## LIBER PRIMUS SENTENTIARUM.

### DE DEI UNITATE ET TRINITATE.

### DISTINCTIO I.

#### Cap. I.

*Omnis doctrina est de rebus vel de signis.*

Veteris ac novae Legis continentiam diligenti indagine etiam atque etiam considerantibus nobis praevia Dei gratia innotuit, sacrae paginae tractatum circa res vel signa praecipue versari. Ut enim egregius doctor Augustinus ait in libro de Doctrina christiana[^1]: «Omnis doctrina vel rerum est, vel signorum. Sed res etiam per signa discuntur. Proprie autem hic res appellantur, quae non ad significandum aliquid adhibentur; signa vero, quorum usus est in significando». Eorum autem aliqua sunt, quorum omnis usus est in significando, non in iustificando, id est[^2], quibus non utimur nisi aliquid significandi gratia, ut aliqua Sacramenta legalia; alia, quae non solum significant, sed conferunt quod intus adiuvet, sicut evangelica Sacramenta. «Ex quo aperte intelligitur, quae hic appellentur signa, res illae videlicet, quae ad significandum aliquid adhibentur. Omne igitur signum etiam res aliqua est. Quod enim nulla res est, ut in eodem Augustinus ait, omnino nihil est; non autem e converso[^3] omnis res signum est», quia non adhibetur ad significandum aliquid. Cumque his intenderit theologorum speculatio studiosa atque modesta, divinam Scripturam formam praescriptam in doctrina tenere advertet. De his ergo nobis aditum ad res divinas aliquatenus intelligendas, Deo duce, aperire volentibus disserendum est; et primum de rebus, postea de signis disseremus.

#### Cap. II.

*De rebus quibus fruendum est, vel utendum, et de his quae fruuntur et utuntur.*

«Id ergo in rebus considerandum est, ut in eodem[^4] Augustinus ait, quod res aliae sunt, quibus fruendum est, aliae, quibus utendum est, aliae, quae fruuntur et utuntur. Illae, quibus fruendum est, nos beatos faciunt; istis, quibus utendum est, tendentes ad beatitudinem adiuvamur et quasi adminiculamur, ut ad illas res, quae nos beatos faciunt, pervenire eisque inhaerere possimus. Res vero, quae fruuntur et utuntur, nos sumus, quasi inter utrasque constituti», et Angeli et Sancti[^5]. «Frui autem est amore alicui rei inhaerere propter se ipsam; uti vero id quod in usum venerit referre ad obtinendum illud, quo fruendum est; alias abuti est, non uti. Nam usus illicitus abusus vel abusio nominari debet[^6]». «Res igitur, quibus fruendum est, sunt Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus. Eadem tamen Trinitas quaedam summa res est communisque omnibus fruentibus ea, si tamen res dici debet et non rerum omnium causa, si tamen et causa. Non enim facile potest inveniri nomen, quod tantae excellentiae conveniat, nisi quod melius dicitur Trinitas haec unus Deus». Res autem, quibus utendum est, mundus est et in eo creata. Unde Augustinus in eodem[^7]: «Utendum est hoc mundo, non fruendum, ut invisibilia Dei per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta, conspiciantur[^8], id est, ut de temporalibus aeterna capiantur». Item in eodem: «In omnibus rebus illae tantum sunt, quibus fruendum est, quae aeternae et incommutabiles sunt; ceteris autem utendum est, ut ad illarum perfruitionem[^9] perveniatur». Unde Augustinus in libro decimo de Trinitate[^10]: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus ipsis propter se voluntas delectata conquiescit; utimur vero eis quae ad aliud referimus, quo fruendum est».

#### Cap. III.

*Quid sit frui et uti.*

Notandum vero, quod idem Augustinus in libro decimo de Trinitate[^11], aliter quam supra accipiens uti et frui, sic dicit: «Uti est assumere aliquid in

<!-- page 27 -->

facultatem voluntatis; frui autem est uti cum gaudio non adhuc spei, sed iam rei; ideoque omnis, qui fruitur, utitur; assumit enim aliquid in facultatem voluntatis cum fine delectationis. Non autem omnis, qui utitur, et fruitur; si id quod in facultatem voluntatis assumit, non propter ipsum, sed propter aliud appetit».

Et attende, quod[^12] videtur Augustinus dicere, illos frui tantum, qui in re gaudent, non iam in spe; et ita in hac vita non videmur frui, sed tantum uti, ubi gaudemus in spe, cum supra dictum sit, frui amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se, qualiter etiam hic multi adhaerent Deo.

Haec ergo, quae sibi contradicere videntur, sic determinamus dicentes, nos et hic et in futuro frui, sed ibi proprie et perfecte et plene, ubi per speciem videbimus quo fruemur; hic autem, dum in spe ambulamus, fruimur quidem, sed non adeo plene. Unde Augustinus in libro decimo de Trinitate[^13]: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus ipsis voluntas propter se delectata conquiescit». Idem in libro de Doctrina christiana[^14] ait: «Angeli illo fruentes iam beati sunt, quo et nos frui desideramus; et quantum in hac vita iam fruimur vel per speculum vel in aenigmate, tanto nostram peregrinationem et tolerabilius sustinemus et ardentius finire cupimus».

Potest etiam dici, quod qui fruitur etiam in hac vita non tantum habet gaudium spei, sed etiam rei, quia iam delectatur in eo quod diligit, et ita iam rem aliquatenus tenet. Constat ergo, quia[^15] debemus Deo frui, non uti. «Illo enim, ut ait Augustinus[^16], frueris, quo efficieris beatus et in quo spem ponis, ut ad id pervenias». De hoc idem ait in libro de Doctrina christiana: «Dicimus ea re nos frui, quam diligimus propter se, et ea re nobis fruendum esse tantum, qua efficimur beati; ceteris vero utendum». Frequenter tamen dicitur frui cum delectatione uti. Cum enim adest quod diligitur, etiam delectationem secum gerit. Si tamen per eam transieris et ad illud, ubi permanendum est, eam retuleris, uteris ea et abusive, non proprie diceris frui. Si vero inhaeseris atque permanseris, finem in ea ponens laetitiae tuae, tunc vere et proprie frui dicendus es; quod non est faciendum nisi in illa Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono[^17]».

##### *Utrum homine sit fruendum, an utendum.*

Cum autem homines, qui fruuntur et utuntur aliis rebus, res aliquae sint, quaeritur, «utrum frui se debeant, an uti, an utrumque». Ad quod sic respondet Augustinus in libro de Doctrina christiana[^18]: «Si propter se homo diligendus est, fruimur eo; si propter aliud, utimur eo: videtur autem mihi propter aliud diligendus. Quod enim propter se diligendum est, in eo constituitur beata vita, cuius etiam spes hoc tempore nos consolatur. In homine autem spes ponenda non est, quia *Maledictus est qui hoc facit*. Ergo si liquide advertas, nec seipso quisquam frui debet, quia non se debet diligere propter se, sed propter illud quo fruendum est». Huic autem contrarium videtur quod Apostolus ad Philemonem[^19] loquens ait: *Ita, frater, ego te fruar in Domino*. Quod ita determinat Augustinus[^20]: «Si dixisset tantum *te fruar*, et non addidisset *in Domino*, videretur finem dilectionis ac spem constituisse in eo; sed quia illud addidit, in Domino se finem posuisse eodemque frui significavit». «Cum enim», ut idem Augustinus ait, «homine in Deo frueris, Deo potius quam homine frueris».

##### *Utrum Deus nobis fruatur, an utatur.*

Sed cum Deus diligat nos, ut frequenter Scriptura dicit, quae eius dilectionem erga nos multum commendat, quaerit Augustinus[^21], quomodo diligit, an ut utens, an ut fruens, et procedit ita: «Si fruitur nobis, eget bono nostro, quod nemo sanus dixerit; ait enim Propheta[^22]: *Bonorum meorum non eges*. Omne enim bonum nostrum vel ipse est, vel ab ipso est: non ergo fruitur nobis, sed utitur. Si enim nec fruitur nobis nec utitur, non invenio, quomodo diligat nos». «Neque tamen sic utitur nobis, ut nos aliis rebus. Nos enim res, quibus utimur, ad id referimus, ut Dei bonitate perfruamur; Deus vero ad suam bonitatem usum nostrum refert: ille enim miseretur nostri propter suam bonitatem, nos autem nobis invicem propter illius bonitatem; ille nostri miseretur, ut se perfruamur, nos vero invicem nostri miseremur, ut illo fruamur. Cum enim nos alicuius miseremur et alicui consulimus, ad eius quidem facimus utilitatem eamque intuemur, sed et nostra fit consequens, cum misericordiam, quam aliis impendimus, non relinquit Deus sine mercede. Haec autem merces summa est, ut ipso perfruamur[^23]». Item: «Quia bonus est, sumus, et inquantum sumus, boni sumus. Porro quia etiam iustus est, non impune mali sumus, et in quantum mali sumus, in tantum etiam

<!-- page 28 -->

minus sumus. Ille igitur usus, quo nobis utitur Deus, non ad eius, sed ad nostram utilitatem refertur, ad eius vero tantummodo bonitatem[^24]».

##### *Utrum virtutibus sit fruendum, an utendum.*

Hic considerandum est, utrum virtutibus sit utendum, an fruendum. Quibusdam videtur, quod eis sit utendum et non fruendum, et hoc confirmant auctoritate Augustini[^25], qui, ut praetaxatum est, dicit, non esse fruendum nisi Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono. Item dicunt, ideo non esse fruendum eis, quia propter se amandae non sunt, sed propter aeternam beatitudinem. Illud autem, quo fruendum est, propter se amandum est. Sed quod virtutes propter se amandae non sint, immo propter solam beatitudinem, probant auctoritate Augustini, qui in libro decimo tertio de Trinitate[^26] contra quosdam ait: «Forte virtutes, quas propter solam beatitudinem amamus, sic persuadere nobis audent, ut ipsam beatitudinem non amemus; quod si faciunt, etiam ipsas utique amare desistimus, quando illam, propter quam solam istas amavimus, non amamus». Ecce his verbis videtur Augustinus ostendere, quod virtutes non propter se, sed propter solam beatitudinem amandae sint. Quod si ita est, ergo eis fruendum non est. Aliis vero contra videtur, scilicet quod eis fruendum sit, quia[^27] propter se petendae et amandae sunt. Et hoc confirmant auctoritate Ambrosii[^28], qui ait super illum locum Epistolae ad Galatas: *Fructus autem spiritus est caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia* etc.: «Haec non nominat opera, sed fructus, quia propter se petenda sunt». Si vero propter se petenda sunt, ergo propter se amanda. Nos autem harum quae videtur[^29] auctoritatum repugnantiam de medio eximere cupientes, dicimus, quod virtutes propter se petendae et amandae sunt, et tamen propter solam beatitudinem. Propter se quidem amandae sunt, quia delectant sui possessores sincera et sancta delectatione et in eis pariunt gaudium spirituale. Verumtamen non est hic consistendum, sed ultra gradiendum. Non hic haereat dilectionis[^30] gressus, neque hic sit dilectionis terminus, sed referatur hoc ad illud summum bonum, cui soli omnino inhaerendum est, quia illud propter se tantum amandum est, et ultra illud nihil quaerendum est; illud est enim supremus finis. Ideo Augustinus dicit, quod eas diligimus propter solam beatitudinem, non quin[^31] eas propter se diligamus, sed quia id ipsum, quod eas diligimus, referimus ad illud summum bonum, cui soli inhaerendum est, et[^32] in eo permanendum finisque laetitiae ponendus; quare virtutibus non est fruendum. Sed dicet aliquis: Frui est amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se ipsam, ut praedictum est; si ergo virtutes propter se amandae sunt, et eis fruendum est. Ad quod dicimus: in illa descriptione, ubi dicitur *propter se ipsam*, intelligendum est tantummodo, ut scilicet ametur propter se ipsam tantum, ut non referatur ad aliud, sed ibi ponatur finis, ut supra ostendit Augustinus dicens[^33]: «Si inhaeseris atque permanseris, finem ponens laetitiae tuae, tunc vere et proprie frui dicendus es. Quod non est faciendum nisi in illa Trinitate, id est, summo et incommutabili bono». Utendum est ergo virtutibus et per eas fruendum summo bono; ita et de voluntate bona dicimus. Unde Augustinus in libro decimo de Trinitate[^34] ait: «Voluntas est per quam fruimur»; ita et per virtutes fruimur; non eis, nisi forte aliqua virtus sit Deus, ut caritas, de qua post tractabitur[^35].

##### *Epilogus.*

Omnium igitur, quae dicta sunt, ex quo de rebus specialiter tractavimus, haec summa est[^36]: quod aliae sunt, quibus fruendum est, aliae, quibus utendum est, aliae, quae fruuntur et utuntur; et inter eas, quibus utendum est, etiam quaedam sunt, per quas fruimur, ut virtutes et potentiae animi, quae sunt naturalia bona. De quibus omnibus, antequam de signis tractemus, agendum est, ac primum de rebus, quibus fruendum est, scilicet de sancta atque individua Trinitate.

## BOOK ONE OF THE SENTENCES.

### ON THE UNITY AND TRINITY OF GOD.

### DISTINCTION I.

#### Chapter I.

*All teaching is about things or about signs.*

As we, by God's grace going before us, considered again and again with diligent investigation the contents of the Old and New Law, it became known to us that the treatment of sacred Scripture is chiefly concerned with things or with signs. For, as the eminent doctor Augustine says in his book *On Christian Doctrine*[^1]: «All teaching is either of things or of signs. But things also are learned through signs. Properly however things are here called those which are not employed to signify something; while signs are those whose use lies in signifying». But of these there are some whose whole use is in signifying, not in justifying — that is to say[^2], those which we use only for the sake of signifying something, like certain Sacraments of the Law; and others, which not only signify but also confer that which inwardly assists, as the evangelical Sacraments. «From this it is plainly understood what are here called signs, namely those things which are employed to signify something. Every sign therefore is also some thing. For that which is no thing, as in the same place Augustine says, is altogether nothing; not however conversely[^3] is every thing a sign», because it is not employed for signifying something. And when the studious and modest speculation of theologians applies itself to these matters, it will recognise that the divine Scripture observes a prescribed form in its teaching. Concerning these things, therefore, we who wish, God leading, to open up some access toward understanding divine things, must discourse; and we shall treat first of things, afterwards of signs.

#### Chapter II.

*On the things which are to be enjoyed or to be used, and on those which enjoy and use.*

«This therefore must be considered in things, as in the same place[^4] Augustine says, that some things are those which are to be enjoyed, others which are to be used, others which both enjoy and use. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed; by these which are to be used we are helped, while striving toward blessedness, and as it were supported, so that we may be able to reach and cleave to those things which make us blessed. The things which enjoy and use are we ourselves, constituted as it were between the two», both Angels and Saints[^5]. «But to enjoy is to cleave with love to some thing for its own sake; to use is to refer that which has come into use toward obtaining that which is to be enjoyed; otherwise it is to abuse, not to use. For an illicit use ought to be named an abuse or misuse[^6]». «The things therefore which are to be enjoyed are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet this same Trinity is a certain supreme thing and common to all who enjoy it — if indeed it ought to be called a thing and not the cause of all things, if even cause. For a name cannot easily be found which befits such great excellence, unless that it is better said: This Trinity is one God». But the things which are to be used are the world and what is created in it. Whence Augustine in the same place[^7]: «This world must be used, not enjoyed, so that the invisible things of God may be seen, being understood through the things that are made[^8] — that is, that from temporal things eternal things may be grasped». Likewise in the same place: «Among all things, those alone are to be enjoyed which are eternal and unchangeable; the rest must be used, so that we may attain to the enjoyment of those[^9]». Whence Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^10]: «We enjoy those things known, in which the will, delighted for their own sake, comes to rest; but we use those things which we refer to something else, which is to be enjoyed».

#### Chapter III.

*What it is to enjoy and to use.*

But it must be noted that the same Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^11], taking *to use* and *to enjoy* otherwise than above, says thus: «To use is to take up something into

<!-- page 27 -->

the power of the will; but to enjoy is to use with joy not still of hope, but already of the reality; and therefore everyone who enjoys also uses, for he takes up something into the power of the will with the end of delight. But not everyone who uses also enjoys; if that which he takes up into the power of the will he seeks not on its own account, but for the sake of something else».

And note that[^12] Augustine seems to say that those alone enjoy who rejoice in the reality, not yet in hope; and so in this life we do not seem to enjoy, but only to use, where we rejoice in hope — even though it was said above that to enjoy is to cleave with love to some thing for its own sake, in which way also many here cleave to God.

These things, then, which seem to contradict one another, we resolve thus, saying that we enjoy both here and in the future, but there properly and perfectly and fully, where by sight we shall behold what we shall enjoy; here, however, while we walk in hope, we do indeed enjoy, but not so fully. Whence Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^13]: «We enjoy those things known, in which the will, delighted for their own sake, comes to rest». The same in the book *On Christian Doctrine*[^14] says: «The Angels enjoying Him are already blessed by that whom we also desire to enjoy; and the more we already enjoy in this life — whether through a mirror or in a riddle — the more tolerably we bear our pilgrimage and the more ardently we desire to end it».

It may also be said that he who enjoys, even in this life, has not only the joy of hope but also of the reality, because he is already delighted in what he loves, and so already in some measure holds the thing. It stands therefore that[^15] we ought to enjoy God, not use Him. «For by that», as Augustine says[^16], «you enjoy by which you are made blessed and in which you place your hope, that you may come to it». On this the same says in the book *On Christian Doctrine*: «We say that we enjoy a thing which we love for its own sake, and that we are to enjoy a thing only by which we are made blessed; the rest, however, are to be used». Yet frequently it is said *to enjoy* with the sense of *to use with delight*. For when that which is loved is present, it brings delight with it. If, however, you pass through it and refer it to that wherein one must abide, you use it, and abusively; you are not properly said to enjoy. But if you cleave and abide, placing the end of your gladness in it, then you are truly and properly to be said to enjoy; which is not to be done except in that Trinity, that is, the supreme and unchangeable good[^17]».

##### *Whether man is to be enjoyed or used.*

But since men, who enjoy and use other things, are themselves certain things, it is asked, «whether they ought to enjoy themselves, or use, or both». To which Augustine in the book *On Christian Doctrine*[^18] thus replies: «If man is to be loved for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for the sake of another, we use him: to me, however, it seems that he is to be loved for the sake of another. For that which is to be loved for its own sake is that in which the blessed life is constituted, the hope of which also consoles us in this time. But hope is not to be placed in man, for *Cursed is he who does this*. Therefore, if you note clearly, no one ought even to enjoy himself, because one ought not to love oneself for one's own sake, but for the sake of that which is to be enjoyed». But to this seems contrary what the Apostle in speaking to Philemon[^19] says: *So, brother, I shall enjoy thee in the Lord*. Which Augustine thus settles[^20]: «If he had said only *I shall enjoy thee*, and had not added *in the Lord*, he would have seemed to set the end of love and of hope in him; but because he added that, he signified that he had set his end in the Lord and that he was enjoying the same». «For when», as the same Augustine says, «you enjoy a man in God, you enjoy God rather than man».

##### *Whether God enjoys us or uses us.*

But since God loves us, as Scripture frequently says, which much commends His love toward us, Augustine asks[^21] how He loves us, whether as one using or as one enjoying; and he proceeds thus: «If He enjoys us, He has need of our good, which no sane man would say; for the Prophet says[^22]: *Of my goods Thou hast no need*. For all our good either is Himself or is from Him: He does not therefore enjoy us, but uses us. For if He neither enjoys us nor uses us, I do not see how He loves us». «Yet He does not so use us as we use other things. For we refer the things which we use to this, that we may enjoy the goodness of God; but God refers our use to His own goodness: for He has mercy on us because of His own goodness, but we on one another because of His goodness; He has mercy on us, that we may enjoy Him fully, but we have mercy on one another, that we may enjoy Him. For when we have mercy on someone and counsel someone, we do it indeed for his usefulness and look to that, but ours follows as a consequence, since God does not leave without reward the mercy which we show to others. But this reward is the highest, that we may enjoy Him fully[^23]». Likewise: «Because He is good, we are; and inasmuch as we are, we are good. Further, because He is also just, we are not evil with impunity, and inasmuch as we are evil, by so much also

<!-- page 28 -->

we are less. That use therefore by which God uses us is referred not to His utility, but to ours; to His, however, only to His goodness[^24]».

##### *Whether the virtues are to be enjoyed or used.*

Here it must be considered whether the virtues are to be used or enjoyed. To some it seems that they are to be used and not enjoyed, and they confirm this by the authority of Augustine[^25], who, as has been noted above, says that none is to be enjoyed except the Trinity, that is, the supreme and unchangeable good. Likewise they say that they are not to be enjoyed because they are not to be loved for their own sake, but for the sake of eternal blessedness. But that which is to be enjoyed is to be loved for its own sake. And that the virtues are not to be loved for their own sake, but rather for blessedness alone, they prove by the authority of Augustine, who in the thirteenth book *On the Trinity*[^26] says against certain ones: «Perhaps the virtues, which we love only for the sake of blessedness, dare to persuade us thus, that we should not love blessedness itself; if they do this, we cease at any rate to love them also, when we do not love that for which alone we have loved them». Behold, by these words Augustine seems to show that the virtues are to be loved not for their own sake, but for blessedness alone. And if this is so, therefore they are not to be enjoyed. But to others on the contrary it seems, namely that they are to be enjoyed, because[^27] they are to be sought and loved for their own sake. And this they confirm by the authority of Ambrose[^28], who says, on that passage of the Epistle to the Galatians: *But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience* etc.: «He does not name these works, but fruits, because they are to be sought for their own sake». But if they are to be sought for their own sake, therefore they are to be loved for their own sake. We, however, desiring to remove from the midst the apparent[^29] repugnance of these authorities, say that the virtues are to be sought and loved for their own sake, and yet on account of blessedness alone. For their own sake indeed they are to be loved, because they delight their possessors with sincere and holy delight and bring forth in them spiritual joy. Nevertheless one must not stop here, but pass beyond. Let not the step of love[^30] adhere here, nor let the term of love be here, but let this be referred to that supreme good, to which alone wholly one must cleave, because that alone is to be loved for its own sake, and beyond it nothing is to be sought; for that is the supreme end. Therefore Augustine says that we love them for blessedness alone — not but that[^31] we love them for their own sake, but because that very fact, that we love them, we refer to that supreme good, to which alone we must cleave, and[^32] in which we must abide and place the end of gladness; wherefore the virtues are not to be enjoyed. But someone will say: To enjoy is to cleave with love to some thing for its own sake, as has been said; if therefore the virtues are to be loved for their own sake, they too are to be enjoyed. To which we say: in that description, where it is said *for its own sake*, it must be understood only thus, that namely it should be loved for its own sake alone, so that it should not be referred to another, but the end should be placed there, as Augustine showed above saying[^33]: «If you cleave and abide, placing the end of your gladness, then you are truly and properly to be said to enjoy. Which is not to be done except in that Trinity, that is, the supreme and unchangeable good». Therefore the virtues are to be used and through them the supreme good is to be enjoyed; and so likewise we say of the good will. Whence Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^34] says: «The will is that by which we enjoy»; and so also through the virtues we enjoy; not them, unless perhaps some virtue be God, as charity, of which it will be treated afterwards[^35].

##### *Epilogue.*

Of all things therefore that have been said, since we have specially treated of things, this is the sum[^36]: that some are those which are to be enjoyed, others which are to be used, others which enjoy and use; and among those which are to be used there are also certain ones through which we enjoy, such as the virtues and powers of the soul, which are natural goods. Concerning all these, before we treat of signs, it must be dealt with, and first concerning those things which are to be enjoyed, namely concerning the holy and undivided Trinity.

---

apparatus.la: Omnes codd. cum edd. 1, 6, 8 *Angeli sancti*. Pro utraque lectione militant rationes; unde nihil immutavimus. Lectio *Angeli sancti* comprehendit sub *nos sumus* omnes homines bonos, sive sint in via, sive in patria; et addit *sancti* ad *Angeli*, ut excludantur daemones, cum damnati nullo modo Deo fruantur. Altera vero lectio ex una parte ponit *nos*, qui soli stricto sensu constituti sumus inter res, quibus fruendum, scil. Deo, et quibus utendum ut mediis ad Deum, ex altera parte beatos Angelos et Sanctos, qui proprie fruuntur Deo nec indigent uti mediis ad ultimum finem, sed tamen aliquo modo creaturis uti possunt ad alios fines.
apparatus.en: All the codices, together with edd. 1, 6, 8, read *Angeli sancti* ("holy Angels"). Reasons support each reading; hence we have altered nothing. The reading *Angeli sancti* comprehends under *we ourselves* all good men, whether they be on the way or in the fatherland, and adds *sancti* to *Angeli* in order to exclude the demons, since the damned in no way enjoy God. The other reading places on one side *we*, who alone in strict sense are constituted between the things to be enjoyed — namely God — and the things to be used as means to God; and on the other side the blessed Angels and Saints, who properly enjoy God and do not need to use means toward the ultimate end, yet can in some way use creatures for other ends.

apparatus.la: Aug. loc. cit. c. 4. et proximus locus, qui incipit: *Res igitur*, ibid. c. 5.
apparatus.en: Augustine at the place cited, c. 4; and the next passage, which begins *Res igitur* ("Therefore the things"), in the same place, c. 5.

apparatus.la: Libr. I. c. 4. et proximus locus ibid. c. 5.
apparatus.en: Book I, c. 4; and the next passage in the same place, c. 5.

apparatus.la: Rom. I, 20.
Vat. et edd. 1, 2, 4 *fruitionem*, contradicentibus textu Augustini et codd. cum aliis edd.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition and edd. 1, 2, 4 read *fruitionem* ("enjoyment"), against the text of Augustine and the codices together with the other editions.

apparatus.la: Cap. 10. n. 13. — Vat. cum cod. A et omnibus edd., excepta 8, in principio propositionis: *Idem* loco *Unde Augustinus*.
apparatus.en: C. 10, n. 13. — The Vatican edition, with codex A and all the editions except 8, at the beginning of the sentence reads *Idem* in place of *Unde Augustinus*.

apparatus.la: Cap. 11. n. 17. — In fine textus cod. B, ed. 1 et originale habent *appetivit* pro *appetit*.
apparatus.en: C. 11, n. 17. — At the end of the text codex B, ed. 1, and the original have *appetivit* for *appetit*.

apparatus.la: Vat. cum codd. B C et edd. praeter 6 et 8 *quia*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition with codices B C and the editions except 6 and 8 read *quia*.

apparatus.la: Cap. 10. n. 13. — Integrum textum posuimus ex cod. D et ed. 1. Vat. cum ceteris edd. et codd. *fruimur cognitis, in quibus voluntas est*. Suspicamur autem, pro *est* legendum esse *etc*. Nomen *Augustinus*, quod deerat post *Unde*, suffectum est ex codd. C D et edd. 1, 8.
apparatus.en: C. 10, n. 13. — We have set down the integral text from codex D and ed. 1. The Vatican edition with the other editions and codices reads *fruimur cognitis, in quibus voluntas est* ("we enjoy things known, in which the will is"). We however suspect that for *est* should be read *etc*. The name *Augustinus*, which was lacking after *Unde*, has been supplied from codd. C D and edd. 1, 8.

apparatus.la: Libr. I. c. 30. n. 31. — Scripturae locus, quem hic respicit Augustinus, est I. Cor. 13, 12.
apparatus.en: Book I, c. 30, n. 31. — The Scripture passage which Augustine here looks to is 1 Cor. 13:12.

apparatus.la: Solummodo edd., exceptis 1, 8, legunt *igitur quod*. Tum Vat. contra codd. et edd. 1, 8 post *frui* addit *et*.
apparatus.en: Only the editions, except 1, 8, read *igitur quod*. Then the Vatican edition, against the codices and edd. 1, 8, after *frui* adds *et*.

apparatus.la: Libr. I. de Doctr. christ. c. 33. n. 37; proximus locus ibid. c. 31. n. 34.
apparatus.en: Book I, *On Christian Doctrine*, c. 33, n. 37; the next passage in the same place, c. 31, n. 34.

apparatus.la: Loc. cit. c. 33. n. 37. — In fine huius auctoritatis codd. omnes et edd. 1, 8 adiiciunt *in* ante *summo*; sed infra circa finem in eodem S. Aug. loco solummodo cod. B cum iisdem duabus edd. Cum autem *in* desit in originali, nihil immutavimus.
apparatus.en: Place cited, c. 33, n. 37. — At the end of this authority all the codices and edd. 1, 8 add *in* before *summo*; but lower down, near the end in the same passage of St. Augustine, only codex B with the same two editions [do so]. Since however *in* is lacking in the original, we have altered nothing.

apparatus.la: Libr. I. c. 22, sed plura secundum sensum excerpta sunt. — Insuper mss. omnes et edd. 1, 8 male et contra textum Augustini omittunt *nos* ante *consolatur*. Verba, quae sequuntur: *In homine* etc., alludunt ad Ierem. 17, 5.
apparatus.en: Book I, c. 22, but several things have been excerpted according to the sense. — Moreover all the mss. and edd. 1, 8 wrongly and against the text of Augustine omit *nos* before *consolatur*. The words which follow, *In homine* etc., allude to Jeremiah 17:5.

apparatus.la: Vers. 20. — Immediate ante Vat. cum edd. 1, 7 contra codd. et ceteras edd. *videri non debet* pro *videtur*.
apparatus.en: Verse 20. — Immediately before, the Vatican edition with edd. 1, 7, against the codices and the other editions, reads *videri non debet* for *videtur*.

apparatus.la: De Doctr. christ. c. 33. n. 37, ubi in originali: *Inde ad Philemonem Paulus: Ita frater, inquit, ego te fruar in Domino. Quod si non addidisset in Domino, et te fruar tantum dixisset, in eo constituisset spem beatitudinis suae*. — In fine huius loci codd. A C D bene *eodemque se frui*. — Proximus locus habetur ibidem.
apparatus.en: *On Christian Doctrine*, c. 33, n. 37, where in the original: *Inde ad Philemonem Paulus: Ita frater, inquit, ego te fruar in Domino. Quod si non addidisset in Domino, et te fruar tantum dixisset, in eo constituisset spem beatitudinis suae* ("Then to Philemon Paul: 'So, brother,' he says, 'I shall enjoy thee in the Lord.' Which, if he had not added *in the Lord*, and had said only *I shall enjoy thee*, he would have placed the hope of his blessedness in him"). — At the end of this passage codices A C D rightly read *eodemque se frui*. — The next passage is found in the same place.

apparatus.la: De Doctr. christ. c. 31. n. 34. — Mox Vat. *diligat* pro *diligit* contra textum Augustini, codd. et fere omnes edd. Postea verbis *si fruitur* hic et paulo infra post *nec fruitur* additum est *nobis* ex cod. D et edd. 1, 8.
apparatus.en: *On Christian Doctrine*, c. 31, n. 34. — Soon after, the Vatican edition reads *diligat* for *diligit*, against the text of Augustine, the codices, and nearly all the editions. Afterwards, to the words *si fruitur* here and a little below after *nec fruitur*, *nobis* has been added from codex D and edd. 1, 8.

apparatus.la: Psalm. 13, 2. — Mss. ABCE cum edd. 1, 8 *indiges* pro *eges*, sed repugnante Augustino cum Vulgata.
apparatus.en: Psalm 13:2. — Mss. ABCE with edd. 1, 8 read *indiges* for *eges*, but against Augustine with the Vulgate.

apparatus.la: Ibid. c. 32. n. 33; in quo textu post *misericordiam quam* codd. A B E et edd. 1, 8 pro *aliis* legunt *alii*; cod. D *alicui*; et mox pro *perfruamur* Vat. cum paucis edd. *fruamur*.
apparatus.en: Same place, c. 32, n. 33; in which text after *misericordiam quam* codices A B E and edd. 1, 8 read *alii* for *aliis*; codex D *alicui*; and soon for *perfruamur* the Vatican edition with a few editions reads *fruamur*.

apparatus.la: Ibid.; in quo textu Vat., ordine verborum non bene inverso, legit *Porro etiam quia*, et paulo post pro *Ille igitur* eadem legit *Ille ergo*.
apparatus.en: Same place; in which text the Vatican edition, with the order of words not well inverted, reads *Porro etiam quia*, and a little after, for *Ille igitur*, the same reads *Ille ergo*.

apparatus.la: Loc. cit. c. 33. n. 37; vide supra in medio huius capituli. — Paulo ante cod. C *confirmatur auctoritate*; cod. D *confirmant auctoritates* et paulo infra *probant auctoritates*.
apparatus.en: Place cited, c. 33, n. 37; see above in the middle of this chapter. — A little before, codex C [reads] *confirmatur auctoritate*; codex D *confirmant auctoritates* and a little below *probant auctoritates*.

apparatus.la: Cap. 8. n. 11. — Paulo ante mss. BCE *sunt* pro *sint*.
apparatus.en: C. 8, n. 11. — A little before, mss. BCE read *sunt* for *sint*.

apparatus.la: Solus cod. D *et propter*, sed male.
apparatus.en: Codex D alone [reads] *et propter*, but wrongly.

apparatus.la: Super Epist. ad Galatas c. 5, 22: «Non dixit: *opera spiritus caritas est*, sed *fructus spiritus*». — Verba, quae sequuntur: «quia propter se petenda sunt», idem Lombardus habet *Collect. in Epist. Pauli ad Gal.* Patrolog. Lat. tom. CXCII, col. 160: «Fructus autem: quasi dicat, haec quae enumeravi, sunt opera carnis; sed ista sunt opera spiritus, quae sequuntur, quae tamen non nominat opera, sed *fructus*, quia propter se petenda sunt». Ex his confirmatur lectio codd. et ed. 1: *haec non nominat*, dum ceterae edd. legunt *Hic non nominat*; Vat. et ed. 4 *At hic* etc. Deinde pro *nominat* cod. D *nominantur*. Postea Vat. et edd. 2, 4, 7, 9 *ergo et propter*; omisimus *et*, postulantibus mss. et aliis edd. Denique edd. 1, 3, 8 adiungunt *amanda sunt*.
apparatus.en: On the Epistle to the Galatians c. 5, 22: «He did not say *the works of the Spirit is charity*, but *the fruit of the Spirit*». — The words which follow, «because they are to be sought for their own sake», the same Lombard has in his *Collectanea in Epist. Pauli ad Gal.*, PL tom. CXCII, col. 160: «*Fructus autem*: as if he said, these which I have enumerated are works of the flesh; but these which follow are works of the Spirit — which however he does not name *opera*, but *fructus*, because they are to be sought for their own sake». From these is confirmed the reading of the codices and ed. 1: *haec non nominat*, while the other editions read *Hic non nominat*; the Vatican edition and ed. 4 [read] *At hic* etc. Then for *nominat* codex D [reads] *nominantur*. Afterwards the Vatican edition and edd. 2, 4, 7, 9 read *ergo et propter*; we have omitted *et*, the mss. and other editions requiring it. Finally edd. 1, 3, 8 add *amanda sunt*.

apparatus.la: Codd. ABE et edd. 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 *videntur*.
apparatus.en: Codd. ABE and edd. 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 read *videntur*.

apparatus.la: Vat. perperam *delectationis*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition wrongly [reads] *delectationis*.

apparatus.la: Vat. *quod*, edd. 5, 8, 9 *qui*, sed recte codd. et aliae edd. *quin*, quia Magister hic mediam viam tenet inter negantes et asserentes virtutes propter se amandas esse.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition [reads] *quod*, edd. 5, 8, 9 *qui*, but rightly the codices and other editions [read] *quin*, since the Master here holds the middle way between those who deny and those who assert that the virtues are to be loved for their own sake.

apparatus.la: Vat. sola praetermittit *et*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition alone omits *et*.

apparatus.la: De Doctr. christ. l. c. 33. n. 37; in quo textu praeter Vat. ceterae edd. et codd. omittunt *tuae* post *laetitiae*; sed retinuimus cum originali, quia supra in eodem textu omnes concorditer sic legunt.
apparatus.en: *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, c. 33, n. 37; in which text, except the Vatican edition, the other editions and the codices omit *tuae* after *laetitiae*; but we have retained it with the original, because above in the same text all read so concordantly.

apparatus.la: Infra d. 17. Edd. 1, 3, 8 *postea* loco *post*.
apparatus.en: Below, d. 17. Edd. 1, 3, 8 [read] *postea* in place of *post*.

apparatus.la: Codd. omnes omittunt *est*, et item postea codd. ABC cum edd. 1, 8 post *utendum*. Denique cod. D legit *animae* pro *animi* et cum ed. 1 *dona* pro *bona*.
apparatus.en: All the codices omit *est*, and likewise afterwards codd. ABC with edd. 1, 8 [omit it] after *utendum*. Finally codex D reads *animae* for *animi* and with ed. 1 *dona* for *bona*.

questions.title: Dist. 1, Divisio Textus
questions.titleLa: Commentarius in Distinctionem I — Divisio textus et tractatio quaestionum
questions.titleEn: Commentary on Distinction I — Division of the text and treatment of the questions
questions.latin:
<!-- page 29 -->

### DIVISIO TEXTUS.

In parte ista incipit tractatus libri, qui dividitur in quatuor libros partiales. Prima pars habet duas partes. In prima parte venatur Magister materiam huius libri et per consequens aliorum. In secunda exsequitur divisionem suam, quae incipit ibi distinctione secunda[^1]: *Hoc itaque vera ac pia fide* etc.

Item prima pars, in qua venatur materiam, habet duas[^2] partes. In prima parte venatur materiam per divisiones, et ideo primo ponit divisionem, per quam distinguuntur tres libri a quarto, scilicet per *res* et *signa*. Secundo[^3] ponit divisionem, per quam distinguitur primus liber a tribus aliis, quae est per *frui* et *uti*, ibi: *Id ergo in rebus considerandum*[^4].

Item, prima pars habet tres particulas. In prima proponit divisionem et auctoritate Augustini confirmat eam, quae est, quod tota doctrina theologica est de rebus, vel de signis, id est, subiectum commune theologiae in haec duo dividitur. In secunda membra divisionis explanat, ibi: *Proprie autem hic res appellantur*, ostendens, quid sit res et quid signum secundum membra praedictae divisionis. In tertia vero particula divisionem ad propositum applicat, ibi: *Cumque his intenderit theologorum speculatio*, dicens, quod de rebus et signis sit[^5] dicturus, primo tamen de rebus.

Item, pars illa, in qua ponit divisionem per *frui* et *uti*, per quam primus liber distinguitur ab aliis tribus, habet duas partes. In prima ponit divisionem et explanat ipsam[^6]. In secunda quae dicta sunt epilogat, ibi: *Omnium igitur, quae dicta sunt* etc. Prima igitur pars habet tres partes: in prima ponit divisionem in res, quibus fruendum, et res quibus utendum: in secunda ad maiorem evidentiam assignat quasdam definitiones, ibi: *Frui autem est amore inhaerere* etc. In tertia vero proponit et determinat quasdam dubitationes, ibi: *Cum autem homines, qui fruuntur et utuntur* etc.

Et in prima particula primo ponit divisionem secundum auctoritatem Augustini, secundo exemplificat, ibi: *Illae, quibus fruendum* etc.[^7]

*Frui autem est amore inhaerere.* Haec secunda[^8] particula illius partis, in qua ponit divisionem in qua distinguitur primus liber ab aliis tribus, quae est de quibusdam notificationibus, quatuor habet particulas. Primo enim ponit notificationes *frui* et *uti*; secundo applicat eas ad propositum, scilicet ad res, quibus fruendum est[^9] et utendum, ibi: *Res igitur quibus fruendum*; tertio comparat ad alias assignationes, ibi: *Notandum vero, quod idem Augustinus*; quarto, quia videntur[^10] sibi contradicere, movet et determinat quandam dubitationem, ibi: *Et attende quod videtur Augustinus dicere* etc.

*Cum autem homines, qui fruuntur et utuntur.* Haec tertia pars, in qua movet et tractat dubitationes quasdam, habet tres partes secundum tres dubitationes, quarum[^11] prima est, utrum homo homine debeat frui, *secunda*, utrum Deus homine fruatur, vel utatur, et hanc movet ibi: *Sed cum Deus diligat* etc.; tertia quaestio[^12] est, utrum virtutibus sit fruendum, vel utendum, ibi: *Hic considerandum est, utrum virtutibus* etc. Et in qualibet istarum trium partium primo movet quaestionem, secundo motam determinat, tertio determinationem per auctoritatem confirmat. Et particulae in suis locis sunt manifestae.

<!-- page 30 -->

## SENTENTIARUM LIB. I.

### TRACTATIO QUAESTIONUM.

Ad evidentiam definitionum et aliorum, quae Magister ponit de his verbis *frui* et *uti*, sex quaeruntur in parte ista, quorum tria pertinent ad *uti*, tria ad *frui*.

*De uti tria quaeruntur.*

Primo quaeritur, quid sit *uti* per essentiam.

*Secundo*, utrum omni creato contingat uti.

*Tertio*, utrum solo bono creato sit utendum.

*De frui similiter quaeruntur tria.*

*Primo*, quid sit *frui* per essentiam.

*Secundo*, utrum bono increato fruendum sit.

*Tertio*, utrum fruendum sit ipso solo bono increato.

---
questions.english:
<!-- page 29 -->

### DIVISION OF THE TEXT.

In this part begins the treatise of the book, which is divided into four partial books. The first part has two parts. In the first part the Master pursues the subject-matter of this book and, in consequence, of the others. In the second he carries out his division, which begins there in the second distinction[^1]: *Therefore by true and pious faith* etc.

Likewise the first part, in which he pursues the subject-matter, has two[^2] parts. In the first part he pursues the subject-matter by divisions, and so first he sets down a division, by which the three books are distinguished from the fourth, namely by *things* and *signs*. Secondly[^3] he sets down a division, by which the first book is distinguished from the three others, which is by *to enjoy* and *to use*, there: *That therefore in things is to be considered*[^4].

Likewise, the first part has three small parts. In the first he proposes the division and confirms it by the authority of Augustine, which is, that the whole of theological doctrine is about things or about signs, that is, the common subject of theology is divided into these two. In the second he explains the members of the division, there: *Properly however here things are called*, showing what is a thing and what is a sign according to the members of the aforesaid division. In the third small part he applies the division to the matter at hand, there: *And when toward these the speculation of theologians shall have been directed*, saying that he is about to speak[^5] of things and of signs, yet first of things.

Likewise, that part, in which he sets down the division by *to enjoy* and *to use*, by which the first book is distinguished from the other three, has two parts. In the first he sets down the division and explains it[^6]. In the second he sums up what has been said, there: *Therefore of all the things which have been said* etc. Therefore the first part has three parts: in the first he sets down the division into things, by which one ought to enjoy, and things by which one ought to use: in the second, for greater clarity, he assigns certain definitions, there: *To enjoy however is to cleave to with love* etc. In the third he proposes and determines certain doubts, there: *When however men, who enjoy and use* etc.

And in the first small part he first sets down the division according to the authority of Augustine, secondly he exemplifies, there: *Those, by which one ought to enjoy* etc.[^7]

*To enjoy however is to cleave to with love.* This second[^8] small part of that part, in which he sets down the division in which the first book is distinguished from the other three, which is concerning certain notifications, has four small parts. For first he sets down the notifications of *to enjoy* and *to use*; secondly he applies them to the matter at hand, namely to the things by which one ought to enjoy[^9] and to use, there: *The things therefore by which one ought to enjoy*; thirdly he compares to other designations, there: *Now it must be noted, that the same Augustine*; fourthly, since they seem[^10] to contradict each other, he raises and determines a certain doubt, there: *And note that Augustine seems to say* etc.

*When however men, who enjoy and use.* This third part, in which he raises and treats certain doubts, has three parts according to three doubts, of which[^11] the first is, whether man ought to enjoy man; *the second*, whether God enjoys or uses man, and this he raises there: *But since God loves* etc.; the third question[^12] is, whether the virtues are to be enjoyed or used, there: *Here it must be considered, whether the virtues* etc. And in each of these three parts he first raises the question, secondly he determines what has been raised, thirdly he confirms the determination by authority. And the small parts are manifest in their places.

<!-- page 30 -->

## BOOK I OF THE SENTENCES.

### TREATMENT OF THE QUESTIONS.

For the elucidation of the definitions and of the other matters which the Master sets down concerning these words *to enjoy* and *to use*, six [questions] are inquired into in this part, of which three pertain to *to use*, three to *to enjoy*.

*Concerning to use three are inquired.*

First it is asked, what is *to use* by essence.

*Secondly*, whether to use befalls every created thing.

*Thirdly*, whether one ought to use only a created good.

*Concerning to enjoy likewise three are inquired.*

*First*, what is *to enjoy* by essence.

*Secondly*, whether the uncreated good is to be enjoyed.

*Thirdly*, whether it is to be enjoyed only the uncreated good itself.

---

apparatus.la: Vat., post *suam* addendo *et hoc*, transponit verba *dist. 2* ante relativum *quae*, sed contra mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, by adding *and this* after *suam*, transposes the words *dist. 2* before the relative *quae*, but against the manuscripts and edition 1.

apparatus.la: Vat. paulo infra, contradicentibus mss. et ed. 1, tertium membrum subdivisionis adiungendo ponit hic *tres* loco *duas*; sed falso, uti ex dicendis patebit. Error editorum Vat. forte inde provenit, quod ipsi putarent, per verba immediate sequentia *In prima parte* significari primam partem subdivisionis, cum tamen revera per illa nihil aliud significetur nisi prima pars principalis i. e. tota prima distinctio.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition a little below, with the manuscripts and edition 1 contradicting [it], by adjoining a third member of the subdivision, puts here *three* in place of *two*; but falsely, as will be clear from what is to be said. The error of the Vatican editors perhaps arises from this, that they thought, by the words immediately following *In the first part* the first part of the subdivision was signified, when however in truth by those words nothing else is signified except the first principal part, i.e. the whole first distinction.

apparatus.la: Auctoritate codd. et ed. 1 substituimus *secundo* pro *in secunda*, postulante hoc insuper contextu, cum *secundo* referatur ad *primo* paulo superius positum.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the codices and of edition 1 we have substituted *secundo* for *in secunda*, the context moreover demanding this, since *secundo* refers to *primo* placed a little above.

apparatus.la: Nullo adstipulante mss. nec favente ed. 1, Vat. adiungit hic *In tertia determinat dubitationes quasdam ex praemissis ortas, ibi: Cum autem homines, qui fruuntur*; sed falso, cum haec pars sit tertia particula subdivisionis partis primae, sicuti infra expresse habetur.
apparatus.en: With no manuscript supporting and edition 1 not favoring [it], the Vatican edition adjoins here *In the third he determines certain doubts arising from what has gone before, there: When however men, who enjoy*; but falsely, since this part is the third small part of the subdivision of the first part, as is expressly held below.

apparatus.la: Contra antiquiores codd. et ed. 1 minus bene Vat. *fuerit*. Mox codd. CS cc *Iterum* pro *Item*.
apparatus.en: Against the older codices and edition 1, less well the Vatican edition [reads] *fuerit*. Shortly after, codices CS, cc [read] *Iterum* in place of *Item*.

apparatus.la: Fide mss. et ed. 1 supplevimus *et explanat ipsam* et mox ex fere omnibus codd. cum ed. 1 post *Prima* addidimus *igitur*, pro quo codd. P et Q habent *iterum*.
apparatus.en: On the faith of the manuscripts and of edition 1 we have supplied *et explanat ipsam* and shortly afterwards from almost all the codices together with edition 1 after *Prima* we have added *igitur*, in place of which codices P and Q have *iterum*.

apparatus.la: Ita mss. cum ed. 1; in Vat. autem subdivisio, quae incipit a verbis *Et in prima particula* usque ad *Frui autem*, deest.
apparatus.en: Thus the manuscripts together with edition 1; in the Vatican edition however the subdivision, which begins from the words *Et in prima particula* up to *Frui autem*, is absent.

apparatus.la: Vat. hic interserens verbum *est*, ob variatam constructionem in fine propositionis ante *quatuor* praefixam habet particulam *et*; insuper in media propositione post *divisionem* pro *in qua ponit* *per quam*, sed contradicentibus mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition here inserting the word *est*, on account of the varied construction at the end of the proposition before *quatuor* has the particle *et* prefixed; moreover in the middle of the proposition after *divisionem* [it has] *per quam* in place of *in qua ponit*, but with the manuscripts and edition 1 contradicting.

apparatus.la: Fide mss. et ed. 1 addimus *est*.
apparatus.en: On the faith of the manuscripts and of edition 1 we add *est*.

apparatus.la: Ita plurimi codd. ut ACFGIKRTVXWZ etc. et ed. 1 necnon textus Magistri Sentent. contra Vat., quae habet *videretur*, et aliquos codd. ut HLOS, qui legunt *videtur*.
apparatus.en: Thus the great majority of codices such as ACFGIKRTVXWZ etc. and edition 1 as well as the text of the Master of the Sentences against the Vatican edition, which has *videretur*, and against some codices such as HLOS, which read *videtur*.

apparatus.en: From the older manuscripts and edition 1 we have supplied *quarum*, just as also a little below after *fruatur* we have substituted *vel* in place of *et*.

questions.latin:
<!-- page 30 -->

### Articulus I. *Quid sit uti et de utibili.*
### Quaestio I. *Utrum uti sit actus voluntatis, an rationis, vel omnis potentiae.*

Circa primum[^1] de uti, quid sit per essentiam, utrum sit actus voluntatis, an rationis, sic proceditur. Quod sit actus voluntatis ostenditur sic.

1. Ab actu utendi denominatur unusquisque bonus[^2]; sed nullus dicitur bonus nisi ab actu voluntatis: ergo actus utendi pertinet ad voluntatem.

2. Item, Augustinus decimo *de Trinitate*[^3]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis»: ergo uti est actus voluntatis.

3. Item, hoc videtur per divisionem ipsius uti contra alia, quia decimo *de Trinitate*[^4] dividit Augustinus haec tria, ingenium, doctrinam et usum, et dicit, quod ingenium respicit, quid homo possit, doctrina, quid homo sciat, usus, quid[^5] velit: ergo usus est actus voluntatis.

4. Item, «Opposita nata sunt fieri circa idem»[^6]; sed uti et abuti sunt opposita, ergo cum abuti sit solius voluntatis, quia eius solius est peccare: ergo et uti similiter erit actus solius voluntatis.

**Contra:** 1. Usus sive assuefactio est via in habitum acquirendum[^7]; sed omnis potentia nata est acquirere habitum: ergo uti videtur esse omnis potentiae.

2. Item, omnis potentia mediante operatione sua ordinatur in finem[^8]; sed eo dicitur aliquid utibile sive uti, quo in finem est ordinabile; sed ordinari in finem mediante propria operatione est omnis potentiae: ergo et uti similiter.

3. Item, sicut Augustinus dicit et habetur in littera[^9], uti est id quod in usum venerit referre etc. Sed eius est referre, cuius est conferre; sed conferre est solius rationis, ergo et referre: ergo et uti a definitione.

4. Item, ars utitur suis instrumentis[^10]; sed ars est in potentia rationali sive cognitiva, cum sit scientia: ergo cum habitus et actus sint eiusdem potentiae, si ars est in potentia rationali, et usus similiter erit in eadem.

> **Conclusio.** Uti quinque modis potest intelligi: si sumitur communissime et communiter, est actus omnis potentiae; si sumitur proprie, magis proprie et propriissime, est actus voluntatis.

**Respondeo**[^11]**:** Dicendum, quod uti quinque modis accipitur, et secundum hoc diversificatur secundum rem et secundum definitionem.

Accipitur enim usus sive uti communissime, secundum quod dividitur contra otium vel otiositatem, pro naturali operatione debita cuilibet rei, sive

<!-- page 31 -->

ad quam unaquaeque res ordinatur, et secundum hoc dicit Philosophus[^12]: «Cuius usus bonus etc.».

Secundo modo dicitur communiter; et sic usus dividitur contra dissuetudinem. Et hoc modo definitur a Victorino[^13]: «Usus est actus frequenter elicitus a potentia», et hoc modo potest dici, quod est actus omnis potentiae nec addit super actum nisi frequentiam.

Tertio modo accipitur uti proprie; et sic dividitur contra habitus memoriae et intelligentiae, scilicet[^14] contra ingenium et doctrinam. Et sic definitur ab Augustino decimo *de Trinitate*: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis», et sic dicit actum voluntatis proprie.

Quarto modo accipitur magis proprie; et sic dividitur contra actum quietativum, scilicet contra frui. Et sic definitur ab Augustino[^15]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis propter aliud», et sic est actus voluntatis ut ad aliud relatae.

Quinto accipitur propriissime; et sic dividitur contra actum inordinatum, scilicet contra abuti. Et sic definitur ab Augustino *de Doctrina christiana*[^16]: «Uti est id quod in usum venerit referre ad id, quo fruendum est», et sic uti dicit actum voluntatis relatum et ordinatum in finem.

Ratio ergo diversarum notificationum est multiplex acceptio eius quod est uti; et ratio multiplicis acceptionis est oppositio eius ad diversa.

Si ergo quaeratur, cuius potentiae est[^17] actus: dicendum, quod, communissime et communiter loquendo, est actus omnis potentiae; et sic non loquitur Augustinus; proprie vero, magis proprie et propriissime actus est ipsius voluntatis.

**Ad argumenta in contrarium:**

1. Et sic patet primo obiectum in contrarium, scilicet quod[^18] sit omnis potentiae.

2. Quod obiicitur secundo, quod omnis potentia refertur in finem per actum suum; dicendum, quod illa potentia dicitur uti suo actu, quae est domina sui actus; et talis potentiae est referre suum actum, non tantum referri. Et quoniam sola voluntas est domina sui actus et sola est se ipsam movens, ideo ipsa sola est, cuius est active uti. Aliis autem potentiis contingit uti materialiter et passive, quia habent referri, et non referre. Et hinc est, quod ab Augustino dicitur[^19]: «Uti est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis»; facultas enim dicitur eius dominium, quo faciliter potest in actum suum tanquam illius princeps.

3. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod rationis est referre; dicendum, quod dupliciter est referre, scilicet per collationem et illationem, sicut praemissae referuntur ad conclusionem; et hoc est rationis, et hoc non est uti. Et est referre per[^20] inclinationem et ordinationem ad aliud; et hoc est proprie voluntatis, quia potest aliquid assumere quiescendo ibi, vel aliud intendendo; et hoc est referre[^21], per quod definitur uti etc.

4. Ad illud quod obiicitur de arte, dicendum, quod ars dicit quod est operationis, et quod est speculationis. Secundum quod dicit[^22] quod est speculationis, non habet uti, et sic est rationis; secundum vero quod dicit quod est operationis, sic extenditur ad voluntatem et eam regulat in utendo.

questions.english:
<!-- page 30 -->

### Article I. *What use is, and concerning the useful.*
### Question I. *Whether use is an act of the will, of reason, or of every faculty.*

Concerning the first[^1] point about use — what it is by essence, whether it is an act of the will or of reason — one proceeds thus. That it is an act of the will is shown thus.

1. By the act of using, each one is called good[^2]; but no one is called good except from an act of the will: therefore the act of using pertains to the will.

2. Likewise, Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^3]: "To use is to take up something into the faculty of the will": therefore to use is an act of the will.

3. Likewise, this is apparent by the division of use itself against other things, because in the tenth book *On the Trinity*[^4] Augustine divides these three — talent (*ingenium*), doctrine, and use — and says that talent regards what a man can do, doctrine what a man knows, use what[^5] he wills: therefore use is an act of the will.

4. Likewise, "Opposites are by nature produced about the same thing"[^6]; but to use and to misuse are opposites; therefore, since to misuse belongs to the will alone, because to sin belongs to it alone: therefore to use will likewise be an act of the will alone.

**On the contrary:** 1. Use or habituation is the way to acquiring a habit[^7]; but every faculty is by nature able to acquire a habit: therefore use seems to belong to every faculty.

2. Likewise, every faculty is ordered to an end through its own operation[^8]; but something is called useful or to be used insofar as it is orderable to an end; but to be ordered to an end through its proper operation belongs to every faculty: therefore use likewise.

3. Likewise, as Augustine says and as is held in the *Lectio* [of the Master][^9], to use is to refer that which has come into use, and so on. But it belongs to that which can refer, to which it belongs to compare; but to compare belongs to reason alone, therefore so does to refer: therefore so also does to use, from its definition.

4. Likewise, art uses its own instruments[^10]; but art is in the rational or cognitive faculty, since it is a science: therefore, since habit and act belong to the same faculty, if art is in the rational faculty, use likewise will be in the same.

> **Conclusion.** Use can be understood in five ways: if it is taken most commonly and commonly, it is an act of every faculty; if it is taken properly, more properly, and most properly, it is an act of the will.

**I respond**[^11]**:** It must be said that use is taken in five ways, and accordingly it is diversified both with respect to the thing and with respect to the definition.

For use or *uti* is taken most commonly insofar as it is divided against idleness or leisure, for the natural operation due to any given thing, or that

<!-- page 31 -->

to which each thing is ordered; and according to this the Philosopher says[^12]: "Whose use is good, etc."

In a second mode it is said commonly; and thus use is divided against disuse. And in this mode it is defined by Victorinus[^13]: "Use is an act frequently elicited from a faculty," and in this mode it can be said that it is an act of every faculty, and it adds nothing to the act except frequency.

In a third mode use is taken properly; and thus it is divided against the habits of memory and intelligence, namely[^14] against talent and doctrine. And thus it is defined by Augustine in the tenth book *On the Trinity*: "To use is to take up something into the faculty of the will," and thus it names an act of the will properly.

In a fourth mode it is taken more properly; and thus it is divided against the quietative act, namely against enjoyment (*frui*). And thus it is defined by Augustine[^15]: "To use is to take up something into the faculty of the will on account of another thing," and thus it is an act of the will as referred to another.

In a fifth mode it is taken most properly; and thus it is divided against the disordered act, namely against misuse (*abuti*). And thus it is defined by Augustine *On Christian Doctrine*[^16]: "To use is to refer what has come into use to that which is to be enjoyed," and thus *uti* names an act of the will referred and ordered to an end.

Therefore the reason for the diverse definitions is the manifold acceptation of *uti*; and the reason for the manifold acceptation is its opposition to diverse things.

If, then, it be asked of which faculty it is[^17] the act: it must be said that, speaking most commonly and commonly, it is the act of every faculty; and in this way Augustine does not speak; but properly, more properly, and most properly, it is the act of the will itself.

**To the arguments on the contrary:**

1. And thus the first objection on the contrary side is clear, namely that[^18] it is of every faculty.

2. As to what is objected secondly, that every faculty is referred to its end through its own act: it must be said that that faculty is said to use its own act which is mistress of its act; and it belongs to such a faculty to refer its act, not only to be referred. And since the will alone is mistress of its act and alone is self-moving, therefore it alone is that to which it belongs actively to use. To the other faculties, however, it pertains to be used materially and passively, because they are referable, not refer-ers. And hence it is that it is said by Augustine[^19]: "To use is to take up something into the faculty of the will"; for *facultas* is called its dominion, by which it can easily proceed into its act as the prince of that act.

3. To what is objected, that to refer belongs to reason: it must be said that to refer is twofold, namely by collation and by inference, as premises are referred to a conclusion; and this belongs to reason, and this is not to use. And there is to refer by[^20] inclination and ordering to another; and this belongs properly to the will, because it can take up something either by resting in it or by directing it toward another; and this is to refer[^21] by which use is defined, and so on.

4. To what is objected concerning art, it must be said that art expresses both what belongs to operation and what belongs to speculation. According to what it says[^22] belongs to speculation, it has no use, and so it belongs to reason; but according to what it says belongs to operation, it extends to the will and regulates it in using.

apparatus.la: Consentientibus mss. et ed. 1, restituimus verba *Circa primum* et mox mutavimus *aut* in *an*, quod et grammatice melius est.
apparatus.en: With the agreement of the manuscripts and the first edition, we have restored the words *Circa primum*, and we have at once changed *aut* into *an*, which is also grammatically better.

apparatus.la: Forsitan respicitur illud Aristot. II. *Ethic.* c. 3. in fine: *Qui enim bene his* (voluptatibus et doloribus) *utetur, bonus; qui male, erit malus.*
apparatus.en: Perhaps reference is being made to that passage of Aristotle, *Ethics* II, c. 3, at the end: "For he who uses these things (pleasures and pains) well, will be good; he who uses them badly, will be evil."

apparatus.la: Cap. 11. n. 17; vide supra in lit. Magistri, c. 3. in initio.
apparatus.en: Chap. 11, n. 17; see above in the Master's text, c. 3, at the beginning.

apparatus.la: Ibidem, paulo ante; et XI. *de Civ. Dei*, c. 25.
apparatus.en: Ibid., a little before; and *On the City of God* XI, c. 25.

apparatus.la: Cod. X hic iterum addit *homo*.
apparatus.en: Codex X here again adds *homo*.

apparatus.la: Aristot., *de Praedicam.* c. de Oppositis circa finem: *Palam vero est, quod circa idem aut specie aut genere nata sunt fieri contraria.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Categories*, chapter on Opposites, near the end: "It is plain that contraries are by nature produced about the same thing, either in species or in genus."

apparatus.la: Idem B. Albert., S. I. tr. 2. q. 8. m. 1. his verbis exprimit: *Secundo dicitur uti rei exercitium ad inducendum habitum, secundum quod dicit Victorinus in Rhetoricis suis* (seu Comment. in Rhetor. Ciceronis, l. c. 25. et n. c. 89.), *quod natura habilem facit, ars potentem, usus facilem.* — Vide et Aristot., II. *Ethic.* c. 1.
apparatus.en: The same point Blessed Albert, *Summa* I, tr. 2, q. 8, m. 1, expresses in these words: "Secondly, *uti* is called the exercising of a thing for the inducing of a habit, in accordance with what Victorinus says in his *Rhetorica*" (or *Commentary on Cicero's Rhetoric*, l. c. 25 and n. c. 89), "that nature makes one apt, art makes one able, use makes one ready." — See also Aristotle, *Ethics* II, c. 1.

apparatus.la: Vide Aristot., IX. *Metaph.* text. 16. (Ed. Paris. VIII. c. 8.). — Mox codd. C F G H K L O R S U cc et ed. 1 *utile* pro *utibile*; cod. Z *utile sive utibile quo* etc.
apparatus.en: See Aristotle, *Metaphysics* IX, text 16 (Paris ed. VIII, c. 8). — Soon after, codices C F G H K L O R S U cc and ed. 1 read *utile* for *utibile*; cod. Z, *utile sive utibile quo*, etc.

apparatus.la: Hic, c. 2. — Faventibus mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, 6, pro *infra* substituimus *in littera*. In conclusione huius argumenti Vat. *ergo referre et per consequens uti*; praeferimus tamen lectionem fere omnium mss. et ed. 1 tanquam distinctiorem.
apparatus.en: Here, c. 2. — With the support of the manuscripts and editions 1, 2, 3, 6, we have substituted *in littera* for *infra*. In the conclusion of this argument the Vatican edition has *ergo referre et per consequens uti*; we however prefer the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and ed. 1 as more distinct.

apparatus.la: Aristot., I. *de Anima*, text. 53. (c. 3.). — Circa finem argumenti mendum Vat. *ponentis* sic pro *si* castigatur ex mss. et ed. 1. — Mox Vat. post *usus* addit *sive uti*; quod deest in antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the Soul* I, text 53 (c. 3). — Near the end of the argument the Vatican error *ponentis sic* in place of *si* is corrected from the manuscripts and ed. 1. — Soon after, the Vatican edition adds *sive uti* after *usus*; this is absent from the older manuscripts and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: Plures codd. ut A I T etc. *Solutio* pro *Respondeo*.
apparatus.en: Several codices, such as A, I, T, etc., have *Solutio* in place of *Respondeo*.

apparatus.la: Sententia: *Cuius usus bonus est, ipsum quoque bonum est*, verbotenus legitur apud Boethium, *de Differentiis topicis*, libr. II. circa medium, in quo libro auctor proponit locorum topicorum divisiones, quae ex una parte, duce Aristotele, a Themistio, et ex altera parte a Cicerone exhibentur, earumque differentias indicat.
apparatus.en: The sentence *Whose use is good, that itself is also good* is read verbatim in Boethius, *On Topical Differences*, book II, near the middle, in which book the author sets out the divisions of topical places — which on one side are presented by Themistius (following Aristotle) and on the other by Cicero — and indicates their differences.

apparatus.la: Fabius Marius (Laurentius) Victorinus, Rhetor († inter 370–382), qui praeter opuscula theologica contra Arianos varios confecit libros philosophicos et rhetoricos; sic transtulit Porphyrii librum *de Praedicabilibus* in linguam latinam (cfr. Boeth., Dialogus I. in Porphyrium) scripsitque commentarium in Rhetorica et Topica Ciceronis (cfr. Boeth. Comment. in Topica Ciceronis; et ed. Operum Ciceronis per Orelli, ubi Victorini Comment. in Rhetor. invenitur). Licet definitio *usus*, de qua hic agitur, explicite non inveniatur in praenotatis Victorini operibus, colligi tamen posse videtur ex supra (argum. 1. ad opp.) allatis eius verbis una cum hac *exercitationis* definitione, quam in Comment. super I. Rhetor. Ciceronis, c. 2. proponit: *Exercitatio est suscepti operis continuatio.* Cfr. et ibid. c. 28., ubi de definitione *habitus* agitur, in qua ponitur *usus sive exercitatio*.
apparatus.en: Fabius Marius (Laurentius) Victorinus, Rhetor († between 370 and 382), who, besides theological tracts against the Arians, composed various philosophical and rhetorical books; thus he translated Porphyry's book *On the Predicables* into Latin (cf. Boethius, *Dialogus I in Porphyrium*) and wrote commentaries on Cicero's *Rhetorica* and *Topica* (cf. Boethius, *Comment. in Topica Ciceronis*; and the edition of Cicero's works by Orelli, where Victorinus's *Commentary on the Rhetoric* is found). Although the definition of *use* here in question is not explicitly found in Victorinus's noted works, it nevertheless seems gatherable from the words of his cited above (argum. 1 on the opposite side) together with this definition of *exercise* which he sets out in his *Commentary on Cicero's Rhetoric* I, c. 2: "Exercise is the continuation of an undertaken work." Cf. also ibid. c. 28, where the definition of *habit* is treated, in which *use or exercise* is set down.

apparatus.la: Perturbatam lectionem Vat. *et* pro *scilicet* emendavimus ope mss. et sex primarum edd. Vide etiam supra fundam. 3, sicuti et de sequenti definitione ab Augustino data cfr. fundam. 2.
apparatus.en: We have emended the corrupt Vatican reading *et* in place of *scilicet* with the help of the manuscripts and the first six editions. See also above, fundamentum 3, and likewise concerning the following definition given by Augustine, cf. fundamentum 2.

apparatus.la: Vide hic lit. Magistri c. 3. in princ. — In fine propositionis Vat. male et contra mss. et ed. 1 *relative* pro *relatae*.
apparatus.en: See here the Master's text, c. 3, at the beginning. — At the end of the proposition the Vatican edition wrongly, and against the manuscripts and ed. 1, has *relative* in place of *relatae*.

apparatus.la: Vide supra in lit. Magistri c. 2, in quo textu codd. A F G H I K S X Y etc. sibi non constantes habent *venit* pro *venerit*.
apparatus.en: See above in the Master's text, c. 2, in which text codices A F G H I K S X Y etc., inconsistent with themselves, have *venit* in place of *venerit*.

apparatus.la: Codd. S Y Z satis bene *sit*. Mox Vat., reluctantibus mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, post *quod* addit *duobus primis modis est actus omnis potentiae, tribus vero ultimis est actus ipsius voluntatis*; sed superflue, quia verbis immediate sequentibus idem dicitur. Dein multi codd. ut C F K L M O R S U V W X Y Z etc. cum edd. 2 et 3 post *communissime*, omissis verbis *et communiter*, transponunt ea post *Augustinus* simulque omittunt *et propriissime*, sic legendo: *Communiter vero et proprie actus est ipsius voluntatis*; quae lectio praecedentibus manifeste contradicit. Codd. D P Q T post *propriissime* addunt *loquendo*, id est tribus ultimis modis.
apparatus.en: Codices S, Y, Z [read] *sit* well enough. Soon after, the Vatican edition, against the manuscripts and editions 1, 2, 3, adds after *quod*: *in the first two modes it is an act of every faculty, but in the last three modes it is an act of the will itself* — but superfluously, since the same thing is said in the words immediately following. Then many codices, such as C F K L M O R S U V W X Y Z etc., together with editions 2 and 3, after *communissime*, omitting the words *et communiter*, transpose them after *Augustinus* and at the same time omit *et propriissime*, so reading: *But commonly and properly it is an act of the will itself*; which reading manifestly contradicts what precedes. Codices D P Q T after *propriissime* add *loquendo*, that is, in the last three modes.

apparatus.la: Supple cum cod. bb *uti*; Vat. autem praeter fidem mss. et ed. 1 hic addit *uti communissime sumtum*, qua additione non quidem falsus, sed alius sensus obtinetur; in lectione siquidem mss. a S. Doctore hic non datur explicita responsio ad primo obiectum, sed breviter repetitur ipsa obiectio; e contra est in lectione Vat.
apparatus.en: Supply with codex bb *uti*; the Vatican edition, however, beyond the faith of the manuscripts and ed. 1, here adds *uti communissime sumtum* — by which addition not indeed a false but a different sense is obtained; for in the reading of the manuscripts no explicit response is here given by the Holy Doctor to the first objection, but the objection itself is briefly repeated; the contrary is the case in the Vatican reading.

apparatus.la: Postulante maiore parte codd. F G H I R S T etc. et ed. 1, posuimus modum passivum pro activo *Augustinus dicit*.
apparatus.en: At the demand of the greater part of the codices F G H I R S T etc. and ed. 1, we have set down the passive mode in place of the active *Augustinus dicit*.

apparatus.la: Cod. D *secundum*.
apparatus.en: Codex D [reads] *secundum*.

apparatus.la: Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc addit *quo vel*, quod tamen abest ab antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, with the later codex cc, adds *quo vel*, which however is absent from the older manuscripts and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: Ed. 1 hic et paulo infra *illud* loco *quod dicit*.
apparatus.en: Ed. 1, here and a little below, [reads] *illud* in place of *quod dicit*.
