questions.titleLa: Utrum omni creato utendum sit
questions.titleEn: Whether every created thing is to be used
questions.latin:
<!-- page 32 -->

### Articulus I. Quaestio II. *Utrum omni creato utendum sit.*

Secundo, viso quid sit *uti* per essentiam, quaeritur de *utibili*, utrum scilicet omni creato sit utendum. Et quod sic, videtur hoc modo.

1. *Proverbiorum* decimo sexto[^1]: *Universa propter semetipsum operatus est Deus*: ergo omnia sunt ordinabilia in Deum; sed omne ordinabile in Deum contingit ordinare; sed ordinando ad Deum ordinabile recte utimur: ergo si omnia contingit ordinare, omnibus est utendum.

2. Item, ens et bonum convertuntur, sicut vult Dionysius[^2]; sed omnia sunt entia: ergo omnia sunt bona. Sed omne bonum diligendum: ergo omne creatum est diligendum; sed non est diligendum propter se: ergo propter aliud; sed hoc est uti: ergo uti contingit omni creato.

3. Item, omni virtute contingit recte uti[^3]: ergo opus omnis virtutis est rectus usus; sed usus alicuius virtutis est respectu mali poenae, ut patientiae, alicuius respectu mali culpae, ut poenitentiae: ergo malis omnibus, scilicet culpae et poenae, contingit recte uti: ergo multo fortius bonis: ergo etc.

4. Item, «Opposita nata sunt fieri circa idem[^4]»; sed omnibus contingit abuti: ergo omnibus contingit recte uti: ergo utendum est omni creato.

**Contra:**

1. Caritas est, per quam recte utimur, quia omnia ordinantur in finem per caritatem quaecumque recte ordinantur; sed sicut dicit Augustinus *de Doctrina christiana*[^5]: «Tantum quatuor diligenda sunt ex caritate et tria tantum creata, ut nos, proximus et corpus proprium»: ergo tantum tria referuntur sive ordinantur in finem per caritatem, cum non sit uti recte nisi per caritatem: ergo tantum tribus est utendum, non ergo omni creato.

2. Item, omnia, quibus utimur, subiacent nostrae voluntati; sed quaedam sunt, quae non subiacent nostrae voluntati, ut necessaria et perpetua: ergo illis non est utendum.

3. Item, omne illud, quo recte utimur, bono fine facimus; sed quaedam sunt, quae nullo bono fine possunt fieri, ut mentiri et talia, «quae mox nominata coniuncta sunt malo[^6]»: ergo talibus non est utendum.

4. Item, virtute non contingit male uti, sicut patet ex eius definitione[^7]: ergo ab oppositis malo culpae sive vitiis non contingit recte uti: ergo non omnibus aliis a Deo est utendum.

### Conclusio.

> Non omni re creata possumus uti ut instrumento neque ut habitu neque ut actu, omni tamen re uti possumus ut obiecto, sed quadrupliciter, vel operando, vel acceptando, vel tolerando, vel respuendo.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod uti aliquo dicitur quatuor modis: aut sicut instrumento, quo operamur, sicut aliquis utitur[^8] instrumento vel organo; et sic non omnibus contingit uti, utpote potentiis, quae sunt pure naturales, accipiendo *uti* proprie, sicut accipit Augustinus[^9]; aut sicut habitu, quo regulamur, utpote virtute; et sic non omnibus contingit recte uti, ut habitu vitii, quo potius contingit obliquari; aut sicut actu, quo movemur; et sic non omni actu contingit bene[^10] uti, sicut illis

<!-- page 33 -->

quae mox nominata coniuncta sunt malo; aut sicut obiecto, ad quod inclinamur; et sic omnibus contingit uti et abuti. Omnia enim possunt sumi in facultatem voluntatis ad approbandum vel respuendum; et hoc patet per Augustinum libro *octoginta trium Quaestionum*[^11]: «Utimur assumendis vel respuendis ad valetudinem, tolerandis ad patientiam, ordinandis ad iustitiam».

Item, Augustinus decimo *de Trinitate*[^12]: «Voluntas totam intelligentiam capit, dum utor omni eo quod intelligo»; sed mala intelliguntur: ergo contingit uti malis.

Aliter tamen utimur bonis, aliter malis. Ratio enim ordinationis in bonis non tantum est ex parte ordinantis, sed etiam ex parte ordinati, quia per se bona sunt utibilia et ordinabilia, et de sui natura; sed in malis ratio ordinationis non est ex parte ordinatorum, sed potius ex parte ordinantis; et ideo mala non dicuntur utibilia.

Unde nota, quod, cum *uti* sit assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis, hoc potest esse quadrupliciter: vel in facultatem voluntatis operantis[^13], sicut est de his quae proprie pertinent ad usum humanum; vel in facultatem voluntatis acceptantis, sicut est dilectio proximi et huiusmodi; vel in facultatem voluntatis tolerantis, sicut sunt mala poenae; vel in facultatem voluntatis respuentis, et sic assumuntur mala culpae et ordinantur. Primis duobus modis intelligitur illud: «Cuius usus bonus etc.».

**Ad opposita:**

1. Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur de caritate, quod tantum tria creata[^14] sunt diligenda; dicendum, quod diligi aliquid ex caritate hoc est ordinari in summum bonum, quod per se caritas diligit. Hoc autem contingit dupliciter: aut enim contingit ordinare quod natum est devenire in finem; et sic tantum tria creata diligenda sunt ex caritate; aut illud per quod devenire est in summum bonum; et quia hoc potest esse suo modo per omnem creaturam, omnis creatura potest diligi ex caritate, et omni creatura contingit uti.

2. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod non omnia subiacent voluntati; dicendum, quod aliquid[^15] dicitur subesse dominio voluntatis dupliciter: aut quantum ad esse ipsius rei; et sic non omnia subiacent; aut quantum ad actum voluntatis, qui est in respuendo ipsam rem vel approbando, et hoc[^16] propter se vel propter aliud; et tali modo omnia subiacent voluntati nostrae, scilicet quantum ad actum appetitionis vel respuitionis, licet non primo modo.

3. 4. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod quaedam nullo bono fine possunt fieri, similiter, quod semper vitiis abutimur; dicendum, quod obiicitur secundum viam, qua contingit uti aliquo ut actu medio; et sic non contingit[^17] uti peccato; vel sicut habitu regulante, similiter; contingit tamen eo uti sicut obiecto recte per motum contritionis et detestationis.
questions.english:
### Article I. Question II. *Whether every created thing is to be used.*

Secondly, having seen what *to use* is per essence, the question is asked about the *useable*, namely whether every created thing is to be used. And that it is so, is shown in this way.

1. *Proverbs* sixteen[^1]: *God has worked all things for his own sake*: therefore all things are orderable to God; but whatever is orderable to God can be ordered; but in ordering to God we rightly use the orderable: therefore if all things can be ordered, all things are to be used.

2. Likewise, being and good are convertible, as Dionysius holds[^2]; but all things are beings: therefore all things are good. But every good is to be loved: therefore every created thing is to be loved; but it is not to be loved for its own sake: therefore for the sake of another; but this is to use: therefore it can be used in the case of every created thing.

3. Likewise, every virtue can be rightly used[^3]: therefore the work of every virtue is right use; but the use of a certain virtue is with respect to the evil of penalty, as patience, of another with respect to the evil of fault, as penitence: therefore all evils, namely of fault and of penalty, can be rightly used: therefore much more strongly, goods: therefore etc.

4. Likewise, «Opposites are naturally to arise about the same thing[^4]»; but all things can be misused: therefore all things can be rightly used: therefore every created thing is to be used.

**On the contrary:**

1. Charity is that by which we rightly use, because all things are ordered to the end through charity, whatever things are rightly ordered; but as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*[^5]: «Only four things are to be loved out of charity, and only three created, namely ourselves, our neighbor, and our own body»: therefore only three are referred or ordered to the end through charity, since there is no right using except through charity: therefore only three are to be used, therefore not every created thing.

2. Likewise, all things which we use are subject to our will; but there are certain things which are not subject to our will, such as necessary and perpetual things: therefore those are not to be used.

3. Likewise, everything that we rightly use, we do with a good end; but there are certain things which can be done with no good end, such as lying and the like, «which, as soon as named, are conjoined with evil[^6]»: therefore such things are not to be used.

4. Likewise, a virtue cannot be ill used, as is clear from its definition[^7]: therefore from things opposite to the evil of fault, that is, from vices, one cannot rightly use: therefore not all things other than God are to be used.

### Conclusion.

> Not every created thing can we use as an instrument, nor as a habit, nor as an act; but every thing we can use as an object, yet in fourfold manner: either by operating, or by accepting, or by tolerating, or by spurning.

**I respond:** It must be said that *to use* something is said in four modes: either as an instrument, by which we operate, just as someone uses[^8] an instrument or organ; and thus it is not possible to use all things, namely the powers which are purely natural, taking *to use* properly, as Augustine takes it[^9]; or as a habit, by which we are regulated, namely virtue; and thus it is not possible to rightly use all things, as the habit of vice, by which rather one can be turned aside; or as an act, by which we are moved; and thus it is not possible to use well[^10] every act, such as those

<!-- page 33 -->

which, as soon as named, are conjoined with evil; or as an object, to which we are inclined; and thus all things can be used and misused. For all things can be taken up into the faculty of the will for approving or spurning; and this is clear from Augustine in the book *On Eighty-Three Questions*[^11]: «We use things to-be-taken-up or to-be-spurned for health, things to-be-tolerated for patience, things to-be-ordered for justice».

Likewise, Augustine in book ten *On the Trinity*[^12]: «The will grasps the whole intellect, while I use all of that which I understand»; but evils are understood: therefore evils can be used.

Yet otherwise we use goods, and otherwise evils. For the ground of the ordering in goods is not only on the part of the one ordering, but also on the part of the thing ordered, because of themselves goods are useable and orderable, and from their own nature; but in evils the ground of ordering is not on the part of the things ordered, but rather on the part of the one ordering; and therefore evils are not called useable.

Hence note that, since *to use* is to take up something into the faculty of the will, this can be in a fourfold manner: either into the faculty of the operating will[^13], as is the case with those things which properly pertain to human use; or into the faculty of the accepting will, as is the love of neighbor and the like; or into the faculty of the tolerating will, as are the evils of penalty; or into the faculty of the spurning will, and thus evils of fault are taken up and ordered. By the first two modes is understood that saying: «Whose use is good etc.».

**To the opposing arguments:**

1. To that which is objected concerning charity, that only three created things[^14] are to be loved; it must be said that for something to be loved out of charity is for it to be ordered to the highest good, which charity loves *per se*. But this happens in two ways: either it is possible to order that which is naturally fitted to come to the end; and thus only three created things are to be loved out of charity; or that through which one comes to the highest good; and because this can be in its own way through every creature, every creature can be loved out of charity, and every creature can be used.

2. To that which is objected, that not all things are subject to the will; it must be said that something[^15] is said to be under the dominion of the will in two ways: either as to the being of the thing itself; and thus not all things are subject; or as to the act of the will, which is in spurning the thing itself or approving, and this[^16] either for its own sake or for the sake of another; and in such a way all things are subject to our will, namely as to the act of seeking-after or spurning, although not in the first way.

3. 4. To that which is objected, that certain things can be done with no good end, similarly, that we always misuse vices; it must be said that the objection proceeds along the way in which one can use something as a middle act; and thus[^17] one cannot use sin; or as a regulating habit, similarly; yet it can be used as an object rightly through the motion of contrition and detestation.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Hanc et sequentem quaestionem antiqui doctores sub una quaestione et minus accurate tractare solent. — Ostensum iam supra est, quod *uti* in sensu activo sit solius voluntatis; in secunda hac quaestione inquiritur, ad quae obiecta se extendat usus voluntatis, sive quibus rebus *uti* passive conveniat. In responsione S. Doctor primo ponit quadruplicem distinctionem circa obiecta voluntatis ordinanda et resolvit quaestionem in genere. Quoad primum membrum huius distinctionis, patet quod voluntas non possit omnia assumere in facultatem suam, ut iis utatur sicut instrumento. Nam aliquae potentiae ipsius animae non subiacent imperio voluntatis; unde vocantur pure naturales, ut potentiae vegetativae. Secundo, incidendo in specialem quaestionem, scil. quo sensu quis malis uti possit, iterum quadrupliciter distinguit modum voluntatis ordinantis, scil. operantis, acceptantis, tolerantis et respuentis. Hic usus mali ex parte ordinantis est «usus per accidens», ut bene dicit Richard. (hic q. 2. ad ult.), «eo quod ordinatum aliunde accipit ordinabilitatem, scil. a voluntate». — Circa hanc quaestionem de usu mali S. Thom. (hic loc. cit.) aliis verbis quam S. Bonaventura loquitur, sed in sententia nulla est differentia, immo in S. II. II. q. 78. a. 4. Angelicus etiam in modo loquendi cum illo convenit.

**II.** Alex. Hal., S. p. III. q. 61. m. 1. — Scot., hic q. 3. et 5. et Quodl., q. 17. — S. Thom., hic q. 2. a. 3; S. I. II. q. 16. a. 3. — B. Albert. M., hic a. 10. et 11. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 1. a. 2. ita presse sequitur S. Doctorem, ut Dionys. Carth. de ipso dicat: «Petrus, qui scripsit post Bonaventuram, ex ipso Bonaventura suam responsionem videtur sumsisse». — Richard., hic a. 1. q. 2. — Aegid. R., hic 2. princ. q. 3. — Henr. Gand., S. a. 72. q. 3. n. 11. — Durand., hic q. 4. — Dionys., hic q. 2. — Biel, hic q. 1.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** This and the following question the ancient doctors are accustomed to treat under one question and less accurately. — It has already been shown above, that *to use* in the active sense belongs only to the will; in this second question it is asked, to what objects the use of the will extends, or with what things *to use* in the passive sense agrees. In the response the holy Doctor first sets down a fourfold distinction concerning the objects of the will to be ordered and resolves the question in general. As to the first member of this distinction, it is clear that the will cannot take up all things into its faculty, so as to use them as an instrument. For some powers of the soul itself are not subject to the command of the will; whence they are called purely natural, such as the vegetative powers. Secondly, falling into a special question, namely in what sense one can use evils, again he distinguishes in fourfold manner the mode of the ordering will, namely operating, accepting, tolerating, and spurning. This use of evil on the part of the one ordering is a «use *per accidens*», as Richard well says (here q. 2. ad ult.), «because the ordered thing receives its orderability from elsewhere, namely from the will». — Concerning this question of the use of evil, St. Thomas (here at the cited place) speaks in other words than St. Bonaventure, but in substance there is no difference; indeed in *Summa* II–II, q. 78, a. 4, the Angelic Doctor also agrees with him even in the mode of speaking.

**II.** Alex. of Hales, *Summa* p. III, q. 61, m. 1. — Scotus, here q. 3 and 5, and *Quodl.*, q. 17. — St. Thomas, here q. 2, a. 3; *Summa* I–II, q. 16, a. 3. — Bl. Albert the Great, here a. 10 and 11. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 1, a. 2, so closely follows the holy Doctor that Dionysius the Carthusian says of him: «Peter, who wrote after Bonaventure, seems to have taken his response from Bonaventure himself». — Richard, here a. 1, q. 2. — Giles of Rome, here 2. princ. q. 3. — Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 72, q. 3, n. 11. — Durandus, here q. 4. — Dionysius [the Carthusian], here q. 2. — Biel, here q. 1.

---

apparatus.la: Vers. 4, ubi Vulgata pro *Deus* legit *Dominus*. — Mox et pluries in seqq. argg. posuimus *contingit* loco *convenit*. Notamus hic et pro semper, quod codd. praesertim antiquiores saepissime ista duo vocabula eodem modo exhibeant abbreviata, ita ut sive *contingit* sive *convenit* legi possit.
apparatus.en: Verse 4, where the Vulgate reads *Dominus* (Lord) instead of *Deus* (God). — Hereafter and several times in the following arguments we have placed *contingit* in place of *convenit*. We note here once for all that the codices, especially the older ones, very often present these two words abbreviated in the same way, so that either *contingit* or *convenit* may be read.

apparatus.la: Cap. 5. *de Div. Nom.*, ubi secundum textum Graecum legitur: *Non aliud dicit esse bonum et aliud ens*. — Mox cod. *cc* *sed si omnia*.
apparatus.en: Chapter 5 of *On the Divine Names*, where according to the Greek text it is read: *He does not say that the good is one thing and being another*. — Next, codex *cc* reads *sed si omnia* (but if all).

apparatus.la: Elicitur ex definitione virtutis, quam August., II. *de Lib. Arb.* c. 18. et 19. ponit: *Bona qualitas mentis, qua recte vivitur et nemo male utitur*. — Mox multi codd. ut C G H K O P Q R S U etc. et edd. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 post *poenae* omittunt *ut patientiae*, quod tamen codd. praedicti postea male loco *ut poenitentiae* ponunt, editiones autem praeallegatae verbis *ut poenitentiae* praemittunt.
apparatus.en: Drawn from the definition of virtue which Augustine, *On Free Choice* II, c. 18 and 19, sets down: *A good quality of mind, by which one lives rightly and which no one uses ill*. — Next, many codices such as C G H K O P Q R S U etc. and editions 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, after *poenae* omit *ut patientiae*, which however the said codices afterward wrongly put in place of *ut poenitentiae*; the editions just cited prepose the words *ut poenitentiae*.

apparatus.la: Aristot., *de Praedicam.* c. de Oppositis circa finem. Vide supra q. I. fundam. 1.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Categories*, the chapter on Opposites, near the end. See above q. I, fundament 1.

apparatus.la: Lib. I. c. 23. n. 22: *Cum ergo quatuor sint diligenda: unum, quod supra nos est; alterum, quod nos sumus; tertium, quod iuxta nos est; quartum, quod infra nos est: de secundo et quarto nulla praecepta danda erant*. — Et ibidem c. 26. n. 27: *Quod si te totum intelligas, id est animum et corpus tuum et proximum tuum, id est animum et corpus eius*. — Cod. *W* post *caritate* addit *scilicet Deus*. — Paulo ante fide codd. et ed. 1 addidimus *sicut*.
apparatus.en: Book I, c. 23, n. 22: *Since therefore there are four things to be loved: one, which is above us; another, which we ourselves are; a third, which is alongside us; a fourth, which is below us: concerning the second and the fourth no precepts had to be given*. — And in the same place, c. 26, n. 27: *But if you understand yourself whole, that is your soul and your body, and your neighbor, that is his soul and body*. — Codex *W* after *caritate* adds *scilicet Deus* (namely God). — Slightly earlier, on the faith of the codices and ed. 1, we have added *sicut*.

apparatus.la: Aristot., II. *Ethic.* c. 6: *Quaedam enim confestim nominata convoluta sunt cum malitia*. (Translatio antiqua in ed. Operum S. Thomae a P. Fiaccadori 1866. tom. 21.)
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* II, c. 6: *For certain things as soon as named are wrapped up with wickedness*. (Old translation in the edition of the Works of St. Thomas by P. Fiaccadori, 1866, tom. 21.)

apparatus.la: August., II. *de Lib. Arb.* c. 18. et 19. n. 50. Vide paulo supra fundam. 3.
apparatus.en: Augustine, *On Free Choice* II, c. 18 and 19, n. 50. See slightly above, fundament 3.

apparatus.la: Substituimus ex fere omnibus mss. et ed. 1 *aliquis utitur* pro *utimur*. Cod. *V* *sicut aliquo utimur*. Mox ex plurimis codd. cum ed. 1 bis substituimus *utpote* loco *ut puta*.
apparatus.en: From almost all manuscripts and ed. 1 we have substituted *aliquis utitur* (someone uses) for *utimur* (we use). Codex *V* reads *sicut aliquo utimur* (as we use something). Next, from very many codices with ed. 1, we have twice substituted *utpote* for *ut puta*.

apparatus.la: Quatenus *uti* est assumere aliquid in facultatem voluntatis. Vid. supra q. 1. Cfr. etiam Aristot., I. *Ethic.* c. ult., ubi agit de potentiis, quae non subiacent imperio rationis et voluntatis.
apparatus.en: Inasmuch as *to use* is to take up something into the faculty of the will. See above, q. 1. Compare also Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I, last chapter, where he treats of the powers which are not subject to the command of reason and the will.

apparatus.la: Vat. cum cod. *cc* male omittit *bene*, quod antiquiores mss. ac ed. 1 suppeditant, mutavimusque *convenit* in *contingit*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition with codex *cc* wrongly omits *bene*, which the older manuscripts and ed. 1 supply; and we have changed *convenit* into *contingit*.

apparatus.la: Quaest. 30: *Sic enim utitur suo corpore: quibusdam assumendis vel respuendis ad valitudinem, quibusdam tolerandis ad patientiam, quibusdam ordinandis ad iustitiam, quibusdam considerandis ad aliquod veritatis documentum*. — In quo textu plurimi codd. ut A B C D F G H I K S T W Z etc. omittunt *assumendis vel*, pro quo ed. 1 ponit *conferendis aut*.
apparatus.en: Question 30: *For thus he uses his body: by taking up or spurning some things for health, by tolerating some for patience, by ordering some for justice, by considering some for some demonstration of truth*. — In which text very many codices such as A B C D F G H I K S T W Z etc. omit *assumendis vel*, for which ed. 1 puts *conferendis aut*.

apparatus.la: Cap. 11. n. 18: *Voluntas etiam mea totam intelligentiam, totam memoriam meam capit, dum toto utor, quod intelligo et memini*.
apparatus.en: Chapter 11, n. 18: *My will also grasps my whole intellect and my whole memory, while I use the whole of what I understand and remember*.

apparatus.la: Renitentibus mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, Vat. pro *operantis* ponit *imperantis*, sed mendose, quia hoc membrum non excludit tria alia membra divisionis. Eamdem distinctionem Petr. a Tar., hic q. 1. a. 2. breviter sic proponit: *Potest aliquid assumi in facultatem voluntatis quadrupliciter: vel voluntatis operantis, ut bona nostra, vel approbantis, ut aliena bona, vel tolerantis, ut mala poenae propria et culpae alienae, vel respuentis, ut mala culpae propriae*.
apparatus.en: Against the manuscripts and editions 1, 2, 3, the Vatican puts *imperantis* (commanding) for *operantis* (operating), but erroneously, because this member does not exclude the three other members of the division. The same distinction is briefly proposed by Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 1, a. 2, thus: *Something can be taken up into the faculty of the will in fourfold manner: either of the operating will, as our own goods, or of the approving, as the goods of another, or of the tolerating, as the evils of penalty of oneself and of fault of another, or of the spurning, as the evils of one's own fault*.

apparatus.la: Codd. cum ed. 1 omittunt *creata*, quod, ut certo subintelligendum, claritatis gratia retinuimus, praesertim cum et paulo post in mss. inveniatur. Mox Vat., post *caritate* omisso *hoc*, propositionem ipsam exhibet modo activo: *diligere aliquid ex caritate est ordinare*, renitentibus tamen mss. et ed. 1. — Obiectionem, quam hic S. Doctor solvit, infra d. 17. p. 1. q. 2. sub alio respectu pertractat.
apparatus.en: The codices with ed. 1 omit *creata*, which, as certainly to be understood, we have retained for the sake of clarity, especially since it is also found shortly after in the manuscripts. Next the Vatican, having omitted *hoc* after *caritate*, presents the proposition itself in the active mode: *to love something out of charity is to order [it]*, though against the manuscripts and ed. 1. — The objection which the holy Doctor here resolves, he treats below at d. 17, p. 1, q. 2, under another aspect.

apparatus.la: Nullo suffragante ms. nec ed. 1, Vat. *aliquis*.
apparatus.en: With no manuscript or ed. 1 supporting it, the Vatican reads *aliquis* (someone).

apparatus.la: Cod. *Z* hic non male addit *vel*.
apparatus.en: Codex *Z* here not badly adds *vel* (or).

apparatus.la: Postulantibus fere omnibus mss. et ed. 1, substituimus *sic* pro *hoc modo*, et bis *contingit* loco *convenit*. Mox mendum Vat. *recto per modum* castigavimus ex mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: At the demand of almost all manuscripts and ed. 1, we have substituted *sic* (thus) for *hoc modo* (in this way), and twice *contingit* in place of *convenit*. Next we have corrected the Vatican error *recto per modum* (rightly through the mode) from the manuscripts and ed. 1.

questions.latin:
<!-- page 34 -->

### Quaestio III. *Utrum solo bono creato utendum sit.*

Tertio, ostenso, utrum omni creato sit utendum et[^1] omni alio a Deo, est quaestio, utrum solo bono creato sit utendum. Et quod sic, videtur.

1. «Omne bonum aut est finis, aut ad finem[^2]»; sed solo bono, quod est ad finem, est utendum, quia ratio utilis est ducere in finem: ergo cum solum bonum creatum sit ad finem, solo bono creato est utendum.

2. Item, omne bonum aut est creatum, aut increatum. Sed si contingit uti bono increato, contingit illud referre ad aliud: aut ergo ad creatum, aut[^3] increatum; sed non ad increatum, quia non est nisi unum increatum: ergo ad creatum. Sed sic refertur terminus ad viam et causa ad effectum; sed hoc est abusio, non usus: ergo solo bono creato sive creatura est utendum.

3. Item, Augustinus in libro octoginta trium *Quaestionum*[^4] dividit honestum contra utile: ergo nullum utile honestum vel e converso; sed Deus est honestum per essentiam: ergo Deo non est utendum.

4. Item, videtur quod non solum non sit utendum Deo sive bono increato, sed uti eo semper sit peccatum mortale, quia Augustinus in libro octoginta trium *Quaestionum*[^5] dicit: «Summa perversitas est frui utendis et uti fruendis»; sed qui utitur bono increato, utitur bono fruendo: ergo etc.

**Contra:**

1. Contingit Deo recte servire intuitu mercedis, quia multi sunt boni mercenarii, ut dicit Ambrosius[^6]; sed non contingit Deo servire nisi amando: ergo contingit Deum recte amare intuitu mercedis; sed sic amans utitur Deo, quia refert ad aliud: ergo etc.

2. Item, sic summa bonitas habet se ad amorem, sicut[^7] summa veritas ad cognitionem; sed contingit veritatem creatam cognoscere clarius sine praeiudicio summae veritatis et sine errore: ergo similiter contingit aliam bonitatem quam summam ardentius diligere sine praeiudicio summae bonitatis et deordinatione: ergo contingit amore ordinato aliud plus diligi quam Deum: ergo contingit Deum diligi propter aliud ordinate et ita uti eo.

3. Item, videtur quod nullum peccatum sit, cum quis utitur Deo propter suam salutem, quia «cuius finis bonus, ipsum bonum[^8]»; sed huius usus bonus est, scilicet nostra salus: ergo usus Dei bonus: ergo non erit peccatum.

4. Item, usus Dei aut est bonus; et sic utendum Deo; aut est malus; et sic Deus malus, quia «cuius usus malus, ipsum malum[^9]»; quod si Deus bonus, et eius usus bonus: ergo Deo est utendum.

> **Conclusio.** Solo bono creato est utendum, et bono increato uti est abuti.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod solo bono creato est utendum, quia, si bono increato utimur, semper est abusus, et abusus talis est mortale peccatum propter perversitatem in finem[^10] cum delectatione, et propter voluntatis inordinationem, quae minus diligit ipsum quo utitur, quam propter quod utitur.

<!-- page 35 -->

**Ad argumenta:**

1. Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur, quod contingit recte servire Deo intuitu mercedis; dicendum, quod illa merces aut est ipse Deus, sicut dixit Abrahae Genesis decimo quinto[^11]: *Ego merces tua*; et sic intuens mercedem non utitur, quia non refert ad aliud; aut merces illa est aliud, et tunc potest eam quis intueri aut ut causam[^?] moventem; et sic est malus mercenarius[^12]; aut ut rationem inducentem; et sic bonus, et hoc modo non utitur.

2. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod clarior cognitio creaturae non praeiudicat Creatori, ergo etc.; dicendum, quod non est simile, quia claritas cognitionis non est in nostra potestate, sed ardor affectionis est in nostra potestate; ideo requiritur a nobis, quod istum ordinemus, non illam[^13]. Aliquis tamen actus cognitionis est in nostra potestate, utpote actus fidei, quo si aliquis assentiat veritati primae propter aliud, bene praeiudicat veritati, sicut amare propter aliud, bonitati.

3. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod finis usus Dei est bonus; dicendum, quod finis dicitur bonus dupliciter: aut quantum ad substantiam, aut quantum ad intentionem finiendi; et propositio illa intelligitur quantum ad intentionem finiendi, et haec[^14] consistit in recta ordinatione.

4. Ad ultimum dicendum, quod illa propositio[^15] intelligitur de habentibus ordinationem ad finem, sed non de ipso fine. — Vel intelligitur de actu naturali ipsarum rerum et proprio, qui frequentius ab ipsa re elicitur, non de ordinatione in[^16] finem; et sic non valet propositio ad propositum.
questions.english:
### Question III. *Whether only a created good is to be used.*

Thirdly, it having been shown whether every created thing is to be used and[^1] every other thing besides God, the question is whether only a created good is to be used. And that it is so, seems [the case].

1. «Every good is either an end, or [ordered] to an end[^2]»; but use is only of the good which is to an end, since the rational character of the useful is to lead to the end: therefore, since only a created good is to an end, only a created good is to be used.

2. Likewise, every good is either created or uncreated. But if it is possible to use an uncreated good, it is possible to refer it to another: either, therefore, to a created [good], or [to an] uncreated[^3]; but not to an uncreated, since there is only one uncreated: therefore to a created. But thus the term is referred to the way, and the cause to the effect; but this is abuse, not use: therefore only a created good or creature is to be used.

3. Likewise, Augustine in the book *On the Eighty-Three Questions*[^4] divides the honorable against the useful: therefore no useful thing is honorable, or conversely; but God is the honorable by essence: therefore God is not to be used.

4. Likewise, it seems that not only is God or the uncreated good not to be used, but to use Him is always a mortal sin, since Augustine in the book *On the Eighty-Three Questions*[^5] says: «It is the highest perversity to enjoy things to be used and to use things to be enjoyed»; but he who uses an uncreated good, uses a good [meant] for enjoying: therefore etc.

**On the contrary:**

1. It is possible to serve God rightly with a view to reward, since there are many good hirelings, as Ambrose says[^6]; but it is not possible to serve God except by loving: therefore it is possible to love God rightly with a view to reward; but the one so loving uses God, since he refers [Him] to another: therefore etc.

2. Likewise, the highest goodness stands to love as[^7] the highest truth stands to cognition; but it is possible to know a created truth more clearly without prejudice to the highest truth and without error: therefore likewise it is possible to love some goodness other than the highest more ardently without prejudice to the highest goodness and without disorder: therefore it is possible by ordered love that another be loved more than God: therefore it is possible that God be loved on account of another in an ordered way, and so to use Him.

3. Likewise, it seems that there is no sin when someone uses God for the sake of his own salvation, since «that whose end is good, is itself good[^8]»; but the use of this is good, namely our salvation: therefore the use of God is good: therefore it will not be a sin.

4. Likewise, the use of God either is good — and so God is to be used; or is evil — and so God is evil, since «that whose use is evil, is itself evil[^9]»; but if God is good, His use is also good: therefore God is to be used.

> **Conclusion.** Only a created good is to be used, and to use an uncreated good is to abuse.

**I respond:** It must be said that only a created good is to be used, since, if we use an uncreated good, it is always abuse, and such abuse is a mortal sin on account of the perversity toward the end[^10] with delectation, and on account of the disorder of the will, which loves less the very thing by which it uses than that on account of which it uses.

**To the arguments:**

1. To that which is objected, that it is possible to serve God rightly with a view to reward; it must be said that that reward is either God Himself, as He said to Abraham, Genesis fifteen[^11]: *I am thy reward*; and so the one looking to the reward does not use [Him], since he does not refer [Him] to another; or that reward is something else, and then someone can look to it either as a cause[^?] [or "the carnal"] moving [him]; and so he is a bad hireling[^12]; or as a reason inducing [him]; and so [he is] good, and in this way he does not use.

2. To that which is objected, that a clearer cognition of the creature does not prejudice the Creator, therefore etc.; it must be said that the case is not similar, since the clarity of cognition is not in our power, but the ardor of affection is in our power; therefore it is required of us that we order this latter, not that former[^13]. Some act of cognition, however, is in our power, namely the act of faith, by which if anyone assent to the first truth on account of another, he indeed prejudices the truth, just as to love on account of another [prejudices] goodness.

3. To that which is objected, that the end of the use of God is good; it must be said that the end is called good in two ways: either as to substance, or as to the intention of finalizing; and that proposition is understood as to the intention of finalizing, and this[^14] consists in right ordering.

4. To the last it must be said that that proposition[^15] is understood of things having ordering to an end, but not of the end itself. — Or it is understood of the natural and proper act of the things themselves, which is most frequently elicited from the thing itself, not of the ordering to[^16] an end; and so the proposition is not valid for the matter at hand.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** In conclusione S. Doctor propositionem, quod bono increato uti sit abusus et peccatum, duplici ratione probat, quae sumitur tum ex parte finis ultimi, tum ex parte voluntatis. Ex parte *finis ultimi* est abusus, quia aversio a fine non fit sine contemtu eius et offensa Dei, uti probatur II. Sent. d. 42. a. 2. q. 1, et a. 3. q. 2; ex parte *voluntatis* propter inordinationem, quia voluntas, quando Deo utitur, in aliquo creato ponit finem; sed finis est melior his quae sunt ad finem (infra d. 29. a. 1. q. 1. in corp.) et «quantum est de se, dicit excessum bonitatis respectu eius, quod est ad finem» (ibid. ad *s.*). Ex quo patet inordinatio in proposito. Voluntas enim in utendo minus diligit medium quam finem. Ad rem facit illud generalissimum principium Aristotelis, toties a S. Doctore repetitum: *Propter quod unumquodque (tale) est, illud magis est.* Cfr. etiam hic dub. 6, ubi dicit, quod omnis res sit aut finis, aut medium ad finem, aut perveniens ad finem. — Quoad solut. ad 1, nempe quomodo Deo servire possimus intuitu mercedis, cfr. II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 3. ad 2. et III. Sent. d. 27. a. 2. q. 2. — Quoad axioma: *Cuius finis bonus, ipsum quoque bonum* (ad 3.), cfr. II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 1.

**II.** Quoad ipsam quaestionem: Alex. Hal., S. p. III., q. 60. m. 3. a. 1. et 2, et p. II. q. 142. m. 2. — Ceteros auctores videsis in Scholio ad praecedentem quaestionem.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** In the conclusion the Holy Doctor proves the proposition, that to use an uncreated good is abuse and sin, by a twofold reason, which is drawn both on the side of the ultimate end and on the side of the will. On the side of the *ultimate end* it is abuse, since aversion from the end does not occur without contempt of it and offense against God, as is proved in II. Sent. d. 42. a. 2. q. 1, and a. 3. q. 2; on the side of the *will*, on account of disorder, since the will, when it uses God, places its end in some created thing; but the end is better than the things which are to the end (below, d. 29. a. 1. q. 1. in the body) and «as far as itself is concerned, expresses an excess of goodness in respect of that which is to the end» (ibid. ad *s.*). Whence the disorder in the matter at hand is evident. For the will in using loves the medium less than the end. To the point applies that most general principle of Aristotle, so often repeated by the Holy Doctor: *That on account of which each thing is (such), is itself more so.* Cfr. also here dub. 6, where he says that every thing is either an end, or a medium to an end, or [something] arriving at an end. — As to the solution to 1, namely how we may serve God with a view to reward, cfr. II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 3. ad 2. and III. Sent. d. 27. a. 2. q. 2. — As to the axiom: *Whose end is good, is itself also good* (ad 3.), cfr. II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 1.

**II.** As to the question itself: Alex. of Hales, S. p. III., q. 60. m. 3. a. 1. and 2, and p. II. q. 142. m. 2. — For other authors see the Scholion to the preceding question.

---

apparatus.la: Codd. R et W *vel* pro *et*.
apparatus.en: Codices R and W [read] *vel* instead of *et*.

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., I. Ethic. c. 1–7; I. Magnor. Moral. c. 3. et III. Topic. c. 1, ubi haec divisio diversimode insinuatur.
apparatus.en: Cfr. Aristotle, I. *Ethics* c. 1–7; I. *Magna Moralia* c. 3, and III. *Topics* c. 1, where this division is insinuated in various ways.

apparatus.la: Cod. A cum ed. 1 satis bene adiungit *ad*. Mox Vat., obnitentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 4, post *unum* omittit *increatum*.
apparatus.en: Codex A with ed. 1 quite suitably adds *ad*. Soon after, the Vatican edition, against the older mss. and ed. 4, omits *increatum* after *unum*.

apparatus.la: Quaest. 30: *Honestum dicitur quod propter se ipsum expetendum est, utile autem quod ad aliud aliquid referendum est.* — Mox ex multis codd. ut A F G H I K T U V aa bb ee ff cum ed. 1 posuimus *vel* pro *et*. Paulo infra Vat. ante *honestum* praemittit *quid*, quod tamen melius cum mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3 omittitur, quia Deus est ipsum honestum per essentiam.
apparatus.en: Question 30: *The honorable is said to be that which is to be sought on account of itself, but the useful that which is to be referred to something else.* — Soon after, from many codices such as A F G H I K T U V aa bb ee ff with ed. 1 we have placed *vel* in place of *et*. A little below, the Vatican edition places *quid* before *honestum*, which however is better omitted with the mss. and editions 1, 2, 3, since God is the honorable itself by essence.

apparatus.la: Quaest. 30: *Omnis itaque humana perversio est, quod etiam vitium vocatur, fruendis uti velle atque utendis frui.*
apparatus.en: Question 30: *Every human perversion, therefore, which is also called vice, is to wish to use things to be enjoyed and to enjoy things to be used.*

apparatus.la: In Evangel. S. Lucae c. 15, ubi iuxta ed. Venet. 1748: *At vero filius, qui habet Spiritus S. pignus in corde, saecularis mercedis lucella non quaerit, quibus serviat. Haeredes sunt etiam mercenarii, qui ducuntur ad vineam. Bonus mercenarius Petrus etc.* — Codex autem, sub n. 507 Bibliothecae Laurentianae Florentiis, membr. in fol. saec. XI. fol. 116. recto, col. 2. ultimam partem sic exhibet: *non quaerit, qui ius servat haeredis. Sunt etiam qui conducuntur ad vineam. Bonus etc.* Cum quo concordat cod. m. Plut. XIV. in fol. saec. XV. libr. VII. c. 35. Lectio istius ed. in verbis et interpunctione errat.
apparatus.en: In [Commentary on] the Gospel of S. Luke c. 15, where according to the Venice edition of 1748: *But truly the son, who has the pledge of the Holy Spirit in his heart, does not seek the petty gains of secular reward, that he may serve them. Heirs too are hirelings, who are led to the vineyard. Peter [is] a good hireling, etc.* — But the codex under n. 507 of the Laurentian Library in Florence, parchment, in folio, of the 11th century, fol. 116 recto, col. 2, gives the last part thus: *he does not seek, who preserves the right of an heir. There are also those who are hired to the vineyard. A good [hireling] etc.* With which agrees cod. m. Plut. XIV., in folio, 15th century, bk. VII. c. 35. The reading of that [Venice] edition errs in wording and punctuation.

apparatus.la: Vat. contra mss. et ed. 1, invertendo comparationem, nempe *sicut summa bonitas, sic summa veritas*, argumentationem, uti ex subnexis patet, perturbat. Mox cod. X post *clarius* satis bene addit *veritate increata*. Dein, faventibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, expunximus *aliquam*, quod Vat. cum recentiori cod. cc praemittit voci *aliam*. In ultima propositione huius argumenti multi codd. CFGKLRSUVW aa bb cum ed. 1 ante *diligi* falso repetunt *plus*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, against the mss. and ed. 1, by inverting the comparison — namely *as the highest goodness, so the highest truth* — disturbs the argument, as is evident from what follows. Soon after, cod. X after *clarius* quite suitably adds *veritate increata*. Then, with the older mss. and ed. 1 in favor, we have expunged *aliquam*, which the Vatican edition with the more recent cod. cc places before the word *aliam*. In the last proposition of this argument many codices CFGKLRSUVW aa bb with ed. 1 falsely repeat *plus* before *diligi*.

apparatus.la: Boeth., II. *de Differentiis topicis*. Locus a fine: *Cuius finis bonus est, ipsum quoque bonum est.* Vide supra q. 1. in corp. Propositio ista derivata esse videtur ex illa Aristot., III. Topic. c. 1: *Cuius finis melior, et ipsum melius.* Ad normam codd. et ed. 1 omisimus *est* et *quoque*, quod Vat. cum Boethio habet.
apparatus.en: Boethius, II. *On Topical Differences*. The passage near the end: *That whose end is good, is itself also good.* See above q. 1. in the body. This proposition appears to be derived from that of Aristotle, III. *Topics* c. 1: *That whose end is better, is itself better.* According to the norm of the codices and ed. 1 we have omitted *est* and *quoque*, which the Vatican edition with Boethius has.

apparatus.la: Boeth., II. *de Differentiis topic.* — Codd. F O X addunt post *malus* particulam *et*. Immediate post ex fere omnibus mss. et ed. 1 substituimus *quod* loco *quia*, cod. R autem habet *ergo si Deus*.
apparatus.en: Boethius, II. *On Topical Differences*. — Codices F O X add the particle *et* after *malus*. Immediately after, from almost all mss. and ed. 1 we have substituted *quod* in place of *quia*, while cod. R has *ergo si Deus*.

apparatus.la: Auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 reiecimus lectionem Vat. *aversionem a fine* tanquam minus rectam, quia talis abusus non dicit solum simplicem aversionem a fine, sed etiam directam perversionem ipsius finis, quatenus nempe ipse finis convertitur in medium. Cod. O post *perversitatem* addit *intentionis*. Cod. R totam propositionem sic exhibet: *et abusus talis semper est mortale peccatum, non* (forsan omissum: *solum*) *propter perversitatem in finem cum delectatione, sed propter voluntatis* etc. Mox maiorem partem codd. ut ACGIKLUVX etc. et ed. 1 secuti, bis pro *utimur* substituimus *utitur*, quod grammatice melius est; alii codd. primo loco habent *utitur*, secundo loco *utimur*. Propositio ista relativa a S. Doctore adducta, quae immediate refertur ad substantivum *voluntatis*, continet implicite rationem inordinationis in voluntate hic notatae; sensus enim est: voluntas ordinata minus diligit ipsum quo *utitur*, i. e. medium, quam propter quod *utitur* i. e. finem; atqui in hoc casu habetur contrarium: ergo voluntas est inordinata.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the mss. and ed. 1 we have rejected the reading of the Vatican edition *aversionem a fine* as less correct, since such abuse signifies not only a simple aversion from the end, but also a direct perversion of the end itself, inasmuch, namely, as the end itself is converted into a means. Cod. O after *perversitatem* adds *intentionis*. Cod. R gives the whole proposition thus: *and such abuse is always a mortal sin, not* (perhaps with *solum* omitted) *on account of perversity toward the end with delectation, but on account of the will's* etc. Soon after, following the greater part of the codices such as ACGIKLUVX etc. and ed. 1, we have twice substituted *utitur* for *utimur*, which is grammatically better; other codices in the first place have *utitur*, in the second place *utimur*. That relative proposition adduced by the Holy Doctor, which immediately refers to the substantive *voluntatis*, contains implicitly the rationale of disorder in the will here noted; for the sense is: an ordered will loves less the very thing by which it *uses*, i. e. the means, than that on account of which it *uses*, i. e. the end; but in this case the contrary obtains: therefore the will is disordered.

apparatus.la: Vers. 1. — Paulo ante exhibemus lectionem codd. RVWXYZ aa bb; alii codd. autem, omisso *Deus*, ponunt *Dominus* post *Abrahae*, a quibus non multum dissidet Vat. legendo: *est ipse, sicut Dominus dixit ad Abraam*. Mox fide antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 post *utitur* expunximus *Deo*.
apparatus.en: Verse 1. — A little before we exhibit the reading of codices RVWXYZ aa bb; but other codices, omitting *Deus*, place *Dominus* after *Abrahae*, from which the Vatican edition does not much differ in reading: *He is Himself, as the Lord said to Abram.* Soon after, on the faith of the older mss. and ed. 1, we have expunged *Deo* after *utitur*.

apparatus.la: Vat. praeter fidem mss. et ed. 1 hic addit *et sic utitur*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, contrary to the testimony of the mss. and ed. 1, here adds *et sic utitur*.

apparatus.la: Vat. post *istum* addit *amorem* et post *illam* adiungit *cognitionem*, quae tamen auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 tanquam superflua expunximus.
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition after *istum* adds *amorem* and after *illam* adjoins *cognitionem*, which however on the authority of the mss. and ed. 1, as superfluous, we have expunged.

apparatus.la: Cod. cc cum ed. 1 *hoc*. Mox antiquiores codd. et ed. 1 omittunt propositionem, quae habetur in Vat. et cod. cc post *ordinatione*, scil.: *et illo modo non contingit uti Deo, quia non convenit ordinari.* — Fusius de hac re tractat S. Doctor II. Sent. d. 28. a. 1. q. 1.
apparatus.en: Cod. cc with ed. 1 [reads] *hoc*. Soon after, the older codices and ed. 1 omit the proposition which is found in the Vatican edition and cod. cc after *ordinatione*, namely: *and in that mode it is not possible to use God, since it is not fitting [for Him] to be ordered.* — The Holy Doctor treats this matter more fully in II. Sent. d. 28. a. 1. q. 1.

apparatus.la: Scilicet, *cuius usus bonus, et ipsum bonum*. — Vat. cum cod. cc paulo ante post *ultimum* praeter fidem antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 addit *scilicet usus Dei aut est bonus aut malus* etc.
apparatus.en: Namely, *that whose use is good, is itself also good*. — The Vatican edition with cod. cc a little before, after *ultimum*, contrary to the testimony of the older mss. and ed. 1, adds *namely the use of God is either good or evil*, etc.

apparatus.la: Ex mss. et ed. 1 substituimus *in* loco *ad*. — De hoc secundo responsionis membro vide supra q. 1. circa principium conclusionis.
apparatus.en: From the mss. and ed. 1 we have substituted *in* in place of *ad*. — On this second member of the response see above q. 1. near the beginning of the conclusion.

questions.titleLa: Utrum frui sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium
questions.titleEn: Whether enjoyment is an act of the will, or of the other powers
questions.latin:
<!-- page 35 -->

### Articulus II. *Quid sit* frui.

Habito de *uti* et *utibili*, consequenter quaeritur de *frui* et *fruibili*, et primo, quid sit *frui* per essentiam, utrum scilicet sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium.

### Quaestio Unica. *Utrum frui sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium.*

1. Quod sit actus voluntatis, videtur per primam definitionem, quae est: *Frui est amore inhaerere* etc.[^1]; sed amor est voluntatis: ergo et *frui* similiter. Si dicas, quod amor sumitur ibi communiter, secundum quod est in qualibet vi respectu sui actus; contra: in omnibus aliis definitionibus idem dicitur. Unde dicitur in sequenti[^2]: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus voluntas delectata conquiescit». Quietatio autem voluntatis est.

<!-- page 36 -->

Et in alia[^9] similiter: «Frui est uti cum gaudio». Gaudium autem ad voluntatem proprie pertinet.

2. Item, ostenditur ratione, quia fruitione delectamur[^10], secundum quod delectabile est differentia boni, cum sit bonum honestum, conferens et delectabile; bonum autem obiectum est voluntatis: ergo *frui* est solius voluntatis.

3. Item, eo fruimur, quo quietamur; sed quietatio respicit rationem finis, «et finis rationem boni[^11]», et «bonum est obiectum voluntatis»: ergo fruitio, quae ordinat ad illud, similiter.

**Sed contra:**

1. Omnis virtus appetit uniri suo obiecto, quo habito delectatur, si cognoscit, et quiescit: ergo motus cum quietatione et delectatione est omnium virium: ergo cum talis sit fruitio, fruitio erit in omnibus, non tantum in voluntate;

2. Item, absentia rei amatae potius contristat amantem, quam delectat[^12]; quod enim delectat ipsum, hoc est, quia videt ipsam et habet. Si ergo motus fruitionis est cum delectatione vel est ipsa delectatio: ergo hoc[^13] est, quia videt illud in quo est ipsa delectatio; sed visio respicit cognitivam: ergo etc.

3. Item, Augustinus in libro *de Doctrina christiana*[^14]: «Haec est summa merces, ut ipso perfruamur». Sed super illud Psalmi: *Ostendam illi salutare* etc., dicit Glossa[^15], quod «visio est tota merces»: ergo si fruitio est merces, fruitio est visio per essentiam; sed visio est in cognitiva sive in ratione: ergo etc.

4. Item, fide et spe tendimus in Deum: aut ergo fruendo, aut utendo; sed non utendo, cum Deo non sit utendum: ergo fruendo: ergo fide et spe fruimur; sed fides est habitus rationis cognitivae; sed cuius est habitus, eius est actus: ergo actus fruitionis est actus[^16] rationis; similiter videtur de irascibili: ergo etc.

### Conclusio.

> *Frui* sumtum essentialiter est actus voluntatis, sumtum dispositive est actus etiam aliarum potentiarum.

**Respondeo:** Secundum aliquos[^17] *frui* pertinet ad omnes vires; et hoc dicunt, quia omnes vires remunerabuntur; qui dicunt etiam, quod[^18] in gloria erit magis proprie rationis, quia immediatius se habet ad delectationem.

Sed aliter videtur dicendum secundum Augustinum, scilicet quod sit actus ipsius voluntatis. Cum enim tres dentur definitiones de *frui*, omnes dantur penes actum voluntatis, quem tripliciter est considerare. Primo modo communiter, prout dicit motum cum delectatione; et sic definit Augustinus[^19]: «Frui est uti cum gaudio». Secundo modo, prout dicit motum cum quietatione; et hoc modo definitur ab Augustino *de Doctrina christiana*: «Frui est amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se ipsam»; et hoc modo accipitur *proprie*. Tertio modo accipitur, prout complectitur utrumque, scilicet quietationem et delectationem; et hoc modo definitur ab Augustino decimo *de Trinitate*: «Frui est quiescere in cognitis, voluntate propter se delectata», et sic accipitur *propriissime*.

Quia ergo *frui* secundum omnem acceptionem dicit delectationem vel quietem vel utrumque, et omne tale habet rationem boni, et hoc est obiectum voluntatis: ideo loquendo essentialiter, *frui* est actus voluntatis. Sed quia voluntas nec delectatur nec quietatur nisi in eo, quod cognoscit vel per fidem vel per speciem[^20], et in eo, quod habet per spem vel in re, ideo actus aliarum virium ad hunc disponunt, non tamen sunt ipsum *frui*, essentialiter loquendo.

Ex hoc patet solutio[^21] ad illud quod communiter solet quaeri, quare *frui* non definitur per actum cognitionis, sicut delectationis. Tamen[^22] haec quae-

<!-- page 37 -->

stio fundata est super falsum. Augustinus enim ponit in notificatione una, quod est cognitionis, cum dicit: «Frui est quiescere in cognitis»; cadit tamen ibi sicut dispositio.

Ex hoc etiam patet, quare non definitur per fidem et[^23] spem, sicut per caritatem, quia caritas inducitur in concupiscibilem, cuius est *frui*. Tamen ista quaestio similiter fundata est super falsum, quia amor, quo definitur *frui*, est communis ad amorem castum et libidinosum[^24], quo avarus fruitur auro, non proprius ipsius caritatis.

**Ad opposita:**

1. Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur, quod omnis virtus habet delectari et quietari[^25], cum unitur suo obiecto; dicendum, quod ipsa voluntas, ut vult Augustinus[^26], amat sibi et aliis. Et sicut etiam dicit Anselmus[^27]: «Voluntas inclinat alias vires et aliis meretur», ideo eius quietatio et delectatio redundat in alias vires. Unde sicut voluntas non sibi cognoscit, sed ratio cognoscit sibi et voluntati, ita voluntas sibi et rationi delectatur et ipsam quiescere facit.

2. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod amans non fruitur, nisi videat vel habeat; dicendum, quod videre et habere requiruntur ad *frui*, similiter et amare. Nam si quis videt aliquid et habet, nunquam delectatur, nisi amet; aliter tamen requiritur visio quam amor. Nam visio disponit, similiter et tentio, sed amor delicias suggerit. Unde est quasi acumen penetrans[^28], et ideo ei maxime convenit unire et per consequens delectare et quietare: ideo essentialiter, non dispositive, est fruitio. Propter quod est intelligendum, quod actus voluntatis potest dupliciter considerari, scilicet per modum appetitus et[^29] complacentiae. Primo modo antecedere potest ipsam visionem; secundo vero consequitur, et in hoc est perfecta ratio ipsius fruitionis, scilicet in complacentia rei visae et habitae.

3. Ad illud: *Visio est tota merces*; dicendum, quod illud non dicitur proprie, sed per concomitantiam[^30], quia visio et complacentia, in qua est perfecta ratio fruitionis, inseparabiliter se habent.

4. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod fide et spe fruimur; dicendum, quod illud non est verum per se, quia quaelibet harum accipit rationem tendentiae[^31] a caritate; unde fruitio non est ex istis nisi per caritatem. Sola enim caritas considerat finem in ratione finis et obiecti. Unde non dicitur aliquis sperare Deum, sicut amare.
questions.english:
<!-- page 35 -->

### Article II. *What enjoyment is.*

Having treated of *use* and *the useable*, the inquiry next concerns *enjoyment* and *the enjoyable*, and first, what *enjoyment* is essentially — namely, whether it is an act of the will, or of the other powers.

### Sole Question. *Whether enjoyment is an act of the will, or of the other powers.*

1. That it is an act of the will is shown by the first definition, which is: *To enjoy is to cleave by love,* etc.[^1]; but love is of the will: therefore *enjoyment* likewise. If you say that love is taken there commonly, according as it is in any power whatever with respect to its own act; against this: in all the other definitions the same is said. Hence it is said in what follows[^2]: «We enjoy things known, in which the will, delighted, comes to rest.» But rest is of the will.

<!-- page 36 -->

And in another[^9] likewise: «To enjoy is to use with joy.» But joy belongs properly to the will.

2. Likewise, it is shown by reason: because by fruition we are delighted[^10], according as the delightful is a difference of the good, since the good is the honorable, the useful, and the delightful; but the good is the object of the will: therefore *to enjoy* is of the will alone.

3. Likewise, we enjoy that by which we come to rest; but rest regards the formal character of an end, «and an end the formal character of the good[^11]», and «the good is the object of the will»: therefore fruition, which orders to that, likewise.

**On the contrary:**

1. Every power seeks to be united to its object, and, this being had, is delighted (if it knows) and comes to rest: therefore motion together with rest and delight belongs to all the powers: therefore, since fruition is such, fruition will be in all, not only in the will;

2. Likewise, the absence of the loved thing rather grieves the lover than delights him[^12]; for what delights him is the fact that he sees it and has it. If therefore the motion of fruition is with delight, or is delight itself: therefore this[^13] is so because he sees that in which is the delight itself; but vision regards the cognitive [power]: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, Augustine in the book *On Christian Doctrine*[^14]: «This is the highest reward, that we may enjoy himself.» But upon that of the Psalm: *I will show him my salvation,* etc., the Gloss says[^15] that «vision is the whole reward»: therefore if fruition is the reward, fruition is vision essentially; but vision is in the cognitive [power] or in reason: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, by faith and hope we tend toward God: therefore either by enjoying or by using; but not by using, since God is not to be used: therefore by enjoying: therefore by faith and hope we enjoy; but faith is a habit of cognitive reason; but whose is the habit, his is the act: therefore the act of fruition is an act[^16] of reason; the same seems to be the case for the irascible [power]: therefore, etc.

### Conclusion.

> *To enjoy*, taken essentially, is an act of the will; taken dispositively, it is an act also of the other powers.

**I respond:** According to some[^17] *enjoyment* pertains to all the powers; and this they say, because all the powers will be rewarded; who say also that[^18] in glory it will be more properly of reason, because reason has a more immediate relation to delight.

But it seems must be said otherwise according to Augustine, namely that it is an act of the will itself. For since three definitions of *to enjoy* are given, all are given in terms of an act of the will, which can be considered in three ways. *First*, commonly, inasmuch as it signifies motion with delight; and thus Augustine defines it[^19]: «To enjoy is to use with joy.» *Secondly*, inasmuch as it signifies motion with rest; and in this way it is defined by Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*: «To enjoy is to cleave by love to some thing for its own sake»; and in this way it is taken *properly*. *Thirdly*, it is taken inasmuch as it embraces both, namely rest and delight; and in this way it is defined by Augustine in book ten *On the Trinity*: «To enjoy is to come to rest in things known, the will being delighted for their own sake»; and so it is taken *most properly*.

Since, therefore, *to enjoy* according to every acceptation signifies delight or rest or both, and every such thing has the formal character of the good, and this is the object of the will: therefore, speaking essentially, *to enjoy* is an act of the will. But since the will is not delighted and does not come to rest except in that which it knows either by faith or by sight[^20], and in that which it has by hope or in reality, therefore the acts of the other powers dispose toward this, but are not *enjoyment* itself, speaking essentially.

From this is clear the solution[^21] to that which is commonly wont to be asked: why *enjoyment* is not defined by an act of cognition, as it is by [an act of] delight. Yet this[^22] ques-

<!-- page 37 -->

tion is founded upon a falsehood. For Augustine in one notification puts what is of cognition, when he says: «To enjoy is to come to rest in things known»; yet it falls in there as a disposition.

From this also is clear why it is not defined by faith and[^23] hope, as it is by charity, because charity is brought into the concupiscible [power], to which *enjoyment* belongs. Yet this question likewise is founded upon a falsehood, since the love by which *enjoyment* is defined is common to chaste love and to lustful love[^24], by which the miser enjoys gold — not proper to charity itself.

**To the opposites:**

1. To that, then, which is objected, that every power has [the capacity] to be delighted and to come to rest[^25] when it is united to its object; it must be said that the will itself, as Augustine[^26] holds, loves for itself and for the others. And as Anselm[^27] also says: «The will inclines the other powers and merits for the others»; therefore its rest and delight redound to the other powers. Hence, just as the will does not know for itself, but reason knows for itself and for the will, so the will is delighted for itself and for reason, and makes reason come to rest.

2. To that which is objected, that the lover does not enjoy unless he sees or has [the beloved]; it must be said that to see and to have are required for *enjoyment*, likewise also to love. For if anyone sees something and has it, he is never delighted unless he loves; but vision is required otherwise than love. For vision disposes, likewise too holding, but love offers the delights. Hence it is, as it were, a piercing sharpness[^28], and therefore it most befits it to unite and consequently to delight and to bring to rest: therefore essentially, not dispositively, it is fruition. On account of which it must be understood that the act of the will can be considered in two ways, namely by way of appetite and[^29] of complacency. In the first way it can precede the vision itself; in the second it follows, and in this is the perfect formal character of fruition itself, namely in the complacency of the thing seen and had.

3. To that: *Vision is the whole reward*; it must be said that this is not said properly, but by concomitance[^30], because vision and complacency, in which is the perfect formal character of fruition, are inseparably connected.

4. To that which is objected, that by faith and hope we enjoy; it must be said that this is not true *per se*, because each of these receives its character of tending[^31] from charity; whence fruition does not arise from these except through charity. For charity alone considers the end under the formal character of end and of object. Hence no one is said to *hope for* God, as [he is said to] *love* [Him].
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** In solutione principali huius quaestionis, scilicet quod fruitio sit actus voluntatis, omnes antiqui doctores cum Seraphico conveniunt; attamen iam istis temporibus circa quasdam subtiles de hac re quaestiones erant controversiae.

Primo quoad ipsum conceptum fruitionis S. Bonaventura docet, fruitionem praesupponere quidem cognitionem sive visionem tanquam dispositionem, tamen, essentialiter loquendo, ipsam esse actum voluntatis, qui importet tum dilectionem tum delectationem, sive esse formaliter actionem voluntatis, nempe amorosam eius inhaesionem, ad quam sequitur inseparabiliter passio delectationis; cfr. hic ad 2. et dub. 1. 2; III. Sent. d. 29. a. 1. q. 2, et ibid. d. 35. a. 1. q. 1. in corp.; II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 2. ad 4. Hexaem. Serm. 12. in fine. Idem docet Scotus cum suis, Richard. a Med., B. Albert. M., Petr. a Tar., Henr. Gand. — Alii vero doctores volunt, fruitionem esse formaliter ipsam delectationem, non quidem qualemcumque, sed ultimatam, seu quae coniuncta est cum quietatione; ipsam vero non esse amorem nisi connotative et causaliter; ita discipuli S. Thomae, teste Caietano (ad S. I. II. q. 1. a. 1.), Dionys. Carth. aliique.

Secundo, quoad actum, in quo fruitio formaliter consistit, docet S. Bonav., hic ad 1. et 2; II. Sent. d. 24. p. I. a. 2. q. 4: omnem delectationem spiritualem ortum habere ex amore voluntatis, praesupposita perceptione convenientis. Consentiunt Alex. Hal., Henr. Gand., Richard. a Med. qui inter alia dicit: «Actum cognitivae non sequitur delectatio nisi mediante actu appetitivae.» Hoc negatur ab auctoribus secundae sententiae.

Tertio, hinc orta est celebris controversia, praecipue inter asseclas S. Thomae et Scoti agitata, utrum scilicet beatitudo in patria formaliter consistat in actu intellectus sive in visione, qui tum amorem tum delectationem inseparabiliter habet annexa, immo «virtualiter continet et causaliter exerit» (Caietanus), an potius, ut vult Scotus cum aliis multis, in actu voluntatis, qui visionem supponit et delectatione completur. Hanc quaestionem tangit S. Bonav., hic ad 3.; plura vide IV. Sent. d. 49. p. 1. q. 5. Haec controversia cohaeret cum doctrinis psychologicis praecipue de relatione inter intellectum et voluntatem.

**II.** De quaestione hic proposita: Alex. Hal., S. p. IV. q. 26. m. 4. — Scot., hic q. 3. in Oxon. et Report. — S. Thom., hic q. 1. a. 1; S. I. II. q. 11. a. 1. et 2. — B. Albert. M., hic a. 12. et 17. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2. a. 1. — Richard. a Med., hic a. 2. q. 1. — Aegid. R., hic I. princ. q. 1. — Henr. Gand., S. a. 49. q. 6. n. 26.; de delectatione etiam agit S. a. 50. q. 2. — Durand., hic q. 1. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 3. — Biel, hic q. 2.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** On the principal solution of this question, namely that fruition is an act of the will, all the ancient doctors agree with the Seraphic; nevertheless already in these times concerning certain subtle questions about this matter there were controversies.

*First*, as to the very concept of fruition, St. Bonaventure teaches that fruition does presuppose cognition or vision as a disposition; yet, speaking essentially, it is itself an act of the will, which imports both love and delight, that is, it is formally an act of the will — namely its loving adhesion, upon which inseparably follows the passion of delight; cf. here ad 2 and dub. 1, 2; III Sent. d. 29 a. 1 q. 2, and ibid. d. 35 a. 1 q. 1 in corp.; II Sent. d. 38 a. 1 q. 2 ad 4; Hexaem. Sermon 12 at the end. The same is taught by Scotus with his followers, Richard of Mediavilla, Blessed Albert the Great, Peter of Tarantasia, Henry of Ghent. — But other doctors hold that fruition is formally delight itself — not, indeed, any sort, but the ultimate, that is, that which is conjoined with rest; and that fruition is not love except connotatively and causally; so the disciples of St. Thomas, on the testimony of Cajetan (on S. I-II q. 1 a. 1), Denis the Carthusian, and others.

*Secondly*, as to the act in which fruition formally consists, St. Bonav. teaches here, ad 1 and 2; II Sent. d. 24 p. I a. 2 q. 4: that every spiritual delight has its origin from the love of the will, supposing the perception of what is suitable. Alexander of Hales, Henry of Ghent, [and] Richard of Mediavilla agree, who among other things says: «An act of the cognitive [power] is not followed by delight except mediated by an act of the appetitive [power].» This is denied by the authors of the second opinion.

*Thirdly*, hence arose the famous controversy, agitated especially between the followers of St. Thomas and of Scotus, namely whether beatitude in the fatherland formally consists in the act of the intellect or in vision, which has both love and delight inseparably annexed — nay, «virtually contains and causally exerts [them]» (Cajetan); or rather, as Scotus with many others holds, in an act of the will, which presupposes vision and is completed by delight. This question is touched by St. Bonav. here, ad 3; see more in IV Sent. d. 49 p. 1 q. 5. This controversy coheres with psychological doctrines, especially concerning the relation between intellect and will.

**II.** On the question here proposed: Alex. Hal., S. p. IV q. 26 m. 4. — Scot., here q. 3 in Oxon. and Report. — St. Thom., here q. 1 a. 1; S. I-II q. 11 a. 1 and 2. — B. Albert M., here a. 12 and 17. — Peter of Tarantasia, here q. 2 a. 1. — Richard of Mediavilla, here a. 2 q. 1. — Giles of Rome, here I princ. q. 1. — Henry of Ghent, S. a. 49 q. 6 n. 26.; on delight he also treats in S. a. 50 q. 2. — Durandus, here q. 1. — Denis the Carthusian, here q. 3. — Biel, here q. 2.

---

apparatus.la: Auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 removimus particulam *vel*, quae hic a Vat. male additur, quia verbum *libidinosum* large acceptum etiam concupiscentiam oculorum complectitur. Codd. P et Q post *caritatis* addunt *est*; cod. X autem legit: *ideo non est proprius ipsius caritatis*.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the manuscripts and ed. 1 we have removed the particle *vel*, which is here wrongly added by the Vatican edition, because the word *libidinosum*, broadly taken, also embraces the concupiscence of the eyes. Codd. P and Q after *caritatis* add *est*; but cod. X reads: *ideo non est proprius ipsius caritatis*.

apparatus.la: Licet multi mss. utACGKLOSTUVWXYZ omittant *et quietari*, retinendum tamen duximus, tum quia in aliquibus antiquioribus mss. ut F H I etc. invenitur, tum quia superius in ipsa obiectione exhibetur.
apparatus.en: Although many manuscripts — A C G K L O S T U V W X Y Z — omit *et quietari*, we have nevertheless judged it should be retained, both because it is found in some older manuscripts such as F H I, etc., and because it is exhibited above in the objection itself.

apparatus.la: Colligitur ex XV. *de Trin.* c. 22, ubi ostendit, quod memoria, intellectus et amor seu voluntas non sint sua nec sibi, sed supposito agant, quidquid agunt. Et in praecedentibus capitulis trinitatem in anima repertam cum Trinitate divina comparando, c. 17 de Spiritu S. ait: *ipse autem et sibi et illis non nisi diligit*. — Plurimi codd. *ut vult* pro *ut dicit*.
apparatus.en: Gathered from *On the Trinity* XV, c. 22, where he shows that memory, intellect, and love (i.e. will) are not their own nor for themselves, but act for the supposit whatever they do. And in the preceding chapters, comparing the trinity found in the soul with the divine Trinity, in c. 17 he says of the Holy Spirit: *He himself does not love except both for himself and for them*. — Very many codd. [read] *ut vult* for *ut dicit*.

apparatus.la: Libr. *de Concordia praescientiae Dei cum libero arbitrio* c. 11. et 12, ubi dicit, quod voluntas movet omnia instrumenta, quae in nobis sunt, ut manus etc.; et quod ex ipsa «descendit omne meritum hominis». — De doctrina hic posita vide II. Sent. d. 24. p. 1. a. 2. q. 1.
apparatus.en: Book *On the Harmony of God's Foreknowledge with Free Will*, cc. 11 and 12, where he says that the will moves all the instruments which are in us, such as the hands, etc.; and that from it «descends every merit of man». — On the doctrine here set forth, see II Sent. d. 24 p. 1 a. 2 q. 1.

apparatus.la: Hic loquendi modus sumtus est ex Hugonis de S. Victore *Expos. in Dionysii libr. de Caelest. Hierarch.* c. 7.
apparatus.en: This manner of speaking is taken from Hugh of St. Victor's *Exposition on Dionysius' Book on the Celestial Hierarchy*, c. 7.

apparatus.en: Cod. X here repeats *per modum*.

apparatus.en: We have restored, from the manuscripts and ed. 1, the more usual word *concomitantiam* in place of *concomitationem*.
