questions.latin:
<!-- page 38 -->

### Articulus III. *De fruibili.*

Ostenso, quid sit frui per essentiam, quaestio est de fruibili, et

*primo*, utrum Deo contingat frui;

*secundo*, utrum fruendum sit ipso solo.

### Quaestio I. *Utrum Deo sit fruendum.*

Circa primum, quod sit Deo fruendum, ostenditur sic.

**Fundamenta.**

1. «Eo fruendum est, quod beatos nos facit[^1]», quia in beatitudine est recta fruitio; sed Deo beati efficimur, quia ipse est nostra beatitudo: ergo Deo est fruendum.

2. Item, bonum est amabile; ergo magis bonum magis amabile et summe bonum summe amabile[^2]; sed eo fruimur, quod summe amamus: ergo etc.

3. Item, pulcrum delectat et[^3] magis pulcrum magis delectat, ergo summe pulcrum summe delectat; sed eo fruimur, in quo summe delectamur: ergo etc.

**Sed contra:**

**Ad oppositum.**

1. Ubi est fruitio, ibi est delectatio; «sed delectatio est coniunctio convenientis cum convenienti[^4]»; Dei autem ad creaturam nulla est convenientia, immo summa distantia: ergo nec delectatio, ergo nec fruitio.

2. Item, excellens sensibile corrumpit sensum vel saltem contristat, quia delectatio est in mediis[^5]: ergo pari ratione excellens intelligibile corrumpit vel contristat intellectum. Sed Deus est excellentissima lux: ergo contristat, non delectat, ergo etc. Si dicas, quod sensibilis potentia est corruptibilis, non intellectus; hoc non solvit, quia intellectus, dum est in carne, fatigatur et impeditur in actu, corpore corrupto.

3. Item, ubi fruitio, ibi quietatio; sed in infinito non est quietatio, «quia semper est aliquid extra accipere[^6]»: ergo cum Deus sit infinitus, in Deo non est quietatio, ergo nec fruitio.

> **Conclusio.** Deo proprie est fruendum.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod Deo fruendum est, eo quod ipse solus perfecte finit[^7] et delectat ipsam animam propter se et super omnia.

**Ad argumenta.**

1. Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur, quod delectatio est coniunctio convenientis etc.; dicendum, quod[^8] est convenientia per unius naturae participationem vel per comparationem communem[^9]. Prima convenientia facit communitatem univocationis, secunda communitatem analogiae sive proportionis. Et haec est secundum triplicem differentiam: aut secundum similem comparationem duorum ad duo, ut sicut homo ad animal, ita albedo se habet ad colorem; aut secundum dissimilem comparationem duorum ad unum, ut animalis et cibi ad sanitatem; vel

<!-- page 39 -->

secundum comparationem duorum ad invicem, ut puta cum unum est imitatio vel similitudo alterius. Similitudo enim non convenit cum consimili[^10] in tertio, sed se ipsa. Sic est in proposito, quia anima est expressa similitudo Dei. Haec convenientia in uno extremo ponit inclinationem et indigentiam, in alio quietationem et sufficientiam, quia unum[^11] factum est propter alterum, unde ordinatur ad alterum. Et quoniam ad inclinationis quietationem et indigentiae suppletionem, ubi est sensus, est delectatio sive sequitur[^12], ideo anima cum tali modo quietatur a Deo, fruitur eo.

2. Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod excellentia sensibilis corrumpit sensum: ergo etc., dicendum, quod non est simile de intelligere et sentire. Et ad hoc est triplex ratio: una est ex parte virtutis apprehensivae, alia ex parte apprehensi sive obiecti, tertia est ex parte modi apprehendendi.

Ex parte virtutis apprehensivae, quia sensus potest corrumpi, intellectus autem non. Cuius ratio est, quia sensus dependet ab organo, in quo est quaedam medietas et harmonia, quae non tantum corrumpitur per contrarium, sed per excellens; sed intellectus non dependet ab organo, quia est vis immaterialis, ideo non tristatur in excellenti[^13].

Ex parte obiecti non est simile, quia obiectum intelligibile[^14] excellens iuvat et confortat, quia influentia talis cognoscibilis procedit ab intimis et intrat ipsam potentiam, et ideo ipsam confortat et corroborat. Sicut si magnus mons daret virtutem portandi se, facilius ferretur quam parvus; sic est in intelligibili, quod Deus est. Sensibile autem obiectum tantum extra excitat, et ideo hoc corrumpit, illud autem non.

Ex parte modi apprehendendi similiter est dissimilitudo, quia sensus in apprehensione sui obiecti tendit ad exterius, unde percipiendo[^15] illud dispergitur exterius nec fortificatur[^16] interius, ideo debilitatur. Sed obiectum intellectus cum sit intimum ipsi intellectui, in eius perceptione virtus non dispergitur, sed colligitur, et quanto virtus est magis unita, tanto fortior.

3. Ad illud quod obiicitur de infinito; dicendum, quod infinitum dicitur dupliciter, scilicet per privationem perfectionis; et sic materia dicitur infinita, et talis infiniti non est finire, sed potius finiri indiget, secundum quod[^17] est possibile. Alio modo infinitum dicitur per privationem limitationis; et quod sic infinitum est, proprie habet finire, quoniam ultra ipsum, cum non sit maius cogitare, non contingit aliquid appetere. Unde talis infinitas convenit ultimo fini, quae[^18] maxime habet finiendi rationem.
questions.english:
### Article III. *On the enjoyable.*

Having shown what it is to enjoy through essence, the question concerns the enjoyable, and

*first*, whether God can be enjoyed;

*second*, whether He alone is to be enjoyed.

### Question I. *Whether God is to be enjoyed.*

Concerning the first, that God is to be enjoyed, is shown thus.

**Foundations.**

1. "That is to be enjoyed which makes us blessed[^1]," since right enjoyment lies in beatitude; but we are made blessed by God, since He Himself is our beatitude: therefore God is to be enjoyed.

2. Likewise, the good is lovable; therefore the more good is the more lovable, and the supremely good is supremely lovable[^2]; but we enjoy that which we love supremely: therefore etc.

3. Likewise, the beautiful delights, and[^3] the more beautiful delights more; therefore the supremely beautiful delights supremely; but we enjoy that in which we are supremely delighted: therefore etc.

**On the contrary:**

**To the opposite.**

1. Where there is enjoyment, there is delight; "but delight is the conjunction of the fitting with the fitting[^4]"; but there is no fittingness of God to the creature, but rather the greatest distance: therefore no delight, therefore no enjoyment.

2. Likewise, an excelling sensible object corrupts the sense or at least saddens it, since delight lies in middle things[^5]: therefore, by parity of reasoning, an excelling intelligible object corrupts or saddens the intellect. But God is the most excelling light: therefore He saddens, He does not delight, therefore etc. If you say that the sensible power is corruptible, the intellect is not; this does not solve the matter, since the intellect, while it is in the flesh, is wearied and impeded in its act, the body being corrupted.

3. Likewise, where enjoyment is, there is rest; but in the infinite there is no rest, "since there is always something beyond to be received[^6]": therefore, since God is infinite, in God there is no rest, therefore neither enjoyment.

> **Conclusion.** God is properly to be enjoyed.

**I respond:** It must be said that God is to be enjoyed, in that He alone perfectly terminates[^7] and delights the soul itself for His own sake and above all things.

**To the arguments.**

1. To that, then, which is objected, that delight is the conjunction of the fitting etc.; it must be said that[^8] there is a fittingness through participation in one nature, or through a common comparison[^9]. The first fittingness produces the community of univocation, the second the community of analogy or proportion. And this latter is according to a threefold difference: either according to a similar comparison of two to two, as just as man is to animal, so whiteness is to color; or according to a dissimilar comparison of two to one, as of the animal and food to health; or

<!-- page 39 -->

according to a comparison of two to each other, as for instance when one is the imitation or likeness of the other. For a likeness does not agree with that-which-is-like it[^10] in a third [term], but in itself. So it is in the case at hand, since the soul is the express likeness of God. This fittingness, in the one extreme, posits inclination and indigence, in the other rest and sufficiency, since the one[^11] is made for the sake of the other, whence it is ordered to the other. And since, for the rest of the inclination and the supplying of the indigence, where there is sense, there is delight, or [delight] follows[^12], therefore the soul, when it is rested in such a way by God, enjoys Him.

2. To that which is objected, that an excelling sensible object corrupts the sense: therefore etc., it must be said that the case of understanding and sensing is not alike. And for this there is a threefold reason: one is on the part of the apprehending power, another on the part of the apprehended or the object, the third is on the part of the mode of apprehending.

On the part of the apprehending power, since the sense can be corrupted, but the intellect cannot. The reason for this is that the sense depends on an organ, in which there is a certain mean and harmony, which is corrupted not only by the contrary, but by the excelling; but the intellect does not depend on an organ, since it is an immaterial power, and so it is not saddened by an excelling [object][^13].

On the part of the object it is not alike, since an excelling intelligible[^14] object aids and strengthens, since the influence of such a knowable proceeds from interior depths and enters the power itself, and therefore strengthens and fortifies it. Just as if a great mountain were to give the power of bearing itself, it would be borne more easily than a small one; so it is in the intelligible, which God is. But the sensible object only stirs from outside, and therefore this corrupts, but that does not.

On the part of the mode of apprehending there is likewise dissimilarity, since the sense, in the apprehension of its object, tends outward, whence by perceiving[^15] it, it is scattered outwardly and is not strengthened[^16] inwardly, therefore it is weakened. But since the object of the intellect is interior to the intellect itself, in its perception the power is not scattered, but gathered, and the more the power is unified, the stronger it is.

3. To that which is objected concerning the infinite, it must be said that the infinite is said in two ways, namely, by privation of perfection; and thus matter is called infinite, and it is not for such an infinite to terminate, but rather it stands in need of being terminated, insofar as[^17] this is possible. In another way the infinite is said by privation of limitation; and that which is infinite in this way properly has [the power] to terminate, since beyond it, since nothing greater can be conceived, nothing else can be sought. Whence such infinity belongs to the last end, which[^18] most of all has the character of terminating.

apparatus.la: August., I. *De Doctr. christ.* c. 33. n. 37: *Illo enim frueris, quo efficieris beatus.* — In quo textu cod. R post *Illo* addit *solo*.
apparatus.en: Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. I, c. 33, n. 37: *For you enjoy that by which you are made blessed.* — In which text codex R, after *Illo*, adds *solo*.

apparatus.la: Simile argumentum reperitur in Aristot., I. *Ethic.* c. 7, ubi agit de felicitate, quae est bonum optimum, ideoque et maxime exoptandum ac amandum. Cfr. III. *Topic.* c. 1. seq.
apparatus.en: A similar argument is found in Aristotle, *Ethics* bk. I, c. 7, where he treats of happiness, which is the best good, and therefore most to be desired and loved. Cf. *Topics* bk. III, c. 1 and following.

apparatus.la: Supplevimus ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1 particulam *et*.
apparatus.en: We have supplied the particle *et* from the older manuscripts and the first edition.

apparatus.la: Haec delectationis definitio est S. Doctori ceterisque Scholasticis familiaris et convenit cum ea, quam exhibet Avicenna in fine VIII. *Metaph.* c. 7. circa finem: *Delectatio non est nisi apprehensio convenientis, secundum quod conveniens est* — Quae ab Avicenna data definitio fundari videtur in illa, quam Aristot., I. *Rhetor.* c. 11. tradit: *Est autem delectatio motus quidam animae et constitutio simul tota, sensibilis, in existentem naturam* (haec definitio explicatur ab Henr. Gand., S. a. 50. q. 2.). Ed. Paris. 1878 sic Aristot. interpretatur: *Positum sit igitur nobis, voluptatem esse motionem quandam animi et constitutionem subitam sensuque percipiendam in statu conveniente naturae.* Cfr. etiam VII. *Ethic.* c. 11. seq. et praecipue X. *Ethic.* c. 1-5. ac II. *Magnor. Moral.* c. 7, ubi plura ad delectationem (voluptatem) pertinentia explicantur. — Mox, contradicentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, habet Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc *facturam* pro *creaturam*. Paulo post cod. R *infinita* loco *summa*.
apparatus.en: This definition of delight is familiar to the holy Doctor and to the other Scholastics, and agrees with that which Avicenna gives at the end of *Metaph.* VIII, c. 7, near the end: *Delight is nothing other than the apprehension of the fitting insofar as it is fitting* — This definition given by Avicenna seems to be founded on that which Aristotle, *Rhetoric* bk. I, c. 11, transmits: *Delight, however, is a certain motion of the soul and a complete settling, sensible, into its existent nature* (this definition is explained by Henry of Ghent, S. a. 50. q. 2.). The Paris edition of 1878 thus interprets Aristotle: *Let it then be laid down by us that pleasure is a certain motion of the soul and a sudden settling, to be perceived by sense, into a state agreeable to nature.* Cf. also *Ethics* bk. VII, c. 11 and following, and especially *Ethics* bk. X, c. 1-5, and *Magna Moralia* bk. II, c. 7, where many things pertaining to delight (pleasure) are explained. — Next, against the older manuscripts and the first edition, the Vatican edition together with the later codex cc has *facturam* in place of *creaturam*. A little later codex R has *infinita* in place of *summa*.

apparatus.la: Aristot., II. *de Anima*, text. 123. (ed. Paris. Firmin-Didot, III. c. 2.), ubi iuxta ed. Venet. 1489 legitur: *Manifestum autem ex his, et propter quid excellentiae sensibilium corrumpunt sensitiva... Et manifesta est ex hoc causa, propter quam sensibilia intensa corrumpunt instrumenta sensuum.* Et text. 143. (ed. Paris. loc. cit.): *Proportio autem est symphonia... unde et delectabilia quidem sunt, dum dicuntur sincera et mixta entia ad rationem... excellentia autem contristant aut corrumpunt.* Tandem libr. III. text. 29: *Et est delectari aut tristari agere sensitiva medietate ad bonum et malum in quantum talia.* — Vat. rationem additam contra mss. et ed. 1 ita exhibet: *quia vera delectatio non est nisi in mediis*. Cod. X circa finem huius argumenti loco *in carne* ponit *in corpore*.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the Soul* bk. II, text 123 (Paris Firmin-Didot ed., III. c. 2.), where according to the Venice edition of 1489 one reads: *It is manifest from these things, and why the excellences of sensibles corrupt the sense-faculties... And the cause is made manifest from this, on account of which intense sensibles corrupt the instruments of the senses.* And text 143 (Paris ed., loc. cit.): *Proportion, moreover, is a symphony... whence delightful indeed are things said to be sincere and the entities mixed unto reason... but excellences sadden or corrupt.* Finally, bk. III, text 29: *And to be delighted or to be saddened is for the sensitive [faculty] to act by a middle state with respect to good and evil insofar as they are such.* — The Vatican edition, against the manuscripts and the first edition, gives the added reason thus: *since true delight is only in middle things*. Codex X, near the end of this argument, places *in corpore* in place of *in carne*.

apparatus.la: Aristot., III. *Phys.* text. 63. (c. 6.): *Infinitum igitur id est, cuius secundum quantitatem accipientibus semper aliquid accipere extra est; cuius autem nihil est extra, id est perfectum et totum.* — Mox praeter fidem antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 non ita bene Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc *ergo non fruitio*.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* bk. III, text 63 (c. 6.): *The infinite, therefore, is that of which, according to quantity, for those receiving it there is always something to be received beyond; but that of which nothing is beyond is the perfect and the whole.* — Next, against the testimony of the older manuscripts and the first edition, not so well does the Vatican edition together with the later codex cc have *ergo non fruitio*.

apparatus.la: Id est, *quietat*.
apparatus.en: That is, *brings to rest*.

apparatus.la: Corruptam lectionem Vat. et recentioris cod. cc, in qua ponitur *et* pro *vel* et omittitur *communem*, restauravimus ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1. Paulo ante cod. X *dicendum, quod convenientia dicitur vel per*. — De convenientia vide Aristot., *de Praedicam.* c. 1. et VII. *Phys.* text. 21-34. (c. 4.).
apparatus.en: We have restored from the older manuscripts and the first edition the corrupt reading of the Vatican edition and of the later codex cc, in which *et* is put in place of *vel* and *communem* is omitted. A little earlier codex X has *it must be said that fittingness is said either through*. — On fittingness see Aristotle, *Categories* c. 1, and *Physics* bk. VII, text 21-34 (c. 4.).

apparatus.la: Plurimi codd. cum ed. 1 omittunt *se habet*, quod Vat. cum aliquibus tantum codd. hic addit.
apparatus.en: Most codices together with the first edition omit *se habet*, which the Vatican edition, together with only some codices, here adds.

apparatus.la: Plures mss. ut A F G H K S T Y etc. cum ed. 1 *simili*. Mox mendum Vat., quae post *se ipsa* addit *anima*, castigamus ex mss. et ed. 1; cod. X *sed est se ipsa similis*. In lectione in textum recepta *similitudo* sumitur concrete et sensus est: *simile ratione similitudinis convenit immediate cum consimili*. — Paulo post cod. T *homo* pro *anima*; plures vero codd. ut C L R S U omittunt *anima*, sed non bene.
apparatus.en: Several manuscripts such as A F G H K S T Y etc., with the first edition, [have] *simili*. Next, the error of the Vatican edition, which after *se ipsa* adds *anima*, we correct from the manuscripts and the first edition; codex X has *sed est se ipsa similis*. In the reading received into the text, *similitudo* is taken concretely, and the sense is: *the like, by reason of likeness, agrees immediately with the like.* — A little later codex T has *homo* in place of *anima*; several codices however, such as C L R S U, omit *anima*, but not rightly.

apparatus.la: Cod. X hic repetit *unum*.
apparatus.en: Codex X here repeats *unum*.

apparatus.la: Cod. WXZ adiungunt *ibi*, et mox cod. A post *sequitur* repetit *delectatio*.
apparatus.en: Codices W, X, Z add *ibi*, and next codex A, after *sequitur*, repeats *delectatio*.

apparatus.la: Cod. X addit *etiam*. Paulo post codd. aa bb *spiritualis* loco *immaterialis*. Mox codd. inter se non conveniunt; nam codd. A C G I L S T U W post *tristatur* omittunt *in*; codd. R et ff ponunt *ab*; cod. bb vero *ex*; plures autem ut F H K. etc. cum ed. 1 *in*.
apparatus.en: Codex X adds *etiam*. A little later codices aa and bb have *spiritualis* in place of *immaterialis*. Next, the codices do not agree among themselves; for codices A C G I L S T U W, after *tristatur*, omit *in*; codices R and ff put *ab*; codex bb has *ex*; many however, such as F H K etc., with the first edition, have *in*.

apparatus.la: De hac differentia inter sensum et intellectum vide Aristot., II. *de Anima*, text. 123. et 143. paulo supra relatos, et libr. III. text. 4. (ed. Paris. c. 4.): *Necesse est itaque, quoniam (intellectus) omnia intelligit, immixtum esse;* et text. 7: *Quod autem non similis sit impassibilitas sensitivi et intellectivi, manifestum est sensoriis et sensu. Sensus enim non potest sentire ex vehementi sensibili... sed intellectus cum aliquid intellexerit valde intelligibile, non minus intelligit inferiora, sed et magis; sensitivum enim non sine corpore est, hic (intellectus) autem separabilis est.*
apparatus.en: On this difference between sense and intellect see Aristotle, *On the Soul* bk. II, text 123 and 143, recounted a little above, and bk. III, text 4 (Paris ed., c. 4.): *It is therefore necessary, since (the intellect) understands all things, that it be unmixed;* and text 7: *That the impassibility of the sensitive and of the intellective are not alike is manifest in the sense-organs and in sense. For sense cannot sense from a vehement sensible... but the intellect, when it has understood something very intelligible, does not understand inferior things less, but even more; for the sensitive is not without a body, but this (the intellect) is separable.*

apparatus.la: Auctoritate antiquiorum mss. substituimus *intelligibile* loco *intelligentiae*.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the older [manuscripts] we have substituted *intelligibile* in place of *intelligentiae*.

apparatus.en: Thus codices C H K O S T U Y aa bb and the first edition; but codices A F I L M R V W X Z [have] *participando*; the Vatican edition, however, with codex cc, has *per*. Next, codices X and Y have *confortatur* in place of *fortificatur*.

apparatus.en: Codex cc has *scilicet quantum* in place of *secundum quod*.

questions.titleEn: Whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed
questions.latin:
<!-- page 39 -->

### Quaestio II. *Utrum solo Deo sive bono increato fruendum sit.*

Ultimo quaeritur, utrum solo Deo sive bono increato sit fruendum; et quod sic, videtur.

**Fundamenta.**

1. Illo solo est fruendum, quod est propter se diligendum; sed illud solum[^1] est propter se diligendum, quod est propter se bonum; illud autem propter se est bonum, quod bonitatem, quam habet, nec habet ab alio, nec bonitas illa est *ad aliud*; hoc autem est solus Deus: ergo etc.

<!-- page 40 -->

2. Item, illo solo est fruendum, quod quietat animae appetitum; sed animae appetitus non quietatur sufficienter nisi in eo quod est illa perfectius et maius bonum; hoc autem est solus Deus: ergo etc.

3. Item, appetitus non sufficienter quietatur nisi per aliquid, quod animam implet, quia ex ea parte anima deficit in quiete, qua deficit in plenitudine; sed[^2] est capax Dei secundum appetitum: ergo si omne creatum est in infinitum minus illo, nullum supplet animae appetitum. Et hoc est quod dicit Augustinus[^3]: «Animam totius Trinitatis capacem nihil minus quam Trinitas potest implere».

4. Item, bonum, quod potest cogitari, potest appeti: ergo si aliquo maius bonum potest cogitari, maius illo potest appeti; sed omni finito maius potest cogitari: ergo maius potest appeti: ergo nullum finitum terminat animae appetitum sufficienter: ergo solo bono infinito, quod Deus est, est fruendum, quo habito, non potest amplius cogitari nec desiderari.

**Contra:**

1. Videtur, quod bono creato contingat frui, quia, quamvis appetitus materiae sit infinitus, tamen per formam creatam incorruptibilem[^4] sufficienter finitur: ergo similiter videtur, quod sit aliquod bonum creatum, quod sufficienter finiet animae appetitum; sed omni tali est fruendum: ergo aliquo bono creato est fruendum.

2. Item, appetitus humanus est finitae capacitatis, ergo non capit nisi finitum, vel si capiat infinitum, capit finite; ergo si finiatur per illud quod capit, finitur per bonum finitum: ergo videtur, quod aliquo bono finito sit fruendum.

3. Item, specialiter videtur, quod homine sit fruendum, quia omni eo est fruendum, quo Deus fruitur; sed Deus homine fruitur, quia hominem amat; sed amore illo, quo amat se, amat hominem, quia non est in eo[^5] duplex amor; sed primus est fruitionis: ergo et secundus.

4. Item, videtur specialiter de virtute; quia omni eo est fruendum, quod est propter se appetendum; haec est manifesta per se; sed omne bonum honestum est propter se appetendum, «quia honestum est quod sua vi nos trahit et dignitate sua nos allicit», sicut dicit Tullius[^6], et Augustinus dividit honestum contra utile; sed virtus cadit in genere honesti: ergo virtute est fruendum.

5. Item, videtur specialiter de beatitudine. Omni eo est fruendum, quo habito animus quiescit et delectatur et nihil ultra potest quaerere; sed beatitudo creata est huiusmodi: ergo etc.

### Conclusio.

> Solo Deo proprie est fruendum; improprie frui licet bonis spiritualibus, quae delectant et fini sunt coniuncta.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod solo Deo est fruendum, proprie accepto frui, prout dicit motum cum delectatione et quietatione. Sed communiter accepto frui, prout dicit motum cum delectatione tantum[^7], omnibus, quae spiritualiter delectant et coniuncta sunt fini, cuiusmodi sunt fructus, dona et beatitudines, potest frui homo non indebite; sed primo modo solo Deo.

Et ratio huius est, quia nihil potest animam sufficienter finire nisi bonum, ad quod est[^8]. Hoc autem est bonum summum, quod superius est anima, et bonum infinitum, quod excedit animae vires. Cognitio enim animae naturalis[^9] est cognitio non arctata; unde nata est quodam modo omnia cognoscere, unde non impletur cognitio eius aliquo cognoscibili, nisi quod habet in se omnia cognoscibilia et quo cognito omnia cognoscuntur. Similiter affectio eius nata est diligere omne bonum; ergo nullo bono sufficienter finitur affectus, nisi quod[^10] est bonum omnis boni et quod est omnia in omnibus.

<!-- page 41 -->

De quo bono Exodi trigesimo tertio[^11]: *Ostendam tibi omne bonum*. Hoc autem est summum bonum: ergo etc.

Item[^12], nihil sufficienter finit animam nisi bonum infinitum, quia ad hoc, ut finiatur, necesse est, ipsam finiri secundum aestimationem; alioquin non esset beata, nisi se existimaret beatam. Aestimatio autem supergreditur omne finitum, quia omni finito potest maius cogitari aliquid: ergo cum affectio possit[^13] se extendere ubi et aestimatio, necessario affectio animae supergreditur omne finitum; et si hoc, nullo bono finito sufficienter finitur. Fruendum est ergo solo Deo, quia summum bonum et infinitum.

Et non solum Deo fruendum propter perfectam finitionem, sed etiam propter perfectam delectationem. Ad delectationem enim concurrit[^14] delectabile et coniunctio eius cum eo quod delectatur. Omne autem, quod delectat animam, delectat in ratione boni et pulcri; et quoniam solus Deus est ipsa[^15] bonitas et pulcritudo, ideo in Deo solo est perfecta delectatio.

Item, quia ibi est coniunctio; solus autem Deus est qui perfectissime coniungitur. Nam coniungitur secundum[^16] veritatem et intimitatem. Solus enim Deus propter summam simplicitatem et spiritualitatem illabitur animae, ita quod secundum veritatem est in anima et intimior animae quam ipsa sibi.

Omnes enim[^17] hae quatuor rationes ad unam reducuntur, scilicet ad hanc: quia nata est anima ad percipiendum bonum infinitum, quod Deus est, ideo in eo solo debet quiescere et eo frui.

**Ad argumenta pro parte opposita:**

1. *Ad illud* vero quod obiicitur de appetitu materiae; dicendum, quod appetitus materiae ordinatur ad formam tanquam ad perfectionem substantialem, ex qua[^18] et materia fit unum; et ideo necesse est, formam esse eiusdem generis cum materia, nec est omnino supra materiam: ideo finita est omnis talis forma. Talis autem, si sit incorruptibilis, propter unionem[^19] arctat appetitum materiae et arctatum finit; unde non finitur in sua amplitudine. Appetitus autem animae non sic arctatur propter unionem cum appetibili, immo dilatatur; et ideo oportet, quod perficiatur aliquo omnino summo.

2. *Ad illud* quod obiicitur, quod[^20] non capit nisi finite; dicendum, quod infinitum bonum finite capit, quoniam ipsa est finita. Sed quoniam bonum illud est infinitum, ideo ab ipso totaliter absorbetur, ut iam eius capacitas undique terminetur. Unde non tantum gaudebit, sed sicut dicit Anselmus[^21], *in gaudium Domini introibit*. Quod si tantum caperet et non vinceretur nec absorberetur, adhuc posset insurgere appetitus ad amplius aliquid capiendum. Patet igitur, quod ad hoc quod anima compleatur, quamvis capacitatem habeat finitam[^22], tamen necesse est adesse bonum infinitum.

3. *Ad illud* vero quod obiicitur de homine; dicendum, quod Deus diligit hominem, et amor Dei est amor fruitionis; tamen homine non fruitur, quia diligendo se diligit hominem, id est, fruendo se utitur homine. Quod patet sic: quia dilectio Dei ad creaturam non est affectio, sed effectus[^23] communicatio. Communicatio autem secundum rationem habitualem attenditur secundum bonitatem; quia bonum est quod natum est se communicare. Secundum rationem vero actualem attenditur sive respicit voluntatem; quia enim vult, ideo facit. Ratio ergo communicandi venit ex voluntate et bonitate, sicut ratio cognoscendi ab exemplari et intelligentia. Quia igitur ex conversione voluntatis supra suam bonitatem nos diligit[^24], ideo se fruendo nos diligit.

4. *Ad illud* quod obiicitur de virtute, quod virtus est bonum honestum; dicendum, quod bonum honestum dicitur dupliciter: aut quod est pure bonum, aut in quo relucet eius similitudo. Primo modo honesto est fruendum, proprie accepto frui, quia hoc solum terminat et quietat. Secundo modo non, nisi communiter accipiatur, prout dicit delectationem.

<!-- page 42 -->

Huiusmodi enim[^25] propter assimilationem ad Deum habent pulcritudinem, qua nos delectant et alliciunt; tamen in ipsis non est quiescendum, quia tunc amittunt pulcritudinem, quia «virtutes, cum ad se referuntur, superbae sunt et inflatae[^26]».

5. *Ad illud* quod obiicitur de beatitudine; dicendum, quod beatitudo creata non finit appetitum per se, sed per coniunctionem cum increata: unde anima ipsam[^27] diligit propter Deum, non propter se.
questions.english:
### Question II. *Whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed.*

Lastly it is asked whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed; and that it is so, seems [evident].

**Foundations.**

1. That alone is to be enjoyed which is to be loved for its own sake; but that alone[^1] is to be loved for its own sake which is good for its own sake; and that is good for its own sake which neither has from another the goodness it has, nor is that goodness *in relation to anything else*; but this is God alone: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, that alone is to be enjoyed which quiets the appetite of the soul; but the soul's appetite is not sufficiently quieted save in that which is a more perfect and greater good than itself; but this is God alone: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, the appetite is not sufficiently quieted save through something which fills the soul, since the soul fails in rest on that side on which it fails in fullness; but [the soul][^2] is capable of God according to appetite: therefore, if every created thing is infinitely less than that [God], no [created thing] supplies the soul's appetite. And this is what Augustine[^3] says: «Nothing less than the Trinity can fill a soul that is capable of the whole Trinity».

4. Likewise, the good which can be thought can be desired: therefore, if a greater good than some [given good] can be thought, a greater than that can be desired; but a greater than every finite [good] can be thought: therefore a greater can be desired: therefore no finite [thing] sufficiently terminates the soul's appetite: therefore the only infinite good, which is God, is to be enjoyed, which once possessed, nothing further can be thought or desired.

**On the contrary:**

1. It seems that the created good may be enjoyed, since although the appetite of matter is infinite, yet through a created incorruptible form[^4] it is sufficiently terminated: therefore similarly it seems that there is some created good which sufficiently terminates the soul's appetite; but every such [good] is to be enjoyed: therefore some created good is to be enjoyed.

2. Likewise, the human appetite is of finite capacity; therefore it does not grasp save the finite, or if it grasps the infinite, it grasps finitely; therefore if it is terminated by that which it grasps, it is terminated by a finite good: therefore it seems that some finite good is to be enjoyed.

3. Likewise, specially it seems that the human being is to be enjoyed, since that is to be enjoyed by which God enjoys; but God enjoys the human being, since he loves the human being; but with that love with which he loves himself, he loves the human being, since there is not in him[^5] a twofold love; but the first is of enjoyment: therefore also the second.

4. Likewise, specially it seems concerning virtue; since that is to be enjoyed which is to be desired for its own sake; this is manifest per se; but every honorable good is to be desired for its own sake, «since the honorable is what by its own force draws us and by its own dignity attracts us», as Tully[^6] says, and Augustine divides the honorable against the useful; but virtue falls in the genus of the honorable: therefore virtue is to be enjoyed.

5. Likewise, specially it seems concerning beatitude. That is to be enjoyed by the possession of which the mind rests and is delighted, and can seek nothing further; but created beatitude is of this kind: therefore, etc.

### Conclusio.

> God alone is properly to be enjoyed; it is improperly permitted to enjoy spiritual goods, which delight and are conjoined to the end.

**I respond:** It must be said that God alone is to be enjoyed, taking "to enjoy" properly, insofar as it expresses a motion with delight and quieting. But, taking "to enjoy" commonly, insofar as it expresses a motion with delight only[^7], a human being can not unfittingly enjoy all things which spiritually delight and are conjoined to the end—of which kind are the fruits, gifts, and beatitudes; but in the first mode [he can enjoy] God alone.

And the reason for this is that nothing can sufficiently terminate the soul except the good for which it exists[^8]. But this is the highest good, which is above the soul, and the infinite good, which exceeds the powers of the soul. For the soul's natural cognition[^9] is a cognition not constrained; whence it is born in a certain way to cognize all things, whence its cognition is not filled by any cognoscible save what has in itself all cognoscibles and by which once cognized all things are cognized. Likewise its affection is born to love every good; therefore the affection is not sufficiently terminated by any good save by that which[^10] is the good of every good and which is "all in all".

Of which good [it is said] in Exodus the thirty-third[^11]: *I will show thee every good*. But this is the highest good: therefore, etc.

Likewise[^12], nothing sufficiently terminates the soul save the infinite good, because for it to be terminated, it is necessary that it be terminated according to estimation; otherwise it would not be blessed, unless it esteemed itself blessed. But estimation transcends every finite [thing], since something greater than every finite [thing] can be thought: therefore, since affection can[^13] extend itself where also estimation [extends], necessarily the soul's affection transcends every finite [thing]; and if this, [it is] not sufficiently terminated by any finite good. Therefore God alone is to be enjoyed, since [he is] the highest and infinite good.

And not only is God to be enjoyed on account of perfect termination, but also on account of perfect delight. For to delight there concurs[^14] the delightable and the conjunction of it with that which is delighted. But everything which delights the soul delights under the account of good and beautiful; and since God alone is goodness and beauty itself[^15], therefore in God alone is there perfect delight.

Likewise, because there is conjunction; but God alone is the one who is most perfectly conjoined. For he is conjoined according to[^16] truth and intimacy. For God alone, on account of supreme simplicity and spirituality, glides into the soul, so that according to truth he is in the soul and more intimate to the soul than [the soul] itself is to itself.

For all[^17] these four reasons reduce to one, namely to this: that since the soul is born to perceive the infinite good, which is God, therefore in him alone it ought to rest and enjoy him.

**To the arguments for the opposite side:**

1. *To that* which is objected concerning the appetite of matter; it must be said that the appetite of matter is ordered to form as to substantial perfection, out of which[^18] also matter becomes one [thing]; and therefore it is necessary that the form be of the same genus as the matter, nor is it altogether above matter: therefore every such form is finite. But such [a form], if it be incorruptible, on account of union[^19] constrains the appetite of matter and once constrained terminates it; whence it is not terminated in its [own] amplitude. But the appetite of the soul is not so constrained on account of union with the desirable, rather it is dilated; and therefore it is required that it be perfected by something altogether highest.

2. *To that* which is objected, that[^20] [the soul] does not grasp save finitely; it must be said that it grasps the infinite good finitely, since [the soul] itself is finite. But since that good is infinite, therefore by it [the soul] is wholly absorbed, so that its capacity is on every side terminated. Whence it will not so much rejoice, but, as Anselm[^21] says, *it will enter into the joy of the Lord*. For if it merely grasped and were not conquered and absorbed, the appetite could still rise up to grasp something further. It is therefore evident that, for the soul to be completed, although it has a finite capacity[^22], yet it is necessary that the infinite good be present.

3. *To that* which is objected concerning the human being; it must be said that God loves the human being, and the love of God is the love of enjoyment; yet he does not enjoy the human being, since by loving himself he loves the human being, that is, by enjoying himself he uses the human being. Which is evident thus: that God's love toward the creature is not affection, but [a] communication of effect[^23]. But communication, according to habitual account, is attended to according to goodness; since the good is what is born to communicate itself. According to actual account, however, it is attended to or regards the will; since because [God] wills, therefore he acts. Therefore the account of communicating comes from will and goodness, just as the account of cognizing [comes] from the exemplar and intelligence. Since therefore from the conversion of his will upon his own goodness he loves us[^24], therefore by enjoying himself he loves us.

4. *To that* which is objected concerning virtue, that virtue is an honorable good; it must be said that the honorable good is said in two ways: either as what is purely good, or as that in which its likeness shines forth. In the first mode the honorable is to be enjoyed, taking "to enjoy" properly, since this alone terminates and quiets. In the second mode not, unless it be taken commonly, insofar as it expresses delight.

For such [virtues][^25] on account of assimilation to God have beauty, by which they delight and attract us; nevertheless in them one is not to rest, since then they lose their beauty, since «the virtues, when they are referred to themselves, are proud and inflated[^26]».

5. *To that* which is objected concerning beatitude; it must be said that created beatitude does not terminate the appetite per se, but through conjunction with the uncreated: whence the soul loves it[^27] on account of God, not on account of itself.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Omnes antiqui doctores, excepto Durando, conveniunt in ea sententia, quod solo Deo obiective et materialiter sit fruendum, beatitudine vero creata sive beatitudine subiective sumta (ut moderni loquuntur), formaliter tantum. Seraphicus Doctor in solut. ad 5. iam reprobaverat Durandi (hic. q. 2.) singularem et falsam opinionem, quod actus mentis, quo Deus immediate attingitur, sit fruitionis obiectum immediatum, Deus vero eiusdem obiectum remotum.

**II.** Quomodo quis improprie frui possit virtutibus, magis explicatur II. Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 2. ad 3, ubi etiam exponitur, quomodo dona, fructus et beatitudines coniuncta sint fini, qui secundum Scripturam est caritas. — Valde notanda sunt profunda et copiosa argumenta, quibus Seraphicus probat, quod in Deo solo sit perfecta delectatio et quietatio, de quo etiam egregie loquitur II. Sent. d. 16. a. 1. q. 1. Cfr. etiam S. Thom. S. c. Gent. I. c. 43; III. c. 48. 50. — Quoad illapsum Dei in animam cfr. II. Sent. d. 8 p. II. a. 1. q. 2.

Quoad quaestionem principalem vide auctores in Scholio praecedenti.

---
questions.englishScholion:
**I.** All the ancient doctors, except Durandus, agree in this opinion: that God alone is to be enjoyed objectively and materially, but [that] in created beatitude—or in beatitude taken subjectively (as the moderns speak)—only formally. The Seraphic Doctor in the reply to the fifth [objection] had already rejected the singular and false opinion of Durandus (here, q. 2.), [namely] that the act of the mind by which God is immediately attained is the immediate object of enjoyment, while God is the remote object of the same.

**II.** How one can improperly enjoy the virtues is more fully explained in II Sent. d. 38. a. 1. q. 2. ad 3, where it is also expounded how the gifts, fruits, and beatitudes are conjoined to the end, which according to Scripture is charity. — The profound and copious arguments by which the Seraphic [Doctor] proves that in God alone is perfect delight and quieting are greatly to be noted, on which subject he also speaks excellently in II Sent. d. 16. a. 1. q. 1. Cfr. also S. Thom., S. c. Gent. I. c. 43; III. c. 48. 50. — As to the gliding-in of God into the soul, cfr. II Sent. d. 8 p. II. a. 1. q. 2.

As to the principal question, see the authors in the preceding Scholion.

---

apparatus.la: Ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1 adiecimus *solum*, quod male abest a Vat. et recentiore cod. cc. — De hac propositione minore argum. cfr. Aristot., VIII. *Ethic.* c. 5: *Quod enim absolute bonum ac iucundum est, amabile est atque eligibile; unicuique vero quod unicuique est tale.* Cfr. etiam I. *Ethic.* c. 1. 2. et 8, ubi de ultimo fine; et I. *Magnor. Moral.* c. 2, ubi de bono in communi agitur.
apparatus.en: From the older manuscripts and ed. 1 we have added *solum*, which is wrongly absent from the Vatican [edition] and from the more recent cod. cc. — On this minor proposition of the argument, cfr. Aristotle, *Ethics* VIII, c. 5: *For what is good and pleasant in an absolute sense is lovable and choiceworthy; but to each one, what is such for each one.* Cfr. also *Ethics* I, c. 1, 2, and 8, where the ultimate end is discussed; and *Magna Moralia* I, c. 2, where the good in general is treated.

apparatus.la: Supple cum cod. I *anima*. Paulo infra fide codd. cum ed. 1 post *nullum* expunximus *creatum*; cod. W ponit *implet* pro *supplet*.
apparatus.en: Supply *anima* (soul) with cod. I. A little below, on the authority of the manuscripts with ed. 1, after *nullum* we have removed *creatum*; cod. W has *implet* for *supplet*.

apparatus.la: Potius auctor libri *de Spiritu et anima*, c. 27, ubi sic habetur: *Animam tamen hominis, id est mentem, nulla creatura iuxta substantiam implere potest, nisi sola Trinitas.* Et paulo inferius: *Solius enim Trinitatis est intrare et implere naturam sive substantiam, quam creavit.*
apparatus.en: Rather, the author of the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*, c. 27, where it is so stated: *Yet the soul of man, that is, the mind, no creature can fill according to substance, save the Trinity alone.* And a little below: *For it belongs to the Trinity alone to enter and fill the nature or substance which it has created.*

apparatus.la: Vat. et cod. K *creatam corporalem et incorruptibilem*; omnes fere codd. omittunt *corporalem et*; melioris notae codd. ut FGHTW aa bb ee ff et ed. 1 retinent solummodo *incorruptibilem*; alii ut A habent *incorporalem*; solummodo V *corporalem*, X *corruptibilem*; edd. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 *incorporalem et incorruptibilem*. Praeter auctoritatem codd. pro nostra lectione facit eiusdem convenientia tum cum solutione huius obiectionis, tum cum doctrina nostri Doctoris. Intelligi enim potest assertio hic posita tum de caelo empyreo, sicut cod. aa intelligit, addendo: *ut patet in corporibus caelestibus*, tum de ipsa anima, quae iuxta Seraphicum, licet sit spiritualis et incorporea, non omnino expers est compositionis ex forma et materia; et II. Sent. d. 19. a. 1. q. 1. in corp. explicite de ipsa affirmatur, quod appetitum materiae perfecte satiet et quietet. Quoad caelum empyreum Scholastici iuxta Aristotelem communiter asserebant, ipsum esse et incorruptibile et immobile. Cfr. II. Sent. d. 12. a. 2. q. 1. et d. 14. p. I. a. 3. q. 1. et III. Sent. d. 13. a. 1. q. 3. ad 6. — Mox cod. T *finiat* loco *finiet*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican [ed.] and cod. K read *creatam corporalem et incorruptibilem* (created, corporeal, and incorruptible); almost all manuscripts omit *corporalem et*; manuscripts of better repute such as FGHTW aa bb ee ff and ed. 1 retain only *incorruptibilem*; others such as A have *incorporalem*; only V has *corporalem*, X *corruptibilem*; edd. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 *incorporalem et incorruptibilem*. Besides the authority of the manuscripts, our reading is supported by its agreement both with the solution of this objection and with the doctrine of our Doctor. For the assertion posited here can be understood both of the empyrean heaven, as cod. aa understands it, adding: *as is evident in the celestial bodies*, and of the soul itself, which according to the Seraphic [Doctor], although it is spiritual and incorporeal, is not wholly exempt from composition of form and matter; and in II Sent. d. 19. a. 1. q. 1. in the body, it is explicitly affirmed of [the soul] that it perfectly satisfies and quiets the appetite of matter. As to the empyrean heaven, the Scholastics following Aristotle commonly asserted it to be both incorruptible and immobile. Cfr. II Sent. d. 12. a. 2. q. 1. and d. 14. p. I. a. 3. q. 1. and III Sent. d. 13. a. 1. q. 3. ad 6. — Soon after, cod. T reads *finiat* in place of *finiet*.

apparatus.la: Cod. K *Deo* pro *eo*.
apparatus.en: Cod. K reads *Deo* (God) for *eo* (him).

apparatus.la: Libr. II. *Rhetor.* c. 53. (ed. Taurin. 1823): *Nam (honestum) est quiddam, quod sua vi nos allicit ad se, non emolumento captans aliquo, sed trahens sua dignitate.* — De divisione boni, quae ex August. affertur, vide ipsius lib. 83 Qq. q. 30. — Immediate post mendum Vat. *dividitur* loco *dividit* castigamus ex mss. et primis edd.
apparatus.en: *Rhetoric* II, c. 53 (Turin ed. 1823): *For (the honorable) is something which by its own force allures us to itself, capturing not by any gain, but drawing by its own dignity.* — On the division of the good which is adduced from Augustine, see his book *83 Questions*, q. 30. — Immediately after, we correct the Vatican [ed.]'s mistake *dividitur* in place of *dividit* from the manuscripts and the earliest editions.

apparatus.la: Cod. K hic addit *sic*. Mox multi codd. ut AFGHKWXYZ ee etc. cum ed. 1 pro *fini* habent *frui*.
apparatus.en: Cod. K here adds *sic* (thus). Soon after, many manuscripts such as AFGHKWXYZ ee etc. with ed. 1 have *frui* (to enjoy) for *fini* (to the end).

apparatus.la: Vat. addit *creata*, quod tamen deest in mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: The Vatican [ed.] adds *creata* (created), which however is absent from the manuscripts and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: *Naturalis* refertur ad *cognitio*, ita ut sensus sit: *Si inspicias naturam cognitionis, quae animae competit, ipsa non est arctata.* — Vat., contradicentibus mss. et ed. 1, *rationalis* loco *naturalis*, sed non ita bene. — De propositione, quae deinde sequitur, vide Aristot., III. *de Anima*, text. 4. in q. praeced. cit.
apparatus.en: *Naturalis* refers to *cognitio*, so that the sense is: *If you inspect the nature of the cognition which belongs to the soul, it is not constrained.* — The Vatican [ed.], against the manuscripts and ed. 1, has *rationalis* in place of *naturalis*, but not so well. — On the proposition which then follows, see Aristotle, *On the Soul* III, text 4, cited in the preceding question.

apparatus.la: Cod. K adiungit *per illud*, quae additio videtur adiuncta, quia supplendum est *eo* sive *illo*.
apparatus.en: Cod. K adds *per illud* (through that), which addition seems adjoined, since *eo* or *illo* must be supplied.

apparatus.la: Vers. 19.
apparatus.en: [Exodus 33,] verse 19.

apparatus.la: Vat. contra fere omnes mss.: *Similiter* pro *Item* et paulo post ter *existimatio* loco *aestimatio*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican [ed.], against nearly all the manuscripts: *Similiter* (likewise) for *Item* (likewise) and a little after, three times, *existimatio* for *aestimatio*.

apparatus.la: Vat. contra codd. A T aa bb etc. *posset*, sed minus apte, quia agitur hic de naturali consecutione, quae subiecto semper inest. Hinc et immediate post Vat., obnitente maiore parte mss. ut AGKLOTVWXYZ etc. et ed. 1, minus bene *extendere eo, ubi est existimatio*. Cod. cc. *ut* loco *ubi*. Paulo infra auctoritate plurimorum codd. ut ACFGHKLOSTUVWZ etc. cum ed. 1 post *et si* substituimus *hoc* pro *haec*. Cod. K planius *et si hoc, ergo*.
apparatus.en: The Vatican [ed.], against codd. A T aa bb etc., has *posset* (it could), but less fittingly, since the matter here concerns a natural consequence, which is always present in the subject. Hence also, immediately after, the Vatican [ed.], with the greater part of the manuscripts such as AGKLOTVWXYZ etc. and ed. 1 resisting, less well [reads] *extendere eo, ubi est existimatio*. Cod. cc has *ut* in place of *ubi*. A little below, on the authority of very many manuscripts such as ACFGHKLOSTUVWZ etc. with ed. 1, after *et si* we have substituted *hoc* for *haec*. Cod. K more plainly: *et si hoc, ergo*.

apparatus.la: Ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1 substituimus *concurrit* loco *concernitur* et paulo post castigavimus mendum Vat., quae cum recentiore cod. cc habet *delectat* pro *delectatur*. — Cfr. supra a. 3. q. 1. arg. 1. ad opp.
apparatus.en: From the older manuscripts and ed. 1 we have substituted *concurrit* (concurs) in place of *concernitur* (is concerned) and a little after we have corrected the mistake of the Vatican [ed.], which together with the more recent cod. cc has *delectat* for *delectatur*. — Cfr. above, a. 3. q. 1. arg. 1. ad opp.

apparatus.la: Supplevimus ex mss. et ed. 1 *ipsa*, quod Vat. *omittit*.
apparatus.en: We have supplied from the manuscripts and ed. 1 the word *ipsa* (itself), which the Vatican [ed.] omits.

apparatus.la: Cod. W *per*.
apparatus.en: Cod. W reads *per* (through).

apparatus.la: Cod. R *autem*.
apparatus.en: Cod. R reads *autem* (however).

apparatus.la: Supple hic, sicuti et paulo infra, post *omnino* cum cod. T *forma*.
apparatus.en: Supply here, as also a little below, after *omnino* with cod. T the word *forma* (form).

apparatus.la: Multi codd. antiquiores et meliores ut ACFGLORSTUXYZ etc. ponunt *sibi* pro *sui*. Mox cod. T post *unde* falso omittit *non*. — Sententiam hic positam S. Doctor breviter complectitur III. Sent. d. 13. a. 1. q. 3. ad 6. his verbis: *Sicut dicimus de forma caeli, quod complet appetitum materiae, quia materia eius non appetit esse sub ulteriori forma, adeo forma ipsam statuit in actualitate completa.* Cfr. Scot., II *Phys.* q. 1. n. 1. et 15.
apparatus.en: Many of the older and better manuscripts such as ACFGLORSTUXYZ etc. read *sibi* (to itself) for *sui* (of itself). Soon after, cod. T after *unde* wrongly omits *non*. — The opinion here posited the Holy Doctor briefly summarizes in III Sent. d. 13. a. 1. q. 3. ad 6 in these words: *Just as we say of the form of the heaven that it fills the appetite of matter, since its matter does not desire to be under any further form, so the form establishes [the matter] itself in complete actuality.* Cfr. Scotus, *Physics* II, q. 1. n. 1 and 15.

apparatus.la: Subaudi cum cod. X *anima humana*. Mox cod. A post *bonum finite* addit *anima*.
apparatus.en: Understand with cod. X *anima humana* (the human soul). Soon after, cod. A after *bonum finite* adds *anima* (soul).

apparatus.la: *Proslog.* c. 26: «Non ergo totum illud gaudium intrabit in gaudentes, sed toti gaudentes intrabunt in gaudium». Alludit ad Matth. 25, 21. — Immediate post Vat. praeter fidem mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3 *totum* pro *tantum*.
apparatus.en: *Proslogion* c. 26: «Therefore not the whole of that joy shall enter into those who rejoice, but those who rejoice, wholly, shall enter into the joy». He alludes to Matthew 25,21. — Immediately after, the Vatican [ed.], contrary to the manuscripts and edd. 1, 2, 3, [reads] *totum* for *tantum*.

apparatus.la: Plures antiquiorum codd. ut ACGOSTUX bb ee ff cum ed. 1, sensu eodem remanente, *quamvis capacitate habeat finitatem, necesse est.*
apparatus.en: Several of the older manuscripts such as ACGOSTUX bb ee ff with ed. 1, the sense remaining the same, [read] *quamvis capacitate habeat finitatem, necesse est* (although it has finitude in capacity, it is necessary).

apparatus.la: Vat., quae habet *affectus*, emendatur ex mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3, 6.
apparatus.en: The Vatican [ed.], which has *affectus* (affection), is emended from the manuscripts and edd. 1, 2, 3, 6.

apparatus.la: Ed. 1 hic addit *Deus*, quod certe subaudiendum est.
apparatus.en: Ed. 1 here adds *Deus* (God), which certainly must be understood.

apparatus.la: Subaudi cum cod. R *virtutes*. Mox plures antiquiores codd. ut ACFGKLORSUYZ ee post *pulcritudinem* loco *qua* habent *quia*.
apparatus.en: Understand with cod. R *virtutes* (virtues). Soon after, several of the older manuscripts such as ACFGKLORSUYZ ee, after *pulcritudinem*, have *quia* in place of *qua*.

apparatus.la: August., XIX. *de Civ. Dei*, c. 25: *Virtutes, cum ad se ipsas referuntur nec propter aliud expetuntur, etiam tunc inflatae ac superbae sunt.*
apparatus.en: Augustine, *On the City of God* XIX, c. 25: *The virtues, when they are referred to themselves and not sought on account of something else, even then are inflated and proud.*

apparatus.la: Lapsum librariorum Vat. ponentium *ipsa* pro *ipsam* correximus ope mss. et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: A scribal slip of the Vatican [editors], who place *ipsa* for *ipsam*, we have corrected with the help of the manuscripts and ed. 1.

questions.latin:
<!-- page 42 -->

### DUBIA CIRCA LITTERAM MAGISTRI.

### Dub. I.

In parte ista circa litteram quaeruntur plura, et primo de hoc quod dicit: *Eorum vero quaedam sunt, quorum usus omnis est in significando, non in iustificando.* Sed contra: Omnia Sacramenta sunt medicinae, quia secundum Hugonem de sancto Victore[^1] *Sacramenta omni tempore fuerunt medicinae*; sed omnis medicina habet effectum in curando: ergo et Sacramenta similiter; sed ista curatio est iustificatio: ergo omni tempore Sacramenta habuerunt iustificare.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod dupliciter est considerare Sacramenta veteris Legis, scilicet in se sive ratione operis operati; et sic erant tantum ad significandum; vel ratione fidei annexae sive caritatis sive ratione operis operantis; et sic erant ad iustificandum Sacramenta legalia, praeter Circumci\[sionem\][^2].

### Dub. II.

*Omne igitur signum res est aliqua.* Opponitur de ista divisione. Videtur enim Magister male dividere, quia superius non dividitur contra suum inferius; sed res est superius ad signum: ergo etc.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod verum est, quod superius in sua generalitate acceptum non dividitur contra suum inferius; sed contractum[^3] bene potest dividi. Hic autem res[^4] contrahitur ad standum pro re non significante.

### Dub. III.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit Magister: *Non autem e converso omnis res signum.* Videtur enim male dicere, quia signum est quod ducit in aliud cognoscendum; sed omnis res ducit in aliud, quia omnis res est causa, vel effectus. Causa autem ducit in cognitionem effectus[^5] et e converso. Si dicas, quod non omne, quod ducit, est signum, sed quod ducit in prius; tunc omnis creatura est signum, cum ducat in Deum.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod duplex est signum, scilicet naturale et institutum. De primo non intenditur hic, sed de secundo; unde non valet obiectio ad propositum, quoniam hic[^6] intenditur de signo ex institutione, sicut sunt signa vocalia et sacramentalia.

### Dub. IV.

Item videtur Magister male dicere in hoc quod dicit: *Primum de rebus, postea de signis.* Videtur enim dicere[^7] debuisse potius e converso, quia signum ducit in cognitionem rei: ergo prius esset agendum vel dicendum de signis quam de rebus.

<!-- page 43 -->

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod prior est cognitio signi quam rei, respectu cuius est signum; sed non oportet, quod omnis rei. Unde ipse primo agit de rebus, quarum sacramenta non sunt signa.

### Dub. V.

Item videtur, quod ista divisio rerum: *Aliae sunt quibus fruendum* etc., sit male assignata respectu divisi, quia divisum simplicius est dividentibus et dividentibus aliquid est[^8] commune; sed Deo nihil est simplicius nec est aliquid commune Deo et creaturae: ergo etc.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod est divisio unius communis secundum nomen tantum; et sic est divisio aequivoci; est alia divisio communis secundum nomen et rem; et haec est divisio univoci; est etiam tertia medio modo; et ista est analogi, ubi non est communitas secundum unitatem naturae[^9], sed secundum similitudinem proportionis; et haec communitas est rationis.

### Dub. VI.

Item videtur mala divisio quantum ad membra: videtur enim, quod tertium membrum sit superfluum. Omni enim re aut est utendum, aut fruendum: ergo tertium superfluit.

Item, sicut est res, quae fruitur et utitur, ita est res, qua fruendum est et utendum, ut Christus: ergo qua ratione ponitur[^10] tertium membrum, deberet poni quartum.

**Respondeo:** Omnis res, quae est natura aliqua, aut est finis; et sic est res, qua fruendum; aut deducens ad finem; et sic est res, qua utendum; aut ad finem perveniens; et sic est res, quae fruitur et utitur, ut homo: et sic accipiuntur membra. Et est ista divisio satis conveniens huic scientiae, quia cum theologia sit de Creatore et de creaturis, utile est, ut theologus doceat, quomodo homo per alias res tendat in Deum.

### Dub. VII.

Item opponitur de hoc quod dicit: *Res, quibus fruendum*; quia si[^11] tres sunt res per se et non per accidens, et a diversitate rerum est diversitas sive multiplicitas fruitionis: ergo sicut sunt tres res, sic erunt tres fruitiones.

Item, tres articuli sunt, quia[^12] de tribus personis: ergo a simili et tres fruitiones.

**Respondeo:** Quod res accipitur hic communiter ad essentiam et personam propter sui generalitatem; et quia sumtum[^13] est hoc vocabulum *res* ab actu animae, ideo tres dicuntur res, quia tres personae, sed tamen una res, quia una bonitas est in eis. Quia ergo una bonitas, ideo et una fruitio, quamvis tres res. — Et quoniam articulus dicit quid a parte animae distinguentis, scilicet intellectus, et fruitio respicit ipsam[^14] divinam essentiam et bonitatem et unionem affectus communiter, ideo fruitio est una.

### Dub. VIII.

Item obiicitur de hoc quod dicit: *Omnis, qui fruitur, utitur*; quia videtur falsum, quoniam stulti[^15] homines similiter et bestiae fruuntur, quia propter se delectantur in delectabili, sed non utuntur. Si dicas, quod dicitur translative; quare non similiter transfertur verbum *utendi*?

**Respondeo:** *Uti* importat libertatem in sua generali acceptione, in speciali importat libertatem cum relatione ad aliud; *frui* importat libertatem cum delectatione; et licet nec libertas nec collatio[^16] conveniat brutis, convenit eis tamen delectatio. Ideo *uti* nullo modo convenit brutis; *frui* autem convenit eis aliquo modo, licet improprie[^17].

### Dub. IX.

Item videtur male dicere, quod in homine spes ponenda non est, quia[^18] de beata Virgine cantatur *Vita, dulcedo et spes* ab Ecclesia, quae non errat.

<!-- page 44 -->

Item, Ionae primo[^19]: *Accessit ad eum gubernator*; Glossa: « Naturale est homini magis de aliis quam de se in periculis confidere ».

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod sperare de aliquo est dupliciter, aut sicut de adiutore, aut sicut de salvatore. Prima spes potest esse in homine, secunda non. — Vel est sperare finale praemium; et hoc debet esse tantum in Deo; vel temporale beneficium; et hoc potest esse in homine. Primum si ponitur[^20] in homine, meretur maledictionem, secundum non.

### Dub. X.

Item quaeritur, quare dicit de homine: *Itaque frater, ego fruar te in Domino*, magis quam de asino vel de alia creatura, cum in omnibus creaturis reluceat vestigium divinae bonitatis.

**Respondeo:** Quod dicatur[^21] aliquis aliquo frui in Deo, non facit repraesentatio, sed magis inhabitatio. Unde conversa est propria, videlicet haec: *Ego fruar Domino in te*, dum per opera sciam, Deum habitare in te; et est figurativa locutio.

### Dub. XI.

Item quaeritur de hac solutione Augustini, qua solvit auctoritatem praedictam per illam determinationem *in Domino*. Sed Ecclesiastici octavo[^22] simpliciter dicitur: *Fruere magnatis*. Item, Deuteronomii vigesimo octavo[^23]: *Filios generabis et filias, et non frueris eis*; ex hoc implicat, quod, si non peccarent, fruerentur.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod praedicta solutio non est generalis, sed solum ad propositam auctoritatem. Et ideo recurrendum est ad solutionem praedictam extra litteram in quaestionibus[^24], quod, cum *frui* accipiatur communiter et proprie, in praedictis locutionibus accipitur communiter tantum.

### Dub. XII.

Item non videtur valere quod dicit Magister: *Si enim nec fruitur, nec utitur* etc., quia Deus diligit se, non tamen utitur, quia non diligit se propter aliud; nec fruitur, quia ubi fruitio, ibi est inhaerentia et indigentia, ut dicit Augustinus[^25]; Deus autem utroque caret etc.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod fruitio de sui generali ratione dicit amoris unionem, scilicet fruibilis cum fruente. Quoniam igitur contingit aliquid uniri sibi et alii, contingit non tantum frui alio, sed etiam se ipso; sed ubi est unio ad alterum, ibi est dependentia, inhaerentia et indigentia; ubi vero ad se ipsum, si ipsum est summum bonum, ibi[^26] non est inhaerentia nec dependentia vel indigentia, sed omnimoda sufficientia. Si vero ipsum bonum deficiens est, indiget; et inde est, quod solus Deus se ipso perfecte fruitur, nihil autem aliud ab ipso potest perfecte se ipso frui. Solus enim Deus est summum bonum et diligit se fruendo se, diligit etiam alia fruendo se: et ita nec fruitio Dei nec usus est cum indigentia, sicut nostra fruitio et usus.

### Dub. XIII.

Item obiicitur de hoc quod dicit: *Quia bonus est, sumus*: ergo quia ab aeterno bonus est, ab aeterno sumus.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum breviter, quod hoc est, quia *bonus* dicit causam[^27]. Sed est causa naturalis et necessaria, et causa voluntaria. Bonitas autem divina est causa nostri esse et boni esse per modum voluntatis, non naturae; haec autem causa non ponit effectum statim, cum est.

### Dub. XIV.

Item, adhuc obiicitur, quare similiter non sequitur: quia iustus est, iusti sumus[^28]? Si dicas, quod iustitia non est eius dispositio in quantum causa; contra: sapientia est dispositio Dei in quantum causa: ergo pari ratione, quia sapiens est, sapientes sumus. Si tu dicas, quod non est dispositio immediata, sicut bonitas; obiicitur de voluntate, quae est immediatissima, et tamen non sequitur: quia volens est, volentes sumus.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod ratio huius consequentiae triplex est. Una est, quia bonitas est conditio causae in quantum causa; secunda est, quia

<!-- page 45 -->

est proxima ad actum[^29]; tertia, quia dispositio generalis, in qua consistit vestigii ratio; dicit enim respectum ad finem. Unde sicut Deus unus imprimit unitatem, ita bonus bonitatem.

### Dub. XV.

Item obiicitur de hoc quod dicitur: *Ut scilicet ametur propter se ipsam tantum*, quia sicut *per se* ad *per accidens*, ita *propter se* ad *propter aliud*. Sed nihil, quod convenit alicui per accidens, convenit per se: ergo nihil, quod convenit alicui propter aliud, convenit propter se. Si ergo virtutes sunt appetendae propter aliud, non ergo propter se.

**Respondeo:** Sicut dicit Philosophus[^30], « Idem est finis et propter quod ». Finis autem dupliciter est: uno modo finis ultimus, qui propriissime est finis, in quo est status; alio modo finis sub fine, qui[^31] dicitur proprie terminus. Sic et *propter quod* diversificatur; unde uno modo excludit finem, alio modo non, ut dicit Magister.

Quod ergo obiicitur de *per se*; dico, quod, sicut *per se* uno modo opponitur ei quod est *per aliud* — et sic idem est *per se* et *secundum quod ipsum*, sive primum universale[^32] — alio modo opponitur ei quod est *per accidens*: sic et *propter se* dupliciter accipitur. Uno modo opponitur ei quod est *propter aliud*, alio modo ei quod est *per accidens*, quia[^33] ad illud accidentaliter ordinatur. Secundum hoc distinguit Magister *propter se*, et consequenter *honestum* sive *fruibile*, et ipsam denique fruitionem[^34].

### Dub. XVI.

Item obiicitur de hoc quod dicit: *Et quaedam sunt res, per quas fruimur, ut virtutes.* Videtur quod solis potentiis possit frui anima[^35]. Sine omni enim virtute potest frui bono creato; ergo cum magis sit fruibile bonum increatum, et anima magis ad hoc nata est, poterit eo frui solis potentiis.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod summum bonum est quod supra nos est; ad hoc ergo, quod illi uniamur, necessario intervenit duplex medium: medium unum, per quod anima nata est uniri alii a se diverso; et hoc est potentia; aliud speciale[^36] supra hoc, quod ipsam sublevet; et hoc est virtus. Quod obiicitur non est simile, quia potentia per se potest deficere et inclinari, sed non per se elevari[^37].
