apparatus.la: Aliqui codd. cum ed. 1 interserunt *esse.*
apparatus.en: Some codices, with ed. 1, insert *esse.*

apparatus.la: Vers. 1: *Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est et cum illo fuit semper et est ante aevum.* — In sequente propositione ex cod. cc et ed. 1 supplevimus verba *si ante aevum dicit quid increatum*, quibus additis argumentatio redditur planior et magis congruit Alex. Hal., S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 1. arg. 1.
apparatus.en: Verse 1: *All wisdom is from the Lord God and was always with Him and is before the ages.* — In the following proposition, from codex cc and ed. 1 we have supplied the words *if "before the ages" signifies something uncreated*, with which added the argument is rendered plainer and agrees better with Alexander of Hales, S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 1, arg. 1.

apparatus.la: Libr. III. Metro 9. — Paulo inferius codd. P Q *exit ab aliquo* pro *exit ab alio.*
apparatus.en: Book III, metre 9. — A little below, codices P Q [read] *goes forth from something* for *goes forth from another.*
Chapter 10, § 3.

apparatus.la: Plures codd. ut F L U cc et ed. 1 adiiciunt *secundum.* — De *maiori* cfr. Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 105. (c. 11.).
apparatus.en: Several codices, as F L U cc and ed. 1, add *according to.* — On the *major*, cf. Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 105 (c. 11).

apparatus.la: Cod. aa *limitatam habet mensuram*; in cod. F autem hic additur *propriam.*
apparatus.en: Codex aa [reads] *has a limited measure*; but in codex F there is here added *proper.*

apparatus.la: Quaest. 63 ad Oros. q. 40: *Movet itaque se ipsum sine tempore et loco, movet creatum spiritum sine loco temporaliter, movet creaturam corpoream temporaliter et localiter.* Cfr. VIII. de Gen. ad lit. c. 20. n. 39.
apparatus.en: Question 63 to Orosius, q. 40: *He therefore moves Himself without time and place, He moves the created spirit without place, temporally, He moves the corporeal creature temporally and locally.* Cf. *On Genesis to the Letter* VIII, c. 20, n. 39.

apparatus.la: Exposit. in c. 1. Gen., ubi etiam a Lyrano allegatur.
apparatus.en: Exposition on Genesis ch. 1, where it is also cited by [Nicholas of] Lyra.

apparatus.la: Vat. *maioris.* In multis mss. et ed. 1 omittitur particula *non.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition [reads] *of greater.* In many manuscripts and ed. 1 the particle *not* is omitted.

apparatus.la: Cod. O *sicut vult Philosophus*, qui IV. Phys. text. 134. (c. 14.) ait: *Dicitur autem recte, quod numerus quidem est idem ovium [versio Arabico-latina hominum] et canum, si aequalis uterque sit; denarius autem non idem, neque decem eadem.* Cfr. ibid. text. 132. — Vat. cum uno alteroque cod. post *mensurantur* adiungit *et numerantur.*
apparatus.en: Codex O [reads] *just as the Philosopher holds*, who in *Physics* IV, text 134 (c. 14) says: *But it is rightly said that the number is indeed the same of sheep [the Arabic-Latin version: of men] and of dogs, if each is equal; but ten is not the same, nor are ten [units] the same.* Cf. ibid., text 132. — The Vatican edition, with one or another codex, after *are measured* adds *and are numbered.*

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., de Praedicam. c. *de Quantitate*, ubi hae species enumerantur.
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, *Categories*, the chapter *On Quantity*, where these species are enumerated.

apparatus.la: Verba *ad primam partem* supplevimus fide cod. cc et ed. 1.
apparatus.en: The words *for the first part* we have supplied on the faith of codex cc and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 104. (c. 11.): «*Nunc* sequitur id quod fertur, ut tempus motum». Quae verba S. Thomas in Commentario super hunc locum (lect. 18.) ita exponit: «Sicut *tempus* ad motum (se habet), ita et *nunc* ad mobile... Ex hac autem consideratione de facili potest accipi intellectus aeternitatis. Ipsum enim *nunc*, in quantum respondet mobili se habenti aliter et aliter, discernit prius et posterius in tempore et suo fluxu tempus facit, sicut punctus lineam. Sublata igitur alia et alia dispositione a mobili, remanet substantia semper eodem modo se habens; unde intelligitur *nunc* ut semper stans, et non ut fluens nec habens prius et posterius». Secundum Fr. Gulielmum de Marra, II. Sent. d. 2. q. 1. propositio de substantia primi mobilis, quae modo sequitur, est Averrois (VIII. Metaph. text. 12. et I. de Caelo et mundo, text. 95.), qui etiam IV. Phys. text. 104. ait: *Instans quodammodo est quasi idem et nunquam transmutabile, et quodammodo est transmutabile et multiplicabile, et causa in hoc est, quia translatum est tale.* — Vat. contra fere omnes codd. et edd. 1, 2, 3 *Nunc aevi* pro *Nunc enim.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 104 (c. 11): «*The now* follows that which is carried along, as time [follows] motion». Which words St. Thomas, in his Commentary on this passage (lect. 18), expounds thus: «As *time* (is disposed) to motion, so too *the now* to the movable... And from this consideration the understanding of eternity can easily be grasped. For *the now* itself, insofar as it answers to the movable disposed otherwise and otherwise, discerns before and after in time and by its flux makes time, as a point [makes] a line. When, therefore, the one and the other disposition is removed from the movable, the substance remains, ever disposed in the same way; whence *the now* is understood as ever standing, and not as flowing nor as having before and after». According to Friar William of Marra, II Sent., d. 2, q. 1, the proposition concerning the substance of the first movable, which now follows, is Averroes' (*Metaphysics* VIII, text 12, and *On the Heavens and the World* I, text 95), who also in *Physics* IV, text 104 says: *The instant is in a way as it were the same and never transmutable, and in a way it is transmutable and multipliable, and the cause of this is that what is transferred is such.* — The Vatican edition, against almost all the codices and editions 1, 2, 3, [reads] *the now of the age* for *for the now.*

apparatus.la: Qui ideo ab Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 39. seqq. (c. 4.) definitur: *terminus corporis continentis.*
apparatus.en: Which therefore by Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 39 ff. (c. 4), is defined: *the limit of the containing body.*

apparatus.la: Quaest. 72: *An tempora aeterna aevum significavit, inter quod et tempus, hoc distat, quod illud stabile est, tempus autem mutabile?*
apparatus.en: Question 72: *Whether "eternal times" signified the age, between which and time this is the difference, that the former is stable, but time mutable?*

apparatus.la: Solummodo Vat. omittit *idem per essentiam.*
apparatus.en: Only the Vatican edition omits *the same by essence.*

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., I. de Caelo et mundo, text. 100. (c. 9.), ubi caelo et rebus caelestibus attribuit hoc nomen αἰών, quod diversimode vertitur: *aeternitas, sempiternitas, saeculum, aevum.* — Paulo superius Vat. *a tempore* pro *a corporalibus.*
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, *On the Heavens and the World* I, text 100 (c. 9), where he attributes to the heaven and to celestial things this name αἰών, which is variously rendered: *eternity, sempiternity, saeculum, the age.* — A little above, the Vatican edition [reads] *from time* for *from corporeal things.*

apparatus.la: Art. 2. q. 1. et 2.
apparatus.en: Article 2, q. 1 and 2.

apparatus.la: Quaest. 40. et 41, ubi affectionibus Angelorum assignat tempus tanquam mensuram earum. Cfr. supra argum. 1. ad opp. et eius solutio, una cum verbis Augustini, 83 Qq. q. 72, hic in corp. citatis.
apparatus.en: Questions 40 and 41, where he assigns time to the affections of the Angels as their measure. Cf. above, argument 1 to the contrary and its solution, together with the words of Augustine, *83 Questions*, q. 72, cited here in the body.

apparatus.la: Art. 2. q. 3.
apparatus.en: Article 2, q. 3.

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 115. seqq. (c. 12.), ubi ostendit, *in tempore esse* idem esse ac tempore mensurari, non autem idem esse *cum tempore esse*, sicut nec idem est *in loco esse* et *cum loco esse*, adeoque sempiterna, licet sint *cum tempore*, non esse in tempore. — Mox aliqui codd. cum edd. 2, 3, 4 in sensu obiectionis *mensurans* pro *non mensurans*, quod explicat Vat. ponendo *continens.* Paulo superius post *quamvis contineat* supplet cod. N *spiritualia.*
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 115 ff. (c. 12), where he shows that *to be in time* is the same as to be measured by time, but not the same as *to be with time*, just as neither is *to be in a place* the same as *to be with a place*, and so sempiternal things, although they are *with time*, are not in time. — Soon after, some codices with editions 2, 3, 4 [read], in the sense of the objection, *measuring* for *not measuring*, which the Vatican edition explains by putting *containing.* A little above, after *although it contains*, codex N supplies *spiritual things.*

apparatus.la: Huius sententiae videtur fuisse Alex. Hal., S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 1. ad 3. Cfr. infra q. 3. fund. 4. et in corp. — De *quantitate virtutis* I. Sent. d. 17. p. II. q. 1, d. 19. p. I. q. 2; infra d. 15. a. 1. q. 3.
apparatus.en: Of this opinion Alexander of Hales seems to have been, S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 1, ad 3. Cf. below, q. 3, fund. 4, and in the body. — On the *quantity of power*, I Sent., d. 17, p. II, q. 1, d. 19, p. I, q. 2; below, d. 15, a. 1, q. 3.

apparatus.la: Cod. aa *rationem assignare.* — Cfr. q. 3. fundam. 4.
apparatus.en: Codex aa [reads] *to assign the account.* — Cf. q. 3, fundamentum 4.

apparatus.la: Subaudi: *quantum ad esse substantiarum spiritualium.* Hinc cod. O mox perperam *indifferens* pro *differens.*
apparatus.en: Understand: *as to the being of spiritual substances.* Hence codex O soon after wrongly [reads] *indifferent* for *differing.*

apparatus.la: Guliel. de Mara (Marra) hic q. 1, ad eandem obiectionem respondet: *Dicendum, quod Philosophus non enumerat omnes species quantitatis in libro Praedicamentorum, sed tantum famosas, sicut ait Commentator (Averroes), V. Metaph. cap. de Quantitate (text. 18.), ubi ponit Philosophus, motum esse speciem quantitatis.*
apparatus.en: William of Mara (Marra) here, q. 1, to the same objection replies: *It must be said that the Philosopher does not enumerate all the species of quantity in the book of the Categories, but only the famous ones, as the Commentator (Averroes) says, Metaphysics V, the chapter on Quantity (text 18), where the Philosopher posits motion to be a species of quantity.* ---

questions.latin:
<!-- page 58 -->

### Quaestio II. *Utrum omnium aeviternorum sit unum aevum.*

Secundo quaeritur, utrum spiritualia habeant mensuram *unam* per essentiam; et hoc est quaerere, utrum sit *unum aevum* omnium aeviternorum. Et quod non, videtur.

1. Dionysius de Divinis Nominibus[^1]: «Ipse est aevum aevorum»: ergo plura sunt aeva: non per interruptionem, ita quod unum post aliud: ergo per diversitatem simul existentium.

2. Item, unitas accidentis venit ab unitate subiecti[^2]; sed non est ponere unum subiectum omnium aeviternorum, cum quaedam spiritualia non habeant aliquod commune, ad cuius aspectum mensurentur: ergo non est ponere, aevum esse unum. Quod autem nullum habeant tale subiectum, quod sit contentivum spiritualium, hoc apparet, quia illud haberet excellentiam et influentiam et continentiam respectu aeviternorum, sicut primum mobile respectu temporalium; sed tale respectu substantiarum spiritualium inveniri non potest, ut patet discurrenti per singula: ergo etc.

3. Item, omnibus aliis[^3] corruptis, possibile est unicum Angelum remanere, cum non dependeat ab aliis; et si remanet in *esse* completo, habet mensuram consequentem illud *esse*, et hoc est aevum: ergo remanet aevum, quolibet Angelo remanente, et totum remanet et perfectum: ergo quot sunt Angeli, tot sunt aeva.

4. Item, aevum est mensura rei perfectae et multum habentis de specie sive de forma: si ergo[^4] aevum maxime consequitur *esse* completum, cum illud non sit unum numero, sed tantum specie, videtur, quod aevum sit unum tantum secundum speciem.

**Contra hoc:**

1. Arguitur *a simili*. Sicut se habet tempus ad temporalia, ita aevum ad aeviterna; sed tempus est unum, quod mensurat omnia temporalia, sicut Anselmus[^5] dicit et Philosophus: ergo similiter unum est aevum, quod mensurat omnia aeviterna.

2. Item, hoc videtur *a minori*. Maior est varietas et difformitas in rebus mutabilibus quam in rebus immutabilibus: si ergo mutabilia omnia possunt unica mensura per essentiam mensurari, ergo multo fortius aeviterna.

3. Item, hoc videtur *a causa*. Positio enim multorum est, quare *tempus* unum potest esse: quia, quamvis sit accidens, tamen est mensura extrinseca, sicut locus, et quia non est accidens situale; sed hoc totum invenitur in *aevo*: ergo etc.

<!-- page 59 -->

4. Item, si plura sunt aeva, aut ergo *simul*, aut *consequenter*. Non *consequenter*, quia quodlibet sit infinitum a parte post; non *simul*, quia quae sunt simul, sunt in eodem instanti, ergo si aeviterna sunt simul, sunt in eodem *nunc* aevi: ergo si omnium aeviternorum est unum *nunc*, ergo unum *aevum* per essentiam.

### Conclusio

> Licet omnium temporalium sit unum tempus, tamen quot sunt aeviterna, tot sunt aeva.

**Respondeo:** Ad huius quaestionis intelligentiam praenotandum est, qualiter intelligitur unitas in *tempore*. Sciendum autem, quod tripliciter tentaverunt aliqui unitatem *temporis* accipere, secundum quod accidens habet tripliciter comparari ad subiectum. Habet enim ibi *causam*, *existentiam* et *apparentiam*.

Dixerunt ergo aliqui, quod tempus est unum ratione subiecti, in quo primo *est* et per se, quo remoto, removetur et tempus. Unde dixerunt, quod tempus est unum, quia est in primo mobili, cuius motu cessante, cessat et tempus[^6]. — Sed illud non sufficit dicere, quia, sicut dicit Augustinus, si cessaret motus primi mobilis, adhuc posset moveri rota figuli; et constat, quod mensuraretur ille motus: ergo non tantum est ibi, immo et in aliis rebus mobilibus. *Item*, tempus est in affectionibus et cogitationibus liberi arbitrii, quod non subest motui caelesti, sicut vult Augustinus[^7].

Et ideo dixerunt alii, quod tempus est unum ratione subiecti, in quo primo *apparet*. Cum enim tempus sit numerus sive mensura motuum, et numerus iste secundum *essentiam* et *habitum* sit in re mobili vel mota, in qua est prius et posterius, secundum *actualem* vero *numerationem* sit a parte animae, sicut vult Philosophus[^8] et Augustinus, cum anima omnes motus et mutationes numeret aspiciendo ad mensuram motus primi mobilis, scilicet per diem, annum et horam; voluerunt dicere, quod unum est tempus ratione subiecti, in quo primo apparet; quia, etsi omnia habeant proprias periodos, tamen omnia numerantur et mensurantur per mensuram motus regularis et certi et nobis notissimi, scilicet motus mobilis primi. — Sed illud non sufficit, quia dicit Philosophus de Caelo et mundo[^9], quod si essent duo mobilia prima, adhuc unum esset tempus. Tunc non posset dici unum ratione *subiecti*, in quo primo *esset*, nec in quo primo *appareret*, cum utrumque esset aeque primum et evidens; nec ratione *animae*, quia tempus non est numerus numerans, sed numeratus, ut Philosophus[^10] vult, et tempus est dispositio rei extra, non fictio animae.

Et ideo dixerunt tertii profundius, quod unitas temporis sumitur ab unitate subiecti, a quo *causatur*; subiectum autem, a quo causatur, est materia ut mutabilis, et ita ut ens in potentia. Nam materia, ut est in acquisitione formae, mutatur, et sic est ens in potentia; et ideo tempus maxime inter omnia accidentia se tenet plus cum materia. Sicut igitur materia una est per *essentiam*, differens per *esse*, una non unitate *universalitatis* nec *singularitatis*, sed *medio* modo, sic et tempus in omnibus temporalibus[^11].

*Et si quaeras*, unde est hoc, quod *tempus* est unum, cum tamen *motus* sint varii; dicendum, quod *motus* definitur per id ad quod est[^12], unde motus respicit motorem et mobile et terminum; *tempus* autem respicit ipsam durationem variam et successivam, quae venit ex potentia rei mobilis. Et quia motus naturae durantis consimilis est[^13], et natura una, supra quam fundatur, est una numero; ideo tempus non tantum est unum *specie* in omnibus temporalibus, immo etiam quantum ad *essentiam* unum *numero*, differens per *esse*, sicut posuerunt omnes sapientes, qui circa hanc materiam locuti sunt.

*Si autem quaeras*, quare non sic est in aliis *quantitatibus*[^14]; omnes respiciunt materiam; dicendum, quod omnes aliae, etsi *esse incompletum* habeant in materia — nam sunt in materia dimensiones infinitae — tamen *esse completum* ipsarum est a materia existente sub forma. Tempus autem habet *esse* ex hoc, quod materia tendit ad formam, propter hoc quod causatur a motu, qui est «entelechia existentis in potentia[^15]», et ideo tenet se maxime ex parte materiae, et ideo minime distinctum.

<!-- page 60 -->

Nec dico, quod tempus sit in ipsa materia, omni forma circumscripta, quia hoc esset contra Augustinum, duodecimo Confessionum[^16], quia non est vicissitudo aliqua in materia, nisi cum in ea est aliqua forma; sed quamvis sit in materia, quae est sub forma et ab ipsa causatur, magis tamen causatur a materia, ut tendit ad formam, et hoc est in materia ratione suae potentiae.

Secundum hunc triplicem modum nisi sunt aliqui qui unitatem in *aevo* ponere, primo ratione subiecti, in quo primo *est*. Posuerunt enim ordinem in intelligentiis secundum continentiam virtualem, sicut in visibilibus est reperire continentiam localem. Et sicut tempus in primo mobili fundatur, sic aevum[^17] in prima intelligentia, quae virtualiter alias continet, in alias influit. — Sed ista positio non potest stare. Primo, quia omnes intelligentiae in incorruptione habent aequalitatem, sicut in sequenti distinctione dicitur[^18]. Secundo, quia conservatio intelligentiarum immediate pendet ex Deo. Tertio, quia, si illa intelligentia destrueretur, tunc fundamentum aevi periret; et possibile fuit, illam peccasse, immo forte peccavit, cum diabolus credatur fuisse excellentissimus Angelorum[^19].

Et ideo alii conati sunt assignare unitatem ratione subiecti, in quo primo *apparet*, quod quidem est caelum empyreum, in quo non cadit variatio; immo omnimode quietum est[^20]. — Sed nec illud sufficit, quoniam immortalitas et immutabilitas per prius est in substantiis spiritualibus quam corporalibus, cum sint digniores; et dignius non habeat mensurari per aspectum ad minus dignum.

Et ideo tentaverunt alii accipere unitatem ex parte *causae*, qui dixerunt, quod duratio intelligentiarum continuatur et conservatur per *divinam* influentiam, quae quoniam una est, unum est aevum mensurans ipsam. — Sed nec illud potest stare, quoniam influentia illa aut *active*, aut *passive* intelligitur. Si de *activa*, non est aliud quam Deus, qui non habet aevum mensuram. Si de *passiva*, tot sunt aeva, quot sunt suscipientes.

Et ideo non restat alius modus nisi per unitatem *materiae*, sicut prius dictum est de tempore. Sed multi negant, intelligentias habere materiam, et ideo minime distinctum. Nec dico, quod tempus sit in ipsa materia, omni forma circumscripta, quia hoc esset contra Augustinum, duodecimo Confessionum, quia non est vicissitudo aliqua in materia, nisi cum in ea est aliqua forma; sed quidquid sit de hoc, tamen *aevum* respicit *esse actuale* et *esse stabile*, sed *tempus* materiam ut in *potentia*. Et ideo sicut unitas temporis conformatur materiae, sic unitas aevi conformatur formae, non inquam formae, in quantum haec vel illa, sed in quantum immutabilis.

Unde sicut linea in corporibus quantumcumque diversis ponitur eadem *specie*, sic aevum habet unitatem *universalis*, non unitatem, quam habet tempus.

Et sic concedendae sunt rationes probantes, non esse unum aevum aeviternorum, sed multa[^21].

1. Quod ergo obiicitur: sicut se habet tempus ad temporalia; dicendum, quod non est simile, quia cum *tempus*, quantum est de se, respiciat variationem et motum, consequitur ipsa, quorum est mensura, ratione illius principii[^22], per quod sunt entia in potentia; et quia illud unicum dicitur esse per essentiam, ideo et tempus. *Aevum* autem de sui ratione propria respicit *esse completum* et *stabile*, et ideo magis respicit formam: et ideo non habet unitatem nisi *universalitatis* sive conformitatis, sicut et alia accidentia.

2. Quod arguitur *a minori*, quod temporalia habent unam mensuram; iam patet[^23], quod non est locus *a minori*, quia illa variatio, ratione qua dicitur esse in potentia, respicit ipsum materiale principium, et ideo facit recedere a distinctione; non sic est in aevo.

3. Quod obiicitur, quod tempus est unum, quia est accidens extrinsecum, non situatum vel situale; dicendum, quod falsum est: ista enim non est causa, sed magis illa quae praedicta est.

4. Quod obiicitur: si sunt plura aeva, aut simul, aut non simul; dicendum, quod *simul*. — Quod ergo obiicitur: ergo in eodem *nunc*; dicendum, quod esse simul in duratione est dupliciter: aut per mensurae *concomitantiam*, aut per mensurae *unitatem* et indifferentiam. Cum autem dicitur Deus, homo et Angelus esse simul; dicendum, quod hoc dicitur per mensurae *concomitantiam*. Cum autem dicitur: Petrus et Paulus simul sunt vel currunt, hoc potest dici per mensurae *unitatem* et indifferentiam; et ideo non sequitur, quod si aeva aeviternorum sunt simul, quod sint unum.
questions.english:
### Question II. *Whether of all aeviternal things there is one age.*

Secondly it is asked whether spiritual things have *one* measure by essence; and this is to ask whether there is *one age* of all aeviternal things. And that there is not seems true.

1. Dionysius, *On the Divine Names*[^1]: «He is the age of ages»: therefore there are several ages: not by interruption, so that one [is] after another: therefore by the diversity of things existing simultaneously.

2. Likewise, the unity of an accident comes from the unity of the subject[^2]; but one cannot posit one subject of all aeviternal things, since certain spiritual things do not have anything in common at the regard of which they would be measured: therefore one cannot posit that the age is one. And that they have no such subject which would be containing of spiritual things, this appears, because that [subject] would have an excellence and an influence and a containment with respect to aeviternal things, just as the first movable [has] with respect to temporal things; but no such thing can be found with respect to spiritual substances, as is plain to one running through them singly: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, all other things being corrupted, it is possible for a single Angel to remain, since it does not depend on the others[^3]; and if it remains in complete *being*, it has a measure consequent upon that *being*, and this is the age: therefore the age remains, with any Angel whatever remaining, and it remains whole and perfect: therefore as many as the Angels are, so many are the ages.

4. Likewise, the age is the measure of a perfect thing and of one having much of species or of form: if therefore[^4] the age most of all follows complete *being*, since that is not one in number, but only in species, it seems that the age is one only according to species.

**Against this:**

1. It is argued *from a likeness*. As time stands to temporal things, so the age to aeviternal things; but time is one, which measures all temporal things, as Anselm[^5] says, and the Philosopher: therefore likewise the age is one, which measures all aeviternal things.

2. Likewise, this seems so *from the lesser*. There is greater variety and disformity in changeable things than in unchangeable things: if therefore all changeable things can be measured by a single measure by essence, then much more so aeviternal things.

3. Likewise, this seems so *from the cause*. For it is the position of many why *time* can be one: because, although it is an accident, it is nevertheless an extrinsic measure, like place, and because it is not a positional accident; but all this is found in *the age*: therefore, etc.

<!-- page 59 -->

4. Likewise, if there are several ages, then either *simultaneously* or *successively*. Not *successively*, because each would be infinite on the side of the after; not *simultaneously*, because things that are simultaneous are in the same instant, therefore if aeviternal things are simultaneous, they are in the same *now* of the age: therefore if of all aeviternal things there is one *now*, then one *age* by essence.

### Conclusio

> Although of all temporal things there is one time, nevertheless as many as the aeviternal things are, so many are the ages.

**I respond:** For the understanding of this question it must be premised how unity is understood in *time*. Now it must be known that in three ways some have attempted to take the unity of *time*, according as an accident can be compared in three ways to its subject. For it has there a *cause*, an *existence*, and an *appearance*.

Some, then, have said that time is one by reason of the subject in which it primarily and *per se is*, on the removal of which time too is removed. Whence they said that time is one because it is in the first movable, on whose motion ceasing, time too ceases[^6]. — But it does not suffice to say that, because, as Augustine says, if the motion of the first movable were to cease, a potter's wheel could still be moved; and it is evident that that motion would be measured: therefore it is not only there, but also in other movable things. *Likewise*, time is in the affections and thoughts of free choice, which is not subject to the celestial motion, as Augustine holds[^7].

And therefore others have said that time is one by reason of the subject in which it primarily *appears*. For since time is the number or measure of motions, and that number, according to *essence* and *habit*, is in the movable or moved thing, in which there is before and after, but according to *actual numbering* is on the part of the soul, as the Philosopher holds[^8] and Augustine — since the soul numbers all motions and changes by looking to the measure of the motion of the first movable, namely by day, year, and hour — they wished to say that time is one by reason of the subject in which it primarily appears; because, even if all things have their own periods, nevertheless all are numbered and measured by the measure of the regular and certain motion best known to us, namely the motion of the first movable. — But that does not suffice, because the Philosopher says, *On the Heavens and the World*[^9], that if there were two first movables, there would still be one time. Then it could not be called one by reason of the *subject* in which it primarily *was*, nor in which it primarily *appeared*, since each would be equally primary and evident; nor by reason of the *soul*, because time is not numbering number, but numbered, as the Philosopher[^10] holds, and time is a disposition of the thing outside, not a fiction of the soul.

And therefore a third group said more profoundly that the unity of time is taken from the unity of the subject by which it is *caused*; but the subject by which it is caused is matter as changeable, and so as a being in potency. For matter, as it is in the acquisition of form, is changed, and so is a being in potency; and therefore time, among all accidents, holds itself most with matter. As, therefore, matter is one by *essence*, differing by *being*, one not by the unity of *universality* nor of *singularity*, but in a *middle* way, so too time in all temporal things[^11].

*And if you ask* whence this is, that *time* is one, while yet *the motions* are various; it must be said that *motion* is defined by that to which it tends[^12], whence motion regards the mover and the movable and the terminus; but *time* regards the very duration, varied and successive, which comes from the potency of the movable thing. And because the motion of an enduring nature is alike[^13], and the one nature on which it is founded is one in number; therefore time is not only one in *species* in all temporal things, but even as to *essence* one in *number*, differing by *being*, as all the wise have held who have spoken about this matter.

*But if you ask* why it is not so in the other *quantities*[^14] — they all regard matter — it must be said that all the others, even if they have *incomplete being* in matter — for there are infinite dimensions in matter — nevertheless their *complete being* is from matter existing under form. But time has *being* from this, that matter tends toward form, on account of the fact that it is caused by motion, which is «the entelechy of what exists in potency[^15]», and therefore it holds itself most on the side of matter, and therefore is least distinct.

<!-- page 60 -->

Nor do I say that time is in matter itself, all form set aside, because this would be against Augustine, in the twelfth book of the *Confessions*[^16], since there is no vicissitude in matter except when there is some form in it; but although it is in matter, which is under form and is caused by it, it is nevertheless caused more by matter, as it tends toward form, and this is in matter by reason of its potency.

According to this threefold mode there were some who [tried] to posit the unity in *the age*, first by reason of the subject in which it primarily *is*. For they posited an order in the intelligences according to virtual containment, just as among visible things one finds local containment. And as time is founded in the first movable, so the age[^17] in the first intelligence, which virtually contains the others [and] flows into the others. — But this position cannot stand. First, because all the intelligences in incorruption have equality, as is said in the following distinction[^18]. Second, because the conservation of the intelligences depends immediately on God. Third, because, if that intelligence were destroyed, then the foundation of the age would perish; and it was possible for it to have sinned, indeed perhaps it did sin, since the devil is believed to have been the most excellent of the Angels[^19].

And therefore others tried to assign the unity by reason of the subject in which it primarily *appears*, which indeed is the empyrean heaven, in which no variation falls; rather it is wholly at rest[^20]. — But neither does that suffice, since immortality and immutability is prior in spiritual substances than in corporeal ones, since they are worthier; and the worthier should not be measured by regard to the less worthy.

And therefore others attempted to take the unity on the side of the *cause*, who said that the duration of the intelligences is continued and conserved by the *divine* influence, which, since it is one, the age measuring it is one. — But neither can that stand, since that influence is understood either *actively* or *passively*. If of the *active*, it is nothing other than God, who does not have the age as a measure. If of the *passive*, there are as many ages as there are receivers.

And therefore no other mode remains except by the unity of *matter*, as was said before about time. But many deny that the intelligences have matter, and therefore [it is] least distinct. Nor do I say that time is in matter itself, all form set aside, because this would be against Augustine, in the twelfth book of the *Confessions*, since there is no vicissitude in matter except when there is some form in it; but whatever may be the case concerning this, *the age* nevertheless regards *actual being* and *stable being*, but *time* [regards] matter as in *potency*. And therefore, just as the unity of time is conformed to matter, so the unity of the age is conformed to form — not, I say, to form insofar as it is this or that, but insofar as it is immutable.

Whence just as a line in bodies however diverse is posited as the same in *species*, so the age has the unity of a *universal*, not the unity which time has.

And thus the reasons proving that there is not one age of aeviternal things, but many, are to be conceded[^21].

1. As to what is objected, then: as time stands to temporal things; it must be said that it is not similar, because, since *time*, so far as it is of itself, regards variation and motion, it follows the very things of which it is the measure, by reason of that principle[^22] by which they are beings in potency; and because that single [principle] is said to be by essence, therefore time too [is one]. But *the age*, from its own proper account, regards *complete* and *stable being*, and therefore regards form more: and therefore it does not have unity except of *universality* or of conformity, like the other accidents.

2. As to what is argued *from the lesser*, that temporal things have one measure; it is already clear[^23] that there is no place for [an argument] *from the lesser*, because that variation, by reason of which it is said to be in potency, regards the material principle itself, and therefore makes [it] recede from distinction; it is not so in the age.

3. As to what is objected, that time is one because it is an extrinsic accident, not situated or positional; it must be said that it is false: for this is not the cause, but rather that which has been said before.

4. As to what is objected: if there are several ages, then either simultaneously or not simultaneously; it must be said *simultaneously*. — As to what is then objected: therefore in the same *now*; it must be said that to be simultaneous in duration is twofold: either by *concomitance* of measure, or by *unity* and indifference of measure. When it is said that God, man, and Angel are simultaneous, it must be said that this is said by *concomitance* of measure. But when it is said: Peter and Paul are or run simultaneously, this can be said by *unity* and indifference of measure; and therefore it does not follow that, if the ages of aeviternal things are simultaneous, they are one.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Hic agitur de unitate tum temporis, tum aevi, et non de unitate *specifica*, sed de unitate *secundum numerum*, ut pluries notatur in corp. — Loquendo de *tempore*, quatenus est *mensura* rei successivae et non eiusdem *intrinseca* duratio, communior sententia unitatem temporis affirmabat. In quo autem huiusmodi unitas *rationem* suam habeat, disputabatur.

<!-- page 61 -->

Tres opiniones hic recensitas affert etiam S. Thom. (hic q. 1. a. 2; S. I. q. 10. a. 6.), et ipse cum Richard. a Med. primam opinionem approbat, quae rationem unitatis ponit in unitate primi mobilis; tertia vero (quam praefert S. Bonav.), quae hanc unitatem repetit ab unitate subiecti, a quo *causatur*, quod est materia, iuxta eundem «non sufficiens videtur». Sententiae S. Thomae adhaeret B. Albert. (S. p. I. tr. 5. q. 23. m. 3. a. 2.), et quoad *perfectam* rationem temporis etiam Scotus, IV. Sent. d. 48. q. 2, et praecipue de Rerum princ. q. 20, in quo opere a quaestione 18. usque ad q. 24. de tempore et annexis quaestionibus diffuse et subtiliter disputat.

**II.** Quoad unitatem *aevi*, utrum sit admittenda, et quae sit eius ratio, maior fuit opinionum dissensus. Et praenotandum est, opinionem Aristotelis, quod etiam corpora caelestia, saltem primum mobile, inter incorruptibilia et aeviterna locum obtineant, illa aetate communiter receptam fuisse. S. Thom. in Commentar. et cum quadam restrictione etiam in Summa («concedimus ad praesens») docet, quod aevum «est unum ab unitate *esse* simplicissimi aeviternorum, quod est primus Angelus». Hanc sententiam aliquatenus approbat Richard. a Med. («quodam modo habet rationem mensurae, quamvis non plenam»). Sed Petr. a Tar. praefert opinionem secundam, «quod primum subiectum aevi est primum immobile, id est caelum empyreum». Etiam Alex. Hal. (S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 2.) unitatem aevi sustinet, et quoad *rationem* eius tertiae opinioni innititur. — E contrario S. Bonav. negat unitatem aevi et aevum ut mensuram *extrinsecam*. Si autem accipitur aevum pro mensura *intrinseca*, patet quod tot sunt admittenda aeva, quot aeviterna. Huic sententiae assentit etiam Aegid. R., et favet etiam Scotus, quia praefert opinionem, non esse unum aevum omnium aeviternorum ut mensura *extrinseca*, sicut est unum tempus omnium temporalium (hic q. 3. n. 5, q. 2. n. 10; Report. hic q. 1. n. 2, ubi dicit: «Mensurare Angelum inferiorem per *esse* Angeli superioris est aequivocare vocabulum ad mensuram perfectionis»). Tamen idem censet, etiam opinionem S. Thomae esse probabilem, si intelligitur de mensura *extrinseca*.

**III.** Praeter laudatos: B. Albert., S. p. I. tr. 5. q. 23. m. 2. a. 2. partic. 2. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2. a. 2. — Richard. a Med., hic a. 1. q. 3. — Aegid. R., hic q. 1. a. 1. — Durand., hic q. 3. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 2.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** Here the subject is the unity both of time and of the age, and not the *specific* unity, but the unity *according to number*, as is noted several times in the body. — Speaking of *time*, insofar as it is a *measure* of a successive thing and not the *intrinsic* duration of that thing, the more common opinion affirmed the unity of time. But in what this unity has its *ground* was disputed.

<!-- page 61 -->

The three opinions here reviewed are also reported by St. Thomas (here q. 1, a. 2; S. I, q. 10, a. 6), and he himself, with Richard of Middleton, approves the first opinion, which places the ground of the unity in the unity of the first movable; but the third (which St. Bonaventure prefers), which traces this unity back to the unity of the subject by which it is *caused*, which is matter, according to the same [Thomas] «seems insufficient». To the opinion of St. Thomas adheres Bl. Albert (S. p. I, tr. 5, q. 23, m. 3, a. 2), and as to the *perfect* account of time also Scotus, IV Sent., d. 48, q. 2, and especially *On the Principle of Things*, q. 20, in which work from question 18 to q. 24 he disputes about time and annexed questions diffusely and subtly.

**II.** As to the unity of *the age*, whether it is to be admitted, and what its ground is, there was greater dissension of opinions. And it must be premised that the opinion of Aristotle, that even the celestial bodies, at least the first movable, hold a place among incorruptible and aeviternal things, was commonly received in that age. St. Thomas, in the Commentary and, with a certain restriction, also in the Summa («we concede for the present»), teaches that the age «is one by the unity of the *being* of the simplest of aeviternal things, which is the first Angel». This opinion Richard of Middleton in some measure approves («it has in a certain way the account of a measure, though not a full one»). But Peter of Tarentaise prefers the second opinion, «that the first subject of the age is the first immobile [thing], that is, the empyrean heaven». Alexander of Hales too (S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 2) maintains the unity of the age, and as to its *ground* relies on the third opinion. — On the contrary, St. Bonaventure denies the unity of the age and the age as an *extrinsic* measure. But if the age is taken for an *intrinsic* measure, it is plain that as many ages are to be admitted as there are aeviternal things. To this opinion Giles of Rome also assents, and Scotus too favors it, because he prefers the opinion that there is not one age of all aeviternal things as an *extrinsic* measure, just as there is one time of all temporal things (here q. 3, n. 5, q. 2, n. 10; Reportatio, here q. 1, n. 2, where he says: «To measure a lower Angel by the *being* of a higher Angel is to equivocate the term as to a measure of perfection»). Yet the same [Scotus] judges that the opinion of St. Thomas also is probable, if it is understood of an *extrinsic* measure.

**III.** Besides those praised: Bl. Albert, S. p. I, tr. 5, q. 23, m. 2, a. 2, partic. 2. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 2, a. 2. — Richard of Middleton, here a. 1, q. 3. — Giles of Rome, here q. 1, a. 1. — Durandus, here q. 3. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 2.

---

apparatus.la: Cap. 5. § 5, et c. 10. § 3. in fine, ubi loquitur de Deo ut est origo et auctor omnis temporis et aevi.
apparatus.en: Chapter 5, § 5, and c. 10, § 3, at the end, where he speaks of God as the origin and author of all time and of the age.

apparatus.la: Aristot., I. Topic. c. 6. (c. 5.), de quo vide tom. I. pag. 511, nota 6. Cfr. etiam Boeth., de Unitate et Uno.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Topics* I, c. 6 (c. 5), on which see vol. I, p. 511, note 6. Cf. also Boethius, *On Unity and the One.*

apparatus.la: Cod. Q interserit *Angelis*, quod Vat. ponit inferius post *ab aliis.*
apparatus.en: Codex Q inserts *to the Angels*, which the Vatican edition places lower down, after *on the others.*

apparatus.la: Plurimi codd. minus congrue *enim.*
apparatus.en: Very many codices, less fittingly, [read] *for* (*enim*).

apparatus.la: Dialog. de Veritate, c. 13. in fine, ubi ad probandum quod veritas improprie dicatur huius vel illius rei, cum secundum illam sint, adducit simile de tempore: «Quemadmodum dicitur tempus huius vel illius rei, cum unum et idem sit tempus omnium, quae sunt in eodem tempore simul; et si non esset haec vel illa res, non minus esset idem tempus». Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 93. (c. 10.), contra opinionem Platonis, secundum quam tempus est motus totius caeli, et partes eius sunt partes temporis, arguit sic: «Si plures essent caeli, similiter utique esset tempus cuiuslibet ipsorum motus; quare multa tempora simul». Ex quibus verbis deducitur, iuxta mentem Aristotelis unum tantum esse tempus, etiamsi essent plures caeli. Cfr. etiam XII. Metaph. text. 49. (XI. c. 8.).
apparatus.en: *Dialogue on Truth*, c. 13, at the end, where, to prove that truth is improperly said [to be] of this or that thing, since they are according to it, he brings forward a likeness from time: «Just as the time of this or that thing is spoken of, although the time of all things that are simultaneously in the same time is one and the same; and if this or that thing did not exist, it would be no less the same time». Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 93 (c. 10), against the opinion of Plato, according to which time is the motion of the whole heaven, and its parts are parts of time, argues thus: «If there were several heavens, likewise there would be the time of the motion of any one of them; wherefore many times simultaneously». From which words it is deduced that, according to the mind of Aristotle, there is only one time, even if there were several heavens. Cf. also *Metaphysics* XII, text 49 (XI, c. 8).

apparatus.la: Cfr. Averroes, IV. Phys. text. 98. et 130, ubi dicit, tempus sequi motum corporis caelestis et primo inveniri in caelo. — Verba Augustini, quae mox allegantur, sumta sunt ex XI. Confess. c. 23. n. 29: *Audivi a quodam homine docto, quod solis et lunae ac siderum motus ipsa sunt tempora; et nil annui. Cur enim non potius omnium corporum motus sint tempora? An vero, si cessarent caeli lumina, et moveretur rota figuli, non esset tempus, quo metiremur eos gyros?* etc.
apparatus.en: Cf. Averroes, *Physics* IV, text 98 and 130, where he says that time follows the motion of the celestial body and is primarily found in the heaven. — The words of Augustine that are soon adduced are taken from *Confessions* XI, c. 23, n. 29: *I heard from a certain learned man that the motions of the sun and moon and stars are themselves the times; and I did not assent. For why are the motions of all bodies not rather the times? Or indeed, if the lights of heaven were to cease, and a potter's wheel were moved, would there not be a time by which we might measure its turns?* etc.

apparatus.la: Libr. XI. Confess. c. 27. n. 36; VIII. de Gen. ad lit. c. 20. 24. 26; Quaest. 65 ad Orosium, q. 41.
apparatus.en: *Confessions* XI, c. 27, n. 36; *On Genesis to the Letter* VIII, c. 20, 24, 26; *Questions to Orosius* 65, q. 41.

apparatus.la: Libr. IV. Phys. text. 100. seqq. et 130. seq. (c. 11. et 14.). — August., XI. Confess. c. 23. n. 30. seqq. et XII. de Civ. Dei, c. 15. n. 1. seq.
apparatus.en: *Physics* IV, text 100 ff. and 130 f. (c. 11 and 14). — Augustine, *Confessions* XI, c. 23, n. 30 ff., and *On the City of God* XII, c. 15, n. 1 f.

apparatus.la: In cod. T ad marg. a manu quasi suppari habetur: *Immo hoc dicit Philosophus quarto Physicorum (text. 93.); unde haec auctoritas male citatur hic.* Verba Aristotelis vide supra pag. 58, nota 5. — Paulo superius cod. cc et ed. 1 *recti* pro *certi.*
apparatus.en: In codex T, at the margin, by an almost contemporary hand, there stands: *Rather, the Philosopher says this in the fourth [book] of the Physics (text 93); whence this authority is wrongly cited here.* For the words of Aristotle see above, p. 58, note 5. — A little above, codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *right* (*recti*) for *certain* (*certi*).

apparatus.la: Libr. IV. Phys. text. 102. et 131. seq. (c. 11. et 14.).
apparatus.en: *Physics* IV, text 102 and 131 f. (c. 11 and 14).

apparatus.la: Cod. cc cum ed. 1 adiungit *est unum per essentiam*, differens per esse. Paulo superius plures codd. cum ed. 1 *universalis nec singularis* pro *universalitatis nec singularitatis.* — De unitate materiae cfr. d. 3. p. I. a. 1. q. 2. 3.
apparatus.en: Codex cc with ed. 1 adds *is one by essence*, differing by being. A little above, several codices with ed. 1 [read] *universal nor singular* for *of universality nor of singularity.* — On the unity of matter cf. d. 3, p. I, a. 1, q. 2, 3.

apparatus.la: Aristot., V. Phys. text. 4: *Magis autem ab eo in quod, quam ex quo movetur, denominatur mutatio.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* V, text 4: *But change is denominated more from that into which than from that out of which it is moved.*

apparatus.la: Vat. *Et quia tempus naturae duranti consimilius est;* collectioni etiam cod. bb concordat in verbis *naturae duranti.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition [reads] *And because time is more alike to an enduring nature;* codex bb too agrees with this collation in the words *to an enduring nature.*

apparatus.la: Quae supra q. 1. argum. ult. ad opp. enumeratae sunt.
apparatus.en: Which were enumerated above, q. 1, in the last argument to the contrary.

apparatus.la: Aristot., III. Phys. text. 6. (c. 1.). Cfr. supra pag. 34, nota 6.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* III, text 6 (c. 1). Cf. above, p. 34, note 6.

apparatus.la: Cap. 12. n. 15: *Duo reperio, quae fecisti carentia temporibus, cum tibi neutrum coaeternum sit. Unum, quod ita formatum est, ut sine ullo defectu contemplationis, sine ullo intervallo mutationis, quamvis mutabile, tamen non mutatum, tua aeternitate atque incommutabilitate perfruatur. Alterum, quod ita informe erat, ut ex qua forma in quam formam mutationis vel stationis mutaretur, quo tempori subderetur, non haberet.* — Aliquanto inferius Vat. *et sic est* pro *et hoc est.*
apparatus.en: Chapter 12, n. 15: *I find two things which Thou hast made lacking times, although neither is coeternal with Thee. One, which is so formed that, without any defect of contemplation, without any interval of change, although changeable, yet unchanged, it enjoys to the full Thy eternity and immutability. The other, which was so formless that it had not [the means] by which it might be changed from what form into what form of change or of rest, by which it might be subject to time.* — Somewhat lower the Vatican edition [reads] *and so it is* for *and this is.*

apparatus.la: Non pauci codd. supplent *est.*
apparatus.en: Not a few codices supply *is.*

apparatus.la: Dist. 3. p. I. a. 1. q. 2, et dub. 4.
apparatus.en: Distinction 3, p. I, a. 1, q. 2, and dub. 4.

apparatus.la: Cfr. infra d. 6. a. 1. q. 1.
apparatus.en: Cf. below, d. 6, a. 1, q. 1.

apparatus.la: Vide p. II. huius dist. a. 1. q. 1.
apparatus.en: See p. II of this distinction, a. 1, q. 1.

apparatus.la: Cod. cc, ed. 1 et Vat. adiungunt *sicut sunt plures formae.*
apparatus.en: Codex cc, ed. 1, and the Vatican edition add *just as there are several forms.*

apparatus.la: Scilicet *materiae*, quae per *essentiam* una dicitur, infra d. 3. p. I. a. 1. q. 2. 3.
apparatus.en: Namely, *of matter*, which is said to be one by *essence*, below, d. 3, p. I, a. 1, q. 2, 3.

apparatus.la: Ed. 1 cum cod. cc *patet responsio.* Dein non pauci codd. *quia* pro *quod.*
apparatus.en: Ed. 1 with codex cc [reads] *the response is clear.* Then not a few codices [read] *because* (*quia*) for *that* (*quod*). ---

questions.title: Dist. 2, Part 1, Art. 1, Q. 3
questions.titleLa: Utrum spiritualia habeant permanentem, vel successivam mensuram
questions.titleEn: Whether spiritual things have a permanent or a successive measure
questions.latin:
<!-- page 61 -->

### Quaestio III. *Utrum spiritualia habeant permanentem, vel successivam mensuram.*

Tertio quaeritur, utrum spiritualia habeant mensuram *permanentem*, aut *successivam*. Et quod *permanentem*, carentem priori et posteriori, videtur primo *auctoritate*, deinde *ratione*.

1. Et *auctoritate* sic: Augustinus duodecimo de Civitate Dei[^1]: «Immortalitas Angelorum non transit in tempore nec est praeterita, quasi iam non sit, nec futura, quasi nondum sit»: ergo tota est praesens, ergo permanens, non succedens.

2. Item, Augustinus undecimo Confessionum[^2]: «Si praesens tempus staret et non transiret in praeteritum, esset aeternitas»; sed non propter hoc esset aeternitas increata: ergo esset aeternitas creata; et hoc est aevum: ergo aevum habet *nunc* non transiens: ergo etc.

3. Item, Philosophus[^3]: «In perpetuis non differt *esse* et *posse*»: ergo potentia est in toto suo actu, ergo nihil exspectat, ergo totum simul: ergo nulla est ibi successio vel prioritas.

4. Item *ratione*: proprietas debet respondere substantiae, ergo substantiae simplicis mensura debet esse simplex; sed substantia spiritualis est simplex: ergo et eius mensura. Sed eius mensura est aevum: ergo simplex est: ergo non habet prius et posterius.

5. Item, omne successivum reducitur ad permanens, ergo prius et posterius successivum ad prius et posterius permanens[^4]; sed prius et posterius permanens est in sola magnitudine: ergo quod caret priori et posteriori permanente caret et successivo. Sed talis est Angelus: ergo etc.

6. Item, ubi est prius et posterius, ibi necessario cadit aliquid novum, quod de posteriori fit prius, et per hoc lapsus in *praeteritum*, et aliquid novum; sed in perpetuis non est aliqua mutatio[^5]: ergo nec successio.

7. Item, ubi est prius, ibi est aliqua exspectatio respectu eius quod posterius est et nondum habitum est; sed in Beatis perfecte nulla cadit exspectatio, quia evacuatur omnino fides et spes, et habetur omne quod habituri sunt[^6]: ergo nullo modo est ibi prius et posterius.

**Contra:**

1. Hieronymus ad Marcellam[^7]: «Tantum est, qui non novit *fuisse* vel *futurum*»: omnis ergo creatura in sui *esse* habet praeteritionem sive *fuisse* et *fore*: ergo habet in sui *duratione* successionem.

2. Item, Anselmus in Proslogio[^8] tractans illud verbum: *Dominus regnabit in aeternum et ultra*, propter hoc dictum est, non quia post aeternitatem sit aliquid, sed quia Dei aeternitas, quae tota simul est, excedit aeternitatem creaturae, quae non omnino est tota simul; ista est sententia: ergo idem quod prius.

<!-- page 62 -->

3. Item, *ratione* videtur: unitas angelica deficit ab unitate divina, ergo simplicitas aeternitatis creatae a simplicitate aeternitatis increatae: si ergo hoc verum est, ergo habet compositionem aliquo modo. Sed compositio in duratione ponit prius et posterius: ergo etc.

4. Item, hoc ipsum videtur, quia mensura durationis angelicae non est ipse Angelus, immo differt ab Angelo, sicut mensura a mensurato; sed mensura secundum veritatem est in genere quantitatis[^9], et talis est divisibilis, ergo habens partes: ergo etc. *Si tu dicas*, quod est quantitatis *principium* sicut punctus; *contra*: punctus non habet complete rationem mensurae, sed est *principium* mensurae; aevum autem vere et proprie est mensura: ergo non potest esse sicut *principium*.

5. Item, Angeli duratio est infinita: si ergo est tota simul in actu, ergo aliquod creatum est infinitum actu. Sed hoc est impossibile: ergo etc.

6. Item, in eo quod habet totum esse simul, idem est *fuisse* et *esse* et *futurum esse*; sed quod fuit, impossibile est cogitari non fuisse, si intelligatur fuisse: ergo si in aeviterno idem est *fuisse* et *fore*, ergo impossibile est cogitari non fore. Hoc autem falsum est, quia hoc est proprium solius Dei: ergo etc.

7. Item, si totum *esse* praesens est, ergo non differt *esse* et *fuisse*: ergo quod nunc non est, nunquam fuit, et si fuit, est. Sed Deus non potest facere, quod fuit non fuisse[^10]: ergo non potest facere, aeviternum non esse. Sed hoc est manifeste falsum: ergo etc.

8. Item, si totum esse aeviterni simul est, et tota duratio sine priori et posteriori, ergo non est ibi magis longum et minus longum; ergo anima beati Petri nec prius nec diutius fuit in gloria quam anima beati Francisci. Si ergo hoc manifeste falsum est, patet etc.

### Conclusio

> In aevo est aliqua successio, quae non importat prius et posterius cum variatione et innovatione, ut in tempore, sed tantum durationis extensionem.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod circa hoc duplex fuit opinio.

Quidam enim dixerunt, quod aevum est totum simplex, sicut et illud quod mensurat; et *esse* substantiae aeviternae et eius *duratio* est tota simul, non habens successionem prioris et posterioris. Unde dixerunt, aevum non esse proprie quantitatem, sed in genere quantitatis solum esse per reductionem; unde *simplex* est extensione, sed tamen est *quantum* virtute, et adeo quantum, quod sua virtute excedat omne *esse* temporale ad similitudinem aeternitatis increatae. Nam sicut anima simplex est quantum ad quantitatem *molis*, tamen propter suam *virtutem* et simplicitatem est in qualibet parte sui corporis; sic in proposito intelligendum est. — Sed, sicut in opponendo tactum est, si quis ponat aevum omnino simplex, ponet ex hoc non esse veram mensuram; ponet etiam durationem creatam actu infinitam; ponet etiam durationem creatam adeo entem[^11], quod nec Deus destruere, nec intellectus possit cogitare non esse; quae omnia, cum non sint intelligibilia, faciunt, praedictam positionem nec esse rationabilem nec intelligibilem.

Et ideo, cum Sanctorum auctoritates aliud videantur sonare, est aliorum positio probabilior et intelligibilior, quod in aevo est ponere *prius* et *posterius*, et est ponere aliquam *successionem*, aliam tamen successionem quam in tempore. In tempore enim est *successio* cum variatione, et *prius et posterius* cum inveteratione et renovatione. In aevo vero est *prius et posterius*, quod dicit durationis extensionem, quod tamen nullam dicit variationem nec innovationem. Et per hanc distinctionem ad omnia obiecta in contrarium facile est solvere, si quis eam intelligat.

Quod si forte quaeratur: *quomodo* potest esse prius et posterius sine novitate circa esse; dicendum, quod sicut videmus, quod aliter egreditur rivulus[^12] a fonte, aliter radius a sole, sic in proposito videmus. Nam rivulus sic egreditur a fonte, quod nova aqua semper exit, non eadem; radius a sole continue egreditur, non quia semper novum aliquid emittatur, sed quia quod emissum est continuatur; unde solis influentia non est aliud quam continuatio dati. Similiter in *motu*, et in *esse* rei *mobilis* aliqua proprietas habita amittitur, vel non habita acquiritur; sed in *esse* rei *aeviternae* quod primo datum est per continuam Dei influentiam *continuatur*. Nulla enim aevi creatura est omnino actus, nec aliqua eius virtus, unde continue indiget divina virtute cooperante. Ideo, etsi *esse* totum habeat, tamen *continuationem esse* non habet totam simul, et ideo est ibi successio sine aliqua innovatione circa *esse* vel proprietatem absolutam; tamen ibi est vera continuatio, respectu cuius creatura habet *esse* quodam modo in potentia, ac per hoc habet successionem.

<!-- page 63 -->

Solus igitur Deus, qui est actus purus, est actu infinitus, et totum *esse* et possessionem sui *esse* simul habet[^13]. His visis, satis de facili solvuntur obiecta.

1. 2. Quod enim obiicitur de praeterito et futuro et de transitu, dicendum breviter, quod intelligitur de istis, ut dicunt variationem.

3. Quod obiicitur, quod non differt *esse* et *posse*; dicendum, quod verum est de *posse* et *esse*, quod non differt, id est, quod non distat; motus enim et tempus facit distare; in solo autem aeterno verum est, quod potentia omnino sit actus, non in aliqua creatura[^14].

4. Quod obiicitur, quod substantiae simplicis proprietas non potest esse composita; dicendum, quod verum est, si illa proprietas habeat compositionem partium simul entium[^15]; nunc autem non est sic, immo de aevo nunquam est nisi *nunc*, prius, sicut et de tempore dicitur. Et ita bene potest esse in simplici, ut in composito; unde tantam extensionem habet *duratio* unius grani milii, sicut et unius montis.

5. Quod obiicitur, quod *prius* et *posterius* reducitur ad permanens; dicendum, quod verum est, quod ad permanens reducitur; sed non oportet, quod ad *prius* et *posterius* permanens. Empyreum enim durationem habet aeviternam et aeque simplex est sicut duratio Angeli: ergo *prius* et *posterius* in partibus permanentibus non facit aliquid ad hoc.

6. Quod obiicitur de novo et veteri, iam patet: quia nihil est ibi alterationis, est tamen ibi crementum durationis absque omni alteratione absolutae proprietatis. Verum enim est dicere, quod diutius fuit anima Petri, quam anima Francisci[^16], quando in gloriam introivit, sed non est ita circa Deum; non enim diutius duravit hodie quam ante heri.

7. Quod obiicitur de exspectatione, dicendum, quod, sicut est *successio* non per *novi acquisitionem*, sed per *prius dati continuationem*, ita etiam est *exspectatio* non novi habendi, sed continuationis prius habiti, quod quia iam habent, et certi sunt se habituros, ideo potius dicitur *tentio* et *comprehensio* quam *exspectatio*. Et sic patet illud.
questions.english:
### Question III. *Whether spiritual things have a permanent or a successive measure.*

Thirdly it is asked whether spiritual things have a *permanent* or a *successive* measure. And that [they have] a *permanent* one, lacking before and after, seems true first *by authority*, then *by reason*.

1. And *by authority* thus: Augustine, in the twelfth book of *On the City of God*[^1]: «The immortality of the Angels does not pass in time, nor is it past, as though it now were not, nor future, as though it were not yet»: therefore it is wholly present, therefore permanent, not successive.

2. Likewise, Augustine, eleventh book of the *Confessions*[^2]: «If the present time were to stand and not pass into the past, it would be eternity»; but not on that account would it be uncreated eternity: therefore it would be created eternity; and this is the age: therefore the age has a *now* that does not pass: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, the Philosopher[^3]: «In perpetual things *being* and *being able* do not differ»: therefore the potency is in its whole act, therefore it awaits nothing, therefore [it is] all at once: therefore there is no succession or priority there.

4. Likewise *by reason*: a property must correspond to the substance, therefore the measure of a simple substance must be simple; but a spiritual substance is simple: therefore also its measure. But its measure is the age: therefore it is simple: therefore it does not have before and after.

5. Likewise, every successive thing is reduced to a permanent one, therefore the successive before-and-after to a permanent before-and-after[^4]; but the permanent before-and-after is in magnitude alone: therefore what lacks a permanent before-and-after lacks also the successive one. But such is the Angel: therefore, etc.

6. Likewise, where there is before and after, there necessarily falls something new, which from being later becomes earlier, and through this a lapse into the *past*, and something new; but in perpetual things there is no change[^5]: therefore neither succession.

7. Likewise, where there is a before, there is some expectation with respect to that which is later and not yet possessed; but in the Blessed no expectation at all falls, because faith and hope are wholly emptied out, and all that they will have is had[^6]: therefore in no way is there before and after there.

**On the contrary:**

1. Jerome to Marcella[^7]: «He alone is, who does not know *to have been* or *to be about to be*»: every creature, therefore, in its own *being* has a pastness, that is, a *having been* and a *going to be*: therefore it has in its own *duration* a succession.

2. Likewise, Anselm in the *Proslogion*[^8], treating that word: *The Lord shall reign forever and beyond*, [says] this is said not because there is something after eternity, but because God's eternity, which is wholly at once, exceeds the eternity of the creature, which is not wholly at once; this is the sense: therefore the same as before.

<!-- page 62 -->

3. Likewise, it seems so *by reason*: angelic unity falls short of the divine unity, therefore the simplicity of created eternity [falls short] of the simplicity of uncreated eternity: if then this is true, then it has composition in some way. But composition in duration posits before and after: therefore, etc.

4. Likewise, this same thing seems so, because the measure of angelic duration is not the Angel itself, but rather differs from the Angel, as a measure from the measured; but a measure, in truth, is in the genus of quantity[^9], and such a thing is divisible, therefore having parts: therefore, etc. *If you say* that it is the *principle* of quantity, like a point; *on the contrary*: a point does not have completely the account of a measure, but is the *principle* of a measure; but the age is truly and properly a measure: therefore it cannot be like a *principle*.

5. Likewise, the duration of an Angel is infinite: if then it is wholly at once in act, then some created thing is infinite in act. But this is impossible: therefore, etc.

6. Likewise, in that which has its whole being at once, *to have been* and *to be* and *to be about to be* are the same; but what has been, it is impossible to think not to have been, if it is understood to have been: therefore if in the aeviternal *to have been* and *to be going to be* are the same, then it is impossible to think it not going to be. But this is false, because this is proper to God alone: therefore, etc.

7. Likewise, if the whole *being* is present, then *being* and *having been* do not differ: therefore what now is not, never was, and if it was, [now] is. But God cannot bring it about that what has been should not have been[^10]: therefore He cannot bring it about that the aeviternal not be. But this is manifestly false: therefore, etc.

8. Likewise, if the whole being of the aeviternal is at once, and the whole duration without before and after, then there is not there a longer and a shorter; therefore the soul of blessed Peter was neither earlier nor longer in glory than the soul of blessed Francis. If, then, this is manifestly false, it is plain, etc.

### Conclusio

> In the age there is some succession, which does not imply before and after with variation and innovation, as in time, but only an extension of duration.

**I respond:** It must be said that concerning this there was a twofold opinion.

For some have said that the age is wholly simple, just as also that which it measures; and the *being* of the aeviternal substance and its *duration* is wholly at once, not having a succession of before and after. Whence they said that the age is not properly a quantity, but is in the genus of quantity only by reduction; whence it is *simple* as to extension, but is nevertheless *quantitative* in power, and so quantitative that by its power it exceeds all temporal *being* in likeness to uncreated eternity. For just as the soul is simple as to the quantity of *mass*, yet on account of its *power* and simplicity is in every part of its body; so it must be understood in the matter at hand. — But, as was touched on in objecting, if anyone posits the age as wholly simple, he will posit from this that it is not a true measure; he will also posit a created duration actually infinite; he will also posit a created duration so much a being[^11] that neither could God destroy it, nor could the intellect think it not to be; all of which, since they are not intelligible, make that aforesaid position to be neither reasonable nor intelligible.

And therefore, since the authorities of the Saints seem to sound otherwise, the position of the others is more probable and more intelligible, that in the age one must posit *before* and *after*, and one must posit some *succession*, yet a succession other than that in time. For in time there is *succession* with variation, and *before and after* with aging and renewal. But in the age there is *before and after*, which states an extension of duration, which nevertheless states no variation nor innovation. And by this distinction it is easy to solve all the objections to the contrary, if one understands it.

But if perchance it be asked: *how* can there be before and after without newness about being; it must be said that, as we see that a brook flows forth from a spring in one way[^12], a ray from the sun in another, so we see in the matter at hand. For the brook flows forth from the spring in such a way that new water always goes out, not the same; the ray flows forth continuously from the sun, not because something new is always emitted, but because what has been emitted is continued; whence the sun's influence is nothing other than the continuation of what is given. Likewise in *motion*, and in the *being* of a *movable* thing, some property possessed is lost, or one not possessed is acquired; but in the *being* of an *aeviternal* thing what was first given is *continued* through God's continual influence. For no creature of the age is wholly act, nor any power of it, whence it continually needs the divine power cooperating. Therefore, even though it has its whole *being*, it nevertheless does not have the *continuation of being* wholly at once, and therefore there is succession there without any innovation about *being* or absolute property; yet there is there a true continuation, with respect to which the creature has *being* in a certain way in potency, and through this it has succession.

<!-- page 63 -->

God alone, therefore, who is pure act, is infinite in act, and has the whole *being* and possession of His *being* at once[^13]. These things being seen, the objections are quite easily solved.

1, 2. As to what is objected, then, about the past and the future and about transit, it must be said briefly that these are understood as they state a variation.

3. As to what is objected, that *being* and *being able* do not differ; it must be said that it is true of *being able* and *being* that they do not differ, that is, that they are not apart; for motion and time make [them] apart; but in the eternal alone is it true that the potency is wholly act, not in any creature[^14].

4. As to what is objected, that the property of a simple substance cannot be composite; it must be said that it is true, if that property has a composition of parts existing at once[^15]; but now it is not so, indeed of the age there is never anything but *now*, before, just as is said also of time. And so it can well be in the simple as in the composite; whence the *duration* of a single grain of millet has as great an extension as that of a single mountain.

5. As to what is objected, that *before* and *after* is reduced to a permanent thing; it must be said that it is true that it is reduced to a permanent thing; but it is not necessary that [it be reduced] to a permanent before-and-after. For the empyrean has an aeviternal duration and is equally simple as the duration of an Angel: therefore before and after in permanent parts does nothing toward this.

6. As to what is objected about the new and the old, it is already clear: because there is nothing of alteration there, yet there is there an increment of duration without any alteration of an absolute property. For it is true to say that the soul of Peter was [in glory] longer than the soul of Francis[^16], when it entered into glory, but it is not so with regard to God; for He has not endured longer today than before yesterday.

7. As to what is objected about expectation, it must be said that, just as there is *succession* not through *the acquisition of something new*, but through *the continuation of what was given before*, so too there is *expectation* not of having something new, but of the continuation of what was had before, which, because they already have it, and are certain they will have it, is therefore rather called a *holding* and *comprehension* than an *expectation*. And thus that [objection] is plain.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Haec quaestio etiam sub his terminis proponitur: utrum aevum sit mensura simplex sive indivisibilis. S. Thom. in solutione eius cum communiore sententia contra S. Bonaventuram tenet, quod, sicut essentia et *existentia* Angeli simplex est et tota simul, sic etiam *mensura* ipsius excludat omnem successionem, nisi forte quatenus connotat coexistentiam ad tempus. — Sententia S. Bonaventurae duabus innititur distinctionibus. 1. Aliter sentiendum est de *esse substantiali* Angeli, aliter de *duratione* eius: illud *esse* in instanti creationis accipit ac indivisibile et totum simul, non autem *durationem* eius, quae, quia creatura continuo dependet a Deo conservante, non est indivisibilis, sed habet aliquam suo modo successionem. 2. Duplex est successio: *propria*, quae competit tempori secundum prius et posterius et habet variationem et renovationem, quia semper aliquid amittitur, et aliquid acquiritur; et *impropria*, quae competit aevo et non importat nisi durationis extensionem sine variatione vel innovatione. Per creationem res proprie *fit* et acquirit *initium* existentiae et durationis; per conservationem vero non *fit*, sed *continuatur in existentia* et acquirit maiorem durationem, quin in *esse* eius fiat innovatio vel additio. Unde aeviternum in instanti suae creationis totum suum *esse substantiale* habuit, sed non totam suam *durationem*, immo non nisi durationis *initium*. — Admissis his distinctionibus, quas contrariae sententiae fautores non approbant, facile intelligitur, in solo Deo idem esse *essentiam, existentiam, durationem*; in omnibus creaturis autem haec tria distinguenda esse.

**II.** Sententiam S. Thomae sequuntur inter antiquos Scholasticos Alex. Hal., Petr. a Tar., Henr. Gand., Durand., Dionys. Carth. aliique. — B. Albertus consentit S. Bonaventurae. Richard. a Med. utriusque sententiae argg. ponit et solvit, magis tamen inclinat in sententiam S. Thomae. Aegid. R. in re parum a S. Bonav. discedit. Scotus vero (hic q. 1.) in utramque partem disputat et anceps haeret, tamen, testibus Lycheto pluribusque aliis Scotistis, magis inclinat in sententiam S. Bonaventurae. Idem etiam de Rerum princip. q. 22. n. 8. ait: «Vel forte habet [aevum] aliquam naturam successionis, scil. quae est *esse* et *modus* essendi et durandi illorum substantiarum». Nec inter recentiores desunt viri doctissimi, qui sententiam S. Bonaventurae praeferant, vel valde probabilem censent, ut cl. P. Kleutgen S. I., Philosophie der Vorzeit tom. I. Abhandl. 4. c. 1. § 2, qui ut huius opinionis sequaces laudat Conimbricenses Phys. IV. c. 14. q. 2, et P. Silv. Maurum, Quaest. philos. tom. II. q. 32.

**III.** Alex. Hal., S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 3. — Scot., locc. citt. — S. Thom., hic q. 1. a. 1; S. I. q. 10. a. 5. — B. Albert., S. p. I. tr. 5. q. 23. m. 2. a. 2. partic. 1. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2. a. 1. — Richard. a Med., hic a. 1. q. 3. — Aegid. R., hic q. 1. a. 3. — Henr. Gand., Quodl. 5. q. 13. — Durand., hic q. 3. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 2. — Biel, hic q. 1.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** This question is also proposed under these terms: whether the age is a simple or indivisible measure. St. Thomas, in his solution of it, holds, with the more common opinion, against St. Bonaventure, that, just as the essence and *existence* of the Angel is simple and wholly at once, so too its *measure* excludes all succession, except perhaps insofar as it connotes a coexistence with time. — The opinion of St. Bonaventure rests on two distinctions. 1. One must judge otherwise about the *substantial being* of the Angel, otherwise about its *duration*: that *being* it receives in the instant of creation as indivisible and wholly at once, but not its *duration*, which, because the creature continuously depends on God conserving [it], is not indivisible, but has in its own mode some succession. 2. Succession is twofold: *proper*, which belongs to time according to before and after and has variation and renewal, because something is always lost and something acquired; and *improper*, which belongs to the age and implies only an extension of duration without variation or innovation. By creation a thing properly *comes to be* and acquires the *beginning* of existence and duration; but by conservation it does not *come to be*, but is *continued in existence* and acquires a greater duration, without any innovation or addition occurring in its *being*. Whence the aeviternal in the instant of its creation had its whole *substantial being*, but not its whole *duration*, indeed nothing but the *beginning* of duration. — These distinctions being admitted (which the supporters of the contrary opinion do not approve), it is easily understood that in God alone *essence, existence, duration* are the same; but in all creatures these three are to be distinguished.

**II.** The opinion of St. Thomas is followed, among the ancient Scholastics, by Alexander of Hales, Peter of Tarentaise, Henry of Ghent, Durandus, Dionysius the Carthusian, and others. — Bl. Albert agrees with St. Bonaventure. Richard of Middleton sets out and solves the arguments of both opinions, yet inclines more to the opinion of St. Thomas. Giles of Rome departs little in substance from St. Bonaventure. But Scotus (here q. 1) disputes on both sides and remains in doubt, yet, on the testimony of Lychetus and several other Scotists, inclines more to the opinion of St. Bonaventure. The same [Scotus] also says, *On the Principle of Things*, q. 22, n. 8: «Or perhaps [the age] has some nature of succession, namely that which is the *being* and the *mode* of being and of enduring of those substances». Nor among more recent [writers] are there lacking most learned men who prefer the opinion of St. Bonaventure, or judge it very probable, as the distinguished P. Kleutgen S.J., *Philosophie der Vorzeit*, vol. I, Treatise 4, c. 1, § 2, who as followers of this opinion cites the Conimbricenses, *Physics* IV, c. 14, q. 2, and P. Silvester Maurus, *Quaestiones philosophicae*, vol. II, q. 32.

**III.** Alexander of Hales, S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 3. — Scotus, locc. citt. — St. Thomas, here q. 1, a. 1; S. I, q. 10, a. 5. — Bl. Albert, S. p. I, tr. 5, q. 23, m. 2, a. 2, partic. 1. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 2, a. 1. — Richard of Middleton, here a. 1, q. 3. — Giles of Rome, here q. 1, a. 3. — Henry of Ghent, Quodl. 5, q. 13. — Durandus, here q. 3. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 2. — Biel, here q. 1.
