apparatus.la: Libr. III. Phys. text. 32. (c. 4.). — Post primum *ergo* cod. N supplet *in perpetuis*, dein cod. cc et ed. 1 omittunt *toto*; Vat. ponit *exspectatur* pro *exspectat* et in fine argumenti adiungit *et posterioritas.*
apparatus.en: *Physics* III, text 32 (c. 4). — After the first *therefore*, codex N supplies *in perpetual things*, then codex cc and ed. 1 omit *whole*; the Vatican edition puts *is awaited* for *awaits* and at the end of the argument adds *and posteriority.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., de Praedicam. c. *de Quantitate*, duplicem quantitatem distinguit, scil. permanentem et successivam; prior competit iis, «quae constant ex partibus, quae in eis sunt, positionem habentibus ad se invicem» i. e. quae constant ex partibus simul existentibus v. g. linea, superficies; posterior vero convenit iis, quae constant ex non habentibus positionem, sed magis ordinem prioritatis et posterioritatis v. g. tempus. Libr. IV. Phys. text. 99. (c. 11.) dicit, quod prius et posterius in loco, qui habet positionem, primum sunt, deinde etiam in motu et in tempore.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Categories*, the chapter *On Quantity*, distinguishes a twofold quantity, namely permanent and successive; the former belongs to those things «which consist of parts that, being in them, have a position with respect to one another», i.e. which consist of parts existing at once, e.g. a line, a surface; the latter belongs to those which consist of [parts] not having position, but rather an order of priority and posteriority, e.g. time. *Physics* IV, text 99 (c. 11) says that before and after are first in place, which has position, then also in motion and in time.

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 97. seqq. (c. 11.).
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 97 ff. (c. 11).

apparatus.la: Vide I. Cor. 13, 10. seqq.
apparatus.en: See 1 Cor. 13:10 ff.

apparatus.la: Verba, quae sequuntur, non sunt Hieronymi, sed Isidori, VII. Etym. c. 1. n. 12. Cfr. de hoc tom. I. pag. 146, nota 4.
apparatus.en: The words that follow are not Jerome's, but Isidore's, *Etymologies* VII, c. 1, n. 12. Cf. on this vol. I, p. 146, note 4.

apparatus.la: Cap. 20, ubi tripliciter exponitur, quod Deus sit etiam ultra ea, quae finem non habebunt, scil. quia ipsa sine Dei conservatione esse non possunt, tum quia ipsa cogitari possunt habere finem, tum quia ipsa de sua aeternitate nondum habent quod futurum est, et iam non habent quod est praeteritum, cum Dei et illorum aeternitas sit Deo tota praesens. — Textus s. Scripturae est Exod. 15, 18. — Circa finem argumenti cod. cc et ed. 1 *excedit creaturam* pro *excedit aeternitatem creaturae.*
apparatus.en: Chapter 20, where it is expounded in three ways that God is even beyond those things which will not have an end, namely because they cannot be without God's conservation, both because they themselves can be thought to have an end, and because they themselves, of their own eternity, do not yet have what is future, and now do not have what is past, since God's eternity and theirs is wholly present to God. — The text of Scripture is Exod. 15:18. — Near the end of the argument codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *exceeds the creature* for *exceeds the eternity of the creature.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., X. Metaph. text. 2. (IX. c. 1.): *Maxime autem mensuram esse cuiusque generis primum et maxime proprie quanti*; hinc enim et ad alia advenit; mensura enim id est, quo quantum cognoscitur. Cfr. q. 1. ad 6.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Metaphysics* X, text 2 (IX, c. 1): *But that the measure is most of all the first of each genus and most properly of the quantitative*; for hence it comes also to the others; for a measure is that by which the quantitative is known. Cf. q. 1, ad 6.

apparatus.la: Cfr. I. Sent. d. 42. q. 3.
apparatus.en: Cf. I Sent., d. 42, q. 3.

apparatus.la: Cod. cc, ed. 1 et Vat. *existentem*; Vat. insuper *a Deo* pro *adeo.*
apparatus.en: Codex cc, ed. 1, and the Vatican edition [read] *existing*; the Vatican edition moreover [reads] *by God* for *so much*.

apparatus.la: Multi codd. cum Vat. *fluvius* contra codd. A cc et ed. 1. Mox non pauci codd. *videndum*, aliqui *vide*, cod. aa *esse videtur*, cod. cc et ed. 1 *videtur* pro *videmus.*
apparatus.en: Many codices with the Vatican edition [read] *river* against codices A cc and ed. 1. Soon after, not a few codices [read] *it must be seen*, some *see*, codex aa *it seems to be*, codex cc and ed. 1 *it seems* for *we see.*

apparatus.la: Alluditur ad illam Boethii, V. de Consol. prosa 6, definitionem: *Aeternitas est interminabilis vitae tota simul et perfecta possessio.* — Vat. *posse* pro *possessionem.*
apparatus.en: Allusion is made to that definition of Boethius, *On Consolation* V, prose 6: *Eternity is the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life.* — The Vatican edition [reads] *to be able* for *possession.*

apparatus.la: Aliis verbis: *In perpetuis non differt esse et posse* i. e. potentia non distat ab actu sive non praecedit actum, sed simul sunt; non autem intelligitur ita, quod in substantiis spiritualibus, excepto Deo, non differant actus et potentia, immo vere differunt; sed potentia non praecedit actum sicut in istis inferioribus, quae motui et tempori subiiciuntur. Dictio «tempus facit distare» est ex Aristotele. Cfr. infra pag. 66, nota 2. — Aliquanto superius non pauci codd. cum edd. 1, 3, 4 *quod verum est de posse ad esse* pro *quod verum est de posse et esse.*
apparatus.en: In other words: *In perpetual things being and being able do not differ*, i.e. potency is not apart from act, or does not precede act, but they are at once; it is not, however, understood thus, that in spiritual substances, except God, act and potency do not differ — indeed they truly differ; but potency does not precede act as in these lower things, which are subject to motion and time. The phrase «time makes [them] apart» is from Aristotle. Cf. below, p. 66, note 2. — Somewhat above, not a few codices with editions 1, 3, 4 [read] *that it is true of being able toward being* for *that it is true of being able and being.*

apparatus.la: Cod. cc et ed. 1 *in aevo*; cod. aa *hic.* Immediate ante Vat. *existentium* pro *entium.* Paulo inferius post *potest esse* in cod. cc et ed. 1 suppletur *duratio aevi.*
apparatus.en: Codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *in the age*; codex aa *here.* Immediately before, the Vatican edition [reads] *existing* for *being [parts].* A little below, after *can be*, in codex cc and ed. 1 there is supplied *the duration of the age.*

apparatus.la: Fide plurium codd. ut A K L O V Z bb adiecimus *anima Francisci*, quae verba etiam in ult. fundam. inveniuntur. Paulo superius cod. aa *Unde nunc* pro *Verum enim*, qui dein post *Petri* bene adiungit *in gloria.*
apparatus.en: On the faith of several codices, as A K L O V Z bb, we have added *the soul of Francis*, which words are also found in the last fundamentum. A little above, codex aa [reads] *Whence now* for *For it is true*, which then, after *Peter*, well adds *in glory.* ---

questions.titleLa: Utrum aevum praecedat aliquo modo tempus
questions.titleEn: Whether the age in any way precedes time
questions.latin:
<!-- page 64 -->

### Articulus II. *De mensura angelicae naturae in comparatione ad mensuram rei corporalis.*

Consequenter quaeritur de mensura substantiae spiritualis in comparatione ad mensuram rei corporalis. De qua tria quaeruntur.

Primum est, utrum aevum praecedat tempus aliquo prioritatis genere.

Secundum, utrum inter aevum et tempus cadat mensura mediae naturae.

Tertio, utrum res spirituales et corporales, sive aeviternae et temporales fuerint simul productae.

### Quaestio I. *Utrum aevum praecedat aliquo modo tempus.*

Circa primum sic. Quod aevum sit prius tempore, ostenditur:

1. Per illud Boethii de Consolatione[^1] loquentis ad Deum:

> *Qui tempus ab aevo*
> *Ire iubes;*

sed tempus ire ab aevo non potest intelligi nisi vel ratione causalitatis, vel durationis, vel excellentiae, quia deficit ab aevo: ergo videtur omnino intelligendum, quod aevum sit tempore prius.

2. Item, omnis motus et mutatio ad immobile reducitur tanquam ad prius[^2]: ergo et mensura mobilis ad mensuram rei immobilis: ergo et tempus ad aevum tanquam ad prius. *Prima* consequentia manifeste est vera, quia omne fluxibile ad stans tanquam ad prius reducitur. Et *secunda* consequentia tenet secundum rationem proportionis, quia, sicut se habet mensuratum ad mensuratum, sic mensura ad mensuram: ergo etc.

3. Item, a priori et posteriori in *magnitudine* causatur prius et posterius in *motu*, et a priori et posteriori in *motu* causatur prius et posterius in *tempore*[^3]: ergo per naturam prior est magnitudo et magnitudinis *esse*, quam sit *esse* temporis; et substantiae primi corporis mensuratur aevo, motus vero tempore: ergo aevum prius est tempore.

4. Item, aevum fuit a principio creaturae, scilicet et Angeli; sed tempus coepit cum motu primi mobilis, qui incepit, ut dicitur, die quarto, vel saltem ante secundum diem non potuit incipere[^4]: ergo aevum duratione praecedit tempus.

**Contra:**

1. Beda[^5] dicit, quod quatuor fuerunt primo creata, et inter illa enumerat *tempus*; *aevum* autem non enumeratur inter primo creata; et est creatum: ergo posterius.

2. Item, Richardus de sancto Victore[^6] dicit et accipit ab Augustino, quod omne quod coepit, coepit ex tempore; sed aevum coepit: ergo coepit ex tempore. Sed quod incipit ex tempore non antecedit tempus, sed potius consequitur vel concomitatur: ergo aevum non potest esse ante tempus.

3. Item, tempus est mensura mutationis; sed aevum est mensura stabilis et fixi: ergo cum ante *esse creatum* praecedat ipsa creatio, quae est mutatio, ergo tempus est ante aevum.

4. Item, prius est[^7] quod imperfectum est, deinde quod perfectum; sed tempus est mensura secundum esse imperfectum, quod est esse in potentia, aevum vero secundum esse actuale et completum: ergo tempus per naturam est ante aevum. — Quaeritur igitur de *ordine* temporis ad aevum, et e converso.

### Conclusio

> Distincto quadruplici sensu termini tempus, asseritur, quod in tertio sensu aevum et tempus sunt simul duratione, sed aevum est prius dignitate; in quarto sensu aevum praecedit tempus et duratione et dignitate.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod *tempus* accipi consuevit quadrupliciter in scripturis Sanctorum, scilicet *communissime*, *communiter*, *proprie* et *magis proprie*. *Communissime* tempus dicit mensuram cuiuslibet durationis creatae; per quem modum accipitur a Beda, cum dicit, quod quatuor fuerunt primo creata, inter quae enumerat tempus. — *Communiter*; sic dicit mensuram mutationis cuiuscumque, sive illius quae est de *non-esse* in *esse*, sive alterius quae est de *uno esse* in *aliud esse*; et sic

<!-- page 65 -->

accipitur illud quod dicit Richardus, quod omne quod coepit, ex tempore coepit; et habetur in Glossa, in principio Genesis[^8]: *In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram*, scilicet temporis. — Tertio modo accipitur *proprie*; et sic dicit mensuram variationis successivae, sive sit successiva successione regulari et continua, sive non; et sic dicit Augustinus ad Orosium[^9]: «Affectiones variae Angelorum mensurantur tempore et omnis variatio rerum». — Quarto modo accipitur *magis proprie*; et sic dicitur mensura motus sive variationis successivae et continuae et regulatae secundum regulam motus octavae sphaerae; et sic consuevit accipi a Philosopho[^10]: sed ista est coarctata temporis acceptio.

Cum igitur quaeritur de *ordine*, dicendum, quod si tempus accipiatur primo modo, sic includit *aevum*; et sic temporis ad aevum nullus est ordo; si autem secundo modo, sic tempus praecedit aevum secundum rationem intelligendi, sicut creatio *esse* creatum. Si autem tertio modo, aevum et tempus simul sunt *duratione*, sed aevum prius est *dignitate*. Si autem quarto modo, sic aevum praecedit tempus et *duratione* et *dignitate*. — Ex his patet quaestio principalis, et obiectiones adductae pro magna parte.

Quod enim ostenditur, quod aevum praecedit tempus; intelligitur vel tertio modo, et ita praecedit dignitate; vel quarto modo, et ita duratione.

1. Quod tamen ostenditur, quod praecedat causalitate; dicendum, quod illud non oportet; neutra harum mensurarum est ab alia[^11], sed a Deo producente utrumque indivisibile, scilicet *nunc* aevi et *nunc* temporis. Unde quod dicitur, quod tempus exit ab aevo, hoc dicitur, quia deficit ab illo et defluit continua deperditione; sed in aevo est fixio sine deperditione et novi acquisitione.

2. Quod obiicitur de reductione ad immobile, dicendum, quod verum est ex parte motoris, et illum non oportet esse creatum, et similiter nec mensuram oportet esse creatam: et ideo non oportet, tempus reduci ad aevum sicut ad prius.

3. Ad illud quod obiicitur de priori et posteriori magnitudinis et motus et temporis, dicendum, quod non causatur a priori et posteriori in *magnitudine* prius et posterius in *motu* vel tempore, nisi secundum quod magnitudo illa est mobilis; et sic habet mensurari per *nunc* temporis, non aevi; nam sicut *tempus* mensurat motum, sic *nunc temporis* mensurat ipsum mobile in quantum mobile.

4. Quod ultimo obiicitur, patet, quod[^12] procedit de quarta acceptione temporis.

Rationes vero ad oppositum procedunt de tempore secundum primam acceptionem vel secundam, ut patet aspicienti, excepta ultima, quae accipitur a comparatione imperfecti ad perfectum. Ad quam respondendum: quod imperfectum praecedit perfectum, verum est, ubi[^13] sunt circa idem; sed circa diversa est e converso. Et ideo potius potest argui oppositum quam propositum per illud medium.
questions.english:
### Article II. *On the measure of the angelic nature in comparison with the measure of a corporeal thing.*

Consequently it is asked about the measure of a spiritual substance in comparison with the measure of a corporeal thing. Concerning which three things are asked.

The first is, whether the age precedes time by any genus of priority.

The second, whether between the age and time there falls a measure of a middle nature.

The third, whether spiritual and corporeal things, that is, aeviternal and temporal, were produced simultaneously.

### Question I. *Whether the age in any way precedes time.*

Concerning the first, thus. That the age is prior to time is shown:

1. Through that [verse] of Boethius, *On Consolation*[^1], speaking to God:

> *You who bid time*
> *go forth from the age;*

but time's going forth from the age cannot be understood except either by reason of causality, or of duration, or of excellence, because it falls short of the age: therefore it seems altogether to be understood that the age is prior to time.

2. Likewise, every motion and change is reduced to the immobile as to something prior[^2]: therefore also the measure of the movable to the measure of the immobile thing: therefore also time to the age as to something prior. The *first* consequence is manifestly true, because everything flowing is reduced to the standing as to something prior. And the *second* consequence holds by the account of proportion, because, as the measured stands to the measured, so the measure to the measure: therefore, etc.

3. Likewise, from before and after in *magnitude* is caused before and after in *motion*, and from before and after in *motion* is caused before and after in *time*[^3]: therefore by nature magnitude and the *being* of magnitude is prior to the *being* of time; and the substance of the first body is measured by the age, but its motion by time: therefore the age is prior to time.

4. Likewise, the age was from the beginning of the creature, namely also of the Angel; but time began with the motion of the first movable, which began, as is said, on the fourth day, or at least could not begin before the second day[^4]: therefore the age precedes time in duration.

**On the contrary:**

1. Bede[^5] says that four things were created first, and among them he enumerates *time*; but *the age* is not enumerated among the things created first; and it is created: therefore [it is] later.

2. Likewise, Richard of Saint Victor[^6] says, and takes it from Augustine, that everything that began, began from time; but the age began: therefore it began from time. But what begins from time does not antecede time, but rather follows or accompanies [it]: therefore the age cannot be before time.

3. Likewise, time is the measure of change; but the age is the measure of the stable and fixed: therefore, since before *created being* there precedes creation itself, which is a change, therefore time is before the age.

4. Likewise, that which is imperfect is prior[^7], then that which is perfect; but time is a measure according to imperfect being, which is being in potency, but the age according to actual and complete being: therefore time is by nature before the age. — It is asked, therefore, about the *order* of time to the age, and conversely.

### Conclusio

> The fourfold sense of the term *time* being distinguished, it is asserted that in the third sense the age and time are simultaneous in duration, but the age is prior in dignity; in the fourth sense the age precedes time both in duration and in dignity.

**I respond:** It must be said that *time* has been customarily taken in four ways in the writings of the Saints, namely *most commonly*, *commonly*, *properly*, and *more properly*. *Most commonly* time states the measure of any created duration; in which mode it is taken by Bede, when he says that four things were created first, among which he enumerates time. — *Commonly*; thus it states the measure of any change whatever, whether of that which is from *non-being* into *being*, or of another which is from *one being* into *another being*; and thus

<!-- page 65 -->

is taken that which Richard says, that everything that began, began from time; and it is had in the Gloss, at the beginning of Genesis[^8]: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth*, namely [in the beginning] of time. — In the third mode it is taken *properly*; and thus it states the measure of a successive variation, whether it be successive by a regular and continuous succession or not; and thus Augustine says, to Orosius[^9]: «The varied affections of the Angels are measured by time, and every variation of things». — In the fourth mode it is taken *more properly*; and thus it is called the measure of motion or of a successive and continuous variation regulated according to the rule of the motion of the eighth sphere; and thus it has been customarily taken by the Philosopher[^10]: but this is the restricted acceptation of time.

When, therefore, it is asked about the *order*, it must be said that if time is taken in the first mode, then it includes *the age*; and so there is no order of time to the age; but if in the second mode, then time precedes the age according to the manner of understanding, as creation [precedes] *created being*. But if in the third mode, the age and time are simultaneous in *duration*, but the age is prior in *dignity*. But if in the fourth mode, then the age precedes time both in *duration* and in *dignity*. — From these things the principal question is plain, and the objections adduced for the most part.

For what is shown, that the age precedes time, is understood either in the third mode, and so it precedes in dignity; or in the fourth mode, and so in duration.

1. As to what is nevertheless shown, that it precedes by causality; it must be said that this is not necessary; neither of these measures is from the other[^11], but from God producing each indivisible, namely the *now* of the age and the *now* of time. Whence what is said, that time goes forth from the age, is said because it falls short of it and flows away by continual loss; but in the age there is a fixity without loss and without acquisition of anything new.

2. As to what is objected about reduction to the immobile, it must be said that it is true on the side of the mover, and that [mover] need not be created, and likewise neither need the measure be created: and therefore it is not necessary that time be reduced to the age as to something prior.

3. As to that which is objected about the before and after of magnitude and of motion and of time, it must be said that before and after in *motion* or time is not caused from before and after in *magnitude*, except insofar as that magnitude is movable; and so it has to be measured by the *now* of time, not of the age; for as *time* measures motion, so the *now of time* measures the movable itself insofar as it is movable.

4. As to what is objected last, it is plain that it[^12] proceeds from the fourth acceptation of time.

But the reasons to the contrary proceed concerning time according to the first acceptation or the second, as is plain to one looking, except the last, which is taken from the comparison of the imperfect to the perfect. To which it must be responded: that the imperfect precedes the perfect is true where[^13] they are about the same thing; but about diverse things it is the reverse. And therefore the opposite can rather be argued than the proposition by that middle term.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Quadruplex temporis distinctio sumta est ex Alex. Hal., S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 1. § 1, et fere eisdem verbis repetitur a Petr. a Tar. (hic q. 2. a. 2. quaestiunc. 2, et quando agit de hac ipsa quaest. ibid. a. 3.). Differentia inter tempus 3. et 4. modo sumtum a Richard. a Med. (hic a. 2. q. 2.) ita explicatur: «Tempus dupliciter potest accipi, scil. *communiter* pro quacumque mensura *esse* existentis in variatione [sive sit successionis continuae, sive non], et *proprie*, scil. secundum quod est *continuatio* motus ab anima numerata, qua, mediante motu, cuius est passio, mensurat anima durationes motuum aliorum» etc. (cfr. Schol. ad a. 1. q. 1.). Dionys. Carth. (hic q. 2.) de hac quaest. refert tantum verba Petri a Tar.

---
questions.englishScholion:
**I.** The fourfold distinction of time is taken from Alexander of Hales, S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 1, § 1, and is repeated in nearly the same words by Peter of Tarentaise (here q. 2, a. 2, quaestiuncula 2, and where he treats this very question, ibid. a. 3). The difference between time taken in the 3rd and 4th mode is explained thus by Richard of Middleton (here a. 2, q. 2): «Time can be taken in two ways, namely *commonly*, for any measure of the *being* of what exists in variation [whether it be of continuous succession or not], and *properly*, namely according as it is the *continuation* of motion numbered by the soul, by which, through the mediation of motion, of which it is a property, the soul measures the durations of other motions» etc. (cf. the Scholion on a. 1, q. 1). Dionysius the Carthusian (here q. 2) of this question reports only the words of Peter of Tarentaise.

---

questions.title: Dist. 2, Part 1, Art. 2, Q. 2
questions.titleLa: Utrum inter tempus et aevum sit aliqua mensura media
questions.titleEn: Whether between time and the age there is any middle measure
questions.latin:
<!-- page 65 -->

### Quaestio II. *Utrum inter tempus et aevum sit aliqua mensura media.*

Secundo quaeritur, utrum inter tempus et aevum sit aliqua mensura media. Et quod non, videtur:

1. Primo per Philosophum, qui dividit substantias mensuratas in libro de Causis[^1] sic, quod «inter substantiam, cuius substantia et actio est in momento aeternitatis, et substantiam, cuius substantia et actio est in momento temporis, est substantia media, cuius substantia est in momento aeternitatis, et actio in momento temporis». Si ergo omnis substantia creata ad aliquam istarum habet reduci; et ad has mensurandas sufficiunt tempus et aevum: ergo etc.

<!-- page 66 -->

2. Item, hoc ipsum videtur per Dionysium de Divinis Nominibus[^2]: «Aevi proprietas est sine alteratione et secundum totum metiri; temporis vero quod in alteratione aliter et aliter se habens; media vero entium, quae illinc quidem aevo, illinc tempore participant». Ergo omnia quae sunt, totaliter aevo, vel totaliter tempore, vel partim aevo et partim tempore mensurantur: ergo non est tertia mensura alia ab his.

3. Item, omne creatum aut est stabile et incorruptibile, aut variabile et corruptibile; sed primum mensuratur aevo, et secundum tempore: ergo nihil est medium inter aevum et tempus.

4. Item, *esse* omnis creati aut est *terminabile* aut *interminabile*. Si est *terminabile*, sic mensuratur tempore, quod est principium corruptionis, quia facit distare quod est[^3]. Si vero *interminabile*, sic aevo: ergo non videtur, quod sit aliquod tertium mensurans praeter haec duo.

**Contra:**

1. Ante quartum diem non erat tempus, quia dicitur in factione luminarium: *Erunt in signa et tempora et dies et annos*[^4]; et constat, quod non solum erat aevum, cum essent aliqua corporalia, ut herbae et arbusta: ergo erat alia mensura: ergo etc.

2. Item, post diem iudicii non erit tempus, secundum quod iurat Angelus in Apocalypsi[^5]; tamen erit successio et variatio in tormentis, quae non poterit aevo mensurari: ergo necesse est mensuram tertiam ab his ponere.

3. Item, in affectionibus Angelorum est intensio et variatio, et ipsi sunt supra tempus, sicut dicitur in libro de Causis[^6]: ergo mensura illa affectionum est supra tempus; sed non potest esse aevum, cum in aevo non cadat variatio: ergo oportet, quod sit alia mensura.

4. Item, Angelus cum convertitur ad Deum, elevatur supra tempus: ergo illa conversio, et illud quod in illa conversione accipit[^7], supra tempus est; et mensura supra tempus debet mensurari; sed Angelus ibi aliquid cognoscit quod potest desinere cogitare: saltem ergo illud non potest mensurari aevo, quod est mensura rei interminabilis, nec tempore: ergo etc.

### Conclusio

> Si tempus accipitur proprie, tunc inter aevum et tempus non est medium re, sed solum ratione differens; si autem magis proprie, tunc est media mensura differens, ab antiquis vocata saeculum.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod secundum quod tempus dividitur contra aevum, in duabus scilicet acceptionibus ultimis prius positis[^8], dupliciter potest accipi, aut scilicet prout dicit mensuram *cuiuslibet* durationis variae sive variationis successive; et sic inter aevum et tempus non est medium *re*, sed solum *ratione*; non, inquam, est medium differens ab utroque in genere *mensurae*, sed medium in genere *mensuratorum*, participans utrumque, ut est illa substantia, quae est in confinio aeternitatis et temporis. — Et sic procedunt omnes rationes ad primam partem, ut patet aspicienti de facili.

Aliter vero accipitur tempus prout est mensura variationis, in qua est successio habens *continuationem* et *regulationem* a motu orbis primi; et haec mensura habet finem et desinet esse. Et inter hanc et aevum est ponere mediam mensuram, in qua est *variatio*, nec oportet quod sit *desitio*, vel primi motus *regulatio*; cuiusmodi fuit in triduo conditionis rerum, et qualis erit in inferno post diem extremum. Et haec ab antiquis doctoribus appellata est *saeculum*[^9]. — Et hoc concludunt rationes ad oppositum; et sic patet totum.

<!-- page 67 -->
questions.english:
### Question II. *Whether between time and the age there is any middle measure.*

Secondly it is asked whether between time and the age there is any middle measure. And that there is not seems true:

1. First, through the Philosopher, who divides measured substances, in the book *de Causis*[^1], thus, that «between a substance whose substance and action is in the moment of eternity, and a substance whose substance and action is in the moment of time, there is a middle substance, whose substance is in the moment of eternity, and whose action [is] in the moment of time». If, then, every created substance has to be reduced to one of these; and to measure these, time and the age suffice: therefore, etc.

<!-- page 66 -->

2. Likewise, this same thing seems so through Dionysius, *On the Divine Names*[^2]: «It is the property of the age to be measured without alteration and according to the whole; but of time, that which holds itself otherwise and otherwise in alteration; but the middle of beings, which partake on the one side of the age, on the other of time». Therefore all things that are, are measured either wholly by the age, or wholly by time, or partly by the age and partly by time: therefore there is no third measure other than these.

3. Likewise, every created thing is either stable and incorruptible, or variable and corruptible; but the first is measured by the age, and the second by time: therefore there is nothing middle between the age and time.

4. Likewise, the *being* of every created thing is either *terminable* or *interminable*. If it is *terminable*, then it is measured by time, which is the principle of corruption, because it makes apart that which is[^3]. But if *interminable*, then by the age: therefore it does not seem that there is any third [thing] measuring besides these two.

**On the contrary:**

1. Before the fourth day there was no time, because it is said, at the making of the luminaries: *Let them be for signs and for times and for days and years*[^4]; and it is evident that there was not only the age, since there were some corporeal things, like herbs and shrubs: therefore there was another measure: therefore, etc.

2. Likewise, after the day of judgment there will be no time, according to what the Angel swears in the Apocalypse[^5]; yet there will be succession and variation in the torments, which cannot be measured by the age: therefore it is necessary to posit a third measure besides these.

3. Likewise, in the affections of the Angels there is intensity and variation, and they themselves are above time, as is said in the book *de Causis*[^6]: therefore that measure of the affections is above time; but it cannot be the age, since in the age no variation falls: therefore it is necessary that there be another measure.

4. Likewise, an Angel, when it is converted to God, is elevated above time: therefore that conversion, and that which it receives in that conversion[^7], is above time; and a thing above time must be measured [by something above time]; but the Angel there knows something which it can cease to think: therefore at least that cannot be measured by the age, which is the measure of an interminable thing, nor by time: therefore, etc.

### Conclusio

> If time is taken properly, then between the age and time there is nothing middle in reality, but [something] differing only in reason; but if [taken] more properly, then there is a middle measure differing [from both], called by the ancients the saeculum.

**I respond:** It must be said that, according as time is divided over against the age, namely in the two last acceptations posited before[^8], it can be taken in two ways: either, that is, insofar as it states the measure of *any* varied duration or of successive variation; and thus between the age and time there is nothing middle *in reality*, but only *in reason*; not, I say, is there something middle differing from both in the genus of *measure*, but [something] middle in the genus of *the measured*, partaking of both, as is that substance which is in the confine of eternity and of time. — And thus all the reasons proceed to the first part, as is easily plain to one looking.

But in another way time is taken insofar as it is the measure of variation, in which there is succession having *continuation* and *regulation* from the motion of the first orb; and this measure has an end and will cease to be. And between this and the age one must posit a middle measure, in which there is *variation*, [but] it need not be [that there is] *cessation*, or *regulation* of the first motion; of which kind there was in the three days of the founding of things, and such as there will be in hell after the last day. And this has been called by the ancient doctors the *saeculum*[^9]. — And this the reasons to the contrary conclude; and thus the whole is plain.

<!-- page 67 -->
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Orta est haec quaestio ex difficultatibus, quae in argg. pro parte affirmativa recensentur, scil. quod ante motum firmamenti et post iudicium non sit tempus, et tamen aliqua duratio successiva; quae etiam in Angelis est quoad *affectiones*, licet ipsi quoad substantiam sint supra tempus. — Solutio supponit distinctionem in praeced. quaest. factam circa tempus in 3. et in 4. sensu acceptum. Si tempus sumitur in sensu ultimo, ita ut importet mensuram *regulatam a motu primi mobilis*, tunc, deficiente hoc motu, actualis variatio et mutatio indiget alia mensura, differente et ab aevo et a tempore in dicto sensu sumto, quae quasi medium obtinet inter utrumque. De hac nonnullorum sententia, confirmata auctoritate Haymonis, plura dicit Alex. Hal. (S. p. I. q. 12. m. 9. a. 4. § 2.), quem sequuntur S. Bonav., Petr. a Tar. et Richard. a Med. — Alii sine ista distinctione simpliciter negant, esse mediam illam mensuram.

**II.** Specialis difficultas est de mensura affectionum et actuum intellectualium in Angelis. S. Thom., S. I. q. 10. a. 5. ad 1, de mente plurimorum dicit, quod «Angeli quantum ad affectiones et intelligentias, in quibus est successio, mensurantur *tempore*... quantum vero ad eorum *esse* naturale mensurantur *aevo*; sed quantum ad *visionem gloriae* participant aeternitatem». Sed Scoto (hic q. 4; Report. hic q. 1; de Rerum princ. q. 1. a. 2.) non placet nec prima nec ultima positio; ipse enim nititur probare, *omnes Angelorum operationes*, quae sunt superiores, etiam liberae et beatificae, mensurari *aevo*, et tantum *transeuntes* tempore.

**III.** Praeter laudatos: B. Albert., S. p. I. tr. 5. q. 23. m. 2. a. 1. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2. a. 2. quaestiunc. 2. — Richard. a Med., hic a. 2. q. 1. — Aegid. R., hic a. 5. dub. later. in fine. — Henr. Gand., Quodl. 12. q. 8. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 2.

---
questions.englishScholion:
**I.** This question arose from the difficulties which are reviewed in the arguments for the affirmative part, namely that before the motion of the firmament and after the judgment there is no time, and yet [there is] some successive duration; which also is in the Angels as regards their *affections*, although they themselves as regards their substance are above time. — The solution presupposes the distinction made in the preceding question concerning time taken in the 3rd and in the 4th sense. If time is taken in the last sense, so that it implies a measure *regulated by the motion of the first movable*, then, this motion failing, actual variation and change needs another measure, differing both from the age and from time taken in the said sense, which holds as it were a middle between both. Of this opinion of several [authors], confirmed by the authority of Haymo, Alexander of Hales says more (S. p. I, q. 12, m. 9, a. 4, § 2), whom St. Bonaventure, Peter of Tarentaise, and Richard of Middleton follow. — Others, without this distinction, simply deny that there is that middle measure.

**II.** A special difficulty concerns the measure of the affections and intellectual acts in the Angels. St. Thomas, S. I, q. 10, a. 5, ad 1, on the mind of most says that «the Angels, as regards their affections and intellections, in which there is succession, are measured by *time*... but as regards their natural *being* are measured by the *age*; but as regards the *vision of glory* they partake of eternity». But it does not please Scotus (here q. 4; Reportatio here q. 1; *On the Principle of Things* q. 1, a. 2), neither the first nor the last position; for he strives to prove that *all the operations of the Angels*, which are higher, even the free and beatific ones, are measured by the *age*, and only as *passing* by time.

**III.** Besides those praised: Bl. Albert, S. p. I, tr. 5, q. 23, m. 2, a. 1. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 2, a. 2, quaestiuncula 2. — Richard of Middleton, here a. 2, q. 1. — Giles of Rome, here a. 5, dub. later. at the end. — Henry of Ghent, Quodl. 12, q. 8. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 2.

---

apparatus.la: Cap. 10. § 3: *Proprietas aeterni* [versio in oper. S. Thomae: *aevi*] *est antiquum et immutabile et universale esse* ... apparatus.en: Chapter 10, § 3: *The property of the eternal* [the reading in the works of St. Thomas: *of the age*] *is to be ancient and immutable and universal being* ... [the reading ibid.: *and to be measured as a whole according to the whole*]. *Time*, however, they speak of in generation and corruption and in changeable things ... *and [that which] holds itself otherwise [at one time] and otherwise [at another]* ... *but the middle of existing and made things, whatsoever they be, partake on the one side of the eternal, on the other of time.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 117. (c. 12.): *Corruptionis enim causa per se tempus est; numerus enim ipsius motus est* ... *tus autem distare facit quod est* [recentior versio: *expellit quod inest*]. Cfr. ibid. text. 128. (c. 13.).
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* IV, text 117 (c. 12): *For time is per se the cause of corruption; for it is the number of motion itself* ... *but it makes apart that which is* [a more recent version: *expels that which is within*]. Cf. ibid., text 128 (c. 13).

apparatus.la: Gen. 1, 14: *Et sint in signa* etc.
apparatus.en: Gen. 1:14: *And let them be for signs* etc.

apparatus.la: Cap. 10, 6: *Et tempus non erit amplius.*
apparatus.en: Chapter 10:6: *And there shall be time no longer.*

apparatus.la: Prop. 29: *Omnis substantia simplex est stans per se ipsam*, scilicet per essentiam suam: quod est, quia creata sine tempore, et est in substantialitate sua superior substantiis temporalibus. Et in prop. 30, substantiae sempiternae dicuntur quod sunt supra tempus. — In fine argumenti Vat. *quod sit in alia mensura* pro *quod sit alia mensura.*
apparatus.en: Proposition 29: *Every simple substance is standing through itself*, namely through its own essence: which is so, because it is created without time, and is in its substantiality superior to temporal substances. And in prop. 30, the sempiternal substances are said to be above time. — At the end of the argument the Vatican edition [reads] *that it be in another measure* for *that there be another measure.*

apparatus.la: Supple: *Angelus.* Vat. cum paucis codd. *accipitur.* Paulo inferius ed. 1 cum pluribus mss., variata interpunctione, *potest desinere cogitare saltem*: ergo.

apparatus.la: In corp. quaest. praeced.
apparatus.en: In the body of the preceding question.

apparatus.la: Damasc., II. de Fide orthod. c. 1. inter varias *saeculi* acceptiones hanc affert: «Quin saeculum quoque dicitur non tempus nec temporis pars ulla solis motu ac cursu definita sive ex dierum noctiumque serie conflata, sed ille velut temporalis motus ac spatium, quod una cum iis quae aeterna sunt, protenditur. Quod enim iis quae tempori subsunt, tempus est, hoc perpetuis est saeculum». Et Haymo, in expos. Epist. ad Titum, 1, 2: *Saecularia* dicuntur a *saeculo*, quod in se resolvantur (revolvantur?), Varrone teste. Saecula autem computantur ex eo, quo materies informis per species discreta est, et ex quo Deus dixit: *Fiat lux, et facta est lux* (Gen. 1, 3.); ex eo enim coepit varietas temporis et vicissitudo horarum pariterque dierum in semet resolvi (revolvi?); antea vero, ut doctores dicunt, non erat *tempus*, sed *aevum*, quod solummodo *esse* habebat.
apparatus.en: Damascene, II *On the Orthodox Faith*, c. 1, among the various acceptations of *saeculum* brings forward this one: «Indeed the saeculum is also said [to be] not time nor any part of time defined by the motion and course of the sun or composed of the series of days and nights, but that, as it were, temporal motion and span which extends together with the things that are eternal. For what to the things subject to time is time, this to perpetual things is the saeculum». And Haymo, in his exposition of the Epistle to Titus, 1, 2: *Secular things* are so called from *saeculum*, because they are resolved (revolved?) into themselves, on the testimony of Varro. The *saecula* are reckoned from that point at which formless matter was distinguished into [its] species, and from which God said: *Let there be light, and there was light* (Gen. 1:3); for from that point began the variety of time and the vicissitude of hours and likewise of days to be resolved (revolved?) into itself; but before, as the doctors say, there was no *time*, but the *age*, which had only *being*. ---

questions.title: Dist. 2, Part 1, Art. 2, Q. 3
questions.titleLa: Utrum spirituales et corporales substantiae simul creatae sint
questions.titleEn: Whether spiritual and corporeal substances were created simultaneously
questions.latin:
<!-- page 67 -->

### Quaestio III. *Utrum spirituales et corporales substantiae simul creatae sint.*

Tertio quaeritur, utrum spirituales substantiae et corporales simul sint creatae. Et videtur, quod sic.

1. In Genesi[^1]: *In principio creavit Deus* etc.; Glossa: «id est spiritualem et corporalem naturam».

2. Item, duodecimo Confessionum[^2]: «Duo invenio, quae fecisti carentia temporibus: unum, quod tua immutabilitate perfruitur, alterum, quod ita informe erat, ut ex forma in quam formam mutaretur, non haberet».

3. Item, *ratione* videtur. Constat, quod Angeli non sunt creati sine loco, quia tunc unus non haberet ordinem ad alium secundum existentiam: oportuit ergo quod fieret empyreum; et iterum, illius concavitas non poterat esse vacua: ergo etc.

4. Item, distinctio dierum attenditur secundum distinctionem rerum[^3], ergo productio ex nihilo praecedit omnem diem: ergo cum materia rerum corporalium sit ex nihilo producta, sicut et natura angelica, quemadmodum natura angelica est ante tempus, similiter videtur, quod materia: et si hoc, ergo in principio durationis: ergo simul.

**Contra:**

1. Ecclesiastici primo[^4]: *Prior omnium creata est sapientia*; constat, quod loquitur de sapientia non divina, sed quae est creata; haec autem est Angelus, ut dicit Glossa. *Si tu dicas,* quod prius est dignitate; obiicitur de Hilario duodecimo de Trinitate[^5]: «Quid magnum, ut ante omnem creaturam Deus Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum genuerit, cum et Angelorum origo terrae creatione reperiatur antiquior».

2. Item, hoc videtur ratione, quam facit Isidorus[^6]: «In rerum conditione primaria conditus est locus poenarum»; sed Deus non praeparavit poenam innocenti: ergo diabolus peccavit ante productionem rerum.

3. Item, videtur, quod non simul potuerint[^7], quia nulla virtus maior est infinita; sed ad productionem unius creaturae necesse est virtutem infinitam exponi: ergo si ad hunc effectum requiritur virtus infinita, et infinito nihil plus potest, ergo virtus illa non potest pro tempore illo alium effectum producere.

4. Item, simplex ad quod se convertit, totaliter se convertit[^8]: ergo si divina virtus est simplicissima, cum se convertit ad aliquem effectum producendum, impossibile est, quod ad aliud se convertat, et ita quod aliud producat: ergo impossibile est, quod simul plura producat.

<!-- page 68 -->

5. Item, quaeritur: quare tantum ista quatuor dicuntur primo esse creata?

### Conclusio

> Quatuor fuerunt primo creata, scilicet caelum empyreum, angelica natura, materia et tempus.

**Respondeo:** Ad praedictorum intelligentiam notandum, quod, sicut extrahitur a Glossa[^9], quatuor fuerunt primo creata, scilicet caelum empyreum, angelica natura, materia et tempus.

Huius autem ratio duplex potest assignari: *una,* quia in principio debuerunt prima in omni genere creari, scilicet in rebus et mensuris, et in rebus corporalibus et spiritualibus, et in corporalibus activis et passivis. Quoniam igitur prima inter substantias spirituales est Angelus, prima inter substantias corporales activas est empyreum, et prima inter passivas est materia elementorum, et prima inter mensuras est tempus, quia non tantum dicit mensuram durationis, sed etiam egressionis: ideo haec quatuor dicuntur primo creata.

Alia ratio potest reddi, quod substantia spiritualis angelica primum debuit fieri tanquam caput et minus dependens, et cum facta fuit, simul habuit distinctionem et ordinem[^10]; sed ordinem existentiae non habuit nisi in aliquo continente: ergo simul factum est caelum empyreum supremum corporum, et ideo capacissimum. Et rursus, cum non posset esse vacuum, necesse fuit, fieri materiam corporalem sive molem; et quia omnis productio est in aliqua mensura, haec tria de necessitate consequitur tempus.

Concedendum igitur, quod quatuor sunt primo creata, et quod angelica natura et corporea simul sunt creatae quantum ad mensurarum concomitantiam, quia simul incepit[^11] duratio materiae et intelligentiae, sicut probatum est.

1. 2. Quod ergo obiicitur, quod *prior omnium* etc.; dicendum, quod, sicut dicit Augustinus in fine duodecimi Confessionum[^12], *prius* dicitur quatuor modis, scilicet *aeternitate, tempore, electione, origine.* Aeternitate Deus praecedit omnia, *tempore* flos fructum, *electione* fructus florem, *origine* sonus cantum. Prioritate ergo *durationis*[^13] nec corporalis natura ante angelicam, nec e converso; prioritate autem *electionis* sive dignitatis *prior omnium creata est sapientia.* — Ad auctoritates Hilarii et Isidori, dicendum, quod ipsi loquuntur secundum illam positionem, quae posuit, creationem tempore praecedere distinctionem. Unde in principio temporis Angelus et materia sunt creata; sed res non fuerunt distinctae usque ad tertium diem. — *Vel* potest dici, quod Hilarius loquitur secundum *opinionem*[^14], et Isidorus de prioritate secundum *praevisionem.*

3. Quod obiicitur, quod Deus totam potentiam exponit ad productionem unius rei; dicendum, quod quamvis *totam* exponat, non tamen *totaliter* exponit. Virtus enim divina non tantum dicitur infinita, quia possit de non-ente facere ens, sed etiam quia non potest tot, quin plura; unde nunquam tot simul producit, quin adhuc possit plura; unde potest, quantum est de se, in infinitum intensione et extensione[^15]. Et ideo non valet illud.

4. Quod obiicitur de simplici, dicendum, quod illud habet locum in illo simplici, in quo simul est simplicitas et finitas; sed de illo, quod simplex est et infinitum simul et semel, veritatem non habet. Illud enim etsi ratione simplicitatis totum se convertat ad id, ad quod se convertit, tamen ratione immensitatis nunquam se totaliter ad effectum producendum convertit.
questions.english:
### Question III. *Whether spiritual and corporeal substances were created simultaneously.*

Thirdly it is asked whether spiritual and corporeal substances were created simultaneously. And it seems that [they were] so.

1. In Genesis[^1]: *In the beginning God created* etc.; the Gloss: «that is, spiritual and corporeal nature».

2. Likewise, the twelfth [book] of the Confessions[^2]: «I find two [things] which you made lacking in times: one which enjoys your immutability, the other which was so formless that it had not [a form] out of which to be changed into [another] form».

3. Likewise, it seems [so] *by reason.* It is established that the Angels were not created without place, because then one would not have an order to another according to existence: it was therefore necessary that the empyrean be made; and again, its concavity could not be empty: therefore etc.

4. Likewise, the distinction of days is reckoned according to the distinction of things[^3], therefore the production out of nothing precedes every day: therefore since the matter of corporeal things was produced out of nothing, just as also the angelic nature, then just as the angelic nature is before time, similarly it seems [so] of matter: and if this [is so], then [it was] at the beginning of duration: therefore simultaneously.

**On the contrary:**

1. Ecclesiasticus, chapter one[^4]: *Wisdom was created before all things*; it is established that it speaks not of divine wisdom, but of that which is created; and this is the Angel, as the Gloss says. *If you say* that it is prior in dignity; the objection [is made] from Hilary, twelfth [book] *On the Trinity*[^5]: «What [is it so] great, that before every creature God should have begotten our Lord Jesus Christ, when even the origin of the Angels is found older than the creation of the earth».

2. Likewise, this seems [so] by the reason which Isidore makes[^6]: «In the primary founding of things the place of punishments was founded»; but God did not prepare punishment for the innocent: therefore the devil sinned before the production of things.

3. Likewise, it seems that they could not [be produced] simultaneously[^7], because no power is greater than the infinite; but for the production of one creature it is necessary that an infinite power be expended: therefore if for this effect an infinite power is required, and to the infinite nothing more can [be added], then that power cannot for that time produce another effect.

4. Likewise, the simple [agent] turns itself wholly to that to which it turns itself[^8]: therefore if the divine power is most simple, when it turns itself to producing some effect, it is impossible that it turn itself to another, and so that it produce another: therefore it is impossible that it produce several [things] simultaneously.

<!-- page 68 -->

5. Likewise, it is asked: why only these four are said to have been created first?

### Conclusion

> Four [things] were created first, namely the empyrean heaven, the angelic nature, matter, and time.

**I respond:** For the understanding of the aforesaid it must be noted that, as is drawn out from the Gloss[^9], four [things] were created first, namely the empyrean heaven, the angelic nature, matter, and time.

A twofold reason for this can be assigned: *one,* because in the beginning the first [members] in every genus had to be created, namely among things and measures, and among corporeal and spiritual things, and among corporeal active and passive [things]. Since therefore the first among spiritual substances is the Angel, the first among corporeal active substances is the empyrean, and the first among the passive [ones] is the matter of the elements, and the first among measures is time — because it states not only the measure of duration but also of issuing-forth: therefore these four are said to have been created first.

Another reason can be given: that the spiritual angelic substance had to be made first as a head and as less dependent, and when it was made, it at once had distinction and order[^10]; but it did not have an order of existence except in some container: therefore at once was made the empyrean heaven, the highest of bodies, and therefore the most capacious. And again, since it could not be empty, it was necessary that corporeal matter or mass be made; and because every production is in some measure, these three of necessity entail time.

It must therefore be granted that four [things] are created first, and that the angelic nature and the corporeal [nature] are created simultaneously as regards the concomitance of the measures, because the duration of matter and of intelligence began[^11] together, as has been proved.

1. 2. To what then is objected, that *[wisdom was created] before all things* etc.; it must be said that, as Augustine says at the end of the twelfth [book] of the Confessions[^12], *prior* is said in four ways, namely *by eternity, by time, by election, by origin.* By eternity God precedes all things, *by time* the flower [precedes] the fruit, *by election* the fruit [precedes] the flower, *by origin* the sound [precedes] the song. By priority therefore of *duration*[^13] neither is the corporeal nature before the angelic, nor conversely; but by priority of *election* or dignity *wisdom was created before all things.* — To the authorities of Hilary and Isidore it must be said that they speak according to that position which held that creation precedes distinction in time. Hence at the beginning of time the Angel and matter were created; but things were not distinct until the third day. — *Or* it can be said that Hilary speaks according to [an] *opinion*[^14], and Isidore of the priority according to *foresight.*

3. To what is objected, that God expends his whole power for the production of one thing; it must be said that although he may expend the *whole* [of it], yet he does not expend it *wholly.* For the divine power is said [to be] infinite not only because it can make a being out of non-being, but also because it cannot [make] so many [things] but [that it can make] more; hence it never produces so many at once but that it can still [produce] more; hence it can, as far as in it lies, [proceed] to infinity in intensity and extension[^15]. And therefore that [argument] does not hold.

4. To what is objected about the simple [agent], it must be said that this holds in that simple [thing] in which simplicity and finitude are together; but of that which is simple and infinite at once and at one time, it is not true. For that [agent], although by reason of [its] simplicity it turns itself wholly to that to which it turns itself, yet by reason of [its] immensity it never turns itself wholly to producing the effect.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Inter doctores Latinos ad quaestionem communiter affirmative respondetur, praesertim post Concil. Lateranense IV., in quo (Cap. *Firmiter*) definitur, quod Deus «*simul ab initio temporis* utramque de nihilo condidit creaturam spiritualem et corporalem». Sed inter Patres, praecipue Graecos, non desunt, qui contrariam sententiam tenent; unde multi opinantur, per dicta verba Concilii contrariam sententiam non esse reprobatam. Etiam S. Thom. in Summa theolog. (loc. cit.) dicit: «Quamvis contrarium non sit reputandum erroneum, praecipue propter sententiam Gregorii Nazianzeni, cuius *tanta est in doctrina* christiana auctoritas, ut nullus unquam eius dictis calumniam inferre praesumserit, sicut nec Athanasii documentis, ut Hieronymus dicit».

**II.** Alex. Hal., S. p. II. q. 19. m. 1. — Loci Scoti collecti a Montefortino, S. tom. II. p. I. q. 61. a. 3. — S. Thom., hic q. 1. a. 3; S. I. q. 61. a. 3; de Potent. q. 3. a. 18. 19. — B. Albert., hic a. 1; S. p. II. tr. 3. q. 11. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 2. a. 3. quaestiunc. 2. — Richard. a Med., hic a. 2. q. 1. — Aegid. R., hic q. 1. a. 1. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 1.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** Among the Latin doctors the question is commonly answered affirmatively, especially after the Fourth Lateran Council, in which (chapter *Firmiter*) it is defined that God «*at once, from the beginning of time*, founded each creature, the spiritual and the corporeal, out of nothing». But among the Fathers, especially the Greeks, there are not lacking those who hold the contrary opinion; whence many think that, by the said words of the Council, the contrary opinion was not reproved. Even St. Thomas in the *Summa theologiae* (loc. cit.) says: «Although the contrary is not to be reckoned erroneous, especially because of the opinion of Gregory Nazianzen, whose *authority in Christian doctrine is so great* that no one ever presumed to bring a calumny against his sayings, just as neither against the writings of Athanasius, as Jerome says».

**II.** Alexander of Hales, S. p. II, q. 19, m. 1. — The passages of Scotus collected by Montefortino, S. tom. II, p. I, q. 61, a. 3. — St. Thomas, here q. 1, a. 3; S. I, q. 61, a. 3; *de Potentia* q. 3, a. 18, 19. — Bl. Albert, here a. 1; S. p. II, tr. 3, q. 11. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 2, a. 3, quaestiuncula 2. — Richard of Middleton, here a. 2, q. 1. — Giles of Rome, here q. 1, a. 1. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 1.

---

questions.titleLa: Utrum caelum empyreum sit, et cuiusmodi sit
questions.titleEn: Whether the empyrean heaven exists, and of what kind it is
questions.latin:
<!-- page 70 -->

### ARTICULUS I.

### *De natura caeli empyrei in se.*

### Quaestio I. *Utrum caelum empyreum sit, et cuiusmodi sit.*

Quaeritur ergo primo de caelo empyreo quantum ad qualitatem naturae, et quaeritur, utrum caelum empyreum sit, et si sit, cuiusmodi sit. Et quod sit, videtur.

1. In quolibet genere mobile praesupponit immobile[^1], quia omne fluxibile ad fixum terminatur; sed corpus caeli siderei est mobile: ergo supra illud de necessitate est ponere ulterius corpus, quod sit *immobile*; hoc autem dico empyreum. *Si tu dicas*, quod non requiritur, quia motus circularis est circa locum et non requirit immobilitatem nisi a parte medii[^2]; *contra*: totum caelum movetur;

<!-- page 71 -->

tunc ergo quaero de ultima superficie caeli, utrum moveatur; constat quod sic; sed omne mobile est in loco[^3], quia «non quaereretur locus, nisi esset motus»: ergo etc.

2. Item, in quolibet genere multiforme praesupponit uniforme, sicut multa praesupponunt unum[^4]; sed caelum sidereum est multiforme: ergo ultra illud et supra est corpus *uniforme*; hoc autem dicimus empyreum: ergo etc.

3. Item, in quolibet genere, in quo est ponere infimum et medium, est ponere supremum; sed gradus in corporibus attenditur secundum gradus perspicui et lucis; sed invenitur corpus opacum simpliciter, ut terra, et simpliciter[^5] secundum totum opacum: ergo si complementum est in corporibus, debet esse corpus simpliciter et secundum totum *luminosum*; hoc dico empyreum: ergo etc.

4. Item, habitatio habitatori debet respondere: ergo cum aliquis locus tenebrosus damnatis debeatur, ergo per oppositum videtur, quod lucidus debeatur Beatis[^6].

**Contra:**

1. Quod non conveniat universo, quod illud sit corpus *uniforme*, videtur, quia corpora mundi principalia creata sunt ordinata et ornata: ergo cum ornatus consistat in maiori distinctione et pulcritudinis additione, impossibile est, corpus illud esse uniforme.

2. Item, lux se diffundit secundum omnem differentiam positionis, ergo sursum et deorsum; sed lux solis maxime est diffusionis inter corpora mundi: ergo sursum se diffundit, cum non habeat obstaculum. Ergo cum non se habeat semper uniformiter, modo illuminat unam partem empyrei, modo aliam: ergo corpus illud non est uniforme in luminositate, ut videtur.

3. Item, quod non conveniat esse aliquod caelum *immobile*, videtur, quia omne caelum necessario est sphaericae figurae, sicut probat Philosophus[^7], et rei veritas est; sed sphaerica figura apta est omnino motui: ergo omne caelum, eo ipso quod caelum, est mobile: ergo etc.

4. Item, quod propinquius est motori citius et velocius movetur[^8]; sed corpus supremum est tale: ergo non solum moveri, sed etiam velocissime moveri competit sibi.

5. Item, hoc nobilitatis est in caelo, ut moveatur — unde orbis primus, scilicet caeli stellati, movetur velocius, et ratio huius est, ut assimiletur suo motori[^9] — sed quanto aliquod corpus superius, tanto nobilius et motori similius et tanto mobilius: ergo si empyreum est ultra firmamentum, non est ergo immobile.

### Conclusio

> Est caelum empyreum, et quidem uniforme, immobile et perfecte luminosum.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod quamvis Sancti parum loquantur de hoc caelo, quia latet nostros sensus, et philosophi adhuc minus, tamen ponere est caelum empyreum, sicut dicit sacra Scriptura: *In principio creavit Deus caelum et terram*[^10]. Strabus exponit de empyreo, et hoc probat per litteram sequentem, quia firmamentum et caelum aqueum facta sunt secundo die. Et Damascenus[^11] hoc exponit: *In principio creavit Deus caelum*, id est «sine stellis sphaericae formae».

Ponendum est etiam illud caelum, quia persuadet ratio finis triplex. Una est *perfectio universi*, alia est propter *motum firmamenti*, et tertia principalis propter *habitationem hominis beati*. Et quoniam finis imponit necessitatem his quae sunt ad finem, propter *perfectionem*[^12] *universi* necesse est, ipsum esse *uniforme*, quia, cum sit caelum luminosum difforme, si non esset uniforme, non esset universum completum. Propter *motum firmamenti* ponendum est ipsum *immobile*, ut motus mobilis fiat circa immobile, scilicet centrum, et intra continens immobile et locans[^13], scilicet empyreum.

<!-- page 72 -->

Propter *habitationem hominis beati* ponendum est ipsum *luminositatis* perfectae, ut habitatio congruat suo habitatori. — Ex his igitur colligitur, quare sit factum, et cuius sit dispositionis inter alios caelos, quia *uniforme, immobile et luminositatis perfectae*.

1. Quod obiicitur, quod non est uniforme, quia[^14] ornatum; dicendum, quod ipsa lux propter sui nobilitatem est sibi ornatus; quoniam ergo corpus illud est luminosum per totum, alio ornatu non indiget. — Vel potest dici, quod, sicut illud caelum decoratum est *astris*, ita istud Angelis, qui sunt quasi astra caeli empyrei, iuxta illud Iob trigesimo octavo[^15]: *Cum me laudarent astra matutina.* Et iterum, *astra* eius erunt homines beati, et quasi *sol* eius erit Agnus Dei.

2. Quod obiicitur, quod sol diffundit lumen in ipsum empyreum; dicendum, quod illius corporis non est recipere lumen, ad minus[^16] ab inferioribus. Et ratio huius est limitatio virtutis a parte solis, quia nihil agit ultra terminum sibi a Deo constitutum. Unde sicut ignis stat, cum pervenit ad horizontem, nec ultra progreditur, et terra, cum pervenit ad centrum; ita solis radii non protenduntur extra firmamentum, quia lucerna est huius visibilis orbis. — Alia ratio est, quia maior influentia absorbet minorem; et ideo tanta est illius caeli influentia, quod ad ipsum non pervenit minor, sicut candela non illuminat solem.

3. 4. Quod obiicitur, quod est mobile, quia sphaericum et propinquum[^17]; dicendum, quod ad motum non sufficit sphaerica figura, sed etiam necessarius est, ut dicunt aliqui, locus continens; et rationabile videtur. Necessarius est etiam absque dubio effectus, vel utilitas mobilis vel alterius. Quoniam ergo caelum illud non est in alio, et quoniam est uniforme per totum, per sui motum nihil faceret; et ideo est immobile. Similiter, quia est uniforme, non habet moveri, quia non habet dextrum et sinistrum. — Sed prima ratio de immobilitate non habet multam necessitatem, cum motus circularis secundum Philosophum[^18] non requirat locum *in quo*, sed *circa quem*. Secunda de utilitate similiter, quia similiter posset dici de aqueo; eodem modo de tertia[^19]. Praeterea, dextrum et sinistrum sunt in caelo non ratione diversitatis partium, sed ratione influentiae motoris; et illud satis faciliter probatur, quia dextrum et sinistrum non mutatur, quamvis omnes partes caeli mutentur.

Et ideo ratio, quare non movetur, est, quia Deus nihil influit super ipsum ad motum, sed ad quietem tantum; et sicut influentia Dei movet firmamentum, sic quietat empyreum. — Ratio autem huius est, quia locus ille est regio deputata his qui omni modo in statu sunt et quiete; et ita patet, quod non magis appropinquat motori, ut *motor* est, sed ut est *stabiliens*. — Ex hac ratione, scilicet quia est, ut sit locus Beatorum, accipitur triplex eius proprietas[^20], scilicet *immobilitas, uniformitas* et *luminositas*. Et haec est ratio magis catholica, quia etiam motus caeli stellati non est nisi propter obsequium hominis viatoris; unde numero electorum completo, non erit amplius revolutio. Rationes autem philosophicae[^21], quae assignantur de motu caeli, apud fideles plus habent vanitatis quam veritatis, si quis diligenter aspiciat.

5. Quod enim obiicit de assimilatione, responderi potest, quod illa causa est nulla, sed impletio numeri electorum. — Vel dicendum, quod est assimilatio in *essendo*, et est assimilatio in *causando*. Verbum Philosophi non habet veritatem primo modo, quia Deus et motor caeli est immobilis; sed secundo modo, quia per sui motum est causa generationis[^22]. Quia ergo empyreum non assimilaretur in *causando*, si moveretur, et esset minus simile in *essendo*; ideo simpliciter dicendum, ipsum esse immobile. Et sic patent omnia.

questions.english:
### ARTICLE I.

### *On the nature of the empyrean heaven in itself.*

### Question I. *Whether the empyrean heaven exists, and of what kind it is.*

It is asked, therefore, first concerning the empyrean heaven as to the quality of [its] nature, and it is asked whether the empyrean heaven exists, and, if it exists, of what kind it is. And that it exists, it seems.

1. In every genus the mobile presupposes the immobile[^1], because everything flowing terminates at something fixed; but the body of the starry heaven is mobile: therefore above it of necessity one must posit a further body, which is *immobile*; and this I call the empyrean. *If you say* that [this] is not required, because circular motion is around a place and does not require immobility except on the part of the center[^2]; *on the contrary*: the whole heaven moves;

<!-- page 71 -->

then therefore I ask concerning the outermost surface of the heaven, whether it moves; it is established that [it does] so; but everything mobile is in a place[^3], because «a place would not be sought, were there not motion»: therefore etc.

2. Likewise, in every genus the multiform presupposes the uniform, just as the many presuppose the one[^4]; but the starry heaven is multiform: therefore beyond and above it there is a *uniform* body; and this we call the empyrean: therefore etc.

3. Likewise, in every genus in which there is something lowest and something intermediate to posit, there is something highest to posit; but grade in bodies is reckoned according to the grades of the transparent and of light; but a body is found wholly opaque, like earth, and wholly[^5] opaque throughout: therefore if there is a completion in bodies, there must be a body wholly and throughout *luminous*; and this I call the empyrean: therefore etc.

4. Likewise, the dwelling ought to correspond to the dweller: therefore since some dark place is owed to the damned, then by the opposite it seems that a bright [place] is owed to the Blessed[^6].

**On the contrary:**

1. That it does not befit the universe that it be a *uniform* body, seems [so], because the principal bodies of the world were created ordered and adorned: therefore since adornment consists in greater distinction and the addition of beauty, it is impossible that that body be uniform.

2. Likewise, light diffuses itself according to every difference of position, therefore upward and downward; but the light of the sun is of the greatest diffusion among the bodies of the world: therefore it diffuses itself upward, since it has no obstacle. Therefore since it does not behave always uniformly — now it illumines one part of the empyrean, now another: therefore that body is not uniform in luminosity, as it seems.

3. Likewise, that it does not befit there to be any *immobile* heaven, seems [so], because every heaven is necessarily of spherical figure, as the Philosopher proves[^7], and the truth of the matter is [so]; but a spherical figure is apt for motion entirely: therefore every heaven, by the very fact that it is a heaven, is mobile: therefore etc.

4. Likewise, what is nearer to the mover moves more quickly and more swiftly[^8]; but the highest body is such: therefore not only to be moved, but also to be moved most swiftly, befits it.

5. Likewise, it belongs to [the] nobility in a heaven that it be moved — whence the first orb, namely that of the starry heaven, moves more swiftly, and the reason for this is that it may be assimilated to its mover[^9] — but the higher some body [is], the nobler and the more like the mover and the more mobile [it is]: therefore if the empyrean is beyond the firmament, it is therefore not immobile.

### Conclusion

> The empyrean heaven exists, and indeed [it is] uniform, immobile, and perfectly luminous.

**I respond:** It must be said that although the Saints speak little of this heaven, because it is hidden from our senses, and the philosophers [speak of it] still less, nevertheless one must posit that there is an empyrean heaven, as Scripture itself says: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth*[^10]. Strabus expounds [this] of the empyrean, and he proves this by the following text, since the firmament and the watery heaven were made on the second day. And Damascene[^11] expounds it [thus]: *In the beginning God created heaven*, that is, «without stars, of spherical form».

That heaven must also be posited because a threefold reason of end persuades [it]. One is the *perfection of the universe*, another is on account of the *motion of the firmament*, and the third [and] principal is on account of the *dwelling of blessed man*. And since the end imposes necessity on the things which are for the end, on account of the *perfection*[^12] *of the universe* it is necessary that it be *uniform*, because, since [if] it were a non-uniform luminous heaven, were it not uniform, the universe would not be complete. On account of the *motion of the firmament* it must be posited *immobile*, so that the motion of the mobile may take place around the immobile, namely the center, and within a containing immobile and locating [body][^13], namely the empyrean.

<!-- page 72 -->

On account of the *dwelling of blessed man* it must be posited of perfect *luminosity*, so that the dwelling may be congruous to its dweller. — From these [things], therefore, it is gathered why it was made and of what disposition it is among the other heavens, namely *uniform, immobile, and of perfect luminosity*.

1. To what is objected, that it is not uniform because[^14] adorned; it must be said that the light itself, on account of its nobility, is its own adornment; since therefore that body is luminous throughout, it needs no other adornment. — Or it can be said that, just as that [starry] heaven is adorned with *stars*, so this [empyrean is adorned] with the Angels, who are as it were the stars of the empyrean heaven, according to that [text] of Job thirty-eight[^15]: *When the morning stars praised me.* And again, its *stars* will be the blessed men, and as it were its *sun* will be the Lamb of God.

2. To what is objected, that the sun diffuses light into the empyrean itself; it must be said that it does not belong to that body to receive light, at least[^16] from things below. And the reason for this is the limitation of power on the part of the sun, because nothing acts beyond the term set for it by God. Hence, just as fire stops when it reaches the horizon, nor goes further, and earth [stops] when it reaches the center; so the sun's rays are not extended beyond the firmament, because [the sun] is the lamp of this visible orb. — Another reason is that a greater influence absorbs a lesser one; and therefore so great is the influence of that heaven that a lesser one does not reach it, just as a candle does not illumine the sun.

3. 4. To what is objected, that it is mobile because spherical and near[^17]; it must be said that for motion a spherical figure does not suffice, but there is also necessary, as some say, a containing place; and [this] seems reasonable. There is also necessary, without doubt, an effect, or the utility of the mobile or of another. Since therefore that heaven is not in another, and since it is uniform throughout, by its motion it would do nothing; and therefore it is immobile. Likewise, since it is uniform, it does not have [the property] to be moved, because it does not have right and left. — But the first reason concerning immobility does not have much necessity, since circular motion, according to the Philosopher[^18], does not require a place *in which*, but [a place] *around which*. The second, concerning utility, likewise, because the same could be said of the watery [heaven]; in the same way concerning the third[^19]. Moreover, right and left are in the heaven not by reason of a diversity of parts, but by reason of the influence of the mover; and that is proved easily enough, because right and left do not change, although all the parts of the heaven change.

And therefore the reason why it does not move is that God infuses nothing into it toward motion, but only toward rest; and just as the influence of God moves the firmament, so it brings the empyrean to rest. — But the reason for this is that that place is a region deputed for those who are in every way in [a state of] stability and rest; and so it is clear that it does not approach the mover more [in so far] as it is *mover*, but [in so far] as it is *stabilizing*. — From this reason, namely because it is [there] so that it may be the place of the Blessed, its threefold property is taken[^20], namely *immobility, uniformity*, and *luminosity*. And this is the more catholic reason, because even the motion of the starry heaven is only on account of the service of wayfaring man; whence, the number of the elect being completed, there will be no further revolution. But the philosophical reasons[^21] which are assigned concerning the motion of the heaven, among the faithful have more of vanity than of truth, if one looks diligently.

5. As to what he objects concerning assimilation, it can be answered that that cause is null, but [the cause is] the filling-up of the number of the elect. — Or it must be said that there is an assimilation in *being*, and there is an assimilation in *causing*. The saying of the Philosopher does not have truth in the first way, because God and the mover of the heaven is immobile; but [it has truth] in the second way, because by its motion it is the cause of generation[^22]. Since therefore the empyrean would not be assimilated in *causing*, if it were moved, and would be less similar in *being*; therefore it must be said simply that it is immobile. And so all [the objections] are clear.

**I.** S. Bonav. (Breviloq. p. II. c. 3.) distinguit «tres caelos principales, scil. empyreum, crystallinum et firmamentum. Intra firmamentum autem, quod est caelum stellarum, continentur septem orbes planetarum, qui sunt saturnus, iupiter, mars, sol, venus, mercurius, luna... et sic procedendo a summo cardine caeli usque ad centrum terrae, decem concurrunt orbes caelestes et quatuor sphaerae elementares». Plura de his vide hic dub. 2, infra d. 14. per totam, d. 12. a. 2. q. 1. 2. 3. — Ex sacra Scriptura satis constat, esse aliquem locum ut habitaculum statui Beatorum congruum, qui ab antiquis doctoribus vocabatur *caelum empyreum*. De natura eius, sicut et de numero, motu et qualitatibus caelorum in genere, illa aetate exortae sunt non paucae quaestiones, quae pro conditione scientiae de rebus physicis et astronomicis tunc vigentis a theologis non sine multis controversiis solvebantur. Non tamen est opinandum, illos doctores multas de istis rebus assertiones habuisse ut spectantes ad fidem, vel ut certas. Ipse S. Bonav. pluries observat, suas conclusiones videri tantum probabiliores. Nemo negare potest, nostra aetate, mediante accuratiore observatione, rerum naturalium scientias progressum fecisse maximum, multasque assertiones Aristotelis de hac re omnium calculo nunc iure reprobari, quae tunc omnium doctorum sententia approbatae erant. Quare non paucae sententiae et multa argumenta de rebus physicis, quae hic et in nonnullis aliis quaestionibus sequentibus occurrunt, nunc obsoleta sunt. Hinc superfluum videtur singulorum magistrorum de his sententias annotare, sed sufficiat indicare auctores de hac et seq. quaest. tractantes.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** St. Bonaventure (*Breviloquium* p. II, c. 3) distinguishes «three principal heavens, namely the empyrean, the crystalline, and the firmament. Within the firmament, however, which is the heaven of the stars, are contained the seven orbs of the planets, which are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, the Moon... and so proceeding from the highest hinge of the heaven down to the center of the earth, ten celestial orbs and four elemental spheres concur». More on these see here dub. 2, below d. 14 throughout, d. 12, a. 2, q. 1, 2, 3. — From sacred Scripture it is sufficiently established that there is some place as a dwelling congruous to the state of the Blessed, which by the ancient doctors was called the *empyrean heaven*. Concerning its nature, as also concerning the number, motion, and qualities of the heavens in general, in that age there arose not a few questions, which, given the condition of the science of physical and astronomical matters then flourishing, were resolved by the theologians not without many controversies. Yet it is not to be supposed that those doctors held many of their assertions about these matters as pertaining to faith, or as certain. St. Bonaventure himself repeatedly observes that his conclusions seem only [the] more probable. No one can deny that in our age, by means of more accurate observation, the natural sciences have made the greatest progress, and that many assertions of Aristotle on this matter are now by everyone's reckoning rightly rejected, which then by the opinion of all the doctors were approved. Hence not a few opinions and many arguments about physical matters, which occur here and in some other following questions, are now obsolete. Hence it seems superfluous to annotate the opinions of the individual masters on these [matters], but let it suffice to indicate the authors treating of this and the following question.

**II.** Alexander of Hales, S. p. II, q. 19, m. 3, a. 1, 2, 3, and q. 47, m. 1-5. — Scotus, II *Sent.* d. 14, q. 1, 2, 3, and *Reportatio* d. 14, q. 1. — St. Thomas, here q. 2, a. 1-3; S. I, q. 61, a. 4, q. 66, a. 3, q. 68, a. 4. — Bl. Albert, here a. 3-5; S. p. II, tr. 3, q. 12. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 3, a. 1, 2, 3. — Richard of Middleton, here a. 3, q. 1, 2, 3. — Giles of Rome, here q. 2, a. 1, 2, 3, 4. — Durandus, here q. 1, 2. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 3, 4. — Biel, II *Sent.* d. 14, q. unic.
