apparatus.la: Cfr. tom. 1. pag. 78, nota 2. et pag. 157, nota 11. — Paulo superius Vat. *cuiusmodi naturae* pro *cuiusmodi*.
apparatus.en: Cf. tom. 1, p. 78, note 2, and p. 157, note 11. — A little above, the Vatican edition [reads] *cuiusmodi naturae* ["of what kind of nature"] for *cuiusmodi* ["of what kind"].

apparatus.la: Vide Aristot., VIII. Phys. text. 76. (c. 9.), ubi probat, motum circularem ex sua natura esse continuum, quia in ipso per se non distinguitur principium, medium et finis; haec enim tria pertinent ad centrum, *circa quod*, non *ad quod* movetur.
apparatus.en: See Aristotle, VIII *Physics* text 76 (c. 9), where he proves that circular motion is of its nature continuous, because in it of itself beginning, middle, and end are not distinguished; for these three pertain to the center, *around which*, not *toward which*, [the thing] moves.

apparatus.la: Aristot., V. Phys. text. 8. (c. 1.): «Omne quod movetur, in loco est». Sequens prop. est Aristot., IV. Phys. text. 32. (c. 4.), quam Vat. invertit *non quaereretur motus, nisi esset locus.* Nonnulli codd. *nisi esset locus motus (localis motus?)* quod respondet Aristot. textui.) — Notamus, quod in hoc argumento proponitur solutio difficultatis, quae animos Commentatorum Aristotelis, IV. Phys. text. 43. (c. 5.), diu agitabat, et quam Averroes ita proponit: «Accidit in eo magna quaestio, quoniam manifestum est, ipsum (totum orbem) moveri, et cum omne motum sit in loco, necesse est, ut totus orbis sit in loco: ergo sumus inter duo: aut ponere, quod aliquid motum non est in loco, aut ponere, quod locus est inane (vacuum) et dimensio». Refutatis dein opinionibus Ioannis Grammatici, Themistii, Alfarabii, Avempacis, ipse tenet, quod ultima sphaera seu caelum dicatur esse *in loco* per accidens, in quantum centrum terrae, *circa quod* revolvitur et cuius indiget tanquam quiescentis et fixi, habet *esse in loco*.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, V *Physics* text 8 (c. 1): «Everything that is moved is in a place». The following proposition is Aristotle, IV *Physics* text 32 (c. 4), which the Vatican edition inverts: *motion would not be sought, were there not a place.* Some codices [read] *nisi esset locus motus (localis motus?)*, which corresponds to Aristotle's text). — We note that in this argument is proposed the solution of a difficulty which long agitated the minds of the Commentators on Aristotle, IV *Physics* text 43 (c. 5), and which Averroes proposes thus: «There arises in this a great question, since it is manifest that it (the whole orb) is moved, and since everything moved is in a place, it is necessary that the whole orb be in a place: therefore we are between two [alternatives]: either to posit that something moved is not in a place, or to posit that a place is something empty (a void) and dimension». Then, the opinions of John the Grammarian, Themistius, Alfarabi, [and] Avempace having been refuted, he himself holds that the outermost sphere or heaven is said to be *in a place* per accidens, in so far as it has *being in a place* [through] the center of the earth, *around which* it revolves and which it needs as something at rest and fixed.

apparatus.la: Aristot., II. de Caelo et mundo, text. 22. (c. 4.): Prius natura in unoquoque genere est unum multis.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, II *On the Heaven and the World*, text 22 (c. 4): Prior by nature in each genus is the one to the many.

apparatus.la: In nonnullis codd. ut X Z deest *simpliciter.* Vat. legit *Sed invenitur corpus opacum simpliciter et secundum totum, ut terra.* Ed. 4, retenta lectione codd., ultimam propositionis partem sic exhibet *ut terra, et simpliciter et secundum totum opacum, ut firmamentum.*
apparatus.en: In some codices, as X Z, *simpliciter* is lacking. The Vatican edition reads *But a body is found wholly opaque and throughout, like earth.* Ed. 4, the reading of the codices being retained, presents the last part of the proposition thus: *like earth, both wholly and throughout opaque, like the firmament.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., de Mundo, c. 7. (c. 6.) de habitatione Dei loquens ait: *Quem locum tum Uranon ab origine vocis dicimus quasi terminum extimum supremorum corporum, tum etiam Olympum ut usquequaque lucidum, ab omni caligine secretum motuque omni incondito* etc.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the World*, c. 7 (c. 6), speaking of the dwelling of God, says: *Which place we call both Uranon from the origin of the word, as it were the outermost term of the highest bodies, and also Olympus as everywhere bright, secluded from all darkness and from all disordered motion* etc.

apparatus.la: Libr. II. de Caelo et mundo, text. 22. seqq. (c. 4.).
apparatus.en: Book II *On the Heaven and the World*, text 22 and following (c. 4).

apparatus.la: Aristot., VIII. Phys. text. 84. (c. 10.): Celerrime moventur quae proxima sunt moventi. Cfr. de Mundo, c. 7. (c. 6.).
apparatus.en: Aristotle, VIII *Physics* text 84 (c. 10): Most swiftly move the things which are nearest to the mover. Cf. *On the World*, c. 7 (c. 6).

apparatus.la: Averroes super XII. Metaph. text. 37: Primum enim caelum movetur ab isto motore secundum desiderium, ut assimiletur ei secundum suum *posse*, sicut amatum movetur, ut assimiletur suo amato; alia autem corpora caelestia moventur secundum desiderium ad motum primi corporis etc. Cfr. etiam Avicenna, IX. Metaph. c. 2. seqq.
apparatus.en: Averroes on XII *Metaphysics* text 37: For the first heaven is moved by that mover according to desire, that it may be assimilated to it according to its *capacity*, just as the beloved is moved that it may be assimilated to its lover; but the other celestial bodies are moved according to desire toward the motion of the first body etc. Cf. also Avicenna, IX *Metaphysics* c. 2 and following.

apparatus.la: Gen. 1, 1. — Verba Strabi vide hic, lit. Magistri, c. 4.
apparatus.en: Genesis 1:1. — For the words of Strabus see here, the text of the Master, c. 4.

apparatus.la: Libr. II. de Fide orthod. c. 6.
apparatus.en: Book II *On the Orthodox Faith*, c. 6.

apparatus.la: Cod. Z *propter perfectam rationem*, qui subinde post *si non esset* adiungit *empyreum quod est.*
apparatus.en: Codex Z [reads] *on account of [its] perfect character*, which thereupon, after *si non esset*, adds *empyreum quod est.*

apparatus.la: Plurimi codd. cum ed. 1 *et locum*, in aliquibus tamen codd., ed. 1 et in anecdoto compendio Commentarii S. Bonaventurae, scripto a Fr. Gulielmo de Mara, habetur *locans.*
apparatus.en: Most codices, with ed. 1, [read] *et locum* ["and place"]; in some codices, however, [in] ed. 1, and in the unpublished compendium of the Commentary of St. Bonaventure written by Fr. William de la Mare, is found *locans* ["locating"].

apparatus.la: Vat. cum nonnullis codd. perperam addit *non.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, with some codices, wrongly adds *non.*

apparatus.la: Vers. 7, in cuius expositione Gregor., XXVIII. Moral. c. 14. n. 34, Angelos vocat astra matutina, homines redemtos autem astra vespertina. — In fine solutionis alluditur ad Apoc. 21, 23.
apparatus.en: Verse 7, in the exposition of which Gregory, XXVIII *Morals*, c. 14, n. 34, calls the Angels morning stars, but redeemed men evening stars. — At the end of the solution allusion is made to Apocalypse 21:23.

apparatus.la: Vat. *lumen maius.* Paulo inferius cod. H *ad suam sphaeram* pro *ad horizontem* (in codd. et primis edd. *horizonta*; codd. N aa adiungunt *suum*). Dein post *progreditur* in codd. A U additur *et mare cum pervenit ad littus.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition [reads] *lumen maius* ["greater light"]. A little below, codex H [reads] *ad suam sphaeram* ["to its sphere"] for *ad horizontem* ["to the horizon"] (in the codices and the first editions *horizonta*; codices N aa add *suum*). Then after *progreditur*, in codices A U is added *and the sea, when it reaches the shore.*

apparatus.la: Supple cum Vat. *motori*, quae etiam aliquanto inferius pro *vel utilitas* ponit *videlicet utilitas.*
apparatus.en: Supply, with the Vatican edition, *motori* ["to the mover"], which also a little below, for *vel utilitas* ["or the utility"], puts *videlicet utilitas* ["namely the utility"].

apparatus.la: Cfr. supra pag. 70, nota 4, et l. de Caelo et mundo, text. 5. (c. 2.), ubi ait: «Circularis igitur [motus] est, qui circa medium fit». Libr. II. de Caelo et mundo, text. 27. (c. 4.) probat, caelum esse sphaericae figurae, ex hoc quod in omnibus aliis motibus accideret, et locum et vacuum esse extra lationem caeli, quod est impossibile. — Cfr. in eodem libro text. 7. seqq. (c. 2. seqq.) cum Comment. Averrois, quae spectant ad ea quae sequuntur de dextro et sinistro in caelo et de eius influentia.
apparatus.en: Cf. above p. 70, note 4, and the book *On the Heaven and the World*, text 5 (c. 2), where he says: «Circular [motion], therefore, is that which takes place around the middle». Book II *On the Heaven and the World*, text 27 (c. 4), proves that the heaven is of spherical figure, from the fact that in all other motions there would result both a place and a void outside the bearing of the heaven, which is impossible. — Cf. in the same book text 7 and following (c. 2 and following) with the Commentary of Averroes, [the things] which pertain to what follows concerning right and left in the heaven and concerning its influence.

apparatus.la: Intellige: dici posset respectu caeli aquei. — Vat., interpunctione variata, sic: *Secunda de utilitate non similiter, quia similiter posset dici de aqueo: eodem modo de tertia, quia dextrum* etc. Codd. sunt divisi inter se quoad primam propositionis partem; nam aliqui ut T Y aa cc cum ed. 1 pro *utilitate* substituunt *inutilitate*, retinentes particulam *non*, excepto cod. aa, quem in hoc sumus secuti; alii consentiunt lectioni Vat., quae explicatur ex cod. 1: *Secunda de utilitate non valeret similiter.* Quoad alteram partem codd. et primae edd. sunt contra Vat., quae etiam paulo inferius cum nonnullis mss. ponit *non mutantur* pro *non mutatur.*
apparatus.en: Understand: it could be said with respect to the watery heaven. — The Vatican edition, with the punctuation varied, [reads] thus: *The second, concerning utility, not similarly, because the same could be said of the watery [heaven]: in the same way concerning the third, because right* etc. The codices are divided among themselves as to the first part of the proposition; for some, as T Y aa cc with ed. 1, for *utilitate* substitute *inutilitate*, retaining the particle *non*, except codex aa, which we have followed in this; others agree with the reading of the Vatican edition, which is explained from cod. 1: *The second, concerning utility, would not similarly hold.* As to the other part the codices and the first editions are against the Vatican edition, which also a little below, with some manuscripts, puts *non mutantur* for *non mutatur.*

apparatus.la: Cod. cc et ed. 1 *accipitur triplex ratio, secundum quod est triplex eius proprietas.*
apparatus.en: Codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *a threefold reason is taken, according as its property is threefold.*

apparatus.la: Vat. *Philosophi.* Aliquanto inferius cod. cc et ed. 1 *inspiciat* pro *aspiciat.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition [reads] *Philosophi* ["of the Philosopher"]. A little below, codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *inspiciat* for *aspiciat.*

apparatus.la: Cfr. Aristot., II. de Gener. et corrupt., text. 56. seqq. (c. 10.). — Mox Vat. *non magis assimilaretur* pro *non assimilaretur.*
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, II *On Generation and Corruption*, text 56 and following (c. 10). — Shortly after, the Vatican edition [reads] *non magis assimilaretur* for *non assimilaretur.* ---

questions.title: Dist. 2, Part 2, Art. 1, Q. 2
questions.titleLa: Utrum caelum empyreum influat in haec inferiora
questions.titleEn: Whether the empyrean heaven influences these lower things
questions.latin:
<!-- page 73 -->

### Quaestio II. *Utrum caelum empyreum influat in haec inferiora.*

Secundo quaeritur de empyreo quantum ad virtutem influentiae. Et quaeritur, utrum empyreum influat in haec inferiora, an non. Et quod sic, videtur.

1. In quolibet creato, quod est perfectum et completum, est substantia, virtus et operatio[^1]: ergo in ipso empyreo. Si ergo habet virtutem, aut operatur in id quod supra, vel in id quod iuxta, vel in id quod infra. Non in id quod supra, planum est; nec in id quod iuxta, quia ipsum est supra omnia corpora: ergo videtur, quod per illam virtutem influit in id quod infra; aut virtus et substantia eius erit otiosa, quod est plane inconveniens.

2. Item, omnia corpora propter humanum obsequium sunt facta, unde «sumus nos finis quodam modo omnium eorum quae sunt[^2]»: ergo si empyreum aliquid est, de aliquo servit homini; sed hoc non faceret, nisi aliquid in haec inferiora influeret: ergo etc.

3. Item, quanto aliquod corpus situ est superius, tanto inter corpora nobilius est[^3], et quanto nobilius, tanto potentius et melius, et quanto potentius et melius, tanto in agendo et influendo efficacius: si ergo caelum empyreum est supremum, ergo videtur, quod sit maxime influens in haec inferiora.

4. Item, quanto lumen[^4] est maius, tanto magis se diffundit et multiplicat: si ergo empyreum inter corpora est luminosum maxime, ergo maxime diffusivum; sed lumen illud non privatur efficacia vegetandi et conservandi, quemadmodum nec lumen firmamenti: ergo videtur, quod empyreum in haec inferiora magis sit influens.

**Contra:**

1. Influentia caelestis corporis maxime consistit in diffusione luminis et caloris; sed empyreum non calefacit[^5], nec ista corpora inferiora irradiat: ergo videtur, quod nulla sit influentia empyrei in haec inferiora.

2. Item, corpora, quae sunt infra firmamentum, sufficienter influunt ad vegetationem et generationem in his inferioribus faciendam: ergo «si natura nihil frustra facit[^6]», videtur, quod alterius caeli influentia nulla sit, cum nullius sit opportunitatis.

3. Item, influentia caeli debet esse conformis ei a quo est, debet etiam nihilominus esse conformis ei a quo recipitur; sed caelum empyreum est

<!-- page 74 -->

incorruptibile, uniforme, quietissimum, statui et quieti gloriae deputatum, haec autem, quae infra sunt, habent omnino oppositas conditiones: ergo videtur, quod nullo modo super corpora inferiora influere habeat[^7].

4. Item, si influit super corpora, aut ergo ad nobiliorem effectum, quam sit influentia octavae sphaerae, aut ad *minus nobilem*, aut ad *eundem* effectum. Ad *eundem* non *oportet*; ad *minus nobilem* non *decet*, cum illud corpus sit nobilius; ad *magis nobilem* non *potest*: ergo nullo modo influit. *Probatio*: quod non *possit* in magis nobilem, videtur. Nam, sicut volunt philosophi et communiter tenent viri physici[^8], influentia caeli est operans ad productionem animae sensibilis; sed supra animam sensibilem non est nisi rationalis, haec autem nulli corpori est subiecta, immo est a creatione pura: ergo nullo modo potest eminentior esse influentia quam supra animam sensibilem; et supra hanc influit firmamentum sufficienter cum his quae sunt infra: ergo videtur, quod nulla sit influentia empyrei existentis supra. *Si tu dicas*, quod influit non ratione animae in se, sed ratione dispositionis a parte corporis; *contra*: anima rationalis unitur mediante vi sensitiva et vegetativa, et corpus disponitur ad susceptionem animae mediante complexione aequali et spiritu triplici, scilicet vitali, naturali et animali[^9]; et ad haec omnia influit hoc caelum sidereum sufficienter: ergo redit idem quod prius.

### Conclusio

> Caelum empyreum in corpora inferiora aliquam habet influentiam.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod circa hoc duplex fuit opinio.

Quidam namque dixerunt, quod caelum empyreum influit in haec inferiora, et influentia nobilissima. — Cum enim sit corpus, necesse est, *influentiam* suam, si qua est, esse corporalem. *Rursus*, cum sit excellentissimum inter corpora caelestia, influit super corpora nobilissima, et talia sunt corpora humana, quae sunt ordinata ad nobilissimam formam, scilicet animam rationalem, quae maiorem et nobiliorem dispositionem exigit in sua materia. Cum igitur natura lucis disponat ad vitam, et triplex sit vita secundum triplicem differentiam animae, differens gradu et dignitate; tres Deus condidit caelos ordinatos inter se gradu et dignitate, non solum naturae, sed etiam influentiae, ita quod caelum *sidereum* de se ordinatur ad conciliationem elementorum, ad susceptionem vegetabilis, *crystallinum* ad susceptionem sensibilis, sed *empyreum* ad susceptionem rationalis.

Et hoc quidem rationabile videtur non solum ratione *ordinis influentiae*, sed etiam ratione *conformitatis naturae*. Caelum enim empyreum est locus spiritualium substantiarum, locus etiam corporum glorificatorum. Et quoniam convenientia est loci ad locatum vel manifesta vel occulta, videtur influentia illius caeli esse consona corporibus nostris et animabus amica, non ratione sui, sed ratione suorum corporum, quae perficiunt et informant[^10].

Alia vero opinio fuit circa hoc omnino isti contraria, quae dixit, quod caeli empyrei in haec inferiora nulla est omnino influentia, quia non habent corpora influentiam nisi secundum ordinem Conditoris, habito respectu ad finem. Quoniam igitur empyreum ad perfectionem universi est conditum, et ut sit locus Beatorum, ideo regio illa[^11] et lux est a nobis remota et occulta, sicut et ipsa gloria, quam per gratiam exspectamus et amamus et credimus, licet non videamus. Et ideo dicunt, quod empyreum non est ad obsequium hominis in praesenti, sed ad obsequium perpetuum; nec melioratur, sed uniformiter in sua dignitate subsistit. Et ideo rationes adductae ad ostendendam influentiam[^12] in haec inferiora secundum hos non valent, quia ordinatio illius corporis ad aliud officium secundum dictamen et imperium Conditoris huiusmodi influentiam non admittit; et hoc solum omnes illas rationes dissolvit.

Quaelibet harum opinionum satis probabilis est; quae autem sit magis vera, non plane apparet. Quis enim novit, si Deus illi caelo hanc occultam influentiam dedit super corpora nostra tum ratione nobilitatis, tum ratione conformitatis? Hoc non est, ut credo, facile refellere nec per violentiam auctoritatis, nec per efficaciam rationis. *Rursus*, quae sit necessitas huius influentiae, nec ratio nec auctoritas manifestat, cum satis videatur sufficere aliorum inferiorum corporum influentia. — Ideo in neutram partem omnino declinando, dicendum videtur, quod cum caelum empyreum sit primum creatum inter corpora, quod est maximum *mole* et *virtute*: quia est maximum *mole*, omnia corpora[^13] locat per ambitum et continentiam; quia maximum

<!-- page 75 -->

*virtute*, cetera vegetat et conservat per suam influentiam. Omittendo igitur illam influentiam, quam dicitur habere super humana corpora, sustineri potest, quod aliquem effectum et aliquam influentiam habeat super corpora inferiora, tanquam primum creatum super sequentia. Et rationes ad hoc inductae sunt concedendae.

1. 2. Quod ergo obiicitur de influentia luminis et caloris, dicendum, quod influentia luminis potest esse dupliciter: vel *manifesta*, vel *occulta*. *Manifesta* influentia est per diaphanum corpus, maxime quando sensu percipitur. *Occulta* influentia est non solum per diaphanum corpus, sed etiam per opacum, sicut virtus stellarum est in mineralia, quae latent sub terra. — Vel potest dici, quod est influentia *mediata* et *immediata*; et possibile est, quod influentia caeli siderei vigoratur ex adiumento luminis superiorum caelorum, et virtutem susceptam desuperius derivat et transmittit ad haec inferiora; et videtur nobis esse propria illorum[^14], cum tamen non sit propria, sed etiam aliena. — Et per hoc patet aliud, quod non est causa sufficiens virtus inferiorum caelorum nisi per adiumentum superiorum.

3. Quod obiicitur de conformitate, dicendum, quod conformis est natura spiritus, qui disponit ad vitam, ipsi luci caelesti quantum ad puritatem; et hac ratione nata est recipere; sed non oportet in omnibus consonare.

4. Quod obiicitur, utrum ad nobiliorem effectum; dicendum secundum primam opinionem, quod ad nobiliorem effectum, quia ad generationem spirituum, qui sunt dispositio ad susceptionem[^15] animae rationalis. — Et si tu obiicias, quod non sunt alii, quam illi qui disponunt ad sensibilem: dicendum, quod etsi non sint omnino alii secundum formam, tamen sunt puriores et excellentioribus et nobilioribus potentiis nati ministrare, secundum quam etiam rationem nobiliorem oportet esse complexionem et organizationem tam humani corporis quam brutalis. — Potest tamen sustineri, quod ad eosdem effectus influunt, nec tamen alterum eorum superfluit, quia virtus caeli inferioris et influentia adiuvatur per virtutem superioris, et virtus superioris operatur mediante virtute et influentia inferioris; ideo neutrum superfluit, sed ad haec inferiora conservanda et perficienda virtus utriusque concurrit[^16].

---
questions.english:
### Question II. *Whether the empyrean heaven influences these lower things.*

Secondly it is asked concerning the empyrean as to the power of [its] influence. And it is asked whether the empyrean influences these lower things, or not. And that [it does] so, it seems.

1. In everything created which is perfect and complete there is substance, power, and operation[^1]: therefore [also] in the empyrean itself. If therefore it has power, it either operates on what is above, or on what is alongside, or on what is below. Not on what is above — that is plain; nor on what is alongside, because it itself is above all bodies: therefore it seems that through that power it influences what is below; or [else] its power and substance will be idle, which is plainly unfitting.

2. Likewise, all bodies were made for the service of man, whence «we are in a certain way the end of all the things which exist[^2]»: therefore if the empyrean is anything, in some respect it serves man; but it would not do this unless it influenced something into these lower things: therefore etc.

3. Likewise, the higher in position some body is, the nobler it is among bodies[^3], and the nobler, the more powerful and better, and the more powerful and better, the more efficacious in acting and influencing: if therefore the empyrean heaven is the highest, then it seems that it is most of all influencing into these lower things.

4. Likewise, the greater the light[^4] is, the more it diffuses and multiplies itself: if therefore the empyrean among bodies is most of all luminous, then [it is] most of all diffusive; but that light is not deprived of the efficacy of vivifying and conserving, just as neither [is] the light of the firmament: therefore it seems that the empyrean influences these lower things more.

**On the contrary:**

1. The influence of a celestial body consists chiefly in the diffusion of light and heat; but the empyrean does not heat[^5], nor does it irradiate these lower bodies: therefore it seems that there is no influence of the empyrean into these lower things.

2. Likewise, the bodies which are below the firmament influence sufficiently for the vivification and generation to be done in these lower things: therefore «if nature does nothing in vain[^6]», it seems that the influence of another heaven is null, since it is of no opportuneness.

3. Likewise, the influence of a heaven ought to be conformed to that from which it is, and ought nonetheless to be conformed to that by which it is received; but the empyrean heaven is

<!-- page 74 -->

incorruptible, uniform, most quiet, deputed to the state and rest of glory; but these [things] which are below have wholly opposite conditions: therefore it seems that it has in no way [the property] to influence over the lower bodies[^7].

4. Likewise, if it influences over bodies, then [it does so] either toward a nobler effect than the influence of the eighth sphere is, or toward a *less noble*, or toward the *same* effect. Toward the *same* — [that] is not *fitting*; toward a *less noble* — [that] is not *becoming*, since that body is nobler; toward a *more noble* — [that it] *cannot*: therefore in no way does it influence. *Proof*: that it *cannot* [influence] toward a more noble [effect], seems [so]. For, as the philosophers hold and the natural scientists commonly maintain[^8], the influence of a heaven is operative toward the production of the sensible soul; but above the sensible soul there is only the rational [soul], and this is subject to no body, indeed is from a pure creation: therefore in no way can there be an influence more eminent than over the sensible soul; and over this the starry [heaven] influences sufficiently with the things which are below: therefore it seems that there is no influence of the empyrean existing above. *If you say* that it influences not by reason of the soul in itself, but by reason of the disposition on the part of the body; *on the contrary*: the rational soul is united by means of the sensitive and vegetative power, and the body is disposed for the reception of the soul by means of an equal complexion and a threefold spirit, namely vital, natural, and animal[^9]; and into all these the starry heaven influences sufficiently: therefore the same [conclusion] returns as before.

### Conclusion

> The empyrean heaven has some influence into the lower bodies.

**I respond:** It must be said that concerning this there was a twofold opinion.

For some said that the empyrean heaven influences these lower things, and [with] a most noble influence. — For since it is a body, its *influence*, if it has any, must necessarily be corporeal. *Again*, since it is the most excellent among the celestial bodies, it influences over the noblest bodies, and such are human bodies, which are ordered to the noblest form, namely the rational soul, which demands a greater and nobler disposition in its matter. Since therefore the nature of light disposes toward life, and life is threefold according to the threefold difference of the soul, differing in grade and dignity; God founded three heavens ordered among themselves in grade and dignity, not only of nature but also of influence, so that the *starry* heaven of itself is ordered to the conciliation of the elements, to the reception of the vegetable [soul], the *crystalline* to the reception of the sensible, but the *empyrean* to the reception of the rational.

And this indeed seems reasonable not only by reason of the *order of influence*, but also by reason of the *conformity of nature*. For the empyrean heaven is the place of spiritual substances, the place also of glorified bodies. And since the suitability of the place to what is located [there] is either manifest or hidden, the influence of that heaven seems to be consonant with our bodies and friendly to [our] souls, not by reason of itself, but by reason of their bodies, which perfect and inform[^10] [them].

But there was another opinion concerning this wholly contrary to that one, which said that of the empyrean heaven there is no influence at all into these lower things, because bodies do not have influence except according to the order of the Creator, regard being had to the end. Since therefore the empyrean was founded for the perfection of the universe, and that it might be the place of the Blessed, therefore that region[^11] and [its] light is remote and hidden from us, just as also is glory itself, which through grace we await and love and believe, although we do not see [it]. And therefore they say that the empyrean is not for the service of man in the present, but for perpetual service; nor is it bettered, but uniformly subsists in its dignity. And therefore the reasons adduced to show an influence[^12] into these lower things, according to these [men], do not hold, because the ordination of that body to another office, according to the dictate and command of the Creator, does not admit such an influence; and this alone dissolves all those reasons.

Each of these opinions is sufficiently probable; but which is the truer does not plainly appear. For who knows whether God gave to that heaven this hidden influence over our bodies both by reason of [its] nobility and by reason of conformity? This is not, as I believe, easy to refute, neither by the force of authority nor by the efficacy of reason. *Again*, what is the necessity of this influence, neither reason nor authority makes manifest, since the influence of the other lower bodies seems sufficiently to suffice. — Therefore, declining wholly to neither part, it seems it must be said that, since the empyrean heaven is the first thing created among bodies, which is the greatest in *mass* and *power*: because it is greatest in *mass*, it locates all bodies[^13] by encompassing and containing [them]; because [it is] greatest

<!-- page 75 -->

in *power*, it vivifies and conserves the rest by its influence. Omitting therefore that influence which it is said to have over human bodies, it can be maintained that it has some effect and some influence over the lower bodies, as the first thing created [influences] over the things following. And the reasons adduced for this are to be granted.

1. 2. To what then is objected concerning the influence of light and heat, it must be said that the influence of light can be twofold: either *manifest* or *hidden*. *Manifest* influence is through a transparent body, especially when it is perceived by sense. *Hidden* influence is not only through a transparent body but also through an opaque one, just as the power of the stars is in the minerals which lie hidden under the earth. — Or it can be said that there is a *mediate* and an *immediate* influence; and it is possible that the influence of the starry heaven is strengthened by the help of the light of the higher heavens, and derives the power received from above and transmits it to these lower things; and it seems to us to be proper to them[^14], although it is not proper [to them], but also from another. — And through this another [point] is clear, that the power of the lower heavens is not a sufficient cause except by the help of the higher ones.

3. To what is objected concerning conformity, it must be said that the nature of the spirit, which disposes toward life, is conformed to the celestial light itself as to purity; and by this reason it is born to receive; but it is not necessary to be consonant in all [respects].

4. To what is objected, whether toward a nobler effect; it must be said, according to the first opinion, that [it influences] toward a nobler effect, because toward the generation of the spirits which are the disposition for the reception[^15] of the rational soul. — And if you object that there are no others than those which dispose toward the sensible [soul]: it must be said that, although they are not wholly other according to form, yet they are purer and born to minister to more excellent and nobler powers, according to which reason also the complexion and organization both of the human body and of the brute [body] must be nobler. — Yet it can be maintained that they influence toward the same effects, nor does either of them become superfluous, because the power and influence of the lower heaven is aided by the power of the higher, and the power of the higher operates by means of the power and influence of the lower; therefore neither becomes superfluous, but for these lower things to be conserved and perfected the power of both concurs[^16].

---

apparatus.la: Vide Dionys. de Caelest. Hierarch. c. 11, ex quo quaedam invenies tom. 1. pag. 79, nota 5. — Paulo inferius cod. N *aut per illam operatur*, plures alii codd. cum ed. 1 incongrue *aut per quam operatur* pro *aut operatur.*
apparatus.en: See Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, c. 11, from which you will find some [things] in tom. 1, p. 79, note 5. — A little below codex N [reads] *aut per illam operatur*, several other codices with ed. 1 incongruously *aut per quam operatur* for *aut operatur.*

apparatus.la: Cfr. supra pag. 46, nota 1. — In Vat. sequens propositio sic sonat: *ergo si empyreum aliquid est, in aliquo servit huiusmodi.*
apparatus.en: Cf. above p. 46, note 1. — In the Vatican edition the following proposition runs thus: *therefore if the empyrean is anything, in some respect it serves [a being] of this kind.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., de Mundo, c. 7. (c. 6.), recitato consensu mortalium, qui Deo summam regionem mundi tribuit et nos ipsos elevare manus facit sursum inter vota concipienda, ait: Quin etiam quae maxime eximia sunt inter res sensu perceptas eundem illa locum obtinent, ut sidera, ut sol et luna.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the World*, c. 7 (c. 6), the consensus of mortals being recited, which attributes the highest region of the world to God and makes us ourselves raise [our] hands upward while conceiving [our] prayers, says: Indeed even the things which are most excellent among the things perceived by sense obtain that same place, like the stars, like the sun and moon.

apparatus.la: Non pauci codd. perperam *bonum.* In fine argumenti cod. cc cum ed. 1 ponit *maxime sit influens* pro *magis sit influens*, ubi cod. 1 addit *quam alia corpora.*
apparatus.en: Not a few codices wrongly [read] *bonum* ["good"]. At the end of the argument codex cc with ed. 1 puts *maxime sit influens* ["is most of all influencing"] for *magis sit influens* ["is more influencing"], where cod. 1 adds *quam alia corpora* ["than the other bodies"].

apparatus.la: Vat. cum paucis mss. prosequitur *quia non est in motu, nec ista corpora inferiora, sicut patet, irradiat.*
apparatus.en: The Vatican edition, with a few manuscripts, continues *because it is not in motion, nor does it irradiate these lower bodies, as is plain.*

apparatus.la: Aristot., III. de Anima, text. 45. (c. 9.). — Aliquanto superius plures codd. cum ed. 1 *intra firmamentum* pro *infra firmamentum.*
apparatus.en: Aristotle, III *On the Soul*, text 45 (c. 9). — Somewhat above, several codices with ed. 1 [read] *intra firmamentum* ["within the firmament"] for *infra firmamentum* ["below the firmament"].

apparatus.la: Cod. cc et ed. 1 *infima.* In fine argumenti cod. bb *influentiam habeat* pro *influere habeat.*
apparatus.en: Codex cc and ed. 1 [read] *infima* ["lowest"]. At the end of the argument codex bb [reads] *influentiam habeat* ["has an influence"] for *influere habeat* ["has [the property] to influence"].

apparatus.la: Sufficiat hic adducere Averroem, qui in suo libro de Substantia orbis (c. 1.) ait: *Calor vero corporum caelestium largitur vitam vegetabilem, sensibilem et animalem.* — Vat. cum nonnullis mss. *viri philosophici.* Paulo superius codd. cum ed. 1 post *quod* subiiciunt *autem*, omissa vel male transposita voce *Probatio* post *ad magis nobilem non potest.* Cod. aa *non mutat* post *immo a creatore est pure* pro *immo est a creatione pura.*
apparatus.en: Let it suffice here to adduce Averroes, who in his book *On the Substance of the Orb* (c. 1) says: *But the heat of the celestial bodies bestows vegetable, sensible, and animal life.* — The Vatican edition, with some manuscripts, [reads] *viri philosophici* ["philosophical men"]. A little above the codices with ed. 1, after *quod*, subjoin *autem*, the word *Probatio* being omitted or badly transposed after *ad magis nobilem non potest.* Codex aa [reads] *non mutat* [...], *immo a creatore est pure* for *immo est a creatione pura.*

apparatus.la: De his cfr. supra d. 1. p. II. a. 1. q. 2. ad 2. 3.
apparatus.en: On these [things] cf. above d. 1, p. II, a. 1, q. 2, ad 2, 3.

apparatus.la: Cod. L *conformant.*
apparatus.en: Codex L [reads] *conformant* ["they conform"].

apparatus.la: Ex cod. cc et ed. 1 supplevimus *illa*, pro quo cod. N *eius.* Aliquanto superius cod. A *secundum ordinationem Conditoris* pro *secundum ordinem Conditoris.*
apparatus.en: From codex cc and ed. 1 we have supplied *illa* ["that"], for which codex N [reads] *eius* ["its"]. Somewhat above codex A [reads] *secundum ordinationem Conditoris* for *secundum ordinem Conditoris.*

apparatus.la: In cod. aa additur *eius.* Paulo ante plures codd. ut U V Z *consistit* pro *subsistit.*
apparatus.en: In codex aa is added *eius* ["its"]. A little before, several codices, as U V Z, [read] *consistit* for *subsistit.*

apparatus.la: Non pauci codd. cum ed. 1 *corporalia.*
apparatus.en: Not a few codices, with ed. 1, [read] *corporalia* ["corporeal [things]"].

apparatus.la: In Vat. deest *illorum.* Dein nonnulli codd. *cum non tantum* pro *cum tamen non.* Melius esset *cum tamen non tantum.*
apparatus.en: In the Vatican edition *illorum* ["of them"] is lacking. Then some codices [read] *cum non tantum* for *cum tamen non.* It would be better [to read] *cum tamen non tantum.*

apparatus.la: Cod. T *receptionem.*
apparatus.en: Codex T [reads] *receptionem* ["the receiving"].

questions.titleLa: Utrum Angeli sint in loco corporeo
questions.titleEn: Whether the angels are in a corporeal place
questions.latin:
<!-- page 75 -->

### ARTICULUS II.

### *De modo, quo Angeli sunt in loco.*

Consequenter circa secundum articulum quaeruntur quatuor.

Primum est, utrum substantiae spirituales sint in loco corporeo.

Secundum est, utrum Angelus sit in pluribus locis simul, aut tantum in uno.

Tertium est, utrum sit in loco punctali, an composito.

Quartum est, utrum plures Angeli possint simul esse[^1] in eodem loco primo.

### Quaestio I. *Utrum Angeli sint in loco corporeo.*

Quaeritur igitur primo, utrum loci corporalis sit locare Angelos. Et quod sic, videtur.

1. Dicit Strabus[^2]: «Statim ut factum est caelum empyreum, repletum est Angelis».

2. Item, Damascenus[^3]: «Caelum est continentia visibilium et invisibilium»; loquitur de empyreo: ergo etc.

3. Item, omne creatum est de universo, ergo est intra primum continens sive ultimum corpus; sed supremum corpus ambiens dicitur empyreum[^4]: ergo omnis creatura continetur infra ipsum: ergo et angelicus spiritus.

4. Item, nulla substantia operatur, nisi ubi est eius virtus[^5]; sed nulla virtus potest elongari a substantia nisi distantia proportionali — nam virtus infinita nullo modo elongatur, virtus finita non potest elongari nisi finite — ergo necesse est, Angelum esse ubi operatur, vel prope. Ergo cum operatur in loco corporali, ut patet in corpore, quod movet, ergo ibi est, vel in loco proximo est: ergo si locus maxime aptus contemplationi est empyreum, videtur, quod ibi sit.

5. Item, spiritus maligni in eodem loco tormentorum habebunt collocari, in quo et homines

<!-- page 76 -->

damnati, sicut dicitur Matthaei vigesimo quinto[^6]: *Ite maledicti* etc.; ergo ab oppositis vel a simili in contrario Angeli cum beatis hominibus in eodem loco corporali erunt; sed locus aptus hominibus beatis est ille qui praedictus est, scilicet caelum empyreum, quod est supremum, quietum, clarum, uniforme et spatiosum: ergo etc.

6. Item, maior requiritur proportio perfectionis ad perfectibile quam locati ad locum; sed videmus, quod substantia spiritualis adeo proportionari potest corporali, et e converso, quod una unitur alteri ut perfectio, ut patet in homine: ergo multo fortius potest una uniri alteri ut locatum loco. Ergo cum caelum empyreum sit nobilissimum corporum simplicium, vel erit in Angelo, vel Angelus in eo; sed ipsum non est in Angelo: ergo e converso.

**Sed contra:**

1. Boethius de Hebdomadibus[^7]: «Communis animi conceptio, quae omnibus videtur, est, incorporeum in loco non esse».

2. Item, Gregorius[^8]: «Locus animae Deus est»; sed non est spiritualior locus animae quam Angeli: ergo si Deus est locus animae, et Angeli.

3. Item, ratione videtur, quia loci ad locatum est mutua indigentia, sicut patet — locatum enim indiget loco suo, ut terra centro; et locus etiam indiget locato, unde refugit vacuitatem; et impossibile est, quod locus sit sine locato, quin aliquid suppleat indigentiam loci[^9] — sed caelum empyreum non indiget Angelis nec aliquis locus, nec similiter Angelus loco, quia, omni corpore circumscripto, adhuc Angelus remaneret et secundum substantiam et secundum operationem, quae est contemplatio: ergo nullo modo est locus Angeli.

4. Item, locus habet influentiam et potentiam super locatum — unde superiora nobiliora locant minus nobilia, sicut patet ex hoc[^10] quod aqua terram, aer aquam, et sic de aliis — sed corporale non habet influere in spirituale nisi secundum ordinem iustitiae, sicut in anima peccatrice vel spiritu: ergo spiritus non habet locum in corpore nisi per culpam.

5. Item, omne locatum habet pondus et inclinationem ad locum; sed Augustinus[^11] dicit: «Quod est pondus in corporibus, hoc est amor in spiritibus»; sed inclinatio amoris angelici est ad bonum spirituale, non ad locum corporalem: ergo non habent locum corporaliter, sed solum spiritualiter.

### Conclusio

> Caelum empyreum locat Angelos ut locus continens, non autem ut mensurans vel conservans.

**Respondeo:** Dicendum, quod caelum empyreum locat Angelos et est locus Angelorum, sicut probant rationes ad primam partem.

Ad intelligentiam autem obiectorum est notandum, quod locus habet triplicem comparationem ad locatum. Comparatur enim primo in ratione *continentis*, secundo in ratione *mensurantis* et tertio in ratione *conservantis*. Continet enim ut vas, mensurat ut quantitas, sed *conservat* ut natura[^12]. — Secundum hanc triplicem habitudinem sunt in loco substantiae *finitae, corporales* et *corruptibiles*: quia finitae et limitatae, sunt in loco continente; quia corporales, in mensurante; quia corruptibiles, in loco conservante. Secundum comparationes duas primas sunt in loco substantiae finitae et corporales, sed incorruptibiles. Secundum primam vero sunt in loco substantiae finitae, spirituales et incorruptibiles, ut Angeli. Et hoc dico in loco corporali; nam Angelus habet locum spiritualem conservantem, scilicet Dei virtutem; locum mensurantem sive circumscribentem, propriae substantiae et[^13] virtutis limitationem sive clausionem; locum vero continentem, non tantum spiritualem, sed etiam corporalem.

Ratio autem, quare Angeli continentur loco sive aliquo ambiente, est ordinatio partium universi. Si enim non haberent aliquid continens, non esset eorum existentia ordinata ad invicem[^14], nec haberet ordinem unus ad alterum; hoc autem non decet universum nec summum opificem. — Ratio autem, quare continentur loco corporali, duplex est: una, scilicet limitatio ipsius spiritus creati. Cum enim spiritus increatus, qui Deus est, habeat in se simplicitatem, per quam est intra omnia, et immensi-

<!-- page 77 -->

tatem, per quam continet omnia et est extra omnia[^15], communicat illas conditiones creaturae eatenus, quatenus nata est recipere. Unde simplicitatem communicat spiritui; sed spiritus non potuit recipere virtutem continentiae. Quia enim simplicitas eius finita est, ideo est hic et nunc[^16]; et quia non habet partem et partem, ideo secundum totum est hic et nunc: et ideo non potest habere universalem capacitatem rerum. Corpus autem, quia compositum est et habet partes innumerabiles, non potuit participare simplicitatem, sed propter partium extensionem potuit recipere capacitatem; ideo Deus fecit unum corpus nobilissimum, quod esset natum omnia ambire, et extra quod omnino nihil esset; et hoc est empyreum; et ideo necesse est, Angelum esse intra ipsum. — Alia ratio est, quia in solo corpore est distinctio. Nam si gratis statur, ceterae creaturae ordinem habent in mundo, distinctionem et positionem habent secundum gradus perfectionum, et ita quod una est hic, et alia ibi, una sursum, et alia deorsum, et[^17] in solo corpore est potentialis distinctio secundum hic et ibi: ideo inter creaturas soli corpori debuit dari universalis potentia locandi, et respectu visibilium et invisibilium, ut sic universum esset unum in omnibus suis partibus ordinatum.

Et sic patet ratio duplex, quare data est corpori potentia locandi spiritum, et spiritum contineri a corpore. Hoc enim exigebat ordo universi tum propter limitationem spiritus creati, tum quia in solo corpore distinctio est secundum hic et ibi.

Concedendae sunt igitur rationes monstrantes, quod caeli empyrei est locare Angelos.

1. Quod enim obiicitur in contrarium primo, quod incorporeum non est in loco; dicendum, quod intelligit[^18] de esse in loco, sicut mensuratum est in mensura.

2. Quod obiicitur, quod locus Angeli et animae Deus est; dicendum, quod intelligit[^19] de loco conservante, non de loco definiente. Et iterum ratio non cogit: quod si Deus est locus[^20], quod nihil creatum locet spiritum.

3. Quod obiicitur, quod loci ad locatum est mutua indigentia; dicendum, quod verum est de his quae locantur propter defectum sui; sed non est verum de his quae locantur propter servandum ordinem universi. — Unde si quaeratur, utrum lapis possit esse extra caelum; dicendum, quod non, tum propter suam indigentiam, quia non haberet locum conservantem, tum quia non patitur hoc ordo universi. Sed de Angelo, quod caelum non exeat, non est ratio loci corporalis indigentia, sed corporis ultimi universalis continentia, secundum quam universum est perfectum et ordinatum.

4. 5. Et ad alias duas[^21] rationes patet responsio, quod[^22] procedunt de esse in loco tanquam in conservante, ratione cuius ponitur influentia in locante, ponitur etiam inclinatio in locato; iste autem modus essendi in loco non convenit Angelo.

questions.english:
### ARTICLE II.

### *On the mode in which the angels are in a place.*

Consequently, concerning the second article, four [things] are asked.

The first is, whether spiritual substances are in a corporeal place.

The second is, whether an Angel is in several places at once, or only in one.

The third is, whether [an Angel] is in a punctual place or a composite [one].

The fourth is, whether several Angels can be at once[^1] in the same primary place.

### Question I. *Whether the angels are in a corporeal place.*

It is asked, therefore, first, whether it belongs to a corporeal place to locate Angels. And that [it does] so, it seems.

1. Strabus says[^2]: «As soon as the empyrean heaven was made, it was filled with Angels».

2. Likewise, Damascene[^3]: «Heaven is the containment of visible and invisible [things]»; he speaks of the empyrean: therefore etc.

3. Likewise, every created thing is of the universe, therefore is within the first container or the ultimate body; but the supreme encompassing body is called the empyrean[^4]: therefore every creature is contained within it: therefore also the angelic spirit.

4. Likewise, no substance operates except where its power is[^5]; but no power can be distanced from the substance except by a proportional distance — for an infinite power is in no way distanced, a finite power cannot be distanced except finitely — therefore it is necessary that the Angel be where it operates, or near. Therefore since it operates in a corporeal place, as is plain in a body which it moves, therefore it is there, or is in the nearest place: therefore if the place most apt for contemplation is the empyrean, it seems that it is there.

5. Likewise, the malign spirits will have to be placed in the same place of torments in which also the men

<!-- page 76 -->

[who are] damned [will be], as is said in Matthew twenty-five[^6]: *Go, you cursed* etc.; therefore from the opposites or from the like in the contrary, the Angels with the blessed men will be in the same corporeal place; but the place apt for blessed men is that which was aforesaid, namely the empyrean heaven, which is supreme, quiet, bright, uniform, and spacious: therefore etc.

6. Likewise, a greater proportion of the perfection to the perfectible is required than of what is located to the place; but we see that a spiritual substance can be so proportioned to a corporeal one, and conversely, that the one is united to the other as a perfection, as is plain in man: therefore much more strongly can the one be united to the other as what is located to the place. Therefore since the empyrean heaven is the noblest of the simple bodies, either it will be in the Angel or the Angel in it; but it is not in the Angel: therefore conversely.

**But on the contrary:**

1. Boethius, *On the Hebdomads*[^7]: «It is a common conception of the mind, which seems [true] to all, that the incorporeal is not in a place».

2. Likewise, Gregory[^8]: «The place of the soul is God»; but there is not a more spiritual place for the soul than for the Angels: therefore if God is the place of the soul, [he is] also [the place] of the Angels.

3. Likewise, it seems [so] by reason, because there is a mutual need of the place to what is located, as is plain — for what is located needs its place, as earth [needs] the center; and the place too needs what is located, whence it flees emptiness; and it is impossible that a place be without what is located, but that something supply the need of the place[^9] — but the empyrean heaven does not need the Angels, nor does any place [need them], nor likewise [does] the Angel [need] a place, because, every body being removed, the Angel would still remain both according to substance and according to operation, which is contemplation: therefore in no way is it the place of the Angel.

4. Likewise, the place has influence and power over what is located [there] — whence the higher, nobler [things] locate the less noble, as is plain from this[^10], that water [locates] earth, air water, and so of the rest — but the corporeal does not have [the power] to influence the spiritual except according to the order of justice, as in a sinful soul or spirit: therefore the spirit does not have a place in a body except through fault.

5. Likewise, everything located has weight and inclination toward the place; but Augustine[^11] says: «What weight is in bodies, this is love in spirits»; but the inclination of angelic love is toward the spiritual good, not toward a corporeal place: therefore they do not have a place corporeally, but only spiritually.

### Conclusion

> The empyrean heaven locates the Angels as a containing place, but not as measuring or conserving.

**I respond:** It must be said that the empyrean heaven locates the Angels and is the place of the Angels, as the reasons for the first part prove.

But for the understanding of the objections it must be noted that the place has a threefold comparison to what is located. For it is compared, first, in the character of *containing*, secondly in the character of *measuring*, and thirdly in the character of *conserving*. For it contains as a vessel, it measures as a quantity, but *conserves* as a nature[^12]. — According to this threefold relation, *finite, corporeal*, and *corruptible* substances are in a place: because finite and limited, they are in a containing place; because corporeal, in a measuring [one]; because corruptible, in a conserving place. According to the first two comparisons, finite and corporeal but incorruptible substances are in a place. According to the first only, finite, spiritual, and incorruptible substances, like the Angels, are in a place. And this I say [as to being] in a corporeal place; for the Angel has a spiritual conserving place, namely the power of God; a measuring or circumscribing place, the limitation or enclosure of its own substance and[^13] power; but a containing place, not only spiritual but also corporeal.

But the reason why the Angels are contained by a place or by something encompassing [them] is the ordering of the parts of the universe. For if they did not have something containing [them], their existence would not be ordered to one another[^14], nor would one have order to another; but this does not befit the universe nor the highest Maker. — But the reason why they are contained by a corporeal place is twofold: one, namely the limitation of the created spirit itself. For since the uncreated spirit, who is God, has in himself simplicity, through which he is within all things, and immensity,

<!-- page 77 -->

through which he contains all things and is outside all things[^15], he communicates those conditions to the creature in so far as it is born to receive [them]. Hence he communicates simplicity to the spirit; but the spirit could not receive the power of containment. For because its simplicity is finite, therefore it is here and now[^16]; and because it does not have part and part, therefore it is here and now according to [its] whole: and therefore it cannot have a universal capacity of things. But the body, because it is composite and has innumerable parts, could not participate simplicity, but on account of the extension of [its] parts it could receive capacity; therefore God made one most noble body, which was born to encompass all [things], and outside of which there would be nothing at all; and this is the empyrean; and therefore it is necessary that the Angel be within it. — Another reason is that distinction is in body alone. For, if it is granted freely, the other creatures have order in the world, [and] have distinction and position according to grades of perfections, and so that one is here and another there, one above and another below, and[^17] in body alone is there a potential distinction according to here and there: therefore among creatures to body alone had to be given the universal power of locating, with respect both to visible and invisible [things], so that thus the universe might be one [thing] ordered in all its parts.

And so the twofold reason is clear, why the power of locating a spirit was given to body, and [why] a spirit is contained by a body. For the order of the universe demanded this, both on account of the limitation of the created spirit, and because in body alone is distinction according to here and there.

The reasons showing that it belongs to the empyrean heaven to locate the Angels are therefore to be granted.

1. For what is objected to the contrary first, that the incorporeal is not in a place; it must be said that it is understood[^18] of being in a place as what is measured is in a measure.

2. To what is objected, that the place of the Angel and of the soul is God; it must be said that it is understood[^19] of a conserving place, not of a defining place. And again the reason does not compel: that if God is the place[^20], [it does not follow] that nothing created locates a spirit.

3. To what is objected, that there is a mutual need of the place to what is located; it must be said that this is true of those [things] which are located on account of a defect of themselves; but it is not true of those which are located for the sake of preserving the order of the universe. — Whence if it is asked whether a stone can be outside the heaven; it must be said no, both on account of its [own] need, because it would not have a conserving place, and because the order of the universe does not allow this. But concerning the Angel, that it does not leave the heaven, the reason is not the need of a corporeal place, but the universal containment of the ultimate body, according to which the universe is perfect and ordered.

4. 5. And to the other two[^21] reasons the response is clear, that[^22] they proceed [on the supposition] of being in a place as in a conserving [one], by reason of which an influence is posited in what locates, and an inclination also is posited in what is located; but this mode of being in a place does not befit the Angel.

<!-- page 78 -->
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** Iam 1. Sent. d. 37. p. II. a. 2. q. 1. 2. 3. tractatum est de motu Angelorum, ubi plura dicta sunt, quae servire possunt ad intelligendas quatuor hic propositas quaestiones de modo, quo Angeli sunt in loco. De proprietatibus loci cfr. ibid. a. 1. q. 1. 2. 3, in specie de differentia inter *esse in loco, esse locatum, esse localem* (ibid. q. 1. ad 1.). Ibidem in corp. enumerantur quatuor leges loci, scil. *continendi, mensurandi, salvandi, terminandi*, hic autem tantum tres, omissa ultima, fortasse quia sub vocabulo *continendi* comprehenditur etiam vocabulum *terminandi*, minus aptum ad significandum modum, quo Angeli in loco definitive sunt praesentes. Manifestum autem est, a loco non posse nec mensurari nec conservari nisi substantiam corporalem. Mensuratur autem Angelus a limitatione propriae substantiae (S. Thom., S. I. q. 30. a. 1. ad 3.) et altiori modo a Deo, qui est omnium mensura extra genus. Conservatur autem Angelus a solo Deo, cuius virtutem S. Bonav. (hic in corp.) vocat *locum spiritualem*, consentiente S. Thoma (1. Sent. d. 37. q. 3. a. 3.). Porro Angelus in stricto sensu etiam non continetur in loco, i. e. sicut mensuratum in mensura, sed continetur in eo «quodam modo», nempe definitive (1. Sent. d. 37. p. II. a. 2. q. 1. in corp.). S. Thom. (S. I. q. 52. a. 1.) vocabulum *continere* non admittere videtur, dicens: «Angelus dicitur esse in loco corporeo non ut contentum, sed ut continens aliquo modo». — Ceterum de ista qualicumque praesentia Angeli in loco non mediocriter illa aetate disputatum est, et quidem tum de facto, utrum sit revera praesens in loco, atque de necessitate, utrum indigeat loco, tum de ratione in genere, quare determinetur ad aliquem locum, tum de modo sive ratione formali huius praesentiae in loco.

**II.** Quoad quaestionem de facto exortae sunt duae opiniones extremae et in verbis quidem oppositae, sed fere in eodem errore sibi propinquae. Quidam enim inter philosophos Arabes dixerunt, quod substantiae separatae *nusquam* sunt secundum substantiam; quae propositio, si intelligitur, quod substantia non sit in loco, reprobata est ab Episc. Paris. a. 1276 (*Collect. iudicior.* p. 192. cap. 7. n. 27.), et a S. Thoma (1. Sent. d. 37. q. 3. a. 1.) nominatur *«haeretica, quia secundum fidem nostram ponimus, Angelos immediate circa nos operari»* (cfr. Alex. Hal., S. p. II. q. 32. m. 2, et propositio a. 1240 damnata, quae 1. Sent. d. 37. p. II. a. 2. q. 1. in Scholio est relata). E contrario Durandus (1. Sent. d. 37. q. 1.) Angelos esse ubique opinatur, sed «absque assertione; solummodo inquirendo et dando occasionem peritioribus ulterius inquirendi». Hanc autem ubiquitatem idem intelligit omnino diversam esse a divina, eamque ponit in eo, quod pro libitu possint ubique operari, in quo totam rationem praesentiae consistere putat. Media autem sententia, quod Angeli nec sint ubique nec nusquam, sed aliquo modo in loco, communissime sustinetur.

**III.** Altera quaestio, utrum Angelus indigeat ex se, quod ad aliquem corporalem locum definiatur, a S. Bonav. (hic ad 3. et clarius infra q. 4. in corp.) in sensu negativo solvitur. Consentiunt Alex. Hal. (loco cit.), S. Thom. (1. Sent. d. 37. a. 1. ad 4.) et Scotus (hic q. 6. n. 11.), qui dicit: «Quod Angelus non necessario est in loco, quia multo magis posset fieri Angelus sine creatione creaturae corporalis, vel facta creatura corporali, posset fieri et esse extra omnem creaturam corporalem. Et tamen in Angelo est potentia passiva, qua posset esse in loco. Et ista potentia vel fundatur immediate in eius substantia, qua posset esse in loco, vel in ipsa, in quantum est natura limitata, actualiter existens, vel in aliquo extrinseco ipsi Angelo, quidquid sit illud. Et ideo non oportet quaerere aliquam intrinsecam rationem essendi Angelum in loco necessario». Sed his suppositis, iterum duplex se offerebat quaestio: 1. quare et quomodo Angelus determinetur in genere, ut sit in aliquo loco et intra mundum; et 2. quid sit illud, per quod actualiter Angelus praesentiam habeat in hoc loco et non in alio. Primam quaestionem hic et infra q. 4. solvit S. Bonav. ita, ut causa finalis sit ordo universi servandus, et causa efficiens divina ordinatio, quae corporali naturae dedit quandam capacitatem continendi universalem, et Angelo quandam potentiam passivam, ut possit contineri in loco. Haec autem ordinatio divina habet rationem tum in limitatione substantiae angelicae, tum quia in solo corpore est et capacitas continendi et distinctio secundum hic et ibi. Eodem modo respondet Alex. Hal. (S. p. II. q. 32. m. 1.) et addit, quod illa proprietas in corporali natura, qua capax est continendi aliquo modo spiritus, «non sit corporalis, ex parte corporis proveniens, sed potius est divinitus data». Item, quod «spiritus angelicus habet ad minus ex parte sua, quod debeat definiri loco, et quod sit hic, ita quod non ibi». Tamen «posset esse, etsi non esset in loco corporali, quoniam ab hac ratione continendi [scil. passive] non dependet *esse* Angeli, sed solum ab hac ratione continendi, qua dicimus, quod Deus continet omnia». Idem autem de hac solutione ait: «Hoc dicimus sine praeiudicio melioris sententiae, quia hoc non invenimus plane determinatum in s. Scriptura nec a Sanctis nec ab expositoribus s. Scripturae». Etiam Scotus hanc doctrinam approbare videtur et (loc. cit. n. 15.) concludit: «Illud quo primo (Angelus) potest esse in loco, est a Deo producente ipsum super creaturam corporalem continentem; sed ex tunc potest reducere se ipsum ad actum istum (scil. ut sit actualiter in loco, et in hoc loco vel illo). — Posteriores scholastici, neglecta hac quaestione, potius disputant de sequenti.

**IV.** Quoad modum huius praesentiae, omnes doctores conveniunt, quod Angelus est in loco non circumscriptive, sed definitive, sive, ut ait Caietanus (in S. I. q. 52. a. 1.), conveniunt «in hoc, quod Angelus est in loco non per quantitatem molis nec per contactum quantitativum, sed per quantitatem et contactum virtualem. Et rursus in hoc etiam convenire omnes videntur, quod contactus ille sit relatio praesentiae Angeli ad locum causaliter, vel formaliter. Sed differentia opinionum et difficultas consistit in assignando, quod sit illius praesentiae fundamentum. Excedit enim evidentia eius humani ingenii capacitatem, propterea quod ex sacris eloquiis habemus, Angelos alicubi esse, et non apparet, quomodo tangant illum locum». — Durandus (loc. cit.) quatuor affert opiniones; sed duae prae aliis sunt celebres. S. Thom. in Summa (loc. cit.) docet, quod «per applicationem virtutis angelicae ad aliquem locum qualitercumque dicitur Angelus esse in loco». Quomodo autem hoc intelligendum sit, a discipulis Angelici non eodem modo exponitur (cfr. Caietan., loc. cit.). Contra sententiam S. Thomae late disputat Scot. (hic q. 6. et Report. q. 2.) et in re convenire videtur cum Richardo a Med. (1. Sent. d. 37. a. 2. q. 1.) dicente: «Ratio applicationis Angeli ad locum est sua simultas cum loco vel cum re in loco existente... sicut formalis ratio applicationis corporis ad locum est circumscriptio». Ambo afferunt articulum ab Episc. Paris. reprobatum, qui est: «Substantiae separatae sunt alicubi per operationem», qui censuratur sic: «Error, si intelligatur, sine operatione substantiam non esse in loco» (*Collect. iudic.* t. 1. p. 192. cap. 7. n. 25, sed cfr. supra Scholion pag. 30). De hac et de altera propositione damnata (supra n. II.) loquuntur etiam Durand. (loc. cit.) et praecipue Henr. Gand. (Quodl. 2. q. 9.), cuius verba notatu digna sunt: «In hoc enim concordabant omnes magistri theologiae congregati super hoc, quorum ego eram unus, unanimiter concedentes, quod substantia Angeli non est ratio, Angelum esse in loco secundum substantiam; et consimili ratione verum est indubitanter, quod si Angelus per potentiam suam, scil. intellectum ac voluntatem, virtutem suam non applicat ad locum operando circa ipsum, quod similiter potentia eius... non est ratio eius essendi ipsum in loco, nisi forte potentia eius sit minoris abstractionis, quam sit eius substantia». Idem in fine asserit, nullam se sustinere nec defendere specialem opinionem de hac re. De hac ultima quaest. S. Bonav., sicut nec Alex. Hal., explicite non tractat. Verba autem eius, incidenter prolata, favent sententiae Richardi, Scoti et Petri a Tar., ut hic q. 3. ad 2, q. 4. in corp.; 1. Sent. d. 37. p. II. a. 1. q. 1. ad 1.

**V.** Praeter locos iam citatos: S. Thom., 1. Sent. d. 37. q. 3. a. 1; Quodl. 1. q. 1. a. 4. — B. Albert., 1. Sent. d. 37. a. 26; S. p. I. tr. 18. q. 73. m. 2. a. 13. — Petr. a Tar., 1. Sent. d. 37. q. 4. a. 1. — Biel, de hac et seqq. qq. hic q. 2. — Alii commentatores de hac et seqq. qq. plerumque agunt 1. Sent. d. 37.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** Already in 1 *Sent.* d. 37, p. II, a. 2, q. 1, 2, 3, the motion of the Angels was treated, where many [things] were said which can serve for understanding the four questions here proposed concerning the mode in which the Angels are in a place. On the properties of place cf. ibid. a. 1, q. 1, 2, 3, in particular on the difference between *being in a place, being located, being local* (ibid. q. 1, ad 1). There in the body four laws of place are enumerated, namely *of containing, of measuring, of saving, of terminating*; here, however, only three, the last omitted, perhaps because under the word *of containing* is comprehended also the word *of terminating*, less apt for signifying the mode in which the Angels are definitively present in a place. But it is manifest that by a place neither can [anything] be measured nor conserved except a corporeal substance. The Angel, however, is measured by the limitation of its own substance (St. Thomas, S. I, q. 30, a. 1, ad 3) and in a higher mode by God, who is the measure of all [things] outside the genus. The Angel, moreover, is conserved by God alone, whose power St. Bonaventure (here in the body) calls a *spiritual place*, St. Thomas consenting (1 *Sent.* d. 37, q. 3, a. 3). Further, the Angel in the strict sense is also not contained in a place, i.e. as what is measured in a measure, but is contained in it «in a certain mode», namely definitively (1 *Sent.* d. 37, p. II, a. 2, q. 1, in the body). St. Thomas (S. I, q. 52, a. 1) seems not to admit the word *to contain*, saying: «An Angel is said to be in a corporeal place not as contained, but as containing in some mode». — Moreover, about this presence of the Angel in a place, of whatever kind, there was no slight dispute in that age, and indeed both about the fact, whether it is really present in a place, and about the necessity, whether it needs a place, and about the reason in general, why it is determined to some place, and about the mode or formal character of this presence in a place.

**II.** As to the question of fact, there arose two extreme opinions, opposed indeed in words, but in nearly the same error close to one another. For some among the Arab philosophers said that separate substances are *nowhere* according to substance; which proposition, if it is understood [to mean] that the substance is not in a place, was reproved by the Bishop of Paris in the year 1276 (*Collection of Judgments* p. 192, cap. 7, n. 27), and by St. Thomas (1 *Sent.* d. 37, q. 3, a. 1) is named *«heretical, because according to our faith we posit that the Angels operate immediately around us»* (cf. Alexander of Hales, S. p. II, q. 32, m. 2, and the proposition condemned in the year 1240, which is reported in 1 *Sent.* d. 37, p. II, a. 2, q. 1, in the Scholion). On the contrary, Durandus (1 *Sent.* d. 37, q. 1) is of the opinion that the Angels are everywhere, but «without assertion; only by inquiring and giving occasion to the more skilled for inquiring further». This ubiquity, however, the same [author] understands to be wholly different from the divine, and posits it in this, that they can at pleasure operate everywhere, in which he thinks the whole character of presence consists. But the middle opinion, that the Angels are neither everywhere nor nowhere, but in a place in some mode, is most commonly maintained.

**III.** The other question, whether the Angel of itself needs to be defined to some corporeal place, is solved by St. Bonaventure (here ad 3 and more clearly below q. 4 in the body) in the negative sense. Alexander of Hales (loc. cit.), St. Thomas (1 *Sent.* d. 37, a. 1, ad 4), and Scotus (here q. 6, n. 11) consent, [the latter] saying: «That the Angel is not necessarily in a place, because much more could an Angel come to be without the creation of a corporeal creature, or, a corporeal creature having been made, [the Angel] could come to be and be outside every corporeal creature. And yet in the Angel there is a passive potency by which it could be in a place. And this potency is either founded immediately in its substance, by which it could be in a place, or in it in so far as it is a limited nature actually existing, or in something extrinsic to the Angel itself, whatever that be. And therefore there is no need to seek some intrinsic reason for the Angel's being necessarily in a place». But these [things] being supposed, again a twofold question offered itself: 1. why and how the Angel is determined in general, so that it is in some place and within the world; and 2. what that is, through which the Angel actually has presence in this place and not in another. The first question here and below q. 4 St. Bonaventure solves so that the final cause is the order of the universe to be preserved, and the efficient cause is the divine ordination, which gave to corporeal nature a certain universal capacity of containing, and to the Angel a certain passive potency, that it might be able to be contained in a place. But this divine ordination has its reason both in the limitation of the angelic substance, and because in body alone there is both a capacity of containing and a distinction according to here and there. In the same mode Alexander of Hales responds (S. p. II, q. 32, m. 1) and adds that that property in corporeal nature, by which it is capable of containing a spirit in some mode, «is not corporeal, coming from the part of the body, but rather is divinely given». Likewise, that «the angelic spirit has at least on its own part [the property] that it ought to be defined by a place, and that it is here, so that not there». Yet «it could be, even if it were not in a corporeal place, since on this reason of containing [namely passively] the *being* of the Angel does not depend, but only on this reason of containing by which we say that God contains all [things]». But the same [author] says of this solution: «We say this without prejudice to a better opinion, because we do not find this plainly determined in sacred Scripture nor by the Saints nor by the expositors of sacred Scripture». Scotus too seems to approve this doctrine and (loc. cit. n. 15) concludes: «That by which first (the Angel) can be in a place is from God producing it over the containing corporeal creature; but from then it can reduce itself to that act (namely that it be actually in a place, and in this place or that)». — The later scholastics, this question being neglected, rather dispute about the following [one].

**IV.** As to the mode of this presence, all the doctors agree that the Angel is in a place not circumscriptively but definitively, or, as Cajetan says (on S. I, q. 52, a. 1), they agree «in this, that the Angel is in a place not by quantity of mass nor by quantitative contact, but by virtual quantity and contact. And again in this also all seem to agree, that that contact is the relation of the Angel's presence to the place causally or formally. But the difference of opinions and the difficulty consists in assigning what is the foundation of that presence. For its evidence exceeds the capacity of human ingenuity, because from the sacred discourses we have [it] that the Angels are somewhere, and it does not appear how they touch that place». — Durandus (loc. cit.) brings forward four opinions; but two beyond the others are famous. St. Thomas in the Summa (loc. cit.) teaches that «by the application of angelic power to some place in whatever manner the Angel is said to be in a place». But how this is to be understood is not expounded in the same mode by the disciples of the Angelic [Doctor] (cf. Cajetan, loc. cit.). Against the opinion of St. Thomas Scotus disputes at length (here q. 6 and *Reportatio* q. 2) and in substance seems to agree with Richard of Middleton (1 *Sent.* d. 37, a. 2, q. 1) who says: «The reason of the application of the Angel to a place is its simultaneity with the place or with the thing existing in the place... just as the formal reason of the application of a body to a place is circumscription». Both bring forward the article reproved by the Bishop of Paris, which is: «Separate substances are somewhere through operation», which is censured thus: «An error, if it is understood [that] without operation the substance is not in a place» (*Collection of Judgments* t. 1, p. 192, cap. 7, n. 25, but cf. above the Scholion p. 30). On this and on the other condemned proposition (above n. II) speak also Durandus (loc. cit.) and especially Henry of Ghent (Quodl. 2, q. 9), whose words are worthy of note: «For in this all the masters of theology gathered upon this [matter], of whom I was one, agreed, unanimously conceding that the substance of the Angel is not the reason of the Angel's being in a place according to substance; and by a like reason it is undoubtedly true that, if the Angel by its potency, namely intellect and will, does not apply its power to a place by operating around it, that likewise its potency... is not the reason of its being in the place, unless perhaps its potency be of less abstraction than its substance is». The same [author] at the end asserts that he sustains nor defends no special opinion on this matter. On this last question St. Bonaventure, like Alexander of Hales, does not explicitly treat. But his words, incidentally uttered, favor the opinion of Richard, Scotus, and Peter of Tarentaise, as here q. 3 ad 2, q. 4 in the body; 1 *Sent.* d. 37, p. II, a. 1, q. 1, ad 1.

**V.** Besides the places already cited: St. Thomas, 1 *Sent.* d. 37, q. 3, a. 1; Quodl. 1, q. 1, a. 4. — Bl. Albert, 1 *Sent.* d. 37, a. 26; S. p. I, tr. 18, q. 73, m. 2, a. 13. — Peter of Tarentaise, 1 *Sent.* d. 37, q. 4, a. 1. — Biel, on this and the following questions here q. 2. — Other commentators on this and the following questions for the most part treat [them in] 1 *Sent.* d. 37.
